D1.justification: V1 promises public code upon acceptance; v2 supplies a repository link. V2 documents sorting/backpropagation behavior, the unseeded MSWD default, timing hardware and detailed DiT training/sampling settings, including AdamW, batch size 60, EMA and three L40S GPUs. These substantially expand reproducibility information while retaining the shared classifier settings.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates classification only. V2 retains the seven classification datasets and adds ImageNet image generation using DiT-XL/2 (Section 5.2.2 and Appendices E/J). Although ImageNet already supplied classification pretraining weights, generating images is a substantially different evaluated task.

E2.justification: Layer Folding, EGP, NEPENTHE and EASIER are retained, while IMP disappears from the ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 comparison. V2 adds comparisons against networks trained from scratch at reduced depths (Appendix H) and SWD, l1, l2, MMD and KL regularizers (Appendix I), substantially expanding the comparator types.

E3.justification: V2 adds critical-path-length, latency and training-time evaluations alongside accuracy/MACs. Its new DiT protocol uses 5,000 finetuning steps and FID on 50,000 generated 256×256 images with 250 sampling steps and guidance 1.5. It also introduces reduced-depth training controls and projection-count/batch-size sweeps. Shared classification training schedules remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original lambda/BI/random-removal ablation survives as v2 Figure 4. New analyses examine block distances versus performance, mismatched dimensions, critical path versus resource consumption, training shallow networks from scratch, post-pruning retraining, projection seeding/count, batch size and alternative discrepancy metrics. Appendix E also analyzes generated-image failures.

E5.justification: The original random-removal error bars over ten seeds are retained. V2 additionally reports standard deviations over five runs for Figure 8, three seeds for the random generation comparator in Figure 3, and timing uncertainty in Tables 1/3/4. These additions concern particular experiments; they do not establish increased repetition of the original results.

E6.justification: V2 adds generation, timing, sensitivity and reduced-depth-control results. Figure 3 newly reports FID 56.2 with LaCoOT versus 118.6 without regularization after removing two DiT blocks. The ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 result of 90.99% at 64.69M MACs is retained, now accompanied by latency measurements. Conversely, the detailed ResNet-18/MobileNetv2 result grids for the five other classification datasets are absent. These are additions and removals, not demonstrated version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The main Wasserstein regularizer and iterative identity-replacement procedure remain. V2 Appendix C adds a limited extension for dimension-changing convolutions: jointly train an alternative average-pooling/1×1-convolution branch through output-distribution matching, then substitute it for the original 3×3 convolution. This changes the replacement procedure for that case.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are extensively rewritten. The former Method section becomes separate Preliminaries and LaCoOT sections, with procedure and properties reordered. Experiments gain separate classification, generation and practical-benefit narratives, while the appendices are reorganized and learning details move from Appendix C to J.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the dominant all-dataset numerical tables with multipanel critical-path trade-off plots and adds timing tables, generated-image grids and ablation charts. Figure 1 is redrawn. The retained BI/random ablation moves from v1 Figure 2 to v2 Figure 4 with a reversed MAC axis and shaded uncertainty, rather than constituting a new experiment.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work are substantially repositioned around foundation models, scaling, pruning and the practical constraints on fusing linearized layers. New discussions include DiT and Pilo et al. (2025). Dedicated comparisons with distribution-discrepancy and Wasserstein-regularized training literature, including Joo et al. (2020) and Karkar et al. (2023), disappear.

T1.justification: V2 Equation 1 inserts the probability weights alpha_i missing from v1's Monge objective, and Section 3.2 restores normalization factors in the block input/output probability measures. The principal Lipschitz, stationary-point, triangle-inequality and gradient arguments remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1's external-method comparison was confined to ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 and lacked measured runtime evidence. V2 substantially strengthens the practical compression case through broader comparisons, measured inference/training costs (Tables 1/3/4), shallow-from-scratch controls (Table 5) and sensitivity/metric analyses (Appendix I). Implementation disclosures also improve reproducibility. Losing several exhaustive classification result grids reduces auditability, but the new controls and direct efficiency measurements provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LaCoOT. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original classification experiments, DiT image-generation results, measured computational costs and additional controlled analyses in Section 5 and the appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification and compression experiments across seven datasets, including accuracy/MAC results and the block-removal ablation in Section 4 and Appendices D–E.

results.title: LaCoOT: Layer Collapse through Optimal Transport

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from a 2.2K-question benchmark of fundamental capabilities to a three-level benchmark with 10,372 questions and integrated insurance scenarios. The abstract and introduction now claim assessment from basic perception through real-world decision tasks, and add headline findings about human comparisons, multi-step reasoning limitations, and prompt mitigation.

C2.justification: v2 interprets scenario failures as limits on multi-step reasoning and recommends restricting near-term deployment to reliable fundamental tasks. It adds explanations of conflicting-prompt failures and distractor-generator bias, alongside proposals involving reasoning datasets, reinforcement learning, and RAG. The public-data mismatch limitation remains, while v1's fundamental-task-only limitation is replaced by discussion of the expanded evaluation.

D1.justification: v2 documents CSV records containing image paths, accompanying text and labels, expert-guided scenario reference answers, and a structured health-underwriting prompt in Figure 3. Conversely, removing Appendix A eliminates the systematic collection of task-specific prompts, options, correct answers, and responses. v1's explicit assurance of balanced correct-option positions also disappears. The dataset/code access statement remains unchanged.

E1.justification: The original four insurance categories and 22 fundamental tasks remain. v2 additionally evaluates five scenarios covering auto claims, accident liability, property risk management, health underwriting, and agricultural claims. These introduce multi-image and image-plus-document reasoning and insurance decisions, using DADA, Fast Furious and Insured, xBD, IU-XRay, and Precision viticulture data.

E2.justification: The main evaluation removes GeminiProVision, Claude3V_Sonnet, and BLIP-2, and adds Gemini 1.5 Flash, GPT-4o-mini, GLM4V-Plus-0111, and Qwen-2.5-VL-32B. A human baseline replaces the displayed random-guess baseline. These are substantive comparator changes, not merely renamed models.

E3.justification: v1 uses 100 examples per fundamental task; v2 uses varying counts up to 500 and specifies stratified sampling for tasks with fewer than 10 labels. Answer extraction changes from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4o. v2 adds selection of three models for scenario evaluation, stepwise regex and numerical-deviation scoring, a six-person human study on 220 questions, and separate prompt and distractor experimental protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled prompt-enhancement experiments across three tasks and five models, plus a 1,500-question ablation comparing GPT-4o-, Claude 3.5 Haiku-, and DeepSeek-V3-generated distractors. The four-category error analysis remains, with Gemini 1.5 Flash replacing GeminiProVision. Conversely, v1's complete collection of qualitative task cases and model responses in Appendix A is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. The new human participant count and experimental sample sizes describe evaluation design, not added uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The main accuracy tables are extensively revised: GPT-4o remains first, but its reported overall score changes from 72.91 in v1 Table 2 to 69.70 in v2 Table 4 under revised sampling and scoring. This is not a same-setting performance decline. v2 adds human, scenario, prompt, and distractor results, including GPT-4o's 9.26% responsible-party identification accuracy in Table 5; Appendix A's individual response results disappear.

M1.justification: v2 Section 4.3 introduces inference-time augmentation of prompts with insurance knowledge, whereas v1 only analyzes errors. This is a limited procedural adaptation; no new model architecture or training objective is introduced.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, benchmark-construction description, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around the three-level task hierarchy and two-stage evaluation. Sections are renamed and reorganized, error analysis gains mitigation discussion, an ablation section is introduced, and Appendix A is removed.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws Figures 1–3 with a task pyramid and scenario components, expands the dataset table, and adds comparison, scenario, prompt, and ablation tables. v1's radar chart and Appendix Figures 6–27 are removed. The error-distribution chart is retained as a reformatted Figure 4.

R1.justification: The literature categories and insurance-benchmark gap argument largely remain. v2 adds Table 1 comparing six existing benchmarks, including potential data overlap, and references for the five scenario datasets. This extends contextual positioning without substantially replacing the related-work framework.

T1.justification: Neither version presents mathematical propositions, proofs, or substantive formal derivations. The expanded task hierarchy and stepwise evaluation descriptions are operational definitions rather than new mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: The five scenario evaluations substantially address v1's acknowledged limitation to isolated fundamental tasks by testing integrated insurance workflows and their intermediate and final decisions. Human references and prompt/distractor experiments add useful diagnostic evidence. Removing Appendix A reduces transparency, and Table 7 contains 5.6-point drops despite the 'within 5%' summary. These reporting weaknesses temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in application-level evaluation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe INS-MMBench, with matchable tasks, datasets, and evaluation sections. The material is readable, including v1's Appendix A. The supplied v2 ends with references and contains no appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 11 LVLMs, a human baseline, scenario-task results, prompt-mitigation experiments, and distractor-generation ablations in Tables 3–7.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 10 LVLMs in Tables 2–3, error analysis in Figure 5, and model-response examples in Appendix A.

results.title: INS-MMBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LVLMs' Performance in Insurance

C1.justification: v2's abstract and contributions add demonstrated policy-evaluation correlation, planning-based policy improvement, and test-time scaling, whereas v1 largely presented downstream policy benefits as prospective. The standalone IRASim Benchmark contribution and the explicit first-to-model-complex-7-DoF-actions priority claim are removed.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning failure-containing training rollouts, joint data/computation scaling, and why additional context frames may help little. Appendix G discusses cost-function failures and dependence on trajectory proposals. The conclusion drops v1's explicit hallucination and inflexible-resolution/action-space limitations while retaining the inference-speed limitation.

D1.justification: v2 adds explicit action-vector conventions and RoboNet padding instructions, new comparator architecture/pretraining details, and documentation of rollout collection, reward modeling, and real-robot trajectory selection. Most original hyperparameter and hardware tables remain. The new applications are documented less completely than the original benchmark training.

E1.justification: v2 adds RoboNet's multiple robot platforms, LIBERO bowl manipulation, Push-T planning, and real-robot drawer-closing and mandarin-placement tasks. Appendix A.4 also adds a physically implausible command scenario. The original three video-generation datasets remain.

E2.justification: The original VDM, LVDM, and Video-Ada comparisons remain. v2 adds MaskViT and iVideoGPT in the RoboNet comparison, GPC-RANK and GPC-RANK+OPT on Push-T, and random trajectory selection for real-robot planning. RoboNet comparator scores are explicitly attributed to prior work rather than new baseline runs.

E3.justification: New protocols include RoboNet prediction of ten frames from two context frames, paired evaluation of four policies in LIBERO and IRASim, and planning evaluation using IoU or task success. The new simulation applications use OpenSora initialization and expert plus post-trained rollouts. Original benchmark splits and short/long-trajectory settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds experiments varying planning candidates and post-trained rollout counts (Table 5), comparing planning cost functions (Table 6), testing one versus two context frames, and checking physically implausible trajectories (Appendix A). These extend the original conditioning comparisons and model-scaling analyses.

E5.justification: v2 adds repetition information: 50 runs per policy/evaluator, average Push-T IoU over 100 trials, and three repetitions of real-robot experiments. It also reports Pearson correlation. These concern new experiments; neither version provides confidence intervals, seed variability, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1-2 remain numerically unchanged as v2 Tables 1 and 3, but Figure 5 revises the Language-Table scaling curves. New results include RoboNet PSNR 24.6, policy-evaluation correlation 0.99, and Push-T IoU rising from 0.637 without planning to 0.961 with K=50 and P=1000. Tables 4-6 and Appendix A add substantial downstream and robustness findings.

M1.justification: The core frame-conditioned diffusion transformer remains, but v2 extends conditioning from one initial image to historical frames. It also introduces a planning procedure that generates outcomes for candidate trajectories and ranks them using predicted rewards or goal-image similarity (Section 4.3 and Appendix G), substantially extending the inference pipeline.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Method exposition is condensed, experiments are reorganized into four application-oriented subsections, and appendix material is expanded and reordered. These are extensive narrative changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a redesigned template with institutional logos, a boxed abstract, colored headings, and revised table/caption styling. It adds policy-evaluation, planning, RoboNet, and robustness displays, rearranges the architecture diagram, and relocates retained appendix figures. Figure 5 also changes the Language-Table axis and curves.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused toward world-model planning and policy evaluation. v2 adds positioning around works such as Cosmos, Genie 2, FLIP, VLMPC, and GPC, expands its treatment of iVideoGPT, and removes several physical-simulator and DAgger references alongside the earlier 7-DoF priority claim.

T1.justification: Equation 1 generalizes the task definition to historical observations, and Equation 3 substantively revises the reverse-diffusion update coefficients. The diffusion loss and Appendix C conditioning equations remain unchanged; no new theoretical guarantees or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a central gap in v1: the proposed usefulness of generated rollouts for evaluating and improving policies was largely untested. Paired LIBERO evaluation, Push-T planning ablations, and real-robot results provide substantial downstream validation (Tables 4-6). These gains outweigh reduced limitation disclosure and overstatement of consistent scaling, which Table 5's small reversals qualify. The new evidence remains limited by narrow task coverage and absent uncertainty intervals.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IRASim, with matching core architecture and original experiments despite the changed title and expanded scope. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds RoboNet evaluation, LIBERO policy evaluation, simulated and real-robot planning, and robustness experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation experiments on RT-1, Bridge, and Language-Table, model-scaling experiments, and a human preference study.

results.title: IRASim: A Fine-Grained World Model for Robot Manipulation

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from detecting generated videos and explaining transferable artifacts to providing an interpretable, quantitative measure of 3D visual coherence. v2 adds core claims of alignment with reconstruction quality and human judgment, generator benchmarking, and synthesis refinement. Fake-video detection becomes a downstream application rather than the principal objective.

C2.justification: v2 interprets classifier confidence as a coherence measure and fusion as capturing more complex inconsistencies. It adds substantive qualifications concerning reconstruction-selection constraints, training-data diversity, and the distinction between visual coherence and comprehensive physical simulation (Appendices M–N). v1 primarily discusses future-generator generalization and limited video length; the latter limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 supplies substantially fuller reproducibility information: scene-cut processing, cropping and resizing instructions, specific feature-extractor variants, network layers and channel counts, and participant screening and rating rubrics (Appendices I–K; Figure A10). Hardware assignments also change: v1 trains classifiers on 4090 GPUs, whereas v2 reports A100 training and 4090 reconstruction. These disclosures go well beyond v1's brief implementation paragraph.

E1.justification: The Pexels/SVD training sources remain, but evaluation expands substantially. v1 evaluates Sora, Pika, and Runway-Gen2 against real videos including Pixabay. v2 evaluates newer generator coverage including Kling, MiniMax, Vidu, Luma, CogVideoX, and Runway-Gen3, and adds static/dynamic reconstruction datasets, ECTV quality evaluation, and video refinement. Pika, Runway-Gen2, and Pixabay are absent from the revised evaluations.

E2.justification: CNNDetection and DIRE remain detection comparators, with NPR added in Table A6. The new quality-evaluation comparisons actually evaluate selected VBench metrics and EvalCrafter against L3DE (Table 4), with another EvalCrafter comparison on ECTV (Table A9). This substantially broadens the comparison methods beyond v1's two image detectors.

E3.justification: Training grows from 6,946 real and 6,946 synthetic videos to 80,000 of each. v2 introduces matched-prompt generator evaluation, reconstruction protocols using 3D-GS/SC-GS and PSNR, selection for successful pose estimation, and human studies including 15 participants rating 300 videos. Accuracy is supplemented by reconstruction and human-agreement metrics. The stated learning rate and batch size remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the original pairwise modality-ensemble ablation with contrastive-loss and addition-versus-concatenation experiments (Table A8). It adds controlled training-diversity analyses for motion and indoor/outdoor scenes (Table A7), quantitative validation of localized artifacts against reconstruction errors and human annotations, and refinement examples. Some qualitative failure motifs recur, but the analytical evidence expands substantially.

E5.justification: Beyond v1's accuracy summaries, v2 introduces Spearman rank-correlation estimation for agreement with reconstruction quality, human ratings, and annotated regions (Tables 2–4; Figure 5). This adds statistical association analysis, but neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 replaces the original detection results and adds extensive validation, ablation, and generator-ranking results. New findings include fusion correlations of 0.7566 with reconstruction quality (Table 2) and 0.6484 with human ratings (Figure 5). Sora detection is reported as 81.33% in v1 Table 3 and 56.31% in v2 Table A6, but changed methods, training data, and test sets prevent interpreting this as a same-setting decline.

M1.justification: v1 combines separately trained classifiers through weighted logit ensembling. v2 introduces a nearest-real-feature contrastive loss and a learned fusion network that concatenates modality features before further convolutional processing (Section 4.2; Appendix J). Appendix H.2 also introduces artifact refinement using localized masks and multiview inpainting. These are procedural changes beyond renaming the framework L3DE.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around L3DE. Data curation, method design, validation, and applications become distinct main sections, while detection, implementation details, and limitations are organized in the supplement. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column presentation to a two-column layout with a new opening overview, reconstruction panels, correlation plots, expanded tables, and detailed architecture diagrams. Qualitative examples are reorganized into reference-frame, artifact-region, and Grad-CAM comparisons in the supplement. Some imagery recurs, but the displays and overall layout are extensively redesigned.

R1.justification: The research positioning shifts from generated-image detection toward video-quality assessment and 3D reconstruction. v2 adds substantive discussion and citations for EvalCrafter, NeRF/Gaussian-splatting reconstruction, and newer generators, while removing the main related-work subsection devoted to generated-image detection. Retained detector citations still support the supplementary detection comparison.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's weighted-logit equation, v2 introduces mathematical definitions for the contrastive objective, clipped reconstruction-quality deficit, and simulation gap G = 1 − S (Equations 1–5). These are limited formal additions supporting the method and evaluation; neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 largely supports its realism interpretation through detection accuracy and selected Grad-CAM examples. v2 adds reconstruction and human-study validation of both scores and localized artifacts, controlled ablations, and substantially fuller implementation documentation. These additions materially strengthen evidence for what the method measures, while Appendix M clarifies its scope. Reconstruction validation remains restricted to successfully reconstructed videos and statistical uncertainty is unreported, but the combined validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title and substantially revised objective, both PDFs develop the same appearance, motion, and geometry framework using SVD-generated training videos. The text, equations, tables, and figures are readable throughout. v1 ends with references; v2 includes supplementary Sections H–N.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction experiments, human studies, generator evaluations, detection results, and ablations in the main paper and supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original detection accuracies, modality ablations, and qualitative Grad-CAM analyses in Tables 2–3 and Figures 1–3.

results.title: How Far are AI-generated Videos from Simulating the 3D Visual World: A Learned 3D Evaluation Approach

C1.justification: The contribution of adaptive local-to-global fusion for SLAM failures is replaced by ground-plane completion for out-of-view contacts and explicit claims of egocentric applicability. The abstract also changes its performance claim from 60% lower error over prior SOTA to 50% over local-to-global methods, while retaining the central optimization-free calibration claim.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of compensation for systematic HMR depth bias, the distinction between local-pose accuracy and global-motion accuracy, and the limitations of fitting one plane on uneven terrain. V1's discussion of fusion-based recovery and EMDB-only evaluation is replaced by explicit limitations concerning catastrophic SLAM failure and long-sequence drift. Remaining errors are increasingly attributed to pose and temporal-consistency limitations.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies RANSAC ground-plane fitting, an RTX 2080 Ti for timing, metric units and RTE normalization, and use of TRAM's released HMR model. It adds a project-page address and named video/PLY resources with viewing instructions. V1's matching and failure thresholds disappear with their associated procedures. Both PDFs still promise code release upon acceptance; actual external resource availability is unverified.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only EMDB2. V2 retains its 25 sequences and adds EgoBody, introducing head-mounted-camera footage with severe body truncation and predominantly invisible contact joints. This materially expands the evaluated input conditions.

E2.justification: V2 adds TRAM to the EMDB2 benchmark and to direct scale-calibration comparisons, alongside a ZoeDepth-fed SLAM comparator (Tables 3–5). PACE, previously compared for runtime, also receives EgoBody accuracy results. The earlier EMDB2 comparators GLAMR, TRACE, SLAHMR, and WHAM remain.

E3.justification: The default experimental configuration changes from CLIFF with DPVO to VIMO with masked DroidSLAM. V2 adds comparisons across HMR and SLAM configurations, ground-truth ground-plane and camera controls, and sequence-length groupings (Tables 2 and 4–6). The existing 100-frame human-motion alignment procedures are retained.

E4.justification: V2 removes the local-to-global fusion ablations, including v1's appendix evaluation on sequences with over 40% human occupancy. It adds ground-plane ablations, component compatibility studies, sequence-length analysis, depth-error and bias studies, and contact-identification validation with a handstand example. The existing footfall/reference-joint analysis is retained as supplementary Figure 10.

E5.justification: V2 introduces boxplots summarizing depth-error, translation-error, and signed-bias distributions (Figure 2 and supplementary Figures 7–8), adding descriptive dispersion reporting absent from v1. These concern variation within the evaluated data; neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 3's reported EMDB2 W-MPJPE/WA-MPJPE/RTE changes from 317.9/108.2/2.2 to 197.2/71.0/1.2 under the revised method and component configuration. V2 adds EgoBody results and extensive calibration results while removing fusion-specific results. Its new Table 4 also reveals a tradeoff: long-sequence ATE-S is worse than TRAM's (1.09 versus 0.80), although W-MPJPE is lower (195.30 versus 218.97). The headline changes do not isolate a same-configuration improvement.

M1.justification: V1 combines nearest-image-keypoint depth matching with a SLAM-failure detector and GLAMR-based motion fusion. V2 replaces correspondence estimation with camera-ray/point-cloud geometry, adds human-guided ground-plane fitting for invisible contacts, and removes the failure detector and fusion procedure (Sections 4.2–4.4). The depth-ratio calibration and sequence-median aggregation remain.

P1.justification: The title, method name, abstract, introduction, and substantial methodological prose are rewritten around 'Humans as Checkerboards.' Preliminaries and methods are reorganized, compatibility analysis becomes a separate subsection, limitations and conclusion are separated, and the supplement gains a structured A–E organization.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, with extensively redrawn pipeline and calibration diagrams, new error-distribution plots, and reorganized comparison tables. Qualitative displays are revised and expanded. V1's Figure 4 moves to supplementary Figure 10, while the camera-calibration trajectory display is retained with revised examples.

R1.justification: V2 substantially develops positioning against TRAM, distinguishing foreground-human depth calibration from background metric-depth calibration. It also expands the single-view metrology discussion and references supporting human priors, ground fitting, and EgoBody. This changes the account of the closest competing approach beyond routine bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: V2 revises the reference-point definition to minimize point-to-ray distance and adds a ray-plane intersection formula and a coplanar-contact assumption (Sections 4.2–4.3). V1's failure-set and motion-fusion formulations disappear. The foundational camera/world transformations and scale-ratio relation remain unchanged; neither version develops theorem or proof results.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for the central calibration idea: it measures the reliability and bias of human-depth predictions, compares directly with TRAM under component controls, and tests the new ground-plane procedure on EgoBody. These address v1's limited validation of its depth assumption and its acknowledged single-dataset coverage. Removing the SLAM-failure fallback narrows robustness, and changed default components prevent attributing headline gains solely to calibration. Nevertheless, the broader, more diagnostic evidence and clearer applicability limits provide a substantial overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same human-guided camera-scale calibration work, renamed from OfCaM to HAC. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial methodological and presentation revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports original EMDB2 and EgoBody evaluations, calibration and compatibility experiments, and supplementary analyses of depth errors and contact identification.

before.justification: V1 reports original EMDB2 human and camera motion evaluations, component ablations, runtime measurements, and an appendix experiment on challenging sequences.

results.title:
Humans as Checkerboards: Calibrating Camera Motion Scale for
  World-Coordinate Human Mesh Recovery

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: noise scheduling corresponds to importance sampling, concentrating computation near log SNR = 0 improves training efficiency, and Laplace benefits ImageNet generation across prediction targets. The new contribution list makes existing claims explicit without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds the interpretation that concentration around intermediate noise levels matters more than the precise schedule family, connects logit-normal flow sampling to this principle, and discusses generalization across conditioning regimes. It also explicitly limits the study's objective to fixed-budget efficiency rather than XL-scale or state-of-the-art performance.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies patch size, conditioning details, continuous implementation and γ = 5 for the weighting baselines. It also supplies CelebA architecture and CC12M preprocessing, CLIP-conditioning and training details. The Laplace code is unchanged; the earlier Appendix B sampling instructions are relocated into Section 2.4.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates class-conditional ImageNet generation at two resolutions. v2 additionally evaluates unconditional face generation on CelebA in 64×64 pixel space and text-conditioned generation on CC12M at 256×256, substantially broadening domains, conditioning requirements and data representations.

E2.justification: The comparator membership in Table 3 remains unchanged. New appendix comparisons introduce Cosine-Ply against Laplace and evaluate Cosine-Ply as a loss weight alongside the retained weighting baselines. Logit-normal flow matching receives analytical discussion, not a newly reported empirical baseline evaluation.

E3.justification: Appendix A.5 adds a distinct protocol: train for one million iterations, fine-tune separately within four timestep bins for 140,000 iterations, and selectively substitute checkpoints during inference. A.7 adds a specified CelebA model configuration and a 200,000-iteration CC12M setup. The original ImageNet evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled tests of which timestep intervals benefit from fine-tuning, a direct comparison of the same sampling distribution used as scheduling versus loss weighting, and matched-initial-noise visual case studies across training checkpoints. These substantially extend v1's prediction-target, resolution and schedule-parameter analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, empirical variability or statistical significance tests. The distributional mean and variance derived in A.4 are theoretical properties, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 3–7 are numerically unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results. Table 9 reports FID-10K of 7.98 for Cosine-Ply versus 8.88 as a loss weight. New Laplace-versus-cosine results include 6.58359 versus 7.93795 on CelebA at 150,000 iterations and 54.3492 versus 58.3619 on CC12M at 200,000 iterations. Additional convergence, interval and visual findings are also reported.

M1.justification: Appendix A.3 introduces Cosine-Ply, which applies a polynomial timestep-sampling transformation before the cosine schedule; A.6 also evaluates its loss-weighting variant. These extend the existing scheduling framework. The original Laplace implementation remains identical.

P1.justification: The introduction and method explanation undergo extensive rewriting, including an explicit contribution list and expanded probability-based narrative. The ablation discussion is expanded, sampling instructions move into the main text, and the appendix is reorganized into eight subsections. These changes exceed simple renumbering or insertion of results.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 8–11 and Figures 4–8, including density plots, interval comparisons, weighting curves and generated-image grids. Figure 2 expands from one convergence panel to two, Figure 3's legend is rearranged, and Table 1 is reformatted. The visual presentation changes substantially despite retained main-table values.

R1.justification: v2 expands background citations and discussion, including Ernie-ViLG 2.0, additional video/3D diffusion work, and Movie Gen in the logit-normal analysis. It elaborates connections to MM-DiT, HDiT and prior noise schedules while retaining the same central research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly defines the normalized polynomial timestep distribution, its sampling transformation and its induced log-SNR density. A.4 derives that logit-normal timestep sampling in flow matching induces a normal log-SNR distribution with mean -2µ and variance 4σ². These extend the mathematical analysis beyond the retained scheduling identities.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on ImageNet and indirect comparisons between sampling and weighting. The new CelebA/CC12M evaluations and controlled interval and sampling-versus-weighting tests strengthen generalizability and support for the central argument. Added derivations and implementation disclosures improve assessability. Repeated-run uncertainty remains absent, and Table 8 inconsistently labels the Laplace parameter in its caption, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same noise-scheduling research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original timestep-interval tests, sampling-versus-weighting comparisons, CelebA and CC12M results, and generated-image comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet-256 and ImageNet-512 experiments, including schedule comparisons, convergence results, prediction-target evaluations and hyperparameter ablations.

results.title: Improved Noise Schedule for Diffusion Training

C1.justification: Both versions claim joint persistent 3D tracking and novel-view synthesis through compact SE(3) motion bases and consolidation of learned priors, with state-of-the-art performance. v2 emphasizes world-coordinate trajectories, but that capability was already specified in v1. The main contribution scope is retained.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 adds a three-part explanation of gains over TAPIR+DA involving shared motion, acceleration regularization and persistent geometry. The limitations discussion broadens dependence on external predictions to geometry and motion and discusses newer alternatives. However, v1's explicit inability to handle large viewpoint changes is omitted without evidence that it was resolved.

D1.justification: New appendices substantially document preprocessing, track sampling and filtering, learning rates, loss weights, batching, regularization, metric-scale alignment and the DynMF implementation. These mostly expand documentation of the retained pipeline. A reproducibility inconsistency remains: v2's main text specifies 1000 initialization iterations, whereas Appendix B.1 specifies 2000 steps.

E1.justification: Alongside the retained iPhone and Kubric evaluations, v2 adds novel-view synthesis on seven NVIDIA scenes captured from a static training camera. Appendix E also adds a qualitative multi-object DAVIS school-girl example. This materially broadens the evaluated data and capture conditions.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds DynMF, DELTA (world), and SpatialTracker (world) to the iPhone comparison while retaining the previous comparators. New Table 3 evaluates Dynamic Gaussian Marbles on NVIDIA. DynMF and Dynamic Gaussian Marbles were already cited in v1 but were not evaluated there.

E3.justification: The stated motion-basis count changes from 20 to 10. The new NVIDIA protocol trains on camera 4 and evaluates cameras 3, 5 and 6 at half resolution using covisibility masks (Appendix F). Added frame-space tracking baselines are transformed into world coordinates. These introduce substantive experimental settings; retained numerical results do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a Per-Gaussian SE(3) ablation to isolate the contribution of shared motion bases, alongside the 2DGS variant comparison and a qualitative DAVIS case study. Existing ablations remain. The Kubric PCA visualization is relocated to Appendix D, not newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. TAPIR uncertainty scores used during optimization concern input confidence, not statistical uncertainty of the reported experimental results.

E6.justification: Original iPhone, Kubric and retained ablation scores are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial result entries. Its 2DGS variant reports EPE 0.097 versus 0.082 for the original model, while LPIPS improves from 0.45 to 0.40. NVIDIA mean PSNR is 23.37 for Ours versus 23.46 for DGM. Reported rendering speed changes from approximately 40 to 140 FPS, without sufficient timing details to establish a controlled speedup.

M1.justification: The shared SE(3) motion-basis representation and trajectory rendering remain. v2 adds an optional 2DGS variant with monocular-normal supervision (Appendix B.2), and introduces MegaSaM initialization followed by joint camera-pose refinement for in-the-wild videos (Section 3.3). These extend the retained reconstruction method.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the method exposition remain. v2 selectively condenses and rewrites the abstract, introduction, baseline descriptions and discussion, makes world-coordinate terminology more explicit, updates authors and affiliations, and organizes additional documentation into appendices.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, with widespread resizing and repositioning of figures and tables. Figure 1 moves onto the title page, Figure 6 moves to the appendix, Table 1 and the ablation table gain rows, and a NVIDIA results table and DAVIS Figure 7 are added.

R1.justification: v2 substantially updates positioning through classical low-rank reconstruction and newer learned reconstruction and tracking work, including DELTA, SpatialTracker, DUSt3R and MonST3R. It replaces v1's absence-of-generic-3D-trackers rationale with a distinction between frame-space and world-space trajectories, and discusses newer joint reconstruction/tracking and motion-segmentation approaches.

T1.justification: Equation 7 changes the mask-loss target from constant 1 to the input mask M, correcting the formal objective to match the stated supervision. Appendix B.2 introduces normal-supervision loss definitions for the 2DGS variant. No new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens reproducibility and empirical assessment through detailed appendices, relevant additional competitors, a direct shared-basis ablation and a distinct static-camera evaluation. The new results expose useful performance tradeoffs while retaining the original evidence. The conflicting initialization budgets and removal of the large-viewpoint limitation temper these gains, but the improved methodological transparency and stronger comparisons provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Shape of Motion and retain matching methods, experiments and visualizations. The complete text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally includes Appendices A-G.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds NVIDIA results, additional comparator and model-variant results, an ablation, and a DAVIS visualization.

before.justification: v1 reports original iPhone tracking and view-synthesis experiments, Kubric tracking results, and component ablations in Tables 1-3.

results.title: Shape of Motion: 4D Reconstruction from a Single Video

C1.justification: V1 claims to introduce video reasoning segmentation and its first model. V3 acknowledges existing VRS approaches and reframes its contribution around overcoming their limitations in long, crowded, rapidly moving, and occluded videos through three modules. Its benchmark contribution also expands to 3,000 videos and 15,000 object descriptions.

C2.justification: V3 introduces explanations involving key-frame error propagation, sampling redundancy, and single-token limitations, and argues against simple static-model adaptation in Appendix A. Appendix E attributes a bystander-selection failure to missing a late-occurring talking action. V1's explicit text-only-input and no-multiround-conversation limitations disappear, without evidence that those restrictions were resolved.

D1.justification: Core hardware, optimizer, loss weights, and training hyperparameters remain essentially unchanged. V3 specifies the extractor implementation and one-third global/two-thirds neighboring-frame sampling, and documents GPT-4V without v1's additional Qwen-VL attribution. It removes the promised code/dataset repository link; this changes access information without establishing actual resource availability.

E1.justification: VideoReasonSeg adds MovieChat and VideoMME sources and explicitly includes long videos exceeding five minutes, extending its temporal and scene coverage. V3 also evaluates MeViS and ReVOS. Ref-YouTube-VOS, Ref-DAVIS17, and the existing VIS benchmarks remain, with VIS evaluation relocated to the appendix.

E2.justification: VideoReasonSeg comparisons remove Mask2Former, VITA, and PixelLM rows and add LMPM, OnlineRefer, VideoLISA, and VISA; LISA configurations change from Llama/Llama2 to LLaVA. The retained referring benchmarks gain URVOS, LBDT, DsHmp, VideoLISA, and VISA comparisons. Appendix A additionally evaluates the direct-adaptation baseline ViLLa†.

E3.justification: VideoReasonSeg changes from 1,934 samples split 1,000/400/534 into train/validation/test to 3,000 videos split 2,000/1,000 into training/validation, with short/long reporting. Segmentation evaluation switches from AP/AR to J&F. New sampling experiments vary reference-frame counts over 0, 6, and 12. The stated core training budget remains unchanged.

E4.justification: The three-row component ablation becomes an eight-configuration study of three modules. V3 adds direct-adaptation and sampling-strategy controls, reference-frame sensitivity, and a temporal-localization failure case. The helmet comparison against LISA/PixelLM is replaced by an occluded-sheep comparison against VISA. The earlier aggregation-strategy study is retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Results remain point estimates; additional ablation configurations do not constitute uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V3 replaces VideoReasonSeg results under its revised dataset and metric and adds MeViS and ReVOS results, including ViLLa J&F scores of 49.4 and 57.0. Reported Ref-DAVIS17 J&F changes from 64.4 to 74.3, while VIS AP changes from 67.1/59.5/46.2 to 67.6/59.9/46.5. These are revised reported results, not controlled same-setting gains.

M1.justification: V3 adds a Grounded-VideoLLM-based Key Segment Extractor that identifies query-relevant intervals and combines global and neighboring reference frames before encoding. This substantially changes video processing. The Context Synthesizer and Hierarchical Temporal Synchronizer largely rename v1's context aggregation module and video-frame decoder, retaining their equations and training objectives.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V1's duplicated Related Works sections are consolidated; task, method, and benchmark material is reorganized under Section 3 with separate module subsections. Terminology changes throughout, and the appendix is reorganized to accommodate discussion and failure analysis.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column presentation. The architecture diagram and introductory examples are substantially redrawn, the qualitative comparison is replaced, and new data and failure examples appear. Tables gain short/long/overall groupings, additional benchmarks, and expanded controls. VIS results move to the appendix; the existing data-generation figures are retained.

R1.justification: V3 substantially repositions ViLLa relative to VISA and VideoLISA, discussing their limitations instead of claiming the first VRS solution. It also adds relevant work including Grounded-VideoLLM, GLaMM, and OMG-LLaVA. This changes the closest-prior-work narrative, beyond citation or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: The task and token definitions, attention and decoder equations (1)–(5), momentum assumption, and training losses retain their mathematical substance. V1's loss equation becomes inline text. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the standard J&F explanation adds no new mathematical result.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens validation through relevant video-reasoning competitors, fuller component ablations, direct-adaptation and sampling controls, and explicit failure analysis. These address v1's limited comparison coverage and component attribution; removing duplicated related work also improves clarity. The omitted release link and limitations are drawbacks, and Table 1 contains an inconsistency: OnlineRefer's overall score is below both subgroup scores. These defects temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in evidence and explanation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ViLLa and VideoReasonSeg, with identifiable correspondence between their methods and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, although revised datasets and protocols prevent some direct score comparisons.

after.justification: V3 reports original benchmark comparisons, component and sampling ablations, a direct-adaptation control, and a qualitative failure analysis in its main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark results and component ablations in Tables 1–7, plus an aggregation-strategy experiment in Appendix C.

results.title: ViLLa: Video Reasoning Segmentation with Large Language Model

C1.justification: The overarching unification, transfer, and state-of-the-art claims remain. However, v2 replaces the explicitly claimed geometric-analysis contribution with TRN and SCA as its central technical contributions, emphasizing temporal/spatial feature aggregation. Its conclusion also introduces claims of reduced deployment complexity and resource demands. This substantially revises the claimed contribution beyond renaming EventMatch to EMatch.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a central explanation that direct voxel encoding wastes temporal structure, motivating recurrent aggregation, and develops the role of contextual attention at locations without events. Sections 4.1 and 4.4 newly attribute joint-model performance and sparse-input generalization to more diverse temporal/spatial training distributions. These extend v1's interpretation of matching, refinement, and transfer convergence.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies 100 ms event windows, crop/full-image sizes, spatial augmentation, flipping probabilities, and ablation parameter counts; hardware changes from RTX 4090 to RTX 3090. Conversely, v1's AdamW weight decay/betas/epsilon, local matching-window sizes, and five-iteration task-switch cadence are omitted. Code remains promised rather than supplied, with v2 specifying release upon acceptance.

E1.justification: DSEC remains the evaluated dataset, with optical flow and stereo matching retained. v2 Section 4.4 and Figure 9 add sparse-input scenarios using one-tenth the accumulation duration and one-sixteenth the event count. These extend input-condition coverage without introducing another dataset or prediction task.

E2.justification: v2 adds ECDDP to the flow comparison and ETAM-TSCLM and TESNet to stereo, while dropping v1's explicitly no-history E-RAFT* and IDNet* comparison rows. The unified-model comparison also adds IDNet and TESNet. Qualitative comparisons replace E-RAFT with IDNet and add TESNet. Concentration Net and Se-cff are the same retained baseline, as confirmed by their cited work.

E3.justification: v1 reports 600k flow, 800k stereo, and 600k joint-training iterations with a maximum learning rate of 1e-4. v2 reports 400k iterations at 3e-4 with batch size four, followed by 150k full-resolution iterations at 1e-5 with batch size one. Voxel bins increase from five to fifteen. Ablations change to a scaled-down joint model trained for 200k plus 10k iterations.

E4.justification: v1's coarse module ablations are replaced by joint-model tests separating TRN/ConvGRU and SCA/attention/FFN/positional encoding, while the propagation ablation is no longer shown. v2 additionally investigates feature-space alignment using PCA, examines sampling-induced distribution shifts, and extends transfer analysis with training curves and single/cross/unified qualitative comparisons.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. v2 Figure 7 shows convergence over training iterations rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Proposed-model results are extensively replaced under changed architecture and training conditions. v1 reports unified EPE/MAE of 0.75/0.54 in Table 3; v2 reports 0.64/0.47 in Table 1. Single-task results change from 0.736/0.519 to 0.67/0.49. v2 also reports new final cross-task results and revised ablation and robustness findings. These are not controlled same-setting gains; rounding of retained baseline scores is not counted.

M1.justification: v2 replaces the shared ResNet encoder with a Temporal Recurrent Network processing voxel groups through residual blocks and ConvGRUs, with a top-down feature pyramid. Flow supervision changes from L1 to L2, loss weighting from 0.7 to 0.8, and flow refinement from six to three iterations. The six-stage self-/cross-attention stack largely persists under the SCA name.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work, and method narrative. It combines the previous formulation and method sections, promotes multi-task training before cross-task analysis, and introduces dedicated ablation and generalization subsections. The title, model terminology, and author list also change.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout and redraws the overview, geometric illustration, and architecture diagrams. It adds a TRN schematic, PCA visualization, convergence plots, and robustness figure; reorganizes qualitative comparisons; and merges task-specific ablations into a joint table with parameter counts. These are extensive display changes, beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially revises positioning around shared correspondence matching versus task-specific regression. v2 expands discussion of joint flow/stereo research with works including SENSE, UNOS, GeoNet, and DF-Net, and explicitly distinguishes its approach from TESNet's flow-guided stereo training. v1's Perceiver IO and unified contrast-maximization discussion is displaced. These are substantive positioning changes beyond citation renumbering.

T1.justification: v1 Section 3 derives camera-projection, motion, and stereo-disparity relationships, including an approximately constant-disparity assumption during event accumulation. This derivation is absent from the supplied v2, which instead presents a general feature-warping objective and separate flow/stereo formulations. The formal stereo-matching objective also changes from squared feature differences to an L1 norm.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification for shared event representations. Compared with v1's coarse ablations and mainly qualitative account of joint-training benefits, it separately tests temporal recurrence and attention components, reports stronger comparisons among training modes, and examines sparse-input behavior against relevant competitors. These additions make the central mechanism and its benefits more assessable. They outweigh the loss of geometric derivation and some implementation detail, although robustness remains qualitative, supplementary material is unavailable, and changed training conditions prevent attributing cross-version gains to individual components.

A1.justification: The PDFs clearly describe successive versions of the same event-based flow/stereo framework, and all supplied pages are readable. However, v1 references an appendix and v2 references supplementary material that neither supplied PDF contains, limiting comparison of those additional details and results.

after.justification: v2 reports original DSEC results, component ablations, feature visualizations, training curves, and qualitative generalization experiments in Tables 1–4 and Figures 5–9.

before.justification: v1 reports original DSEC experiments, including single-task and unified-model results, cross-task transfer experiments, and component ablations in Tables 1–7.

results.title:
EMatch: A Unified Framework for Event-based Optical Flow and Stereo
  Matching

C1.justification: The central uncertainty-estimation and regularization contributions remain. The abstract's claimed Lyft APBEV/AP3D advantage increases from 2.2/1.0 to 4.1/2.0 percentage points; v1 Table 2 actually supports 2.5/1.0. The headline nuScenes advantage of 6.9/2.5 remains unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations linking equal branch-loss weights to balanced learning and earlier attachment to greater auxiliary-branch independence (Appendix A.5), alongside explanations of the granularity results. Appendix A.1 explicitly states that object categories are not modeled. The existing noise/disagreement explanation is largely retained.

D1.justification: V2 adds layer-by-layer architecture specifications, augmentation ranges, point-shuffling instructions, optimizer-policy and learning-rate-clipping details, per-GPU batching, four A6000 GPUs, and training-time estimates (Section 4.1; Appendix A.1–A.2). The code pointer changes from UL3D to UA3D. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing corresponding implementation changes.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate unsupervised object discovery on nuScenes and Lyft, including the same distance ranges. Additional qualitative examples retain the existing distant/small-object scenarios; no new dataset, domain or task is evaluated.

E2.justification: V2 adds box-level and point-cloud-level uncertainty alternatives as evaluated comparators to coordinate-level regularization in Table 2b. The existing supervised, MODEST-PP, MODEST, OYSTER and rule-based comparator memberships remain unchanged in their corresponding comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 adds controlled settings for uncertainty aggregation, auxiliary-loss weights of 0.25/0.5/1/2, and attachment at sa_layer_4/fp_layer_1/fp_layer_2. Existing train/test splits, IoU threshold, distance bins, sampled point counts and epoch budgets are retained. Newly disclosed implementation settings do not establish that existing experiments were rerun differently.

E4.justification: V1 tests rule-based uncertainty, auxiliary width and regularization strength. V2 retains these and adds direct granularity comparisons (Table 2b), auxiliary-loss-weight and attachment-layer sensitivity studies (Appendix A.5), and additional qualitative cases (Figure 5). These substantially expand validation of the central design choices.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Self-training rounds and predicted box uncertainty are not statistical uncertainty estimates for the reported performance.

E6.justification: The reported T=10 Lyft APBEV/AP3D changes from 59.8/56.1 to 61.4/57.1 over 0–80m. The 50–80m entry changes from 28.5/24.9 to 36.8/29.0, while 0–30m falls from 76.0/73.4 to 74.1/71.2 (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 1b). The cause is unspecified. NuScenes main results and existing ablation scores remain unchanged, while substantial new ablation and qualitative results are added.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure remains auxiliary-versus-primary dense prediction disagreement, coordinate-level uncertainty regularization and primary-only inference. V2 expands the equations and architecture description and clarifies pseudo-box supervision; these changes do not establish a revised algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method explanations and experimental narrative undergo extensive rewriting. UL3D becomes UA3D, contribution bullets are consolidated, rule-based baseline definitions move into the ablation discussion, and a structured appendix is added. The editorial changes extend well beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redesigned, and Figures 3–4 gain stronger contrast, revised annotations and reordered panels. Separate benchmark and ablation tables are consolidated into multipart tables. V2 adds architecture and sensitivity tables, further qualitative comparisons and an uncertainty-visualization diagram (Figures 5–6).

R1.justification: V2 adds references including UNION, ProposalContrast, reward finetuning and recent uncertainty work. The uncertainty-regression discussion replaces He et al. (2020) with the distinct He et al. (2019) paper. The overall related-work taxonomy and positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–3 express the same absolute prediction discrepancy, exponential uncertainty weighting and weighted branch-loss combination using more explicit coordinate notation. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 adds a direct test of the central coordinate-level design (Table 2b), supporting sensitivity studies (Appendix A.5), and substantially fuller reproduction details (A.1–A.2). These address important validation and documentation gaps in v1, while redesigned diagrams clarify the method. Unexplained Lyft score revisions and absent repeated-run uncertainty remain limitations, but the substantial quality gain rests on stronger evidence and transparency rather than higher scores alone.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. V1 ends after its references; v2 adds Appendix A. Content can be matched across the UL3D-to-UA3D rename, table consolidation and figure redesigns.

after.justification: V2 retains original detection experiments and reports additional granularity, auxiliary-loss-weight and attachment-layer ablations in Table 2b and Appendix A.5.

before.justification: V1 reports original detection experiments on nuScenes and Lyft, uncertainty ablations in Tables 3–4, and qualitative analyses.

results.title:
Harnessing Uncertainty-aware Bounding Boxes for Unsupervised 3D Object
  Detection

C1.justification: v2 adds an explicit claim of user-controllable face counts and makes balancing compactness with sequence regularity a stated contribution. The central claims of roughly halving token length, improving efficiency and quality, and doubling capacity to 1,600 faces remain.

C2.justification: v2 develops the interpretation that compression alone is insufficient, attributing PolyGen(AMT)'s quality deficit to difficulty referencing previously generated vertices. It also interprets face-count control saturation as prioritizing mesh quality and discusses swap-related tradeoffs. These substantially expand the explanatory discussion. The industrial-readiness limitation is retained unchanged in Appendix B.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands implementation information through coordinate-based deduplication, Chamfer-based filtering of failed mesh2sdf conversions, 10% face-condition dropout, and details of the single-model PolyGen adaptation. Hardware, four-day training duration, and batch size remain unchanged. v1's open-source statement becomes a future code/model release promise; the PDFs do not establish actual resource accessibility.

E1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds evaluation under explicit requested face counts, extending the requirements of shape-conditioned mesh generation. v2 also reports including a small ObjaverseXL portion, while retaining the same mesh domain and 1,600-face limit. The smaller-face subsets used elsewhere are protocol changes within retained coverage.

E2.justification: v1's quantitative comparison uses V2 and its no-AMT variant. v2 retains that comparison and adds Unsort, PolyGen(AMT), and AMT(Swap) in Table 2, plus a direct MeshAnything-versus-V2 user study. PolyGen(AMT) is explicitly an adapted single-model implementation combined with AMT, not unmodified PolyGen.

E3.justification: The reported corpus increases from 100K to 230K pairs, and Section 4.1 changes evaluation size from 2K to 4K, although v2 Section 4.3 still says 2K. New Table 2 experiments use OPT-125M, meshes with at most 400 faces, 10K metric-sampling points, and training perplexity. Appendix A adds face-count scaling and a preference protocol involving 30 meshes and 43 users. The main ablation retains 100K metric-sampling points.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained AMT/no-AMT ablation, Table 2 tests sorting, alternative representation choices, and vertex swapping, examining regularity versus compression. Appendix A.1 adds sensitivity to requested face counts, and Appendix A.2 adds perceptual assessment through a user study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The newly reported number of user-study participants is a study sample size, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces numerical results: CD values in units of 10^-2 for the no-AMT variant and V2 change from 1.454/0.802 to 0.895/0.874, alongside other metric updates. Revised data settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance changes. Tables 2–3 add tokenization and face-control outcomes; Appendix A.2 reports preferences of 67.8% for V2 versus 32.2% for MeshAnything.

M1.justification: v2 extends the stated method with optional vertex swapping using a new special token, face-count conditioning through an additional embedding, and invalid-prediction masking during inference. These change tokenization, conditioning, and decoding beyond the basic AMT procedure described in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, contributions are reordered and expanded, and the quantitative section is reorganized around metrics and tokenization comparisons. v2 introduces supplementary sections and moves the existing limitations paragraph from the combined conclusion section to Appendix B.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. Existing Figures 1–2 are retained but relocated and resized, and Algorithm 1 is reformatted with line numbers. Table 1 gains a sequence-ratio column, and Tables 2–3 introduce new comparison and face-control displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds three language-tokenization references and a reference supporting mesh2sdf processing, while expanding discussion of the already-cited PolyGen representation. The existing mesh-generation and general 3D-generation positioning is largely retained.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds an explicit token-cost argument comparing 3+n with 3n tokens for a vertex referenced n times. The original mesh and face definitions in Equations (1)–(3) remain mathematically equivalent, and no substantial theorem or proof framework is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's quantitative validation centered on one AMT/no-AMT ablation. v2's alternative-tokenization experiments directly examine the roles of compression and ordering, addressing an important gap in support for the central representation claims. Face-control tests and a direct human comparison further strengthen validation. The 4K/2K inconsistency and claims of preserved quality despite mixed Table 2 metrics remain weaknesses, but the added comparative evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MeshAnything V2 and retain matching core methods, equations, figures, and experiments. All material supports comparison: v1 ends with references, while v2 includes additional experiments and limitations in Appendices A–B.

after.justification: v2 reports original results in Tables 1–3, including tokenization comparisons and face-count control, plus a 43-participant user study in Appendix A.2.

before.justification: v1 reports original mesh-generation examples, quantitative AMT ablation results in Table 1, and an empirical token-length comparison.

results.title:
MeshAnything V2: Artist-Created Mesh Generation With Adjacent Mesh
  Tokenization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the central contribution from an entirely synthetic four-task benchmark to a predominantly synthetic five-task benchmark with realistic inputs, accompanied by GRAB-Lite for costly reasoning models. The underlying claim that graph analysis remains challenging and supports straightforward exact-match evaluation is retained.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations concerning robustness to noise and screenshot distractors, limited plotting-library effects, and a transformation-capability threshold crossed by newer models on GRAB-Lite. Appendix C also discusses the computational cost of repeated evaluation and limitations of distance-based metrics with varying answer scales and nonnumeric outputs.

D1.justification: New appendices document screenshot construction, corruption types, GRAB-Lite API routes and reasoning-effort settings, and additional model-version identifiers. The stated release expands to include generation code. The A100 inference estimate changes from about 30 to 45 minutes for the enlarged benchmark; hardware remains the same.

E1.justification: V3 adds the 1114-question Real task to the original four tasks: photographed paper and whiteboard drawings, graphs embedded in screenshots, and corrupted images. These introduce substantially different input conditions. GRAB-Lite mainly resamples the resulting five-task coverage rather than introducing another task.

E2.justification: The original 20-model comparison remains on the original tasks. V3 Table 6 adds 14 newer comparators against three retained models on GRAB-Lite, including GPT-5 variants, o1, newer Claude and Gemini models, and Grok 4. Table 4 also evaluates Gemini 2.0 Flash and 2.5 Flash on Real.

E3.justification: V3 introduces GRAB-Lite with 100 questions per task, approximate category/complexity balancing, mixed plotting libraries, and specified reasoning-effort settings. It also adds a paired 100-question plotting-library protocol and alternative metrics on Real Screenshots. The original exact-matching evaluation remains unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses examine performance across realistic image conditions, sensitivity to plotting-library appearance, and alternative performance metrics. The earlier complexity, answer-extraction, multiple-choice, and OCR analyses are retained; the multiple-choice analysis moves from v1 Section 4.7 to v3 Appendix B.

E5.justification: V3 Appendix C/Table 8 newly reports five-attempt pass@5 and 5/5 reliability for three models on Real Screenshots. This adds repeated-generation assessment without establishing increased repetitions of the original experiments. The existing 95% Wilson confidence intervals and general seed-setting statement are retained.

E6.justification: Original four-task, category, multiple-choice, and OCR scores are retained. Claude 3.5 Sonnet's overall score changes from 21.7% to 21.0% because GRAB now includes Real, not because of a same-setting decline. New results include GPT-5's 46.2% on GRAB-Lite and Claude 3.5 Sonnet's 30.0% versus 26.0% on Matplotlib versus Seaborn plots.

M1.justification: The benchmark-generation pipeline gains screenshot compositing and image corruption, described in Appendix A, plus Seaborn regeneration of half the synthetic GRAB-Lite plots. These are limited construction-procedure extensions; the underlying graph-property generation, inference prompt, and core exact-matching procedure remain.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained, with localized condensation and terminology edits. Complexity and evaluation-protocol discussions are reordered, question-format analysis moves to the appendix, and appendix sections are reorganized around the added material. This is not an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: Figures 2 and 4 are redesigned to include Real examples, the statistics displays are reformatted, and the main results table is compressed and extended. V3 adds Real, GRAB-Lite, metric, and plotting-library tables plus Figure 7. Existing analysis figures are reordered and resized, including a changed evaluation-chart vertical scale.

R1.justification: V3 adds references for newer evaluated models, Seaborn, and additional APIs, and motivates lightweight evaluation through inference-time reasoning costs. The related-work discussion and positioning against existing chart and multimodal benchmarks remain substantially unchanged; publication-metadata updates do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: The greedy-decoding expression is retained, and neither version develops theoretical propositions or proofs. V3's additional empirical metrics do not introduce new formal definitions, derivations, or theoretical guarantees.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially addresses v1's limited input realism and lack of economical evaluation for newer reasoning models through Real and GRAB-Lite, supported by additional validation and reproducibility details. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems: Section 4.3 retains a closed-model superiority claim contradicted by Table 3's GPT-4o mini 7.1% versus TransCore-M 7.9%, and Figure 7's purportedly equivalent Series examples do not match.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GRAB benchmark. Their main text, tables, figures, equations, and appendices are readable and support matching retained material to the additions in v3.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds Real-task and GRAB-Lite evaluations, alternative performance metrics, and a plotting-library experiment.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 20 LMMs, complexity and question-format analyses, evaluation-protocol comparisons, and appendix OCR experiments.

results.title: GRAB: A Challenging GRaph Analysis Benchmark for Large Multimodal Models

C1.justification: The central contribution of combining DDSD and MIMA for efficient, stable adaptation remains. v2 corrects the abstract's claimed ACDC improvement from 1.6 to 0.6 percentage points and focuses its contribution claims on multiple segmentation benchmarks. The roughly twentyfold speed claim, newly emphasized in the abstract, already appeared in v1's body.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of beneficial source forgetting, reconstruction-weight tradeoffs and ADD's fixed-threshold/window failures. Its supplement argues that RGB reconstruction supplies domain-specific cues that help DDSD, extending v1's emphasis on domain-agnostic features and knowledge retention. v1's explicit limitation concerning classification performance is removed.

D1.justification: v2's supplement adds optimizer, learning rate, batch size, masking ratio and patch size, threshold smoothing, loss weights, initialization and hyperparameter-selection details absent from supplied v1. Hardware and adapter-size descriptions are revised. Conversely, v1's explicit project/code URL is omitted from v2; this establishes removal of access information, not disappearance of the resource.

E1.justification: The ImageNet-to-ImageNet-C classification evaluation is removed. v2 adds segmentation on OnDA's synthetic rain conditions and GTA-to-ACDC under the OASIS protocol, using SYNTHIA for validation. Cityscapes-to-ACDC remains, but the represented domains and task coverage change substantially.

E2.justification: v2 adds BeCoTTA and Continual-MAE to the Cityscapes-to-ACDC comparisons, directly compares DDSD with HAMLET's Adaptive Domain Detection, and expands speed comparisons with additional baselines and augmentation-disabled variants. VDP is retained in supplementary Table 9 rather than simply removed from the paper.

E3.justification: v1's speed test uses three rounds and MIMA without DDSD; v2's Table 4 uses ten rounds with DDSD and specifies RTX 6000 Ada hardware. The reported adapter fraction changes from 10% to 0.1% (0.17M parameters). New protocols include 20-round stability testing and SYNTHIA-based hyperparameter selection for OASIS.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands analysis beyond v1's component ablations and coarse tuning-utilization table. It adds DDSD-versus-ADD activation analysis, threshold and reconstruction-weight sensitivity, 20-round stability ablations, source-domain forgetting measurements, augmentation controls and qualitative cases across all four weather domains.

E5.justification: v2 Section 5.3 first reports five-run means and standard deviations for the component ablations in Table 3. v1 provides point estimates without repetition information. This limited reporting addition does not establish that the number of runs increased.

E6.justification: The overall ACDC mean remains 62.2, but reported entries change: Hybrid-TTA's first-round Fog score changes from 69.1 to 70.3 and tenth-round Night from 51.6 to 49.5. v2 adds OnDA results of 66.7, OASIS results of 41.2, Hybrid-TTA++ results of 63.4 and extensive analysis results, while removing classification outcomes. These are revised or newly reported results, not established same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: v1 jointly trains reconstruction and segmentation on source data; v2 explicitly uses a randomly initialized reconstruction decoder without pretraining or warm-up. v2 also introduces sensitivity scaling in DDSD's decision threshold, weights reconstruction loss by lambda_r, and adds the augmentation-enabled Hybrid-TTA++ variant. These revise the stated procedure beyond renaming ET as adapter tuning.

P1.justification: The introduction and method explanations are extensively rewritten. Preliminary material becomes a separate section, DDSD is organized into temporal-correlation and thresholding subsections, and experiments are reorganized into results, ablations and analysis. v2 also adds a structured supplement and removes the standalone limitations paragraph.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the opening display with a performance-versus-FPS plot, redraws the tuning schematic, and revises the pipeline figure to omit source-stage reconstruction training.
