The performance curves are expanded and relocated to Figure 5. Tables are restructured, and detector plots, full-results tables and a multi-weather qualitative gallery are added.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated domain-shift-detection related-work discussion, including HAMLET, OnDA and controllable CTTA, and introduces references supporting the new benchmarks and comparators. Its supplement substantially develops the novelty argument for coupling RGB reconstruction with DDSD relative to Continual-MAE and TTT-MIM. Several broader MIM and multitask discussions from v1 are removed.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions of the decision rule and objective change: v2 compares segmentation loss with lambda_d times the threshold and weights reconstruction loss by lambda_r, unlike v1's unscaled formulations. The underlying EMA and masking definitions remain; neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central mechanism through direct detector comparison, 20-round stability tests, source-forgetting analysis and synthetic-to-real evaluation. Added implementation details and five-run ablation variability address important reproducibility weaknesses, while the abstract's gain is corrected. Classification evidence and its limitation are lost, and reporting inconsistencies remain, including the OnDA source mean of 62.4 in Table 2 versus 59.9 in Table 11. Nevertheless, the stronger evidence for the paper's central segmentation contribution provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Hybrid-TTA by the same authors. Their text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison, including v2's supplementary material and rotated tables. The supplied v1 ends with references.

after.justification: v2 reports original segmentation experiments on Cityscapes-to-ACDC, OnDA and GTA-to-ACDC, alongside ablations, detector comparisons and forgetting analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Cityscapes-to-ACDC segmentation results, ImageNet-C classification results, component ablations and adaptation-speed measurements.

results.title: Hybrid-TTA: Continual Test-time Adaptation via Dynamic Domain Shift Detection

C1.justification: The title changes from over 100 FPS to over 80 FPS, and the conclusion explicitly separates multimodal throughput from throughput on preprocessed events. This qualification was already present in v1's abstract. The contribution list more explicitly foregrounds asynchronous association and efficient modules, while retaining the central fusion, dataset, and occlusion-robustness claims.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation: it attributes small Kalman gains on simple scenes to existing LSTM temporal modeling and image-only EDS degradation to motion blur and a training-domain gap. Supplement B discusses parallelization assumptions and required spatial alignment. The conclusion replaces the separate-training limitation with network-capacity and receptive-field limitations, materially revising the discussion of applicability and failure conditions.

D1.justification: Supplement A supplies event binning, image-training losses and sampling, Kalman initialization, architecture tables, feature dimensions, iteration counts, and uncertainty mappings. v2 also specifies 80,000 uncertainty-training steps, preprocessing costs, a code/data repository link, and dataset licensing. These substantially improve documentation; the newly specified training count does not establish that the training budget changed.

E1.justification: The underlying MultiTrack, MultiFlow, EC, EDS, and DSEC coverage is retained, including synthetic and occluded variants. Supplement B.2 adds targeted overexposure and simulated underexposure scenarios on DSEC, plus low-texture and dim-light EDS examples. These extend tested environmental conditions without introducing a new base dataset.

E2.justification: v2 adds Deep-EV-Tracker(E2VID) to the real-data comparison, FF-KDT to real and occluded comparisons, and CoTracker to the extreme-lighting comparison. HASTE and EKLT also enter the occluded-data accuracy comparison in Table C. Conversely, the standalone KLT occlusion comparison from v1 Table 3 disappears. Comparator coverage is substantially expanded and revised.

E3.justification: The main EC/EDS preprocessing intervals, ground-truth timestamp sampling, and accuracy metrics are retained. New supplementary protocols include long-term evaluation over 81 image and 368 event frames using endpoint error and survival with a 32-pixel threshold, plus runtime comparisons distinguishing ordinary and ideal parallelization. These extend rather than replace the main evaluation design.

E4.justification: Supplement B and C add occlusion-induced degradation comparisons, long-term stability curves, extreme-lighting and low-texture case studies, predicted-uncertainty visualization, component runtime analyses, and displacement-distribution analysis. Existing architectural and training-dataset ablations remain, although v1 Table 3's image-only Kalman ablation on occluded data is removed. The evidence examining robustness and mechanisms expands substantially.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v2's uncertainty visualization concerns the model's predicted measurement uncertainty, not statistical uncertainty in experimental results.

E6.justification: Matched core scores remain unchanged, including full-model EC/EDS expected feature ages of 0.845/0.550. v2 adds extensive comparator, degradation, long-term, runtime, and qualitative results while removing image-only occlusion results. The expanded comparison changes the event-only ranking on EDS: Deep-EV-Tracker(E2VID) reports expected feature age 0.482 versus 0.475 for BlinkTrack with Kalman filtering in Table 1.

M1.justification: The core event/image architecture, dual LSTM, Kalman fusion, and staged training remain consistent. Supplement B.5 adds an optional inference adaptation that replaces the grayscale camera reference with an E2VID reconstruction, permitting event-only input. The expanded architecture and loss descriptions otherwise constitute documentation rather than evidence of a redesigned tracker.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are extensively rewritten, the challenges are reorganized into association, uncertainty-aware fusion, and efficiency, and the method is regrouped around event, image, Kalman, and supervision sections. Terminology shifts from color to image modules, with substantial explanatory expansion and redistribution between the main text and supplement.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, adds an introductory fusion schematic, redraws the architecture and dataset-generation diagrams, and introduces numerous supplementary plots, tables, and visual examples. Existing displays are also reorganized: image-only real-data results move to Table E, the dataset ablation to Table G, and the real/synthetic comparison to Table H.

R1.justification: The rewritten related work adds a dedicated event/frame-fusion discussion and substantive positioning against FF-KDT, ETAP, and the E2VID-based Deep-EV-Tracker extension, emphasizing temporal-resolution and computational tradeoffs. v1's blanket claim of the first event-based feature-tracking dataset is replaced by a more specific emphasis on accurate occluded trajectories and visibility labels.

T1.justification: v1's general Kalman prediction/update equations are retained in Supplement A.3. v2 additionally specifies the four-component state, observation and transition matrices, time-dependent process-noise covariance, and the assumption of no cross-axis covariance. These add formal model specification, but no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the supplied paper by resolving important implementation-documentation gaps and adding targeted evidence about robustness, uncertainty behavior, runtime, and competing methods. The qualified speed claims also improve precision. These gains outweigh the removal of image-only occlusion results and the remaining overbroad superiority language, which does not fully acknowledge the E2VID comparator's higher EDS event-only score. The improvement rests on reproducibility and evidential depth, rather than higher retained benchmark scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BlinkTrack and contain readable, matching methods, datasets, and core results. v1 ends at its references despite mentioning supplementary material; v2 includes Supplement A–C. The supplied contents support comparison, while newly supplied implementation details do not by themselves establish changes to the underlying method.

after.justification: v2 retains original tracking results and adds empirical analyses of long-term stability, challenging lighting, uncertainty predictions, runtime, and training-data displacement distributions.

before.justification: v1 reports original tracking experiments, synthetic-data comparisons, and architectural and training-dataset ablations in Tables 1–4.

results.title: BlinkTrack: Feature Tracking over 80 FPS via Events and Images

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion expand the contributions to include compatibility with 2D GS and geometry reconstruction, while the conclusion adds superiority over previous feed-forward methods in sparse-view settings. The claimed reconstruction latency changes from 1.3 seconds to 1 second. The central claim of instant wide-coverage reconstruction remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of damage from naive opacity pruning, depth supervision encouraging spherical-harmonic color representation instead of translucent floaters, reduced need for regularizers with two-view inputs, and stability from distributing transformer blocks. It replaces v1's speculative explanation of the LPIPS gap with an explanation of reduced floaters through learned priors and regularization. The 64-view scaling and field-of-view limitations remain essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds Gaussian color degree, scale and opacity biases, expanded camera-normalization instructions, refinement learning rates and frozen parameters, and geometry-evaluation implementation details. These substantially expand reproducibility information. However, it omits v1's explicit first-7K-training-scenes disclosure and near-plane settings, including the different setting used without depth supervision; their omission does not establish that those settings changed.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained DL3DV and Tanks and Temples evaluations, v2 adds two-view novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K and zero-shot ScanNetv2 evaluation of image rendering, depth maps and reconstructed meshes. This substantially expands both dataset coverage and evaluated task requirements.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Mip-Splatting and Scaffold-GS alongside the retained 3D GS baseline. New comparisons include pixelSplat, MVSplat and GS-LRM on RealEstate10K, and optimization-based 2D GS on DL3DV and ScanNetv2. Appendix Table 9 additionally contextualizes depth results against COLMAP, Atlas and VoRTX under explicitly different input and supervision conditions.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce a two-view 256-by-256 evaluation, additional 2D GS fine-tuning, and three- or ten-step refinement budgets. ScanNetv2 adds aspect-ratio augmentation, every-80th-frame image evaluation, depth evaluation across keyframes, and mesh construction using every-10th-camera depth maps with 4 cm TSDF voxels. The original main evaluation split and K-means input selection are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds constant-width token-merging controls in Table 4, merging-position ablations in Table 5, RealEstate10K loss ablations in Table 10, and transformer/Mamba ordering experiments in Table 11. These examine separate effects of token width, merging location, regularization applicability and training stability. The original loss and Gaussian-usage analyses remain as Tables 6 and 7.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The expanded results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises the reported 32-view DL3DV PSNR from 23.86 to 24.10 and time from 1.3 seconds to 1 second, and adds 25.60 PSNR after ten refinement steps. Numerous new benchmark and geometry results appear. The four-view final-model ablation changes from 21.25 to 20.43 PSNR, and its parameter count from 162M to 142M. These revisions are not fully explained and do not establish a controlled performance improvement.

M1.justification: v2 Section 4.1 introduces optional post-prediction optimization of Gaussian positions and colors using input-view rendering loss. It also adapts Long-LRM to predict 2D Gaussians through additional fine-tuning. These extend the reconstruction procedure and output representation, while the original hybrid architecture, token merging and regularization losses remain.

P1.justification: The six-section progression and much of the method and training exposition remain. v2 tightens prose and captions, swaps the dataset and implementation subsections, introduces result subheadings, and reorganizes the appendices. Citation style, affiliation text and acknowledgements also change; much of the additional prose documents new scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document from single-column to two-column layout, rearranges Figure 1, expands Figure 3 with additional comparators, and adds color/depth and RealEstate10K figures. Tables are expanded and newly arranged, including compact side-by-side displays. v1's appendix Figure 4 survives as v2 Figure 6, and the original loss and usage tables are retained rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds focused positioning against object-level Gamba/MVGamba and city-scale Gaussian optimization methods. References also expand to support the new baselines, 2D GS adaptation and datasets. The existing related-work framework and central positioning of hybrid, wide-coverage reconstruction remain.

T1.justification: The state-space equations, complexity statements, token-merging mathematics and original loss definitions are retained, with notation and equation-numbering changes. Neither version introduces formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence by replacing a narrow main comparison with several relevant alternatives, adding direct sparse-view comparisons, and separating token-merging effects from token-width choices through additional ablations. ScanNetv2 image, depth and mesh evaluations also provide concrete support for the geometry extension. These gains outweigh the loss of training-subset and near-plane disclosures and the unexplained ablation-score revisions, although those reporting issues reduce reproducibility and confidence in exact numerical comparisons.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Long-LRM. All main-text and appendix pages are readable, including equations, tables and figures, and retained content can be matched across the substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original reconstruction experiments and adds refinement, RealEstate10K, 2D Gaussian and ScanNetv2 results, including additional appendix ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments on DL3DV-140 and Tanks and Temples, architecture and loss ablations, and qualitative results in its appendix.

results.title: Long-LRM: Long-sequence Large Reconstruction Model for Wide-coverage Gaussian Splats

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden SeaS from anomaly-image/mask generation supporting segmentation to unified generation of anomalies, normal images and masks. New central claims concern benefits for synthesis-based and unsupervised anomaly detectors, beyond the retained supervised-segmentation claims.

C2.justification: Appendices A.11–A.12 explicitly qualify generation of extremely subtle defects and distinguish unseen instances within known anomaly types from genuinely unseen types. v2 also explains Textual Inversion shortcomings and interprets detector-augmentation benefits. Earlier discussions emphasizing small supervised models outperforming larger unsupervised detectors are removed with their comparisons.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly specifies forward-diffusion t=1500 and 25 sampling steps, detector checkpoint sources, GLASS foreground-mask omissions and PatchCore preprocessing. These are additional disclosures rather than demonstrated changes to retained experiments. The per-stage resource/time breakdown is removed, while aggregate timings, core training hyperparameters and the code link remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds VisA's 12 object categories alongside the retained MVTec datasets. Evaluation expands beyond anomaly-image generation and supervised segmentation to normal-image generation, anomaly replacement in synthesis-based detectors, and normal-image augmentation for unsupervised detectors.

E2.justification: v2 newly evaluates GLASS, PatchCore, MambaAD and Textual Inversion, and adds a DRAEM control using real training anomalies. CDC is removed from generation comparisons. DRAEM disappears as a synthesis source for the common segmentation networks but appears in new detector-augmentation comparisons. Earlier direct comparisons with RealNet, Shape-guided and FOD are removed.

E3.justification: v2 adds normal-image KID, anomaly-region IC-LPIPS, detector-augmentation protocols, lighting-specific training subsets and a real-anomaly DRAEM control. The RMP ablation baseline is revised from having no components to retaining coarse-mask supervision (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 6), without establishing a rerun. The principal few-shot split and generation-training budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained token, loss, training-strategy and RMP ablations, v2 adds a fixed-prompt ablation, Textual Inversion comparison, lighting/background experiment, small-defect examples and t-SNE analysis of unseen-type generalization. Appendix A.13 adds a substantive control testing whether DRAEM gains exceed those obtained from access to the same real anomalies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run or seed counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations, error bars or significance tests. Both present point estimates; averages across categories or models do not establish repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results, including VisA IS/IC-LPIPS of 1.27/0.26, normal-image KID and detector-augmentation outcomes. Retained MVTec AD generation and per-category segmentation scores are unchanged. Some MVTec 3D AD summaries change: average SeaS image-AUROC becomes 78.38 rather than 78.44, while DFMGAN image-AP changes from 82.83 to 83.83 despite unchanged component rows averaging 82.83.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 adds a normal-image output mode conditioned on the normal token alone, whereas v1 describes inference for abnormal image-mask pairs. The shared U-Net, UA prompts, DA/NA losses, mixed training and RMP architecture remain unchanged; this is a limited extension of the stated inference procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions and conclusion are substantially rewritten around unified generation and broader downstream applications. Experimental discussion and appendices are reorganized, with MVTec 3D AD material redistributed and implementation, ablation and qualitative-result sections reordered.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout. Tables consolidate datasets and image/pixel metrics; retained qualitative displays are merged, relocated or stripped of removed comparators. Figure 1 is redesigned, and normal-generation, feature-visualization, lighting, small-defect and t-SNE displays are added.

R1.justification: The central positioning shifts from anomaly-only versus complete-image generation to one model serving anomaly, normal-image and mask generation, revising the contrasts with AnomalyDiffusion and DFMGAN. References supporting GLASS, MambaAD, PatchCore and VisA are added; references associated with RealNet, Shape-guided, FOD and FID are removed.

T1.justification: The loss equations, attention formulation and Appendix A.2 multi-head-attention argument are retained. Explicit prompt indexing and added qualitative explanations do not introduce a substantive new mathematical definition, derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through defect-region diversity measurements, VisA evaluation and detector-augmentation experiments, including the real-anomaly control in Appendix A.13. Appendices A.11–A.12 also meaningfully constrain the generalization claims. These gains outweigh removed comparator/resource detail and limited reporting defects, including Table 4's inconsistent DFMGAN average. Uncertainty across runs remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SeaS. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds VisA evaluations, detector-augmentation experiments, and further diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-generation, downstream detection and segmentation, and ablation results on MVTec AD and RGB images from MVTec 3D AD.

results.title: SeaS: Few-shot Industrial Anomaly Image Generation with Separation and Sharing Fine-tuning

C1.justification: The central contributions remain preserving generative architectures for open-world referring segmentation and introducing Ref-VPS. v2 explicitly emphasizes benefits from advances in video generation in its abstract and conclusion, but v1 already articulated that relationship in Section 5.3 and discussed interchangeable backbones. The expanded experiments principally strengthen existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations connecting two-stage training to spatial priors, image/video balance to generalization, and VAE reconstruction to mask-domain compatibility. It discusses ambiguous ground truth, the limitations of temporal-consistency measurement and misleading consistency from empty predictions. Existing object-centric bias and fast-motion limitations remain in the appendix.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds Wan's 80k-step schedule, batch size and 17-frame clips, model-specific MeViS fine-tuning schedules, and inference-versus-scoring frame rates. Computational-cost sections document measurement hardware and baseline-estimation procedures. However, v1's exhaustive supervision inventory for the original baselines is omitted, and v2's general eight-GPU training statement is not clearly reconciled with its four-GPU ModelScope cost report.

E1.justification: v2 adds training and evaluation on MeViS, substantially extending evaluation toward motion-dependent referring expressions. The earlier training sources and five evaluation benchmarks remain. Ref-VPS's additional clips retain the same 39 concepts and do not independently establish broader task coverage.

E2.justification: The new MeViS comparison includes VISA-13B, DsHmp and GLUS alongside Referformer. GLUS also joins the existing Ref-VPS comparison in v2 Table 4, whereas v1 Table 3 compared only MUTR, UNINEXT and VD-IT. The original in-domain and BURST/VSPW comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: Ref-VPS changes from 141 clips annotated at 24 FPS to 145 clips annotated at 6 FPS, with ambiguous pixels excluded using Ignore labels. The stated default evaluation resolution changes from original resolution to 512×512. v2 also introduces Wan and MeViS training schedules, controlled resolution/supervision experiments and temporal-consistency evaluation. These establish reported protocol changes without proving that every retained result was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's backbone/CNN ablations, v2 adds latent-versus-pixel supervision, frozen-versus-tuned VAE and MLP-decoder comparisons; training-stage, data-ratio and noise ablations; annotation agreement and VAE reconstruction checks; quantitative failure, temporal-consistency and computational-cost analyses; and ambiguous-scene cases. Earlier backbone, fight-scene, failure-example and concept-coverage analyses are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: Appendix B.3 newly specifies averaging inference measurements over 80 runs, and Appendix A.3 reports inter-annotator agreement. The timing repeats do not establish additional training runs. Neither version reports segmentation-performance seed variability, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds MeViS results of 53.5 and 60.3 J&F for ModelScope and Wan, respectively, plus Wan results and numerous diagnostic outcomes. Matched ModelScope entries change from 40.4 to 37.5 J on BURST and 49.56 to 49.0 on Ref-VPS; several baseline and backbone-ablation values also change. Revised protocols prevent interpreting these as same-setting regressions. Original Table 1 scores are retained with rounding.

M1.justification: v2 adds a principal REM variant using the Wan-14B diffusion transformer alongside the ModelScope model. Its joint spatiotemporal architecture uses single-stage fine-tuning instead of ModelScope's spatial-then-joint training. This substantially extends the implemented model family, while retaining the mask-latent objective, frozen VAE and single-pass decoding.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, benchmark-collection narrative and discussion are extensively rewritten, and terminology changes from 'Referral' to 'Referring'. The appendix is reorganized into dataset, quantitative evaluation, qualitative evaluation and implementation sections. The existing generative-backbone analysis moves from the main text into the supplement.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 becomes a front-page teaser, and existing qualitative comparisons are extensively rearranged. v2 adds an annotation-pipeline diagram, ground-truth/Ignore visualizations and a quantitative failure plot, while expanding and regrouping tables for additional models, comparisons and analyses.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting MeViS, Wan/DiT, GLUS, VISA, DsHmp, reconstruction analysis and annotation-quality evaluation. It extends comparisons to recent language-model-based video segmentation systems. The central positioning against object-centric RVOS and diffusion feature-extractor approaches remains; publication updates and merged duplicate citations are bibliographic changes.

T1.justification: Appendix B.7 adds a formal temporal-consistency metric in Equations (A)-(B), absent from v1. The original diffusion and segmentation Equations (1)-(7) remain substantively unchanged. The new signed IoU-difference definition permits cancellation, limiting its interpretation as temporal stability.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's limited decoder ablation and absence of annotation-agreement measurement, v2 adds controlled supervision/decoder experiments and independent annotation validation, substantially strengthening the central method and benchmark evidence. MeViS and Wan evaluations further test applicability. The flawed signed temporal-consistency definition and inconsistencies in training-cost reporting weaken those particular additions, but the stronger central validation provides a clear substantial net improvement. Revised Ref-VPS scores alone do not establish performance improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReferEverything, the REM framework and Ref-VPS benchmark. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison. Changed evaluation settings limit direct score comparisons, not identification of the revisions.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Wan and MeViS evaluations, annotation-agreement measurements, computational-cost measurements and extensive supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original REM evaluations, backbone and decoder ablations, and qualitative analyses on established datasets and the newly collected Ref-VPS benchmark.

results.title: ReferEverything: Towards Segmenting Everything We Can Speak of in Videos

C1.justification: The shared geometry-guided Gaussian contribution remains, but v3 makes opaque mesh surfaces and efficient occlusion-aware light transport central contributions in its abstract and introduction. Its conclusion emphasizes normal accuracy, material disentanglement and efficiency relative to implicit-field methods, replacing v1's stronger emphasis on NeRF/DTU results and novel-view synthesis.

C2.justification: v1 identifies shadows baked into albedo and leaves ray tracing to future work. v3 explains how occlusion modeling addresses this problem and discusses the remaining indirect-light approximation and path-tracing cost. It adds explanations of deferred shading, coarse-mask applicability, resolution costs and the failure of initial-mesh reconstruction on specular objects, while dropping detailed lighting-inconsistency and underexposure discussions.

D1.justification: v3 supplies implementation details for revised attribute networks and losses, refinement at learning rate 0.001 for 100 steps, and coarse-mask generation using 5,000 3DGS steps. It adds resolution-dependent GPU-memory and runtime information and identifies ReSTIR for path tracing. A project-page link is added, although both conclusions still describe code release as future work.

E1.justification: Synthetic4Relight and TensoIR are retained; TensoIR already appeared in v1 Appendix F.3. v3 adds the Shiny Blender reflective-object suite, Stanford-ORB objects, Garden outdoor captures and scene-level demonstrations using initial meshes. The full NeRF Synthetic NVS evaluation, DTU experiments and dedicated four-scene geometry-recovery suite from v1 are removed.

E2.justification: Within the retained Synthetic4Relight comparison, v3 adds NVdiffrecmc, TensoIR and NeRO. Within TensoIR, it adds NVdiffrecmc, NeRO and GS-Shader. Appendix I introduces MIRRES as a comparator. The earlier NeuS2 geometry comparison and non-relightable NVS comparisons disappear. GS-Shader and GaussianShader refer to the same retained method.

E3.justification: The reported geometry resolution changes from 96 cubed in v1 to 72 cubed for simple shapes and 96 cubed otherwise in v3. Vertex sampling changes from the first 2% to 5% of training. Geometry evaluation shifts from Chamfer distance/F-score to normal MAE, and new protocols measure reflection-direction and transfer-distance errors, refinement displacement and resolution sensitivity.

E4.justification: v3 replaces the earlier residual-color and second-stage analyses with broader ablations of shape alignment, appearance refinement, occlusion and indirect lighting (Table 3). It adds shape-consistency measurements, refinement-displacement measurements, resolution comparisons and path-tracing analysis. v1's quantitative mask-removal and 2D-versus-3D splatting studies, along with exposure-related failure studies, are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeat counts, seed values, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Dataset averages and Monte Carlo rendering calculations do not constitute newly added uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Results are substantially revised. Synthetic4Relight relighting PSNR/LPIPS are 31.65/0.032 in v1 Table 2 and 34.10/0.037 in v3 Table 1; roughness MSE is respectively 0.017 and 0.004. These accompany method and setting changes, not controlled same-setting gains. v3 adds normal, component-ablation, consistency and path-tracing results while removing earlier benchmark and per-scene entries.

M1.justification: Although FlexiCubes and the six-Gaussian MGadapter remain, v3 replaces split-sum rendering plus residual color with Monte Carlo rendering, BVH-accelerated mesh occlusion and directional indirect lighting. It introduces deferred-shading refinement and revises attribute modeling and regularization. Appendices H and I additionally implement existing-mesh initialization and path-tracing variants.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten around light transport. Methodology gains a dedicated light-transport section, experiments are reorganized around inverse rendering and normal quality, and the appendices are substantially restructured. This exceeds terminology changes or relocation of existing material.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. The teaser, pipeline and MGadapter figures are redesigned, and new occlusion, refinement and normal-comparison illustrations replace much of the earlier gallery. Results are consolidated into a multi-dataset table, with new ablation and appendix tables and different visual highlighting.

R1.justification: v3 adds a rendering-equation-evaluation subsection positioning its approach against split-sum, spherical-Gaussian and Gaussian ray-tracing methods. Appendix B.3 substantively distinguishes MGadapter from MeshSplats and other mesh-Gaussian alignment approaches. References and discussion expand to deferred shading, MIRRES, ReSTIR and additional surface-reconstruction methods.

T1.justification: Formal definitions and assumptions change locally: v3 adds the metalness factor to the diffuse BRDF, replaces depth-map-based shape consistency with reflection-direction and transfer-distance criteria, and introduces a monochrome-lighting assumption for regularization. The central MGadapter equations remain. No theorem or proof is added; the referenced error-bound analysis in Appendix B.3 consists of empirical measurements.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's acknowledged shadow-disentanglement deficiency through explicit occlusion modeling and targeted evidence: Table 3 reports relighting PSNR of 27.36 without occlusion versus 29.95 for the full model. Stronger relevant baselines and analyses of alignment, refinement and resource tradeoffs strengthen the central argument. Removed per-scene and failure-case detail, plus unexplained score differences between v3 Tables 1 and 7, limit transparency but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GeoSplatting and retain the same underlying mesh-to-Gaussian framework. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial methodological and experimental revisions.

after.justification: v3 reports original inverse-rendering and normal-estimation results, component ablations, real-world demonstrations, and appendix experiments on shape consistency, refinement, resolution and path tracing.

before.justification: v1 reports original novel-view synthesis, decomposition, relighting, geometry-recovery and ablation results, including additional experiments in Appendices B, D, E and F.

results.title: GeoSplatting: Towards Geometry Guided Gaussian Splatting for Physically-based Inverse Rendering

C1.justification: The central contribution remains uncertainty-aware self-ensembling for few-shot 3DGS, claimed to mitigate overfitting, outperform competitors across four datasets, avoid additional ground-truth signals, and incur negligible additional overhead. The rewritten abstract, introduction, and conclusion largely retain these claims.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly frames perturbation as a tradeoff between model diversity and supervision reliability. It explains failures with overly frequent, strong, or weak perturbations and identifies unreliable models as a target for future outlier identification. These add concrete qualifications to the existing mechanism explanation.

D1.justification: The new supplement supplies operational details missing from v1: threshold parameters r=0.05 and theta=0.01, Gaussian selection through projected overlap, parameter-scaled noise with a multiplier decaying from 0.08 to 0.02, and specific DTU scans requiring random initialization. The direct repository link becomes a project-page link; v3 also introduces inconsistent released-versus-future-release wording.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate few-shot novel-view synthesis on LLFF, DTU, Mip-NeRF360, and 50 sampled MVImgNet scenes. The benchmark view counts remain unchanged. The added analyses use retained LLFF coverage rather than introducing another domain or task.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 2 add DNGaussian participation in the 6-view and 9-view comparisons, where v1 reports dashes. Its 3-view participation and the other benchmark comparator memberships remain unchanged. CoR-GS model-count variants and Random/Gradient-Aware perturbation alternatives already appear in v1.

E3.justification: v3 removes AVGE from Tables 1–3 and adds model-agreement PSNR as a diagnostic. New analyses sweep perturbation intervals from 100 to 900 iterations and fixed noise multipliers from 0.01 to 0.3. The stated default noise distribution is revised to adaptive scaling, while benchmark splits, view counts, and training budgets are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained model-count/speed comparison and perturbation-strategy ablation, v3 adds model agreement versus synthesis quality in Figure 7, interval sensitivity in Figure 9, noise-level sensitivity in Figure 10, and the evolution of the perturbed-Gaussian fraction in Figure 11. These substantially expand examination of the central perturbation mechanism.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty on benchmark estimates. The pixel-level uncertainty computation is part of the algorithm, rather than statistical uncertainty reporting for experimental results.

E6.justification: Shared SE-GS PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS values in Tables 1–4 and the Table 5 ablation values remain unchanged. Newly reported DNGaussian PSNRs are 22.01/22.62 on LLFF and 22.56/25.25 on DTU for 6/9 views. Figures 7 and 9–11 substantially expand findings on diversity, perturbation sensitivity, and the perturbed-Gaussian fraction. AVGE entries disappear, and Figure 5 replaces one qualitative example. These are additional or removed results, not same-setting SE-GS performance gains.

M1.justification: The two-model pipeline, co-pruning, losses, and inference procedure remain. However, Equation 8 changes uncertainty normalization from sqrt(sum)/S to sqrt(sum/S), and Section 4.1 replaces the stated unit-variance perturbations with parameter-scaled Gaussian noise. These are limited revisions to the reported specification; the PDFs do not establish whether implementation or experiments changed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Preliminaries and Motivations become separate subsections, Temporal Samples in 3DGS becomes Uncertainty-Aware Perturbation, and terminology shifts toward perturbed models. A structured supplement expands the explanation of ensemble learning and implementation.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the pipeline and buffer diagrams, adds Figures 7–11, and revises Figure 5 with zoomed details and a box example replacing the watch. Tables 1–3 lose AVGE columns, Table 3 becomes a single-column display, and several figures and tables are relocated. These constitute substantial visual and layout revisions.

R1.justification: v3 adds references on deep ensembles, transformation-consistent self-ensembling, SE-SSD, and Plenoxels, while removing several background references on volume rendering, augmentation, dropout, and left-atrium segmentation. The principal positioning against CoR-GS and other sparse-view reconstruction methods remains.

T1.justification: Equation 8 changes the uncertainty normalization mathematically, moving 1/S inside the square root. The supplement adds explicit definitions of the adaptive threshold in Equation 15 and parameter-dependent noise scale in Equation 16. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 defers essential Gaussian-selection details to supplementary material absent from its PDF and provides limited testing of perturbation settings. v3 supplies operational threshold and noise specifications and targeted diversity, interval, and noise analyses, substantially improving reproducibility and support for the central design. Dropping AVGE and introducing inconsistent code-release wording are narrower drawbacks; the principal benchmark results remain intact.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same SE-GS study, with matching core methods and benchmarks. v3 includes supplementary material absent from the supplied v1; newly documented details can be compared without assuming they represent newly implemented procedures.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds model-diversity analysis and supplementary perturbation sensitivity studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original SE-GS experiments on four datasets, qualitative renderings, and analyses of model count, training speed, and perturbation strategies.

results.title: Self-Ensembling Gaussian Splatting for Few-Shot Novel View Synthesis

C1.justification: Both versions claim that label-converted SA1B-Matte and the decoder/attention improvements enable precise micro-level zero-shot matting and downstream transfer. The principal contributions and MicroMat-3K benchmark claim remain the same; additional experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: V2 explains the mismatch between whole-foreground public matting labels and object/part-level predictions, linking box-prompt failures to SAM ambiguity and discussing dense-point mitigation. It adds substantive transparency limitations, interprets training-data controls and frozen-backbone constraints, and explicitly acknowledges prompt ambiguity and uncertain predictions in the conclusion.

D1.justification: Appendix C.1 newly specifies RITM evaluation with at most 12 points, 10% box perturbation, eight V100 GPUs, and training times of seven and five days. The code-access pointer changes from a repository to a project website. Conversely, v1's explicit COCO 2017 validation/10-point inpainting setup and training-box-perturbation statement are omitted.

E1.justification: V2 adds dedicated transparent-object matting on Transparent-460 and fine-grained segmentation transfer on DIS, COIFT, HRSOD, and ThinObject. These extend the evaluated tasks and data coverage. The original MicroMat-3K, automatic-mask-generation, inpainting, medical, and 3D scenarios remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds GFM and AIM to traditional matting comparisons, IndexNet, MGMatting, and TransMatting to transparency comparisons, and Matte-Any and Matting-Any to downstream comparisons. Table 1 removes SAM2 and SMat, although both remain in appendix Table 6. Table 8 also introduces component-augmented comparison variants.

E3.justification: New evaluations sweep 2–10 point prompts, swap training datasets, test 1% versus 10% training data, and fine-tune ZIM on Transparent-460 while comparing box and trimap inputs. P3M-500-NP is added to public-matting evaluation. The original main-training defaults remain unchanged; newly specified prompt-sampling details alone do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Table 3c adds training-dataset controls for ZIM and Matting-Any; Table 8 tests converter post-processing and training existing models on SA1B-Matte. Figure 8 examines prompt-density sensitivity under domain shift, and Appendix C.1 reports a data-volume check. Original component, object-size, and hyperparameter analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The medical-IoU distribution plot is retained as Figure 15 from v1 Figure 8. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. V2's discussion of uncertain predictions does not add statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V2 adds transfer, training-control, prompt-count, and transparency results; Table 7 reports ZIM MSE 15.55 and SAD 298.78. Matched MicroMat-3K, inpainting, NVOS, and original ablation values remain unchanged, while the complete v1 AM-2K/AIM-500 table is omitted. Figure 8 plots Matte-Any's AIM-500 box MSE near 22, versus 38.497 in v1 Table 2 and about 38.5 in v2 Figure 5; the PDFs do not explain this discrepancy.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.2 retain the same label converter, augmentation and selective learning strategies, losses, hierarchical decoder, and prompt-aware attention. Added fine-tuning and component-transfer experiments do not establish a revised ZIM algorithm. Text and scribble prompting already appear in v1.

P1.justification: The standalone downstream-task section becomes a short Section 5.3 with detailed accounts moved to Appendix B. Appendix material is reorganized into expanded subsections, method explanations are condensed, and the conclusion is rewritten around limitations and future work. This substantially changes the narrative structure.

P2.justification: V2 adds the multipanel transfer chart, domain-shift examples, prompt-count curves, transparency and component-transfer tables, and an expanded training-data ablation table. It removes the original public-matting table, reduces and rearranges Figures 1–2, and relocates numerous downstream figures and tables into the appendix.

R1.justification: New references support transparency and fine-grained segmentation evaluations and identify components such as Grounding DINO and the inpainting model. The related-work narrative and central positioning around SAM generalization and macro-level matting datasets remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The matting-loss and prompt-masked-attention definitions in Equations 1–5 are mathematically unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs, and v2 adds no substantive derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central data-versus-architecture argument through Tables 3c and 8, directly testing explanations that v1 largely supported indirectly. Its domain-shift and transparency analyses also establish important applicability limits. These gains in validation and qualification outweigh the loss of some comparison and protocol detail, although the unexplained Matte-Any discrepancy between Figures 5 and 8 weakens the public-benchmark reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ZIM and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Their contents can be reliably matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds training-dataset controls, downstream comparisons, prompt-count experiments, and transparency evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original MicroMat-3K evaluations, component and hyperparameter ablations, and inpainting, medical segmentation, and 3D segmentation results.

results.title: ZIM: Zero-Shot Image Matting for Anything

C1.justification: v2 expands the main contributions to dynamic-round training, cumulative spatial reasoning and flexible probability-distribution modeling. It also strengthens novelty positioning to the first fully support-free CAPE framework. The claim of outperforming prior five-shot methods was already present in v1 and is not itself a new contribution.

C2.justification: v2 introduces substantive mechanism explanations: dynamic training enables accumulated relational context to help prediction, and decoded distributions can better respect object boundaries than fixed-variance Gaussians. It also interprets new experiments as evidence of robustness to description, resolution and decoding variations. These extend v1's explanations concerning descriptions, backbone tuning and model size.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository hyperlink and decoding parameters such as temperature, top-k and nucleus thresholds. However, it omits v1's explicit split-1 ablation scope, padding rule for incomplete keypoint groups, and some pre-training data and initialization details. Default optimizer, hardware and training-budget disclosures remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: MP-100 and its category coverage remain unchanged. v2 expands evaluation scenarios to train–test description mismatches, including removed or placeholder descriptions, and explicitly examines several occlusion conditions. These extend input-condition coverage without introducing another dataset or pose-estimation task.

E2.justification: GraphCAPE-S and CapeX remain the benchmark comparators. v2 newly evaluates a LocLLM-style training control in Tables 3–4. Figure 5 also introduces a ground-truth-centered, fixed-variance Gaussian as a qualitative reference distribution.

E3.justification: New experiments compare training strategies under single versus cumulative inference, vary description substitution, test resolutions through 336×336, and evaluate seven decoding strategies. The original benchmark splits and default training settings remain. Separately, the stated Hiera token count changes from less than 20% of other encoders' tokens to 20% fewer; no changed implementation or rerun is established.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands diagnostic analyses: cumulative reasoning, training-strategy controls, vague and missing descriptions, resolution sensitivity, decoding alternatives, occlusion cases and predictive-density comparisons (Tables 3–9; Figures 4–5). Earlier instruction, backbone and pre-training ablations largely survive in the appendices rather than being removed.

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly visualizes predictive uncertainty using multiple decoded samples and kernel density estimation. Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests for benchmark scores. The new density visualization does not establish uncertainty in reported PCK averages.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results, including dynamic-training PCK@0.2 of 96.05 with single inference versus 97.28 with cumulative inference, and LocLLM-style mPCK of 84.00 versus fixed-round 91.98. Existing benchmark split scores remain unchanged; Table 2 corrects the query-only average from 91.60 to 92.60. Several retained appendix tables omit previously reported intermediate PCK thresholds.

M1.justification: v2 adds dynamic-round training with variable numbers of keypoints per conversation and cumulative inference that carries earlier keypoint prompts into subsequent predictions (Sections 3.3 and 4.3). These extend the procedure substantially. The fixed-round grouping, DINOv2–LLaMA architecture and three-decimal coordinate representation already existed in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, related-work discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The experimental narrative is reorganized around cumulative reasoning and distribution modeling, while much of v1's main-text ablation discussion moves into an expanded Appendix B. Author affiliation and contact formatting also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 2 to depict coordinate-token decoding, adds occlusion and density figures, and removes v1's qualitative name-variation figure. It adds experimental tables, splits the earlier combined ablation table into separate appendix tables, reduces columns in several retained tables, and relocates the description table and instruction diagrams.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around LocLLM as the closest approach, distinguishes CapeX's skeletal dependence, and connects CapeLLM to chain-of-thought and decoding-based regression. Table 1 changes CapeX's support-free designation from a checkmark to a partial-status triangle. New references support these arguments, while the Long-CLIP citation is removed.

T1.justification: v2 adds Equation (6), a digit-wise conditional probability factorization, and a cited claim that decoding represents a truncated conditional density at resolution 10^(-K). v1 described coordinate encoding without this formal distributional argument. No new proof is supplied within v2.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of CapeLLM's adaptation: Tables 3–4 add the missing LocLLM-style training control and reveal when cumulative inference helps or hurts. New stress tests examine reliability beyond v1's name-variation example, while the benchmark average is corrected and code access is documented. Some reproducibility details are lost and the distribution claims remain qualitatively evaluated, but the stronger controls and diagnostic evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CapeLLM. All 14 pages of each version, including equations, figures, tables and appendices A–C, are readable and support comparison. Retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark and appendix results and adds experiments on training strategies, cumulative inference, input robustness and decoding, plus qualitative density analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original MP-100 benchmark results, architecture and instruction ablations, and additional output-format and pre-training experiments in the appendices.

results.title: CapeLLM: Support-Free Category-Agnostic Pose Estimation with Multimodal Large Language Models

C1.justification: The three central methodological contributions and claims of strong benchmark performance and efficiency remain. v2 removes the abstract's explicit claim of second place in the CVPR24 Occupancy and Flow Prediction Competition, a limited narrowing of its headline achievements.

C2.justification: The supplement adds interpretations concerning applicability to Waymo, object-specific advantages in qualitative examples, and performance tradeoffs underlying the selected denoising duration and sampling density. It also characterizes SurroundOcc's annotation quality and evaluation differences. The original explanations of semantic alignment and competing semantic/flow demands remain.

D1.justification: v2 discloses key defaults such as three inter-object sampling points, six denoising epochs, and 25,088 supervision samples. It adds checkpoint initialization, variant channel sizes, projected-LiDAR 2D supervision, OpenOcc ray-visible training masks, and detailed baseline-result provenance. These substantially improve reproducibility without establishing that retained experiments changed. The repository link is unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds Occ3D-Waymo, extending evaluation beyond nuScenes-derived data, and a camera-plus-depth input scenario. It also evaluates SurroundOcc, which reuses nuScenes but has different annotations and evaluation requirements. These additions substantially broaden the empirical coverage of v1's Occ3D/OpenOcc evaluations.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds multimodal comparators including EFFOcc, SDGOcc, OccFusion, BEVFusion, and FusionOcc. Supplementary comparisons introduce GaussianFormer/GaussianFormer2 and additional temporal methods including CVT-Occ. BEVDetOcc-SOLO becoming BEVDetOcc-SF is a matched rename, not a new comparator.

E3.justification: Added protocols include FlashInternImage-Tiny configurations, SurroundOcc evaluation at 900×1600 without voxel-level temporal fusion and with all-voxel metrics, and Occ3D-Waymo evaluation at 640×960. Existing nuScenes splits and training budgets remain unchanged. Appendix B.5's 'without mask' description conflicts with its masked-metric table labels, leaving that particular setting unclear.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained coarse component ablations in Tables 4–5, Tables A.9–A.12 separately examine depth denoising, occlusion-probability transfer, inter-object sampling, denoising duration, and supervision sampling density. Figure A.7 adds qualitative comparisons of pedestrian, vegetation, traffic-cone, and construction-vehicle predictions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Uncertainty-aware voxel sampling describes the learning procedure, not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Matched original scores remain stable, including ResNet-50 ALOcc-3D's 45.5 masked mIoU and 43.7 RayIoU. v2 adds extensive configuration, class-level, benchmark, and ablation results, including 30.03 mIoU on Occ3D-Waymo and 60.0 masked mIoU for depth-assisted Swin-Base ALOcc-3D. These are additional settings, not same-setting gains. The competition-placement report is removed.

M1.justification: The adaptive lifting, depth denoising, semantic prototypes, and cost-volume flow procedures remain intact. v2 adds a depth-assisted operating configuration that supplies LiDAR-derived depth to adaptive lifting (Table 1, Section 4.3), extending the reported inputs beyond v1's camera-only ALOcc configurations. Most other methodological additions clarify existing components.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, contribution bullets become an integrated enumeration, and the prototype-head and flow-head explanations are reorganized. Terminology and notation are clarified throughout, and structured supplementary sections are added. The editorial revision extends well beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains modality columns and substantial configuration blocks; Table 3 gains supervision and FPS columns. v2 adds Tables A.6–A.12 and qualitative Figure A.7, revises diagram labels and captions, and relocates existing displays. This substantially expands and reorganizes the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds a BEV-detection discussion and citations covering Gaussian occupancy, multimodal fusion, newer temporal methods, and prior AdaOcc work. The central positioning around unified occupancy/flow prediction and comprehensive evaluation remains. LetOccFlow's preprint and publication entries represent the same work.

T1.justification: Appendix E introduces a formal definition of occluded length using a maximal same-class extension along a camera ray, with interior and endpoint conditions. v1 provides probabilistic modeling without this explicit definition. Appendix A's formulas mostly explain existing metrics; no substantial new proof or theoretical analysis is added.

improvement.justification: v1's validation was confined to nuScenes-derived benchmarks and coarse component ablations, with important training details unspecified. v2 adds Waymo evaluation, targeted component studies, qualitative evidence, and checkpoint and baseline provenance, substantially strengthening validation and reproducibility. The supplementary mask-label inconsistency remains, and depth-assisted scores require separate interpretation, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of ALOcc, with matching core methods and experiments. v1 ends with references; v2 adds Supplementary Material A–E. All pages, including figures, equations, tables, and supplementary material, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds backbone configurations, depth-assisted evaluations, SurroundOcc and Occ3D-Waymo experiments, and supplementary ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original occupancy and flow experiments on Occ3D and OpenOcc, including benchmark comparisons, runtime measurements, and component ablations in Tables 1–5.

results.title: ALOcc: Adaptive Lifting-Based 3D Semantic Occupancy and Cost Volume-Based Flow Predictions

C1.justification: The central claims about joint modeling, generative replay, semi-supervised learning, and useful representations are retained. v3 elevates reduced computational cost into an explicit introductory contribution and attributes performance gains to higher-quality rehearsal samples. The principal method contribution and conclusion remain stable.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations connecting logit alignment to distillation, generation precision to classifier performance, and weak classification signals to semi-supervised CIFAR100 difficulties. It also discusses attention's classification–generation tradeoff and two-stage training's stability–plasticity tradeoff. v1's explicit qualification that the method costs more than buffer-based approaches is removed, although generative replay's computational burden remains discussed.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the hidden-for-review code reference with a repository URL and adds model sizes, ResNet152 details for Figure 1, ResNet18 for separate-model ablations, ImageNet100 implementation information, and runtime methodology. It also clarifies initialization from the current global model. Conversely, v1's detailed CPU/GPU specifications and total research-compute estimates are removed.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates CIFAR10 and CIFAR100; v3 additionally evaluates five-task ImageNet100, described as 120,000 training images at 64×64 resolution. This materially extends coverage beyond the original CIFAR collections while retaining their supervised and semi-supervised scenarios.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds EWC, GKD (LwF), MKD (iCaRL), TKD (SS-IL), and ANCL to the existing CIFAR comparisons. Figure 6 adds supervised representation baselines SL, SL+MLP, t-ReX, and SupCon. Conversely, Table 2 removes the semi-supervised oEWC row. These changes substantially broaden the comparator families.

E3.justification: Figure 1 changes from first-task CIFAR100 training for 110 epochs to CIFAR10 training for 100,000 steps with similarly sized models and additional distillation controls. Appendix B revises stated training budgets, including CIFAR10's initial local training from 60,000 to 50,000 steps. New evaluations introduce generative-quality and transfer metrics, controlled A100 runtime comparisons, and reduced-precision training. These reported changes do not establish that retained scores were rerun.

E4.justification: Table 3 adds separate removal of knowledge distillation and two-stage training, previously untested individually. New analyses examine logit-distribution alignment, component behavior across tasks, attention versus pooling, transfer, training loss versus runtime, and sensitivity to β. The earlier representation-drift and UMAP analyses are retained as Figures 7 and 8 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 Section 5.1 explicitly states that evaluated metrics are averaged over three seeds and reported with standard deviations. v3 retains mean±deviation entries but removes this general statement, explicitly documenting three-seed averaging only for Figure 1. This changes reporting scope without establishing an increase or decrease in actual runs.

E6.justification: The main CIFAR JDCL accuracy values remain 83.69, 47.95, and 29.04. v3 adds substantial results, including ImageNet100 accuracy of 54.53±2.15 versus GUIDE's 39.07±1.37, new ablations, and generative-quality, runtime, transfer, and sensitivity measurements. Table 3 changes the full-model entry from 83.3 to 83.7. Figure 1 reports replacement results under changed conditions, not a same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: The main JDCL procedure and losses remain unchanged. Appendix G adds an evaluated architectural alternative that chains attention over UNet representations instead of pooling them. This extends the examined model variants without replacing the main pooling-based method.

P1.justification: Much of the abstract, related work, background, method exposition, and conclusion is retained. Targeted rewrites clarify the motivating experiment and local-to-global training, formalize the introductory pseudocode, and reorganize supplementary sections. The representation-stability discussion moves into the appendix; much of the additional prose accompanies new scientific content.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. Figure 1 is redrawn with a step axis and four curves; the main accuracy/forgetting table is reorganized across main-text and supplementary displays. New mechanism plots, an attention diagram, expanded comparison charts, and numerous additional tables substantially change the visual organization.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for ImageNet, complementary networks, supervised continual representation learning, exemplar-free distillation, and DER transfer measurements. Two-stage training is more explicitly connected to prior approaches. The existing related-work taxonomy and overall positioning are otherwise retained.

T1.justification: The class-incremental assumptions, joint probability factorization, and denoising, classification, distillation, and semi-supervised loss formulations remain mathematically unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs, and the added empirical metrics introduce no substantive formal derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important evidential gaps: Table 3 separately tests distillation and two-stage training, Figure 6 adds supervised representation comparators, and ImageNet100 plus generative-quality analyses substantially broaden validation. These gains outweigh the loss of some uncertainty and compute disclosures. Efficiency claims still require qualification: Table 5 reports standard JDCL at 53.83 GPU-hours versus GUIDE's 30.60; the lower cost applies to JDCL (fast), at 27.21 hours.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JDCL research, with matching core formulations and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial layout changes.

after.justification: v3 retains original JDCL experiments and adds ImageNet100 results, expanded ablations, generative-quality measurements, runtime comparisons, and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original JDCL results on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, including continual classification, semi-supervised learning, component ablations, and representation analyses.

results.title: Joint Diffusion models in Continual Learning

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes coherent correlations, outlier patches and similarity irregularity. V2 makes identifying inter-class correlations as the primary impediment a central contribution, and adds spatial/semantic feature refinement to its main claims. Class-name correction disappears from the contribution statements.

C2.justification: Value reconstruction is reinterpreted as suppressing residual inter-class correlations within imperfect masks, rather than chiefly correcting similarity irregularity after scope restriction. V2 adds substantive discussion of mixed-class masks, mask-downsampling errors, feature/text misalignment and computational bottlenecks, including explanations of branch-specific performance degradation and efficiency tradeoffs.

D1.justification: The core backbone choices, thresholds and sliding-window recipe remain. V2 adds a code-repository pointer, feature weights, the selected 42×42 mask resolution, CPU clustering information, RTX 4090/FP16 measurement conditions, and backbone/pretraining details for alternative mask generators. These extend the implementation documentation without replacing its existing core recipe.

E1.justification: The eight original benchmarks remain. V2 additionally evaluates FoodSeg103, ATLANTIS, CUB-200 and SUIM from MESS (Table 9), extending coverage to food, waterbody, fine-grained bird and underwater segmentation domains.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated comparators including LaVG, NACLIP, Trident, ResCLIP, SC-CLIP, CLIPer, CASS, CAT-Seg and ESC-Net. SCLIP's ViT-L/14 and ViT-H/14 rows disappear, although its ViT-B/16 comparison remains. Supplementary Table 9 additionally compares against OVSeg-L and CAT-Seg-L.

E3.justification: The headline validation splits, mIoU metric and image-resizing/sliding-window settings remain. V2 introduces controlled inter-class interaction proportions, mask-resolution sweeps and computational comparisons using 8×8 versus 32×32 prompt grids. The CLIP-variant analysis also changes its aggregation from eight benchmarks in v1 Table 5 to five background-free benchmarks in v2 Table 7.

E4.justification: V2 adds controlled intra/inter-class correlation analyses, scope reconstruction applied to other methods, mask-resolution sensitivity, separate feature-branch ablations and component-level computational analysis. Conversely, v1's detailed SAM-threshold and DBSCAN-parameter sweeps are absent; mask merging is instead tested through an on/off comparison across several benchmarks.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. V2's added performance differences are point-score comparisons, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1's reported CorrCLIP averages change from 49.7 to 51.0 for ViT-B/16, 51.0 to 53.6 for ViT-L/14, and 50.0 to 52.3 for ViT-H/14. These concern revised CorrCLIP variants on the retained benchmarks, rather than unchanged-method reruns. V2 also supplies new domain-generalization, correlation, feature-refinement and efficiency results.

M1.justification: V2 adds feature refinement through lower-layer spatial features and mask class tokens, substantially changing feature computation (Section 3.4). Its appendix introduces faster variants that replace SAM and omit value reconstruction and mask merging. V1's plural-form class-name correction is no longer included in the described pipeline.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten around the inter-class correlation argument. Method exposition is reorganized into feature refinement and map correction, replacing the earlier combined correction subsection, and v2 adds a structured supplementary narrative. The title is also shortened and refocused.

P2.justification: V1's opening attention visualization and performance curve are replaced by a radar comparison and separate correlation plots. The framework diagram is extensively redrawn, Table 1 gains a denser structure with annotated differences, and qualitative comparisons expand to more methods and supplementary galleries. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands its treatment of recent OVSS approaches, distinguishing self-self attention, lower-layer attention refinement and external foundation-model methods. It positions explicit interaction-scope control against these approaches and adds literature supporting specialized-domain evaluation, fully supervised comparisons and alternative mask generators.

T1.justification: The interaction-matrix definition changes the unsegmented-region term from the broadcast sum of m0 and its transpose in v1 Equation (6) to their outer product in v2 Equation (7), changing the formal mask definition. V2 also introduces the weighted feature-refinement expression in Equation (11). Neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence for its mechanism and applicability through controlled correlation experiments (Figures 2 and 5), broader comparator coverage, specialized-domain evaluations (Table 9), and explicit runtime/memory analysis (Table 11). Branch ablations and discussion of alignment errors and computational limitations make the revised method easier to assess. Although some earlier parameter sweeps disappear and the method becomes more complex, the new evidence addresses important validation and practicality gaps in v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CorrCLIP for open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, and their text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 also includes Supplementary Material, which was inspected.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark evaluations, correlation experiments and ablations, plus supplementary domain-generalization and computational results.

before.justification: V1 reports original segmentation evaluations across eight benchmarks, component ablations, parameter studies and qualitative results.

results.title: CorrCLIP: Reconstructing Patch Correlations in CLIP for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation

C1.justification: The central claims remain first integration of 3DGS into gaze redirection, explicit eye rotation, separate face/eye modeling, expression-guided generalization, and strong performance across four datasets. Subject-specific conditioning receives greater emphasis, and downstream usefulness receives new evidence, but these do not establish a new overarching contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explains EGNR more explicitly through subject-specific information and identity preservation, and discusses why adding it to existing baselines leaves representation limitations. Section 13 newly identifies tracking-related difficulties with glasses, earrings, and hair, supported by Figure 9. These qualify applicability without overturning the original interpretation.

D1.justification: New Sections 9–10 disclose Adam optimization, a 1e-4 initial learning rate with exponential decay, 10 initialization epochs plus 20 pipeline epochs, NVIDIA 4090 hardware, 680 mm normalization, and single-image adaptation timing. They distinguish the VGG-based loss estimator from ResNet50 evaluation. v2 also clarifies Gaussian Head Avatar conditioning and changes the code statement from future release to claimed availability.

E1.justification: ETH-XGaze, ColumbiaGaze, MPIIFaceGaze, and GazeCapture remain the dataset coverage. v2 adds actual evaluation of downstream few-shot gaze-estimator personalization in Section 5.5 and an identity-interpolation demonstration in Section 12.2. v1 mentions the downstream benefit but supplies no corresponding results.

E2.justification: The original comparison methods remain in Tables 1–2. v2 substantially expands the controls with GazeNeRF+EGNR and Gaussian Head Avatar+EGNR in Table 5, testing whether the proposed renderer explains the advantage. Figure 6 includes real-only estimator fine-tuning, while Table 6 adds Wang et al. using explicitly attributed published scores rather than a reproduced experiment.

E3.justification: The existing redirection protocols retain the 14.4K-image training subset, evaluation pairings, resolution, and metrics. New Section 5.5 evaluates estimator fine-tuning with one to nine real calibration images and fixes augmented training sets at 200 real-plus-generated samples. Newly disclosed epoch counts and preprocessing parameters describe existing experiments rather than establish changed settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds cross-dataset component ablations in Table 4 and renderer-transfer controls in Table 5, extending the original within-dataset ablation. Sections 12–13 also add transformed-Gaussian inspection, identity interpolation with fixed gaze and pose, expanded qualitative ablations, and an illustrated accessory-reconstruction failure case.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The new gaze-estimation curves in Figure 6 show point estimates without uncertainty bands or error bars.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their numerical results. Table 3 changes identity similarity without eye rotation from 38.521 to 41.521. v2 adds downstream error curves, cross-dataset ablation scores, renderer-control results, and qualitative findings. Figure 6 places GazeGaussian augmentation lowest in error throughout. New Table 5 also gives Gaussian Head Avatar head error as 8.498, inconsistently with 13.563 in retained Table 1.

M1.justification: The two-stream architecture, eye rotation, expression-guided renderer, and training losses are retained. A localized specification change appears in the gaze-conditioned eye-color MLP: its input changes from Gaussian positions X0e in v1 Equation 7 to Gaussian features z0e in v2 Equation 5. The PDFs do not establish whether this reflects an implementation change or a correction to the written formula.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the method exposition, replaces notation throughout, and consolidates separate attribute descriptions into grouped equations. It introduces a numbered section/subsection hierarchy, revises explanatory passages across the abstract and experiments, and incorporates an organized supplementary narrative. This extends beyond isolated language corrections.

P2.justification: v2 retains the original core figures but redistributes comparison figures and tables within a revised typographic layout. It adds Figure 6, Tables 4–6, and Figures 7–13, covering downstream performance, controls, Gaussian geometry, identity morphing, failures, and expanded visual comparisons. These substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Adam and GaussianHair and sharpens discussion of Gaussian Head Avatar's single-avatar scope. Wang et al., already cited in v1, gains a quantitative literature comparison. The main related-work coverage remains; consolidating Gaussian Head Avatar's preprint/publication references does not remove a distinct work.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4.1 adds explicit covariance, Gaussian-kernel, and alpha-compositing definitions where v1 primarily listed Gaussian attributes and used a rasterization operator. Most subsequent mathematics is retained under renamed notation and consolidated equations, with localized formula corrections. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves evidential support and reproducibility: Section 5.5 supplies results for a downstream benefit previously asserted without supporting outcomes, Tables 4–5 strengthen component attribution and generalization evidence, and Sections 9–10 disclose essential implementation details. The illustrated limitations also improve transparency. These gains outweigh localized inconsistencies, including Gaussian Head Avatar's conflicting head-error entries and the unexplained relationship between 74 FPS and 0.2 seconds per generated image.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GazeGaussian and contain readable text, equations, tables, and figures. Corresponding main-text material can be matched reliably. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 additionally includes supplementary Sections 7–13.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and additionally reports downstream gaze-estimation results, cross-dataset ablations, renderer-enhanced baseline comparisons, and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original gaze-redirection experiments across four datasets, quantitative comparisons in Tables 1–2, and component ablations in Table 3.

results.title: GazeGaussian: High-Fidelity Gaze Redirection with 3D Gaussian Splatting
