C1.justification: The central claim of improving personalized localization through curated instruction tuning while retaining generalization remains. v2 drops the headline contribution of a copying-related metric and explicitly emphasizes GPT-4o's weaknesses and effectiveness across 7B–72B models in the abstract and introduction.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of failure through prompt-format compliance, model-scale effects, and possible difficulty with longer contexts. Section 5 explicitly limits the studied setting to single-object output and hypothesizes a training-data explanation for poor multi-object localization. The earlier copying-based interpretation is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds test-set category, object-density, and conversation counts; exact baseline prompts; the GPT-4o model snapshot and high-detail image setting; and a planned release of the data mixes. Conversely, SEED split sample counts disappear. Training documentation still largely refers to LlamaFactory defaults.

E1.justification: The training datasets and principal localization and generalization benchmarks remain unchanged. Section 5 adds a briefly reported MS-COCO multi-object localization test; v1 mentioned COCO but did not report this evaluation.

E2.justification: Beyond the three original VLM baselines, v2 Table 2 adds Pixtral-12B, GPT-4o, Qwen2-VL-72B, and InternVL2-76B. Tables 7–8 additionally compare IPLoc with CD-ViTO, TFA, and OwlViT, substantially broadening the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 introduces 72B fine-tuning and larger-model evaluations, a denser 1–8-shot ICL-LASOT evaluation, and baseline prompt sweeps with selection by aggregate performance (Appendix D). It removes evaluation with IoUex. The principal mIoU metric and stated 50/50 LaSOT category split remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds extensive prompt-sensitivity experiments and response-level failure cases, a denser shot-count analysis, and 72B generalization-retention checks. Existing data-source, semantic-coherence, pseudo-name, and LLaVA analyses largely remain. The copying examples and IoUex diagnostic in v1 Figures 3–4 are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both principally report point estimates; SEED refers to a benchmark, not random-seed reporting.

E6.justification: Between v1 Table 1 and v2 Table 2, Qwen2-VL-7B's ICL-LASOT 4-shot score changes from 21.89 to 46.29, and IPLoc-7B's Real + Pseudo 8-shot score changes from 33.95 to 55.21. The PDFs do not explain these revisions. Numerous larger-model, detector, prompt-ablation, and multi-object results are added, while the IoUex results and detailed SEED image/video scores are removed.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure remains video-based conversation construction, maximum-interval frame sampling, real/pseudo-name mixing, and LoRA fine-tuning with next-token prediction. Applying this recipe to larger models and testing baseline prompts does not change IPLoc itself.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and results discussion receive targeted rewrites. Model and metric descriptions are removed, ablations are reordered, and limitations and a prompt-ablation appendix are introduced. The main section sequence and most methodological prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 transposes and expands the main results table, replaces several ablation bar charts with tables, revises Figure 1's examples, and adds a shot-count curve, dataset statistics, and extensive prompt/response displays. The older appendix localization examples are retained but redistributed throughout the expanded supplement.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations supporting the new VLM and detector comparisons and discussion of scaling and context length, while removing the earlier Qwen technical-report reference. The related-work section's principal VLM/ICL framing and the claimed novelty of personalized localization remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: v1's Equation 1 defining IoUex, its mathematical explanation, and its multi-shot selection rule are deleted. The conversation and bounding-box notation remain, with no added theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical foundation through stronger VLM and detector comparisons and explicit prompt controls. Appendix D shows why these controls matter: Qwen2-VL-72B's mean score changes from 7.69 with the original prompt to 34.21 with the selected prompt. Scaling and retention checks better support applicability, and the single-object limitation clarifies scope. Removed copying diagnostics and SEED details, unexplained score revisions, and inconsistencies such as Table 4's 72B label versus Section 4.3's 7B description temper, but do not outweigh, these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IPLoc research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, added, and removed content.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds larger-model evaluations, detector comparisons, and quantitative prompt ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original localization experiments, data-curation ablations, and generalization evaluations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Teaching VLMs to Localize Specific Objects from In-context Examples

C1.justification: V1's contribution list claims a proposed contrastive multi-metric quality measure. V2 emphasizes the routing architecture built around multi-metric measures, while Section 4 attributes contrastive scoring to prior work. This narrows the novelty positioning of one component while retaining the central text-to-image routing and dual-gate MoE contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning preference alignment, edge-device suitability, customizable metrics, and semantic robustness across encoders. It removes v1's discussion of diminishing routing benefits at high cloud-routing rates. Its new description of 83.97% as a fraction of the full cloud gain is also imprecise: under the unchanged ΔP formula, v1 Table 2 assigns the cloud itself 80%, rather than 100%.

D1.justification: V2 discloses all ten positive/negative quality-prompt pairs, previously illustrated with only two examples. It adds generator and encoder specifications, explains baseline adaptation, and reports router size, training time, memory use, deployment hardware, and LAION sample counts. These materially expand reproducibility information. V1's statement that generators use official default hyperparameters is dropped.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates COCO2014 captions only. V2 adds training and evaluation on LAION2B-en-aesthetic prompts (Appendix F), extending coverage from concise object descriptions to more colloquial and stylistic requests. The text-to-image routing task remains the same.

E2.justification: The baseline families remain RouteLLM-BERT, RouteLLM-MF, Hybrid LLM, ZOOTER, and random routing. However, v1 compares the learned baselines only for SD3/SD2.1, while its other generator-pair results report RouteT2I alone. V2 Appendix Tables 6–14 add all four learned baselines to those nine already-tested pairs, substantially expanding comparator participation.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce a 20,000-training/10,000-validation LAION split, HPSv2 and MPS scoring at 50% routing, ImageReward analysis by noun count, and Jetson deployment measurements. Generator configurations expand from ten to eighteen pairs, including PixArt-α and Infinity. The stated optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and approximately ten training epochs remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds an empirical test of prompt complexity versus generator quality gaps (Figures 2–3), validation against preference-scoring models (Appendix D), and visual routing case studies (Appendix G). Appendix H also analyzes behavior across encoder and generator architectures. The original three component ablations and their Table 6 values are retained.

E5.justification: V2 Figure 3 introduces shaded bands around the noun-count curves, but neither its caption nor the text identifies what the bands represent or how they were estimated. Neither version specifies seeds or repeated-run counts. The bands therefore cannot reliably be classified as a documented change in statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The headline SD3/SD2.1 results and ablation values remain, but Table 5 revises existing entries: SD3/SDXL at 40% routing changes from 27.10% to 29.78%. V2 adds LAION results, preference scores, additional pair comparisons, and runtime/memory measurements; v1's pairwise win-rate matrix is removed. These are revised and expanded reported results, without evidence establishing an underlying method improvement.

M1.justification: Sections 4–5 retain the contrastive quality scores, PRS normalization and aggregation, dual-gate token-selection MoE, projection and score matrices, multiple prediction heads, and threshold-based routing. Added explanations and generator configurations do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most method exposition remain. V2 revises the title and authorship information, adds acknowledgments, edits related-work and results prose, clarifies metric terminology, and organizes additional material into Appendices A–H. These are targeted editorial and structural refinements rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1, adds prompt examples and complexity plots, removes v1's pairwise win-rate heatmap, and narrows the displayed routing-rate range in the performance curves. It restructures and expands the generator-pair table and adds extensive appendix tables and a routing-example image grid. The architecture diagram is retained with renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 substantially strengthens grounding of the central components: contrastive scoring is attributed to Liang et al. and Wang et al.; metric selection is connected to HEIM, T2I-Scorer, and VisionPrefer; and MoE positioning adds token-mixture and expert-choice work. Related-work discussion further distinguishes T2I from LLM routing, alongside references supporting the new evaluations.

T1.justification: New Appendix B formalizes text and image space cardinalities, defines their logarithmic size ratio, and derives numerical comparisons for CLIP and T5 inputs. V1 only gives the qualitative space-size argument. This is a limited mathematical addition; the core routing equations are retained, and no routing optimality proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow validation through LAION evaluation, preference-scoring models outside the routing objective, broader baseline comparisons, and measured Jetson deployment costs. The complete quality-prompt specification also improves reproducibility. Unexplained score revisions, undefined uncertainty bands, and imprecise normalized-gain interpretations remain weaknesses, but the new evidence materially strengthens assessment of generalization, quality alignment, and practical feasibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RouteT2I, with matching core methods and experiments despite the changed title. The text, equations, figures, and tables support comparison. V1 ends after its references; v2 additionally supplies Appendices A–H, which were included in the assessment.

after.justification: V2 retains original routing experiments and adds LAION results, preference-model scoring, prompt-complexity analysis, additional generator-pair comparisons, and measured deployment costs.

before.justification: V1 reports original COCO routing experiments, comparisons with other routers, results across ten generator pairs, and component ablations in Section 6.

results.title: Adaptive Routing of Text-to-Image Generation Requests Between Large Cloud Model and Light-Weight Edge Model

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion newly claim attacks at any FL round while preserving normal model utility. The central contributions—natural-language targeted inversion, compatibility with reconstruction algorithms, and resistance to existing defenses—retain their original scope.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands applicability explanations and limitations: auxiliary data must represent queried features, advanced VLMs better handle complex queries, and reconstruction deteriorates beyond roughly 16 matches with the tested backend. It also argues that client selection can undermine model-history inspection and explains utility preservation through separate benign aggregation.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 explicitly documents initialization and training steps. The appendix adds HFGradInv integration information and identifies BLIP-based query generation. The repository link, CLIP checkpoint, hardware, optimizer, and reported feature-extraction and poisoning times are retained.

E1.justification: The datasets remain ImageNet, CIFAR-20, FER, and the existing auxiliary sources. V2 modestly extends scenario coverage through caption-defined ImageNet retrieval and explicit background-object targeting in Appendix F. The added CIFAR-20 illustrations and 128-image examples do not introduce new datasets or previously untested batch-size coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 7 adds HFGradInv, previously cited but not evaluated there, alongside retained DLG and InvertingGrad comparisons, each with and without Geminio. The five targeted-attack comparators in Figure 5 and five supplementary label-inference methods remain.

E3.justification: The stated default reconstruction algorithm changes from InvertingGrad to HFGradInv. Appendix F introduces caption-generated queries for randomly selected images, alternative VLM configurations, random versus current-global-model initialization across FL rounds, and a fixed batch of 256 with varying matched-sample counts. The existing CIFAR-20 evaluation and 0.90 gradient-similarity threshold remain.

E4.justification: Appendix F substantially expands analysis of query complexity, VLM choice, attack timing and initialization, reconstruction sensitivity to matched-sample count, and background-object targeting. These investigate generalization and failure conditions beyond v1's retained auxiliary-data, architecture, defense, label-inference, and batch-size analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Existing averaging practices remain, and the additional experiments continue to report point estimates without introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds caption-query, FL-round, matched-count, and VLM results, including SigLIP's 69.54% versus CLIP's 68.13% F1. Figure 7 adds HFGradInv LPIPS values of 0.66 alone and 0.19 with Geminio and revises existing scores. It also corrects Figure 8's prose to match the unchanged bars. Updated reconstructions use a revised default algorithm, preventing a simple same-setting improvement claim.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Figure 2 add an explicit deployment branch: non-victim clients train a benign model, and only their gradients enter its aggregation while the victim receives malicious parameters. This is a limited extension of the described procedure; the VLM-guided loss and soft-label equations remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and portions of the introduction, threat model, and method explanation are rewritten. The appendix is reorganized around new pseudocode and extended analyses, with affiliation and acknowledgement edits. Much of the original experimental narrative and overall section sequence remains intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are redrawn, Figure 4 expands from two to three dataset panels, and Figure 7 gains a third reconstruction method. Main-text plots are resized and rearranged, and the short final appendix example panel is replaced by extensive new plots and reconstruction displays in Figures 26–34.

R1.justification: V2 adds a specific CI-Net scalability comparison and references supporting captioning, auxiliary data, and larger-batch training, while removing several general gradient-inversion citations. Its central positioning as the first natural-language interface for semantically targeted GIAs remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 and the gradient-dominance reasoning remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 restates the existing training mathematics; no new theorem, proof, or substantive formal derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: V1's quantitative validation of language-guided targeting largely relies on CIFAR subclass names. V2 addresses this important gap with caption-based ImageNet evaluation and substantially clarifies applicability through attack-timing tests and an explicit matched-sample capacity limit. These additions strengthen the central claim and expose a meaningful failure boundary; pseudocode also improves inspectability. The stronger utility-preservation claim still lacks a direct utility comparison, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the claim-relevant validation and clearer limitations provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Geminio and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The shared method and experiments can be matched reliably despite the expanded and reorganized supplementary material.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds caption-query evaluation, VLM comparisons, FL-round experiments, and reconstruction-quality analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction experiments on ImageNet, CIFAR-20, and FER, including baseline comparisons, defense evaluations, and supplementary label-inference experiments.

results.title: Geminio: Language-Guided Gradient Inversion Attacks in Federated Learning

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes a broadly applicable module providing reconstruction improvements in supervised and self-supervised settings. v2 makes self-supervised motion modeling the primary contribution, treats supervised use as an extension, claims the first such plug-and-play module, and explicitly claims state-of-the-art self-supervised novel-view synthesis on Waymo and KITTI. These strengthen and refocus the headline scientific claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of DeSiRe-GS and OmniRe improvements, explains the inadequacy of trajectory interpolation for assessing simulation, and discusses embedding-capacity versus computational-cost tradeoffs. The original component-ablation interpretations remain. The lighting limitation is unchanged and merely moves from Section 6 to Appendix E.

D1.justification: v2 supplies embedding dimensions, interpolation details, regularization settings, loss coefficients, LiDAR initialization and filtering, Adam training budgets, warm-up procedures and A800 hardware information. It changes the code statement from a future release to stated availability. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation, although v1's explicit every-tenth/every-fourth-frame evaluation intervals are omitted.

E1.justification: The original Waymo coverage is retained, and KITTI is added. Section 5.3 also evaluates genuinely new camera trajectories shifted left and right by 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 meters, extending evaluation beyond interpolated views along the recorded trajectory.

E2.justification: The original S3Gaussian and StreetGaussian comparison sets remain. New Tables 2 and 4 add reported comparisons involving DeSiRe-GS, OmniRe, S-NeRF, StreetSurf, SUDS, PVG, DeformGS and HUGS, substantially broadening the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: New experiments use four Waymo and three KITTI scenes for the DeSiRe-GS comparison, add a three-camera StreetGaussian setting alongside the original one-camera setting, and evaluate human regions with OmniRe. v2 also introduces FPS and a trajectory-shift protocol using FID against original-trajectory images. Newly disclosed training settings alone do not establish changes to retained experiments.

E4.justification: Appendix D and Table 8 add sensitivity experiments varying Gaussian embedding dimensions across 8/32/128 and temporal dimensions across 1/4/16, including parameter costs. Section 5.3 adds tests of generalization away from the recorded camera trajectory. The original component-removal ablations and motion-deformation comparison are retained.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added experiments continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original component-ablation scores are unchanged. The StreetGaussian+EMD row is revised: full-image PSNR changes from 36.03 to 35.41 and vehicle PSNR from 29.81 to 30.96. v1 describes reconstruction whereas v2 explicitly labels novel-view synthesis, so a same-setting performance change is not established. Substantial new results include DeSiRe-GS, OmniRe, sensitivity tests and trajectory FID, such as 83.48 versus 45.11 at the 0.5-meter offset in v2 Table 5.

M1.justification: v1 states that it uses the baseline losses; v2 introduces neighboring-embedding smoothness and deformation regularization. v2 also adds DeSiRe-GS position/color deformation and OmniRe SMPL pose/shape refinement, and replaces StreetGaussian's additive rotation correction with ordered rotation composition. These are substantive procedural changes beyond the retained motion embeddings and coarse/fine architecture.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, preliminaries, supervised-results discussion and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting or condensation. The method gains finer subsection organization, the experimental narrative is reorganized, and limitations move into the new supplementary structure. These exceed incidental wording changes accompanying added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds tables for DeSiRe-GS, OmniRe, trajectory FID, loss coefficients and embedding sensitivity, plus a new lane-change figure. The StreetGaussian table gains camera-setting blocks. The original ablation figure moves from Figure 5 to Figure 6 and adds pedestrian zooms to retained images; typography, spacing and figure placement also change throughout.

R1.justification: v2 centers DeSiRe-GS and OmniRe in its positioning and presents EMD as filling a specifically self-supervised motion-modeling gap. It removes the directly relevant Bae et al. discussion of embeddings for fast/slow motion while introducing stronger priority claims. Section 2 also changes EmerNeRF's characterization from flow-free in v1 to optical-flow-guided in v2.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation receives localized revisions: v1 Equation 14 sums rotation corrections, while v2 Equation 13 composes them multiplicatively. v2 also supplies explicit SMPL-refinement and neighboring-embedding regularization equations. No theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's broad applicability claim relied on two frameworks evaluated only on Waymo, with little implementation documentation. v2 substantially strengthens that evidence through additional representations, KITTI and off-trajectory evaluation, while examining inference cost and embedding sensitivity. Its training specifications and corrected rotation composition also improve technical inspectability. Omitted holdout intervals and reduced discussion of relevant embedding-based prior work weaken reporting and positioning, but the gains in applicability evidence and reproducibility outweigh these shortcomings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EMD and contain readable text, equations, tables and figures supporting reliable comparison. All supplied pages were inspected: v1 ends with references, while v2 includes supplementary Sections A-E.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments with additional frameworks, KITTI, shifted camera trajectories and embedding dimensions.

before.justification: v1 reports original EMD reconstruction, novel-view synthesis and component-ablation results on Waymo in Tables 1-3 and Figures 3-5.

results.title: EMD: Explicit Motion Modeling for High-Quality Street Gaussian Splatting

C1.justification: The abstract and central contributions retain the same scope: object-dynamics tokens, a detect–segment–track pipeline, and benefits for general video understanding and referring. V2's stronger descriptive language and additional evidence elaborate these existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 develops the earlier general limitations into concrete explanations of context compensating for missed objects and misplaced attention causing errors. It adds a language-alignment explanation for DINOv2's weaker results and discusses the measured 38.5% runtime overhead as a tradeoff. These materially expand mechanism and applicability discussions.

D1.justification: V2 adds egocentric QA construction details, identifies ChatGPT3.5 as the evaluator, and documents runtime. It omits v1's explicit resize-only treatment of object-branch frames and some projector details, including the two-layer LSTM specification. Main hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain unchanged, with Table 8 becoming Table 13.

E1.justification: Section 3.4 and Table 1 add LLaVA-Video instruction data and an explicit egocentric QA dataset constructed from Ego4D and EgoExo4D, covering descriptive through deductive questions. Evaluation benchmarks remain unchanged; TemporalBench was already present in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds LLaVA-OneVision. New Table 8 compares against models replacing the object branch with VideoMAE or UMT-L, introducing a substantive alternative representation comparison. Tables 6–7 also evaluate additional alternatives including Mask2Former, SAM2, and DINOv2-L.

E3.justification: Table 1 increases video instruction samples from 1.4M to 2.7M plus 1M egocentric samples, retaining one training epoch. New experiments introduce pipeline controls, token limits, and a 50-sample timing protocol. V2's blanket 765K Video-LLaVA ablation description differs from v1's specific 100K VideoChat2 subset disclosure for the pretraining ablation; unchanged scores do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: V2 adds systematic pipeline-component tests, DINOv2 and video-encoder comparisons, an object-only ablation, object-token-limit sensitivity, failure cases, and computational-cost analysis. These substantially expand investigation of design choices and practical limitations. The original attention case study and data-scaling analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without seed counts, repeated-training-run information, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The new average runtime over 50 samples adds a measurement protocol, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces headline results under expanded training: VideoOrion's MVBench accuracy changes from 58.3 to 63.5 and Perception-Test from 53.4 to 65.2. VideoOrion+ TemporalBench results change from 20.7/60.4 to 20.3/61.8. Numerous new ablation and failure results are added, including runtime increasing from 8.27 to 11.46 seconds with the pipeline. Referring results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed two-branch architecture, RAM++ key-frame selection, GroundingDINO–SAM–XMem pipeline, object pooling/MLPs, prompts, and three-stage cross-entropy training remain. Newly tested component alternatives are ablation configurations; the default method is retained.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work, methodology, and experimental narrative. It consolidates projector and temporal-understanding analyses into the ablation section, moves TemporalBench from the appendix, and reorganizes the appendices. The author list also changes.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 6, 8, and 10–12 and failure Figures 6–7, expands the projector table, and restructures the training-data table. Existing figures and tables are resized or relocated, with revised captions and substantially reorganized appendix layouts. The retained scaling figure changes from Figure 6 to Figure 8.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion broadens object-segmentation coverage to vision foundation models and tracking, adding works such as SAM2, TrackFormer, and ByteTrack, alongside new dataset and comparator citations. The central positioning relative to Chat-UniVi, Slot-VLM, and Artemis remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The tensor, mask-list, object-token, and key-frame selection definitions in Sections 3.2–3.3 are retained. Neither version supplies substantive theorems or proofs; expanded conceptual explanations do not introduce new formal reasoning.

improvement.justification: V1's pipeline choices and practical failure/cost limitations were weakly evaluated. V2 adds direct component and video-encoder comparisons, complementary-branch tests, failure analysis, and measured overhead, substantially strengthening validation and transparency. Expanded training prevents attributing the new headline scores solely to the method, and some ablation details become less clear, but the added evidence about the central design and its limitations provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VideoOrion and provide readable methods, equations, results, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results and ablations, including additional component comparisons, failure analyses, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original video question-answering, referring, ablation, TemporalBench, and data-scaling results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: VideoOrion: Tokenizing Object Dynamics in Videos

C1.justification: The principal GTJM and DSD contribution claims persist. The dataset contribution is strengthened from a comprehensive dynamic-scene dataset to the claimed first event-inclusive 4D benchmark containing synthetic and real-world scenes, with state-of-the-art performance emphasized in the abstract and introduction.

C2.justification: V2 removes v1's explicit synthetic-only evaluation limitation and proposed future real-world collection, consistent with its added captured-data experiments. It also attributes the blurry-scene advantage to event-based deblurring. The central geometric-consistency and deformation-capacity explanations remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds substantial capture documentation: beam splitter, Prophesee Gen4, Basler ace, STM32 synchronization, rotating turntable, and frame-selection details. Conversely, it removes v1's implementation paragraph specifying PyTorch, random-point initialization, and the 7k threshold/47k joint-optimization budgets; the 3k static warm-up remains elsewhere. Both versions still promise future code and dataset release.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates eight synthetic scenes only. V2 retains these and adds four captured scenes—Excavator, Jeep, Flowers, and Eagle—plus dynamic blurry-scene evaluation. This substantially expands coverage to real sensor data and blurred inputs.

E2.justification: The original synthetic comparator set remains unchanged, and the real-world comparison reuses 4D-GS, Deformable-3DGS, and Event-4DGS. V2 additionally evaluates a blur-adapted Deformable-3DGS comparator in Figure 9; Section 4.2 describes extending comparison methods with blur loss and EDI. DE-NeRF remains unevaluated.

E3.justification: V2 introduces real-video evaluation using downsampled training frames and intermediate test frames, alongside the blurry-scene comparison procedure. The existing synthetic training count and PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FPS metrics persist. Newly specifying uniform synthetic sampling and intermediate test-frame selection documents the protocol without establishing a changed split or rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a motion-blur case study testing the adapted method (Figure 9). The GTJM, DSD, and buffer ablations and existing sensitivity analyses remain, although ablation reporting is condensed to averages. Real-world ablations are referenced but their results are absent from the supplied PDF.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's aggregate ablation scores summarize scenes rather than introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 2 retain their numerical results, including all 224 synthetic comparison values. V2 adds quantitative results for four real-world scenes and a blurry-scene result of 28.98 dB versus Deformable-3DGS's 24.19 dB (Figure 9). These are new evaluations, not same-setting gains over v1. Per-scene ablation entries are replaced by aggregate scores.

M1.justification: The core threshold optimization, event supervision, and dynamic-static decomposition procedures remain unchanged. V2 adds an adaptation using blur loss and EDI for dynamic blurry scenes (Section 4.2), although its detailed implementation is deferred to unavailable supplementary material.

P1.justification: V2 drops 'Fast' from the title, revises the abstract and experimental narrative, replaces 'intensity' with 'brightness,' and clarifies threshold notation. Comparisons gain quantitative, qualitative, and blurry-scene subheadings, but the overall section sequence and most method prose remain.

P2.justification: The experimental presentation is substantially reorganized through a new real-world results table and acquisition, real-world rendering, and blur figures. The synthetic comparison loses its Musicbox row, and the wide per-scene ablation table becomes a compact aggregate table. Existing diagnostic figures are largely retained but relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 expands benchmark novelty positioning and revises its discussion of prior datasets. It removes the dedicated Robust e-NeRF discussion while retaining that citation, and removes Structure-from-Motion Revisited with the initialization paragraph. Most other reference differences are renumbering or metadata updates.

T1.justification: Equations 1–14 retain the same mathematical substance. Distinguishing estimated thresholds with a hat and expanding the event-count summation indices clarify notation rather than introduce new derivations or assumptions. Neither version contains formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly identifies synthetic-only validation as a limitation. V2 substantially addresses it with a documented capture setup and quantitative and qualitative comparisons on four real-world scenes (Table 3; Figures 6 and 8), strengthening evidence for practical applicability. The blur example provides additional support. Removed training details and reduced ablation granularity weaken reproducibility and diagnosis, but the real-sensor validation resolves an important deficiency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GTJM/DSD framework and are readable throughout, including equations, figures, and tables. Both end with references and contain no appendices. Separately referenced supplementary material is not included, so its contents cannot be compared.

after.justification: V2 retains original synthetic experiments and additionally reports real-world reconstruction results and a dynamic blurry-scene comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-scene reconstruction results, baseline comparisons, ablations, and sensitivity analyses in Tables 1–3 and associated figures.

results.title: Event-boosted Deformable 3D Gaussians for Dynamic Scene Reconstruction

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: using 3D information for 2D unsupervised instance segmentation through LocalCut, Spatial Importance Sharpening, and Spatial Confidence, with improved benchmark performance. Updated margins and additional experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: Section 5 adds interpretations concerning robustness to imperfect depth and CutLER's plateau under matched training. The appendix explains the confidence-source comparison, identifies initial semantic-cut failures, and qualifies pseudo-mask evaluation through ImageNet's limited box annotations. The main limitations concerning indistinct boundaries, small objects, and unavailable depth remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Unlike v1's references to unavailable supplementary settings, v3 supplies extraction thresholds, batch sizes, learning rates, optimization, initialization, augmentation, and training budgets in Appendix E and Tables 15–17. It also adds a project-page link, a configuration-file availability statement, and computational-overhead figures. These are substantial disclosures, although the one-versus-three-round inconsistency limits reproducibility.

E1.justification: OpenImages object-detection evaluation is removed from Section 4 and Table 2. ImageNet training and the remaining COCO, COCO20K, LVIS, VOC, Objects365, and KITTI coverage remain. The added ImageNet validation experiment evaluates an existing domain rather than introducing another domain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds UnSAM and removes LOST and MaskDistill, while retaining the principal competing methods. v3 also includes CutLER in the training-round comparison (Table 5) and MaskCut in the direct pseudo-mask comparison (Table 14), extending comparator participation beyond the corresponding v1 analyses.

E3.justification: The main evaluation changes from one to three self-training rounds, with explicit comparisons across matched backbones and rounds in Table 5. v3 adds ImageNet validation bounding-box evaluation and size-specific AP and recall reporting. However, Appendix E.3 and Table 17 still specify one self-training round, conflicting with the main protocol.

E4.justification: v3 adds SIS-only and CRF-versus-depth confidence controls, a lower-quality MiDaS depth test, extended Kick Back & Relax training, direct pseudo-mask evaluation, and qualitative failure analyses. Conversely, Table 4 drops the DINO component-ablation results. The confidence-floor and mask-alignment tests are moved from v1 Table 5 to v3 Table 10, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports independent repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Additional self-training rounds are sequential training stages; Spatial Confidence measures pseudo-mask confidence rather than uncertainty in experimental estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the DiffNCuts model's COCO val2017/COCO20K mask AP of 10.2/10.3 with 10.7/10.9 under increased self-training, so these are not same-setting gains. In-domain LVIS mask AP changes from 5.6 to 4.5 in Table 3. Numerous roundwise, depth, confidence, pseudo-mask, and detailed AP/recall results are also added.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 revises the stated LocalCut procedure: v1 retains only points inside the semantic cut, whereas v3 assigns background z-coordinates to points outside it. This is a localized procedural revision; the three principal components, detector architecture, and loss remain.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the abstract, introduction, method, and conclusion remain intact. Changes include localized rewriting and condensation, reorganized ablation discussion, a structured supplement, updated affiliations, and acknowledgements; there is no wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adds a first-page qualitative/bar-chart overview, redraws the Spatial Confidence diagram, restructures comparison tables with difference rows and revised columns, and adds extensive appendix tables and visualizations. Existing confidence ablations are relocated, and Equation 2's rendering is repaired. These substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds SAM and UnSAM references and distinguishes UnSAM's multi-granularity discovery objective from precise instance segmentation. It removes the dedicated LOST description and OpenImages reference. The broader positioning around CutLER, self-supervised features, and 3D information remains.

T1.justification: The NCut/min-cut formulation, confidence definitions, and loss mathematics remain substantively unchanged, with no new proofs or derivations. v3 repairs the malformed typesetting of Equation 2's already-described normalization to [beta, 1]; this does not introduce a different normalization principle.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens experimental support and technical documentation. Matched backbone/training-round comparisons, confidence-source controls, depth-quality tests, and direct pseudo-mask evaluation better test the proposed mechanisms, while the appendix supplies settings absent from the supplied v1. These gains outweigh the reduced OpenImages coverage and documentation inconsistencies, although the conflicting self-training schedules and occasional table discrepancies still require correction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CutS3D, with matching authors, core components, and experiments. All pages are readable. v3 includes supplementary Sections A–E; the supplied v1 ends after its references despite mentioning supplementary material. Comparisons concern what is present in these PDFs.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results and ablations, including additional training-round comparisons, depth experiments, and ImageNet pseudo-mask evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original instance-segmentation and object-detection results, in-domain self-training experiments, and component ablations in Tables 1–8.

results.title: CutS3D: Cutting Semantics in 3D for 2D Unsupervised Instance Segmentation

C1.justification: The central claims about quadric primitives, geodesic Gaussian weights, and detailed reconstruction remain. v2 adds explicit claims about density consistency during deformation and fewer primitives/potential memory savings, quantifies DTU error reductions as 33% versus 2DGS and 27% versus GOF, and drops stricter sorting from the three highlighted contributions.

C2.justification: v2 develops a substantive explanation of geodesic weights preserving density under deformation and attributes low-texture artifacts to missing multi-view regularization. It presents tighter bounds as addressing the earlier speed problem. However, it removes the fog/transparency limitation and several reconstruction tradeoffs, and replaces v1's acknowledged Neuralangelo gap with overbroad superiority language despite the no-MV variant's 0.71 versus Neuralangelo's 0.61 in Table 1.

D1.justification: v2 documents the tighter bounding construction and mentions GPU memory-access optimization. It removes v1's explicit 60,000-iteration Courthouse/aerial training schedule, densification and opacity-reset settings, baseline gradient threshold, and depth-distortion stop-gradient detail. These are documentation losses; they do not establish that those underlying procedures changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds a weakly textured, geometry-rich Google Scanned Objects subset for geometry-versus-point-count evaluation and primitive visualization (Figures 1 and 11). DTU, Tanks and Temples, Mip-NeRF 360, and the supplementary aerial urban scene were already covered in v1.

E2.justification: DTU Table 1 adds 3DGS, Gaussian surfels, GSDF, GS-pull, and PGSR as evaluated comparators. PGSR also enters the TNT and Mip-NeRF 360 comparisons, while NeuS is removed from TNT Table 2. The qualitative DTU comparisons are expanded to include PGSR and, in the supplement, GOF.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes reported mesh extraction from equally weighted median/expected depth to median depth alone, and the TSDF truncation threshold from 0.002 to 0.02. v2 also introduces gradient-threshold sweeps, fixed-scale and Euclidean-distance controls, and FPS/storage evaluation. These alter evaluation conditions; the PDFs do not establish same-setting comparability for all revised scores.

E4.justification: v1's two-scene curvature study and four-scan sorting study are replaced by six-scene TNT component ablations, including multi-view regularization (v2 Table 4). New controls test fixed disk-like primitives and Euclidean distance (Table 5), while Figure 1 and supplementary Table 6 examine point-count efficiency and tighter bounds. The separate per-tile sorting comparison from v1 is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Gaussian distribution parameters in the method are not uncertainty estimates for experimental results.

E6.justification: DTU mean Chamfer distance changes from v1's 0.73 mm to v2's 0.71 without multi-view regularization and 0.54 with it; TNT mean F1 changes from 0.44 to 0.45 and 0.50, respectively. These are revised results under changed method/settings. Table 3 also revises rendering scores, including 3DGS indoor PSNR from 30.99 to 30.52. New ablation, GSO, and efficiency results substantially expand the evidence.

M1.justification: v2 incorporates PGSR-style multi-view reprojection and photometric regularization into the training objective (Section 3.3); v1 left multi-view constraints for future work. The supplement also introduces a tighter tangent-plane bounding procedure, evaluated as QGS w/ TB, beyond v1's rectangular bounding construction.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, and related-work prose are extensively rewritten. The preliminary exposition is shortened, optimization and ablation narratives are reorganized, and the closing Discussion/Limitation paragraphs are replaced by acknowledgements. This exceeds localized editing or the insertion of new results.

P2.justification: The Courthouse teaser is replaced by a GSO comparison and point-count plot. v2 adds density-deformation illustrations, restructures benchmark and ablation tables, redraws the bounding-box diagram, and adds an efficiency table. Main and supplementary qualitative comparisons are redesigned with additional comparator columns. The aerial comparison is retained and renumbered, not newly added.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around primitive density, shape kernels, and textured primitives, citing work such as GES, Deformable Radial Kernel Splatting, GSTex, and BBSplat. QGS is presented as a geometry-focused framework complementary to these developments. v1's closing orthogonality discussion and some references, including Trim-GS and classic surface-splatting works, are removed.

T1.justification: The supplement adds a mathematical construction for tangent-plane bounds and the truncated pyramid, including v2 Equation 22. It also removes an erroneous intermediate integration-by-parts step containing d cos(x). The principal arc-length, curvature, and rendering-gradient derivations otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification for QGS: Table 5 directly tests the defining quadric and geodesic choices that v1 did not isolate, PGSR comparisons distinguish results with and without multi-view regularization, and supplementary Table 6 evaluates the proposed acceleration. These address important evidential gaps. The gains outweigh material weaknesses: lost large-scene training details and limitations, plus superiority wording that overstates the no-MV results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Quadratic Gaussian Splatting (QGS). Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and five-page supplements are readable and support comparison despite the changed title and substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, expanded component ablations, Google Scanned Objects experiments, and speed/storage measurements, alongside supplementary qualitative results.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction and rendering results on DTU, Tanks and Temples, and Mip-NeRF 360, component ablations, and supplementary aerial-scene results.

results.title: Quadratic Gaussian Splatting: High Quality Surface Reconstruction with Second-order Geometric Primitives

C1.justification: The central claim that preserving important tokens improves generation quality at comparable computational cost remains. v2 broadens the contribution framing from CFG-based selection to a framework accepting different importance signals and explicitly extends its performance claims across U-Net and transformer architectures.

C2.justification: v2 adds a gradient-based saliency interpretation of CFG and revises the step-distilled-model limitation by explaining and demonstrating an attention-map workaround. It acknowledges the alternative’s possible memory cost and suggests weighted importance signals for multi-guidance scenarios. The existing warning about temporal merging reducing video dynamics remains.

D1.justification: v2 supplies implementation information for the extensions, including PixArt-α layer placement, sampling settings and spatial matching, final-block attention-map averaging, and the LCM Dreamshaper v7 configuration. It also supplies new qualitative prompts. Most original sampling, pruning, hardware, and metric-library details remain, with several moved into Appendix B.

E1.justification: Both versions cover text-to-image, image-conditioned multi-view, and text-to-video generation, retaining MS-COCO, GSO, and VBench evaluations. PixArt-α, consistency models, and acceleration combinations expand model configurations without establishing new datasets, task requirements, or input environments.

E2.justification: v2 adds ToFu to the Stable Diffusion quantitative and qualitative comparisons (Table 1 and Figures 5 and 9). It also adds unmerged Zero123++ outputs to the supplementary multi-view comparison (Figure 11). ToMeSD and the qualitative ATC comparison remain.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluation configurations: PixArt-α uses 20 sampling steps, CFG 4.5, and merging in self- and cross-attention layers 7–20; Appendix A adds a four-step consistency model, controlled top/bottom-30% pruning, and acceleration combinations. The design ablation also replaces r=0.6 with r=0.7. Original Stable Diffusion, Zero123++, and AnimateDiff settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of cross-attention importance, whether high-CFG tokens matter more than low-CFG tokens, compatibility with DeepCache/Faster Diffusion/FRDiff, and sensitivity to pruning duration across three tasks (Tables 8, 10, 12, and 15). The original early-pruning and sampling-step analyses remain as Tables 14 and 13.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The additional v2 tables retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive quantitative and qualitative results for ToFu, PixArt-α, cross-attention, consistency models, and supplementary analyses. For example, its new PixArt-α comparison reports FID 34.02 versus ToMeSD’s 65.46 at r=0.5. Within retained multi-view settings, the proposed method’s r=0.6 PSNR changes from 14.83 to 14.85 and LPIPS from 0.269 to 0.263 (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 3). The changed design-ablation rows use different merging ratios, rather than demonstrate same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The core important-token pool, destination sampling, and partitioning procedure remain. v2 adds an implemented cross-attention-based importance variant and uses pixel-location distance instead of feature similarity for PixArt-α matching (Section 4.3 and Appendix B). The original early-pruning procedure is retained in Appendix B.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statements, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around general importance-based merging. The standalone preliminaries section is removed and its relevant explanations integrated elsewhere. Early-pruning discussion and several implementation settings move to the appendix, substantially revising the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the examples in Figures 1 and 4, transposes and expands Figure 5 to include ToFu, and adds PixArt-α visual comparisons. Table 1 gains comparator columns, several new experimental tables appear, and supplementary image grids expand to include additional method variants and unmerged Zero123++ outputs.

R1.justification: v2 adds five cited works, including InstructPix2Pix, Faster Diffusion, ToMA, and LCM-LoRA, while retaining the earlier references. ToFu was already cited in v1 but receives an explicit methodological contrast in v2. Architectural background expands without substantially reorganizing the related-work positioning.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 2 adds the approximate relationship between CFG magnitude and the conditional log-likelihood gradient. It also corrects the ablation discussion’s pool-size expression from (1+r)(1+p) to (1−r)(1+p), matching the formula already used in v1’s method. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1’s broad applicability claim rested on related U-Net-based models and left step-distilled models as a limitation. v2 materially strengthens that evidence through PixArt-α and attention-based consistency-model experiments, a relevant ToFu comparison, and a direct test of CFG token importance (Tables 2, 11, 1, and 10). These additions address important generalization and mechanism-validation gaps. Cross-attention has a stated memory tradeoff and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the overall evidential basis is substantially stronger.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same importance-based token-merging work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, references, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison despite the changed title and organization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds PixArt-α, consistency-model, cross-attention, token-importance, and acceleration-combination experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative and qualitative experiments on text-to-image, multi-view, and video generation, including method ablations and supplementary pruning and sampling-step studies.

results.title: Importance-Based Token Merging for Efficient Image and Video Generation

C1.justification: The three central contributions—a data engine, comprehensive benchmark and grounding/referring model—remain intact. The revised introduction additionally claims that contemporary leading MLLMs struggle with basic document localization and recognition, emphasizing the benchmark's ability to expose these deficiencies.

C2.justification: v2 removes v1's explanations of missed grounding boxes in dense PDFs and vulnerability to changed inference resolution. It adds interpretations of competitors' coordinate-understanding weaknesses and attributes DOGR's remaining Ga F1 limitation to reasoning in Appendix F.3. New ablations receive explanations based on generator instruction-following and annotation precision, while Appendix C's existing failure cases remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds model-specific evaluation prompts, coordinate conversions, output-format rules, ablation construction details and manual hallucination-filtering information. It reports released code, data and model with a repository link instead of promising future release. Conversely, the explicit 20/16 inference-tile settings disappear; the main-text parsing-data count is corrected from 1.4M to 2.1M, already documented in v1's Figure 2 and appendix.

E1.justification: Benchmark evaluation coverage contracts: v2 Figure 4 and Table 2 omit posters from the three combined grounding-and-referring tasks evaluated in v1 Table 2. Poster training data remain, and the other document domains, DocLocal4K, Local15k and ten general benchmarks are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds eleven competing models to DOGR-Bench, where v1 reported only DOGE, and seven MLLM comparators to DocLocal4K. These include GPT-4o, Gemini, Qwen-VL and InternVL variants. Table 3 additionally introduces Qwen2-VL-7B while removing eight older comparators, including Donut, UReader, TokenPacker and QwenVL.

E3.justification: The benchmark changes from 4,144 samples in v1 Table 1 to 3,600 with revised category proportions in v2 Section 4. New comparisons evaluate F1all at IoU 0.1, retain a DOGR row at 0.5 and examine thresholds in Figure 14. New ablations introduce instruction-data controls, 25k-sample generator comparisons and bounding-box perturbations within 30%; the previous tile-count experiment is removed.

E4.justification: v2 adds instruction-tuning data ablation, GPT-4o versus Gemini-generated training-data comparison, accurate versus perturbed bounding-box analysis, IoU sensitivity and baseline grounding failure cases. It removes v1's training/inference tile-count sensitivity study. The parsing-data ablations and existing qualitative examples remain.

E5.justification: New Figure 16 explicitly displays three attempts at the same InternVL2.5-72B grounding query, providing limited repeated-inference evidence of output variability. Neither version provides benchmark-level repeated-run summaries, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces the original benchmark scores with revised results and extensive comparator entries; overall referring accuracy changes from 50.9 to 60.3 under the changed benchmark composition, so this is not an established same-setting gain. New ablation and sensitivity results are added, while tile-count results disappear. The proposed model's ten general-benchmark scores, retained DocLocal4K entries and Local15k Table 8 results are unchanged.

M1.justification: The re-rendering, annotation merging and post-annotation procedures remain unchanged, as do the InternViT/Qwen2 architecture, three-stage training and coordinate representation. Renaming DOGE to DOGR and adding filtering explanations do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and several data-engine passages receive substantial rewriting. Section 6.2 is reorganized around basic capability verification, comparative evaluation and detailed model performance. The revision also renames DOGE throughout, changes author information, adds acknowledgements and inserts a new evaluation appendix before the existing supplementary experiments.

P2.justification: Benchmark statistics move from v1 Table 1 into a redesigned Figure 4. DocLocal4K results are redistributed across v2 Tables 1 and 4, Table 2 expands into a model comparison, Table 3 contracts and Table 5 is replaced. Figures 14–16 and Tables 9–10 are added. Most existing pipeline and qualitative illustrations remain, with a corrected explanatory label in Figure 12.

R1.justification: References are updated with newer Qwen, InternVL and Gemini reports, alongside additions such as PyMuPDF and removals of older background and baseline works. The central positioning relative to DocOwl-1.5, Kosmos-2.5 and Fox remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version presents theoretical propositions or proofs, and the seven-task taxonomy and underlying mathematical descriptions remain unchanged. The added IoU-threshold comparisons concern empirical evaluation settings rather than new theoretical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a central weakness of v1: the proposed benchmark originally lacked competing-model results. Broad comparisons, documented evaluation prompts and controlled data-quality ablations substantially strengthen evidence for the benchmark and data engine. Removing the tile-sensitivity study and inference settings, leaving the benchmark revision underexplained and overstating the reasoning-only bottleneck weaken transparency. Nevertheless, the central empirical case is substantially better supported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same data engine, benchmark and model, renamed from DOGE to DOGR. Their complete main texts, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds baseline comparisons, instruction-tuning and annotation-quality ablations, IoU sensitivity results and baseline failure examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on DOGE-Bench, ten general document benchmarks, DocLocal4K and DOGE-Local15k, together with ablations and qualitative examples.

results.title: DOGR: Towards Versatile Visual Document Grounding and Referring

C1.justification: The headline claims of state-of-the-art single-step decomposition, millisecond inference, and approximately three-second 3D processing remain. The 3D contribution is refined to explicitly incorporate SuperMatMV and joint cross-view prediction, without changing the paper's overall objectives.

C2.justification: New Section 10 explains limitations involving detail sharpness, inability to obtain alternative predictions by rerunning the deterministic model, and difficulty with transparent, multilayered, or highly reflective materials. v4 also interprets training-data diversity as improving generalization and assigns cross-view consistency more directly to SuperMatMV, emphasizing missing-region completion for UV refinement.

D1.justification: v4 adds a project-page link, the expert branches' parameter overhead, RM-channel conventions, and SuperMatMV initialization and training details, including three epochs with batches of eight six-view inputs. It removes v1's exact VGG feature-layer selection. These are targeted additions and losses of reproducibility information alongside the protocol revisions.

E1.justification: v4 adds Digital Twin Catalog to training and image-space evaluation, retaining Objaverse and BlenderVault. It also introduces StanfordORB and a distinct evaluation of complete 3D objects under novel viewpoints and lighting. Conversely, v1's standalone captured-photograph demonstrations in Figure 14 are removed.

E2.justification: v4 adds StableMaterialMV to Table 1 and the corresponding per-dataset comparisons. All six original baselines remain, so comparator membership expands by one relevant multi-view variant.

E3.justification: Reported SuperMat training changes from 100k to 75k objects, three to sixteen rendered lighting conditions, 115 to 30 epochs, batch size 16 to 32, and learning rate 1e-5 to 2e-5. The re-render lighting pool changes from 716 to 50 maps. v4 also explicitly retrains IIR and RGB→X on its data and introduces a 3D evaluation using 28 objects, 60 novel viewpoints, and three environment maps.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained end-to-end, re-render-loss, and loss-function ablations, v4 adds synthetic-only, real-captured-only, and mixed-data training comparisons in Table 3. Table 4 adds numerical evaluation before and after UV refinement, substantially strengthening v1's qualitative analysis of that component.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and averages without independent-run variability, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional experiments retain this reporting practice.

E6.justification: Main and per-dataset results are extensively revised, with new SuperMatMV and DTC entries. New Table 5 reports pipeline relighting PSNRs of 27.00 on BlenderVault and 24.99 on StanfordORB. Table 2 also changes the loss ranking: perceptual loss leads every metric in v1, whereas L1 leads albedo and metallic SSIM in v4. Changed training and evaluation conditions prevent interpreting revised scores as direct same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: v1 processes views independently with SuperMat before UV blending and refinement. v4 introduces SuperMatMV, using 3D self-attention and camera-extrinsic conditioning to jointly decompose six views, and incorporates it into the 3D pipeline. This substantially changes cross-view processing; the original single-view architecture and losses remain.

P1.justification: The main narrative order and much of the prose remain. v4 rewrites portions of the introduction and related work, moves the PBR subsection into the supplement and training-data description into the main experiments, reorganizes supplementary discussions, and updates terminology and affiliations.

P2.justification: Qualitative comparison grids are extensively rebuilt with paired viewpoints and additional multi-view columns. v4 adds novel-view relighting and DTC figures, removes the captured-photograph gallery, adds three experimental tables, and expands the detailed tables with DTC columns. Figure 2 is relocated, while several existing pipeline and result illustrations are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning across material generation, inverse rendering, image decomposition, and UV-space generation. New citations include rendering-aware material estimation, MVDream for multi-view conditioning, and Clay for expert branches, alongside broader generation literature. This changes attribution and contextualization beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The rendering equation, perceptual and re-render losses, and UV-blending mathematics are retained. The PBR formulation moves from v1 Section 3.1 to v4 supplementary Section 6, with equation renumbering but no substantive mathematical revision or new proof.

improvement.justification: v1's central 3D-pipeline claim was supported mainly by qualitative examples. v4 adds quantitative ground-truth novel-view relighting comparisons and UV-refinement validation, addressing an important evidential gap. Training-data ablations, explicit baseline retraining, and substantive limitations further improve rigor. These gains outweigh the loss of the captured-photo gallery and exact VGG-layer specification. The improvement rests on stronger validation and clearer boundaries, not on directly comparing aggregate scores obtained under changed settings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SuperMat and contain readable main texts, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material. Corresponding components and relocated material can be matched reliably despite substantial experimental and methodological additions.

after.justification: v4 reports original SuperMat and SuperMatMV results, training-data ablations, quantitative UV-refinement evaluation, and novel-view relighting experiments in the main text and supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original material-decomposition and relighting results in Table 1, loss-function experiments in supplementary Table 2, and qualitative 3D reconstruction and ablation results.

results.title: SuperMat: Physically Consistent PBR Material Estimation at Interactive Rates

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add central contributions concerning fine-grained occlusion handling through OccNet and OccCFG, complementary depth/normal conditioning, and dual-pathway body representation. V1's broader full-body personalization and user-defined shape-control claims remain, but the claimed technical contribution substantially expands.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies the effectiveness of depth conditioning for fine-grained occlusions and explains complementary depth/normal information, oversaturation from uniformly strong guidance, and SMPLx's difficulty representing muscle versus fat distribution. These substantive mechanism explanations and applicability qualifications extend v1's discussion, while dependence on face networks and fitting accuracy remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: V2 specifies Canny thresholds of 5/15, regional guidance scales of 3/5, conditioning weights of 0.8, and implementation details for CLIP-based body descriptions and regional prompting. Existing backbone, optimizer, hardware, and embedding details largely remain. V1's project-page access pointer is omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions use MPII-derived training data and COCO-WholeBody evaluation covering one to five people, alongside custom scenes, body-shape control, and stylization. Pose-guided generation was already tested in v1 Figure 9(a); v2 substantially expands its evaluation within the existing human-generation coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds pose-generation comparisons with T2IAdapter-SDXL, ControlNet-Flux, and HumanSD-SD2, and evaluates training-data-matched OMG variants and ControlNet-SDXL in Tables S8-S9. The personalization baseline families remain, but Textual Inversion and IPA-Face+OMG disappear from corresponding handshake and birthday qualitative panels (v1 Figure 4; v2 Figure 6).

E3.justification: Denoising steps change from 50 to 30, and the reported single-person:multi-person training ratio reverses from 1:2 to 2:1; the PDFs do not establish whether the latter reflects resampling or correction. V2 adds MPJPE, AP-0.5, IS/KID, and matched-training controls. The personalization study changes from 7 cases/123 participants to 15/103, and a pose study uses 15 cases/114 participants.

E4.justification: V2 adds depth/normal/RGB comparisons, OccNet and OccCFG ablations, spatial-guidance comparisons, conflicting body-composition examples, and a fitting-failure case (Table 5; Figures 9-11 and S22-S23). Body-parameter and conditioning-scale studies remain, while v1's explicit face-masking ablation in Figure 9(b) is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both present point estimates and preference percentages. Changed user-study sample sizes concern evaluation design, without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces overall face/body/CLIP scores of 0.305/0.531/0.252 with 0.317/0.560/0.273 under the revised method and settings, so these are not established same-setting gains. V2 adds pose, image-quality, component-ablation, and fine-tuned-baseline results; updates personalization preferences; and removes v1's cumulative Top-3 preference table.

M1.justification: V1 combines depth-only SCNet with masked face-identity conditioning. V2 adds depth-and-normal SCNets, an occlusion-boundary network trained on masked depth edges, occlusion-dependent residual fusion, and spatially varying classifier-free guidance. It also introduces optional CLIP-derived body descriptions with regional prompting (Sections 3.1-3.3 and B.1).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized into personalization and pose-controlled generation sections. Stylization, efficiency, and body-parameter analysis move into the supplement, and the bibliography now precedes a separately headed supplementary section.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the pipeline and training diagrams, restructures qualitative comparisons into horizontal grids with enlarged detail views, and adds component-analysis and failure-case figures. Table 1 changes from individual identity-count columns to Single/Multi/Total groups and adds pose/image-quality columns. Numerous figures and tables are added, resized, or relocated.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around controllable human generation and spatial guidance, discussing HumanSD, Stable-Pose, HumanLDM, MIMO, StoryMaker, and ID-Patch. It additionally connects its new mechanisms to guidance-related prior work and MultiDiffusion, extending v1's emphasis on personalization and depth-based pose control.

T1.justification: V2 adds mathematical definitions for ray-intersection-based occlusion masks and spatial guidance, and revises residual fusion (Equations 2-5). V1's explicit SMPLx vertex-shaping equation is omitted. These are limited changes to algorithmic formalization; neither version develops theorem/proof-based analysis, and the appendix identity and CLIP metric formulas remain equivalent.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of pose and occlusion claims that v1 supported mainly qualitatively: direct pose metrics, component ablations, and matched-training comparisons in Tables 5 and S8-S9 make the advantages more assessable. Failure analysis also improves transparency. Reporting defects temper these gains: the lowest-KID claim contradicts Table 3 (HumanSD 0.082 versus PersonaCraft 0.091), and Table S6's body-shape total conflicts with Table 1. These defects do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PersonaCraft by the same authors. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original personalization and pose-generation experiments, component ablations, comparisons with fine-tuned baselines, and two user studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-generation experiments, quantitative comparisons, ablations, inference timings, and a user study in the main text and appendix.

results.title:
PersonaCraft: Personalized and Controllable Full-Body Multi-Human Scene
  Generation Using Occlusion-Aware 3D-Conditioned Diffusion

C1.justification: V1 centers its contributions on ObjectRelator for Ego2Exo/Exo2Ego, efficiency and flexibility. V2 explicitly adds construction of HANDAL-X as a contribution and broadens its abstract and introduction's state-of-the-art claim to two benchmarks. The original two-module method claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning cross-dataset transfer, HANDAL-X's easier conditions and robotics relevance, generated-text accuracy, and the practicality of reducing query annotations. It also explains why visibility accuracy is relatively easy. Existing mechanism explanations, failure categories and the limitation of frame-level modeling largely remain.

D1.justification: V2 documents HANDAL-X construction, its 44,202 training and 14,074 test samples, and associated training settings and time. It replaces a promised release with a code-availability statement and project link. Most existing implementation details are retained or relocated, although the expanded learning-rate choices lack an experiment-specific mapping.

E1.justification: V2 adds HANDAL-X, covering cross-view images of manipulable objects intended for robotics applications, alongside the retained Ego-Exo4D domains. It also evaluates first-frame-only queries and includes target-invisible cases when evaluating visibility accuracy, substantially expanding the tested conditions.

E2.justification: The Ego-Exo4D competitors remain XSegTx, XView-XMem, their combination, SEEM and PSALM; Xmem+XSegTx is an abbreviation. HANDAL-X reuses existing image-based comparators. The relocated fusion ablation omits a repeated PSALM row but retains the base-model comparison in its discussion.

E3.justification: V2 adds LE, CA and VA metrics, evaluating VA on all cases rather than only mutually visible objects. New protocols include HANDAL-X pairing at 100-frame intervals, a description audit sampling 50 frames per scenario, and first-frame inference. The stated learning rate changes from 6e-5 to a choice of 6e-5 or 2e-4, without establishing which existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds quantitative description-error assessment and a generated-versus-ground-truth text comparison on human-accepted descriptions (Supplementary Table B). It also tests dependence on frame-level queries through first-frame inference (Table F). Existing fusion, alignment, loss-weight, joint-training and single-condition analyses are retained, including material moved to the supplement.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests. The new description-error rates are experimental point estimates, not an added uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises ObjectRelator's Full-set Ego2Exo IoU from 43.9 to 45.4 and adds LE/CA/VA results. New HANDAL-X results include ObjectRelator versus PSALM at 84.7 versus 83.4 after retraining and 42.8 versus 39.9 when transferring from Ego-Exo4D. Supplementary Tables B and F add description-error rates and first-frame IoUs of 37.0/43.7. The revised learning-rate specification prevents treating the updated Full-set score as a confirmed identical-setting gain.

M1.justification: The core PSALM-based architecture, MCFuse, XObjAlign and two-stage training remain unchanged. Supplementary Section 2.3 adds an inference adaptation: after the first query frame, predictions from previous target-view frames supply subsequent queries. This introduces a limited memory-based procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, five contribution items become three, and baseline and method explanations are revised with new notation. Detailed fusion ablations move into reorganized supplementary sections. The title, author information and acknowledgments also change.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn and annotated, Table 2 expands to multiple metrics, and detailed ablations move into the supplement. Existing description-generation and failure-case figures become larger displays. HANDAL-X, text-quality and first-frame tables and a HANDAL-X montage are added; the original extensive Ego2Exo/Exo2Ego montages are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including HANDAL, CAFuser, XTrack and CamSAM2, and broadens the introductory discussion from video understanding to visual perception. Its central positioning relative to PSALM, universal segmentation and cross-view alignment remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The cross-attention fusion, residual weighting and Euclidean alignment loss retain their mathematical substance. V2's additional forward-pass equations formalize operations already described in v1, while notation is revised. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's single benchmark and qualitative reassurance about generated descriptions. HANDAL-X transfer and retraining comparisons, the quantitative text audit, and first-frame testing address important gaps in generalization and practical applicability while preserving the original ablations. HANDAL-X is easier, the text-ambiguity comparison uses only human-accepted descriptions, and the learning-rate revision leaves the updated Full-set score insufficiently explained. These limits temper individual conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ObjectRelator and provide readable methods, experiments, figures, tables and complete supplementary material. Renamed notation and relocated analyses can be matched reliably across versions.

after.justification: V2 retains original Ego-Exo4D experiments and adds HANDAL-X evaluations, generated-description assessments and first-frame-query results.
