before.justification: V1 reports original ObjectRelator and retrained-baseline experiments on Ego-Exo4D, including component ablations, joint training, single-condition testing and qualitative results.

results.title: ObjectRelator: Enabling Cross-View Object Relation Understanding Across Ego-Centric and Exo-Centric Perspectives

C1.justification: v2 removes the advertised contribution of a new Robust-DC evaluation protocol and the introduction's claim to be the first DC model performing well across broadly varied scenes and patterns. The underlying evaluations remain, as do the central method and zero-shot-performance claims.

C2.justification: v2 attributes mixed-data degradation to blurry NYUv2 labels and expands the explanation for retaining L1 to enforce per-pixel accuracy. It adds discussion of radar accuracy versus sharpness and explicitly extends limitations to radar inputs and large holes in object-removal or inpainting applications.

D1.justification: Core implementation, optimizer, training schedule, hardware and repository disclosures are retained. New reproducibility details include the one-sixth NYUv2 mixture and reduced training budget, DrivingStereo's 500-point sampling, and indoor/outdoor checkpoint selection for Depth Prompting.

E1.justification: v2 adds ZJU-4DRadarCam radar inputs, Carla-Night-DC nighttime scenes, and DrivingStereo under sunny, rainy, foggy and cloudy conditions. Appendix B also introduces training ablations mixing NYUv2 with synthetic data. NYUv2 and VOID evaluation already existed in v1 and is retained.

E2.justification: Depth Prompting joins the ETH3D, KITTI, NYUv2 and VOID comparisons. New Appendix A compares SpAgNet, VPP4DC, TTADC and UniDC, identifying different adaptation settings and the use of copied scores. The radar and nighttime experiments add specialized comparators, including RadarCam-Depth and LDCNet.

E3.justification: v1 reserves 251 KITTI validation images for ablations; v2 evaluates on the official validation set and instead samples 1000 training images for ablations. Figure 6 changes from indoor MAE to outdoor RMSE, and VOID reporting changes from MAE/REL to RMSE/MAE. New protocols include radar depth-range cutoffs and 500-point sampling on DrivingStereo.

E4.justification: New Appendix B tests synthetic-only versus synthetic-plus-NYUv2 training and retrains baselines on matching data. Appendix P explicitly removes L1 from the loss. Appendices C–D add unseen-sensor and nighttime/weather robustness analyses. Existing scale-equivariance, resolution-scaling and sparse-pattern analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version adds repeated-run counts, seeds, significance tests or empirical uncertainty estimates. Figure 3 retains the same Gaussian-noise illustration with a 95% confidence interval; experimental tables continue to report point estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for the new studies and comparators. Retained entries also change: Table 4's three-resolution ETH3D REL changes from 0.059 to 0.064. KITTI-8 MAE changes from 0.622 to 0.597 alongside the revised split, preventing interpretation as a matched-setting gain. Synthetic-pattern appendix breakdowns and view-synthesis scores are retained.

M1.justification: The CompletionFormer backbone, three-resolution depth integration, log-depth and median normalization, combined L1/Laplacian/gradient-matching loss, and DySPN refinement remain unchanged. The new experiments test the existing method.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, with an explicit contribution list. The loss discussion moves before scale normalization, the standalone Robust-DC section becomes part of Experiments, evaluation subsections are reordered, and the appendix is substantially reorganized around new studies.

P2.justification: v2 adds five appendix tables and two qualitative figures. Table 3 is reorganized to incorporate NYUv2, Table 1 gains sparse-depth information, and Figure 6 is redrawn with outdoor RMSE and Depth Prompting. Existing appendix displays are relocated and renumbered, with their content largely retained.

R1.justification: Related work is reframed around generalization across depth patterns versus datasets, distinguishing zero-shot evaluation from test-time adaptation and few-shot learning. v2 adds UniDC, Xu et al.'s domain-agnostic completion work and radar/nighttime/weather literature, while withdrawing the Robust-DC benchmark-novelty positioning.

T1.justification: The Gaussian error-accumulation argument, integration formulation, mathematical assumptions and scale-equivariance lemma and proof are retained. Appendix H becomes Appendix L; notation cleanup and equation renumbering do not substantively change the mathematics.

improvement.justification: v1's comparisons left uncertainty about the contribution of differing training data. v2's controlled retraining in Appendix B and radar/nighttime/weather tests in Appendices C–D substantially strengthen validation of the central generalization claim, while expanded limitations clarify applicability. Reporting problems temper this gain: BP-Net's KITTI-64 MAE conflicts between Table 3 (0.011) and Table l (0.204), and Table i's metric labels conflict with matching entries in Table 4. These localized issues do not outweigh the stronger experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OMNI-DC work. All 24 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds training-data ablations, radar completion, nighttime and weather evaluations, and further loss ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original depth-completion evaluations, component ablations, scale-equivariance experiments and novel-view-synthesis results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: OMNI-DC: Highly Robust Depth Completion with Multiresolution Depth Integration

C1.justification: V2's introduction adds human-interpretable landmark control as a benefit and foregrounds the zero-shot generalization claim previously developed in the appendix. The central contribution—retrieving external structural knowledge to improve garment fidelity—remains. The change from three-level alignment to coarse-to-fine texture alignment largely reorganizes existing components.

C2.justification: V2 expands the practical interpretation through explanations of direct-mask prediction failure, negligible retrieval overhead, user control and commercial logo fidelity. It acknowledges remaining failures on extreme shapes but removes v1's limitation concerning non-end-to-end training and its expertise/coding demands. These changes substantially revise the discussion of applicability and limitations; color-bias limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents FAISS-based parallel retrieval, a retrieval/denoising/captioning timing breakdown, and the raw-image conditioning used for ControlNet. Reported training and annotation hardware changes from A100 to H20 GPUs. Most existing architectural details, hyperparameters, dataset preprocessing and augmentation instructions are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on Viton-HD and DressCode, including upper-body, lower-body and dress subsets, plus extreme-garment and user-controlled shape scenarios. V1's pose-control, finger-refinement and background-replacement demonstrations are removed. The 856-item retrieval expansion and 50-query lower-body/dress study already existed in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: STGarment Table 1 expands from PBE, IP-Adapter and ReferenceNet to also include ControlNet, TryOffDiff and TryOffAnyone. Figure 3 replaces the IP-Adapter/PBE columns with the two garment-restoration methods, and Figure 4 adds TryOffAnyone. IGR is discussed but is not an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: V2 adds DISTS to the evaluation metrics, changes the reported user-study population from 25 to 100 participants while retaining 200 image pairs, and revises StructureNet pretraining from nearly 200 million to 2 million images. New cross-dataset testing distinguishes zero-shot evaluations from Viton-HD-trained checkpoints. These are reported setting changes; the PDFs do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a direct UNet mask-prediction alternative to test the necessity of retrieval, extreme-shape/pattern robustness examples, landmark-manipulation case studies and cross-dataset generalization analysis. Existing embedding, retrieval-size, nearest-neighbor sensitivity and color-failure analyses remain. V1's generic training-free RAG demonstrations are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions describe user-score distributions through means, medians, quartiles and outliers. Neither reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. The changed participant count and plotted scores alter study settings and results, without changing the statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds baseline/DISTS scores, cross-dataset results, mask-prediction results and runtime measurements. For example, Table 3 reports a DressCode-lower FID of 40.5, and Table 2 gives mask prediction an FID of 14.55. The original STGarment RAGDiffusion FID remains 9.990. Figure 4 changes its annotated RAGDiffusion scores from 8.34/8.52 to 8.30/8.86, although v2's prose retains the old values; the participant setting also changed.

M1.justification: V2 adds an optional inference procedure in supplementary Section 6.2: users replace the recommended landmark with another retrieved candidate before denoising. The core StructureNet, SLLE, EP-Adapter, ReferenceNet and PGEA pipeline remains. The Resampler label replacing MLP in Figure 2 clarifies an architecture already documented in v1's appendix.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are substantially rewritten around garment restoration. Structure conditioning moves into Section 3.2, ablations are presented as cumulative component additions, and generalization is promoted into the main experiments. The supplementary rationale is reorganized, and references move after the supplementary material.

P2.justification: V2 expands comparison and ablation tables, adds cross-dataset and timing tables, changes comparison panels and the user-study display, and adds manipulation and extreme-garment figures. The sensitivity and t-SNE plots are merged, existing lower-body examples are partly redisplayed in the main text, and the generic RAG demonstration figure is removed.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion replaces generic image/document restoration with garment restoration, positioning RAGDiffusion against TileGAN, TryOffDiff, TryOffAnyone and IGR. It develops distinctions involving structural errors, commercial detail fidelity and adaptation costs. Additional references support the new metrics, retrieval implementation and benchmark coverage.

T1.justification: V2 corrects Equation 1 by adding the negative sign to the contrastive loss. Supplementary Equation 7 restores multiplication by V_text in the attention formula, omitted in v1. SLLE's assumptions and mathematical construction otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's limited empirical validation by adding garment-restoration competitors, quantitative cross-dataset evaluation and a direct mask-prediction control. These additions test the value and generalizability of retrieval more directly than v1's generic baselines and qualitative transfer examples. Mathematical corrections and implementation disclosures also improve clarity. These gains outweigh the new Figure 4/prose inconsistency and the removal of the multistage-training limitation, although those issues weaken reporting consistency and qualification of practical claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RAGDiffusion and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures and supplementary material. Retained content can be matched across renaming, renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds cross-dataset evaluations, additional comparisons, mask-prediction experiments, manipulation examples and runtime measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original STGarment experiments, component ablations, retrieval analyses, a user study and supplementary generalization demonstrations.

results.title: RAGDiffusion: Faithful Cloth Generation via External Knowledge Assimilation

C1.justification: The central dataset contribution expands from approximately 0.4m to 3.55m instances. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add the substantive claim that TextSSR data improves models already trained with real-world data. The earlier claim to be the first application of diffusion models to assist STR training is removed.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning ST saturation, the usefulness of the VAE quality–accuracy trade-off, and overcoming irregularity through increased data volume. It also acknowledges incomplete contextual-semantic realism and proposes more specific remedies for existing failure modes. The main irregular-text limitations and failure categories remain.

D1.justification: v2 discloses conditioning tensor shapes, the 13-to-4-channel projection, stage-specific GPU-hours, inference timing, and preset augmentation use, and states that TextSSR-F is publicly available. However, the enlarged dataset description omits v1's explicit expansion multiplier and unfiltered generation count. Most existing model and hardware details are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix 6.3.3 and Table 6 add explicit evaluations in French, German, Japanese, and Traditional Chinese, substantially broadening the previously reported English and Chinese evaluation coverage. The generator training corpora and existing STR benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds SynthAdd as a competing training-data source in Table 3 and the NRTR case study. The TextOCR Pseudo comparator in v1 Table 3 disappears from the corresponding scaling table. Tables 1 and 2 retain their comparator membership; SceneVTG-Real is renamed Real-L.

E3.justification: The main usability experiments switch from CRNN, NRTR, and ABINet to CRNN and MAERec, replace approximately 429k supplements with 1.05m and 3.55m configurations, and change the reported training budget from 100k steps to 20 epochs. New protocols include 100 images per added language, multilingual SVTRv2 evaluation, and a 300-instance human audit.

E4.justification: v2 adds a human check of filtering correctness, examples testing erroneous pseudo-labels, downstream NRTR recognition comparisons on difficult text, and additional synthesis cases. These examine important reliability questions beyond the retained component and region-size ablations. Conversely, the standalone 30k anagram-only experiment in v1 Table 3 is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new human audit reports accuracies for three assessors checking different samples; these are not repeated-run or uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v1 Table 4 is replaced by large-scale results under revised settings in v2 Table 3, including new mixed-data averages of 87.08% for CRNN and 95.46% for MAERec. Table 6 adds multilingual accuracies of 68%, 75%, 24%, and 55%; the human audit reports 98.67% correctness. These are newly reported results, not same-setting improvements over v1. Tables 1, 2, and 5 retain their numerical results.

M1.justification: The region-centric diffusion pipeline, word and character conditioning, VAE/CDM objectives, anagram expansion, and OCR filtering are retained. The expanded tensor, projection, and padding descriptions clarify implementation without establishing a changed synthesis procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition, and experimental discussion undergo extensive rewriting. Related-work subsections are reorganized, and Appendix 6.3 is divided into six focused subsections. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 introduces a new opening overview, combines and redraws the architecture and synthesis pipeline, relocates the prior-method pipeline comparison to the appendix, and restructures the large-scale results table. It adds the multilingual table and several analysis figures, expands the synthesis gallery, and reformats retained plots and comparisons.

R1.justification: The broad diffusion-based data-synthesis survey is removed, while STR data scaling and direct synthesis competitors receive more focused treatment. v2 adds works including the STR scaling-law study and DreamText, explicitly discusses limitations of CTIG-DM and SceneVTG, and withdraws the first-attempt novelty claim.

T1.justification: The locality assumption, glyph-feature formulation, squared reconstruction and denoising losses, and factorial permutation count remain equivalent. Revised notation and expanded data-flow explanations introduce no new theoretical result or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for TextSSR's practical usefulness through matched-size SynthAdd comparisons, tests adding synthetic data to an existing real-data training mixture, broader language evaluation, and a human correctness audit. These address important validation gaps in v1. Clearer implementation descriptions and more qualified novelty positioning also help. Removing the pseudo-label comparator and anagram-only control, and omitting updated generation totals, weakens some comparisons and reproducibility, but the overall evidential gains remain substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TextSSR and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material. Renamed methods and relocated content can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and reports revised large-scale recognition results, additional multilingual evaluations, and a human assessment of generated data.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthesis evaluations, downstream recognition experiments, scaling experiments, and component ablations.

results.title: TextSSR: Diffusion-based Data Synthesis for Scene Text Recognition

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions remove the 150% faster-processing claim and instead emphasize a 17.9% Survival50 advantage over an event-only TAP baseline and superiority to feature trackers using events plus frames. The dataset contribution expands from one simulated event dataset to two. The central motion-guidance and temporal-consistency claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for sampling offset-frame features, time-surface advantages over other representations, and the accuracy/computation tradeoff around six iterations. It also explains why missing ground truth for occluded Ev-Davis points limits visualization. The main interpretation based on motion guidance and temporal consistency is retained.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents encoder structure, polarity-separated time surfaces, sampling strides, approximately 340k training samples with 128 points each, augmentations, and spline alignment of feature-tracking ground truth. Reported hardware changes from four to eight A6000 GPUs. Conversely, v1's event-simulation/interpolation recipe and project-page link disappear. Newly disclosed implementation details do not establish that those procedures changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds Ev-Davis, simulated from TAP-Vid-Davis real videos, extending TAP evaluation to scenes with fast motion and frequent occlusion. Ev-PointOdyssey, EC and EDS remain. Feature tracking itself is retained coverage, despite receiving a separate task subsection.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains PIPs++ but removes PIPs, TAPIR, Context-PIPs, EKLT, DeepEvT, E-RAFT and B-FLOW from that comparison, adding CoTracker, CoTracker3 and event-adapted PIPs++/CoTracker3. Table 2 retains EKLT and DeepEvT while adding PIPs++, CoTracker3, FE-TAP, EM-ICP, HASTE, AEB-Tracker and ETAP.

E3.justification: v1 describes 256×320 training followed by 512×640 fine-tuning; v2 reports training at 512×640. v2 introduces event-retrained video trackers as comparison controls, Survival16 evaluation for Ev-Davis, and supplementary experiments at 192×256 without VMA. FPS evaluation is removed. These are changes to reported protocols, not proof of which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The component-ablation design is retained, while supplementary Table 4 and Figure 9 add event-representation comparisons and sensitivity analyses for loss weighting and iteration count. Figure 7 replaces the MLP kinematic-vector correction visualization with an MGM-on/off tracking case. Occlusion and rapid-motion case studies are also revised and expanded.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Figure 8 retains temporal standard deviations of feature activations; these are a feature-consistency analysis, not uncertainty estimates across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 contain substantially revised results. Ours' Ev-PointOdyssey accuracy/Survival50 changes from 0.358/0.553 to 0.362/0.560, and EDS FA/EFA from 0.616/0.529 to 0.713/0.626. Ev-Davis and supplementary results are added; FPS results are removed. Changed training descriptions and MTE scaling prevent interpreting these as unqualified same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The stated supervision changes from MAE in v1 to temporally weighted absolute error with gamma=0.8 in v2 Equation 8. The central MGM and VMAM/VMA architecture remains. Expanded descriptions of feature pyramids, encoder blocks and two temporal convolutions do not independently establish architectural changes.

P1.justification: The method overview and module explanations are substantially rewritten. Experiments are reorganized from combined quantitative/qualitative comparisons into implementation details, TAP, feature tracking and ablations. The paper is retitled MATE, VMAM becomes VMA, and dedicated supplementary sections are introduced.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is extensively redrawn, Table 1 gains a second dataset and loses FPS, and Table 2 gains modality groups and numerous comparator rows. Figures 4–7 replace or expand visual examples; supplementary Table 4 and Figures 9–11 are added. Figure 8 largely retains its existing analysis.

R1.justification: v1 states that event-based TAP has not yet been proposed. v2 discusses FE-TAP and ETAP and positions MATE against their appearance-based matching, materially revising its novelty framing. Additional tracker references support the expanded comparisons, while the simulator and frame-interpolation references are removed.

T1.justification: v2 adds an explicit mathematical definition of temporally weighted supervision in Equation 8, including the gamma-based weighting absent from v1's MAE description. The surface-gradient, plane-fitting and event-rate derivations otherwise remain, with renumbering and notation changes rather than new proofs.

improvement.justification: Ev-Davis and event-adapted TAP comparisons substantially strengthen the evidence for generalization and comparative performance. Targeted ablations and the implementation supplement also address important gaps in assessing and reproducing v1. These gains outweigh the loss of FPS results, simulation instructions and the project link. Claims still need qualification: v2 says it outperforms all feature trackers, but Table 2 reports EC EFA of 0.875 versus ETAP's 0.876.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same event-based tracking framework, renamed MATE in v2. The text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. All supplied material was inspected, including v2's supplementary Sections 6–9; v1 contains no separate supplement.

after.justification: v2 reports original tracking results across four datasets, revised component ablations, and supplementary representation and hyperparameter experiments in Table 4 and Figure 9.

before.justification: v1 reports original tracking experiments on Ev-PointOdyssey, EC and EDS, component ablations, and qualitative analyses in Tables 1–3 and Figures 5–8.

results.title: MATE: Motion-Augmented Temporal Consistency for Event-based Point Tracking

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the headline contributions to synthetic-to-real adaptation, direct robotic policy training and greater asset diversity than synthetic datasets. The third contribution shifts from establishing a benchmark to demonstrating downstream utility. The dataset and dense-prediction contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets URDFormer fine-tuning as improved real-world adaptability and explains how its mesh-fitting and axis-alignment biases motivate bounding-box evaluation. It also omits v1 Section 5.1's explicit exclusion of movable parts without interactable descendants; this omission does not establish that those parts were newly evaluated. Existing size and faucet-failure interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies loss weights, articulation acceptance thresholds, GPT-4o-based class-mass estimates, URDFormer data preparation and robotics hardware/training settings. Most original model settings are retained or relocated, but v1's separate 640-epoch interactable-part training detail is omitted. The embedded project-access link is unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on SceneFun3D, image-based synthetic-to-real transfer using URDFormer, and simulated robotic drawer opening. These substantially extend the evaluated data and task requirements beyond v1's retained Articulate3D, MultiScan, connectivity and LLM insertion experiments.

E2.justification: v1's MultiScan experiment compares only ArtMask3D with and without Articulate3D pretraining. v2 Table 6 additionally compares USDNet against SoftGroup† and Mask3D† on MultiScan. The comparator set for the original Articulate3D experiments remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include selecting and cropping three images per object, assuming known object poses and evaluating part-box AP50 for URDFormer, plus PPO training with 1024 environments for 30,000 iterations. The original 42-scene test split and 2 cm voxelization remain unchanged; newly specified articulation thresholds are additional disclosure.

E4.justification: v2 adds a zero-shot versus fine-tuned URDFormer study testing synthetic-to-real generalization, robotics case studies and train/test label-distribution analysis. The dense-axis/origin ablations, MultiScan pretraining analysis, annotation-agreement check and size/category failure analyses were already present in v1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for model performance. The added experiments continue reporting point estimates without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds SceneFun3D joint articulation scores of 30.5 for USDNet, 22.4 for Mask3D† and 12.8 for SoftGroup†. Table 8 reports URDFormer zero-shot/fine-tuned AP50 of 22.7/35.1 on MultiScan and 16.4/38.2 on Articulate3D; Section 10.2 adds 87% drawer-opening success. Original benchmark, ablation, pretraining and connectivity scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: USDNet matches ArtMask3D's Mask3D backbone, dense origin/axis predictions, query-based axis branch and auxiliary point-to-center branch. Comparing v1 Figure 4 with v2 Figure 3 establishes continuity; the expanded architecture and loss descriptions do not establish an algorithmic revision.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten, USD background is condensed and partly moved to the appendix, and the method receives a dedicated USDNet section. Experiments and downstream applications are reorganized, with corresponding appendix restructuring. The title and model name also change.

P2.justification: Table 1 is substantially redesigned, the annotation and network diagrams are redrawn, and new comparison tables, annotation-tool screenshots, split-distribution plots and robotics illustrations are added. Existing LLM examples, dataset histograms, connectivity plots and error-analysis figures are largely retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial synthetic/generated-assets discussion, including ProcTHOR, HSSD-200, URDFormer and MeshArt, and expands Table 1 to compare diversity and simulation readiness. This strengthens positioning around real-world assets and the synthetic-to-real gap beyond v1's predominantly real-scene annotation comparisons.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4.2 adds explicit mathematical definitions of the auxiliary point-to-center loss and weighted joint training objective. Its cosine-based axis and origin-to-axis distance losses formalize the construction already described in v1. No new theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the dataset's central transfer and simulation utility. Beyond v1's MultiScan pretraining and LLM insertion, it adds synthetic-to-real adaptation, SceneFun3D validation and a trained drawer-opening policy, while documenting losses and evaluation thresholds more clearly. Omitted scope and training details are drawbacks, and uncertainty remains unreported, but the added direct validation provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Articulate3D dataset and prediction framework, renamed from ArtMask3D to USDNet. Both main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds SceneFun3D evaluation, URDFormer adaptation results and simulated robotic manipulation outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation and articulation experiments, ablations, MultiScan transfer results, annotation agreement and connectivity prediction results.

results.title: Articulate3D: Holistic Understanding of 3D Scenes as Universal Scene Description

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds spatial-similarity detection and infringement-feature inversion for assigning responsibility. V2 drops the feature-inversion contribution and centers copyright attribution and adaptive optimization, adding a principal claim of outperforming existing defenses across two attack scenarios.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting attribution scores to memorization, explaining easier detection in general imagery, and identifying detection as the stronger contributor in the component ablation. It removes v1's substantive liability-attribution discussion. The limitations concerning real-world copyrighted images and future attack methods are retained.

D1.justification: V2 adds attribution pseudocode, trigger-prompt templates, baseline implementation descriptions, and disclosures of the default SD v1.4 model, SSCD/Disc-MixUp, guidance scale 7.5, and 1000 diffusion steps. V1's explicit 832-clean-image count and 5.7-second detection timing disappear. Reproducibility remains limited by v2 specifying Adam in the main text but AdamW in the supplement.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates Pokemon character generation. V2 retains this coverage and adds a continual-pretraining scenario using COYO-700M clean images and Midjourney v5 copyright targets, extending evaluation to general imagery. SilentBadDiffusion remains the evaluated attack.

E2.justification: V1 compares defended models with undefended SilentBadDiffusion models. V2 additionally evaluates T2IShield and TERD as defense comparators in Table 2, and TRAK, Journey TRAK, and D-TRAK as detection comparators in Table 3. Previously citing some defenses did not constitute evaluating them.

E3.justification: The detection threshold sweep changes from 0.2/0.25/0.3 to 0.3/0.35/0.4, with the experimental selection changing from 0.25 to 0.35. V2 adds FID/CLIP evaluation over 500 random prompts and specifies an LDS-based threshold procedure for attribution baselines. The 100-epoch budget and 100 generated images per poisoned caption for CIR are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds detection-only and training-only component ablations in Table 5, fixed-versus-adaptive penalty results in supplementary Table 6, and attribution-score analysis in Figure 2. V1 mentions a fixed-coefficient sweep but does not supply these comparative results. The earlier rotation and model-version analyses remain, with revised presentation.

E5.justification: Both versions report 20 independent experiments per evaluated scenario without reporting seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Applying the same practice to the additional scenario does not change uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: At Pokemon poisoning rate 0.1, reported defense CIR/FAE changes from 0.318/84.13 to 0.305/85.93; the undefended values remain 0.650/50.15. These are results for the revised method and threshold, not a controlled same-procedure improvement. V2 also adds substantial baseline, COYO+Midjourney, FID/CLIP, and ablation results.

M1.justification: V1 detects poisoning using an IoU-gated IoU–SSCD score. V2 replaces this with normalized copyright attribution derived from spatially masked similarity and projected model gradients. The training penalty also changes from a fixed coefficient lambda to sample-specific attribution weights, substantially changing both detection and optimization.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution statements, method explanation, and substantial portions of the experimental narrative are rewritten. Related work and preliminaries are reorganized, the feature-inversion subsection is replaced by ablations, and a structured supplement is added. These changes extend beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the framework diagram, expands the rotation illustration with attribution plots, restructures tables around datasets and comparators, and replaces v1's model-version table with bar charts. It adds utility and ablation displays and supplementary comparison images, while removing the liability-allocation diagram.

R1.justification: V2 introduces dedicated data-attribution related work covering TRAK, Journey TRAK, and D-TRAK, and positions CopyrightShield within a detection–cleaning–retraining framework. It removes much of v1's broad adversarial-attack citation discussion and the legal-liability positioning, substantially shifting the research context.

T1.justification: V2 adds projected-gradient attribution definitions and derivations, including kernel construction, Newton influence approximation, Taylor linearization, and the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma in Section 3.2 and supplementary Section 7. This substantially changes the mathematical development from v1's spatial-score and cross-attention motivation. The main-text and supplementary Gram-matrix expressions are not fully consistent.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification: evaluated competitors, component ablations, and FID/CLIP measurements address v1's missing evidence about comparative advantage, component necessity, and generation-quality costs. The additional image domain also tests broader applicability. Threshold, optimizer, and matrix-expression inconsistencies weaken reproducibility, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs clearly describe CopyrightShield and are readable throughout, including their equations, figures, and tables. V2 includes supplementary Sections 7–11; no supplement is appended to the supplied v1 PDF. The judgments concern the material actually supplied.

after.justification: V2 reports original detection, defense, generation-quality, and ablation results on Pokemon and COYO+Midjourney, including supplementary experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original poisoned-sample detection and defense experiments on Pokemon, including numerical results across poisoning rates and Stable Diffusion versions in Tables 1–3.

results.title: CopyrightShield: Enhancing Diffusion Model Security against Copyright Infringement Attacks

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list redefine the methodological novelty around inpainting that separates degradation identification from generation and avoids simulating specific degradation patterns during training. V1 foregrounded a generic inverse-problem formulation and AI-generated driving worlds. The generated-world application remains in v2's appendix but is no longer a headline contribution. The central free-form synthesis objective remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations for LiDAR guidance, domain-specific texture improvement, the training/inference mask gap, and expanding reliable regions during optimization. Appendices A and G discuss limitations of fixed trajectory sampling and failure on completely unseen surfaces. It also interprets slightly lower recorded-view metrics as perceptually negligible. V1's interpretation of its direct video-world-model comparison disappears with that experiment.

D1.justification: V2 specifies edge-mask construction, LiDAR accumulation and motion alignment, fine-tuning for 15,000 iterations with batch size 24 on eight RTX A6000 GPUs, full Waymo segment identifiers, the two ablation segments, and the Faster R-CNN evaluator. Conversely, v1's nuScenes initialization-image list and explicit 50% generated-data mixture are omitted. These omissions do not establish underlying procedural changes. The project address remains equivalent.

E1.justification: V2 adds PandaSet evaluation and aggressive viewpoints involving a 6 m lateral shift or a camera elevated 3 m with 30-degree pitch (Appendices F–G). V1's real nuScenes evaluation and acceleration/deceleration comparisons disappear. Waymo and reconstruction of Vista-generated videos remain; the latter is relocated to Appendix E.

E2.justification: V2 Table 2 adds evaluated comparisons with ReconDreamer and FreeVS alongside DriveDreamer4D. V1's Appendix Table 9 comparison against MagicDrive-t and Vista is removed, although Vista remains the source of generated videos in another experiment. EmerNeRF, S3Gaussian, PVG, and StreetGaussian remain in the main Waymo comparison.

E3.justification: Reported Waymo evaluation changes from 12 to 18 selected sequences and from 640×920 to 640×960 images. V2 adds recorded-trajectory PSNR/SSIM evaluation with every fifth frame held out. Refinement intervals change from 2,000 to 3,000 steps and sampled shifts from 2–4 m to 2–6 m. It also introduces diffusion fine-tuning and revises the generative-baseline comparison protocol. Aggressive viewpoints are explicitly included during optimization.

E4.justification: V2 adds LiDAR-conditioning and fine-tuning ablations (Table 5), a qualitative fine-tuning comparison, aggressive-view tests, an unseen-vehicle-surface failure case, and mask evolution across iterations. Existing mask, buffer, noise-strength, Gaussian-model, progressive-shift, and warping analyses are retained with revisions or relocation. V1's generated-video pose-refinement and depth-prior ablations are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, evaluation seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. V2's random training-mask sampling and changed sequence averages do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Main Waymo and many ablation values change substantially. For example, DriveX's 3 m IoU/AP/FID changes from 0.1755/0.5427/95.60 to 0.2699/0.5712/79.78, under revised method and evaluation settings rather than an isolated same-setting comparison. V2 adds comparator, recorded-view, and PandaSet results while removing earlier result sets. The generated-video FID entries are unchanged between v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 9. V2 Table 2 also shows FreeVS slightly ahead on 3 m lane IoU.

M1.justification: V2 adds driving-domain fine-tuning with edge-aware inpainting masks and colored-LiDAR conditioning accumulated from adjacent frames (Sections 3.3–3.4). This extends v1's use of ViewCrafter and is distinct from the LiDAR depth supervision already present in v1. V2 also removes the need for the earlier foreground-vehicle downweighting. The iterative Gaussian optimization and unreliability-mask framework remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten. V2 separates novel-view regularization, inpainting restoration, and generative-model training into dedicated subsections. Generated-video material moves from the main method/results sections to Appendix E, and the supplementary material is reorganized into Appendices A–G. The title also adds DriveX and changes scene synthesis to view synthesis.

P2.justification: V2 expands Table 1 with recorded-view metrics, restructures Table 2 into different comparison panels, and adds a component-ablation table. Qualitative comparison grids are reorganized, and new figures cover fine-tuning, PandaSet, aggressive viewpoints, failure cases, and mask evolution. The generated-video figure and table are relocated rather than newly added, while the existing mask/refinement illustration gains clearer annotations.

R1.justification: V2 substantially updates positioning through FreeSim, Difix3D+, StreetCrafter, ReconDreamer, and FreeVS. It contrasts its inpainting formulation with approaches requiring degradation-specific training or LiDAR-guided restoration. Earlier inverse-problem references are removed, and the novelty argument shifts toward training a driving-domain generative prior without simulating off-trajectory degradations.

T1.justification: V1's explicit measurement model V' = f(V) + epsilon and its distortion/noise formulation (Equation 3) are omitted in v2's restoration formulation. The Gaussian rendering, photometric loss, trajectory, warping, and mask mathematics are otherwise largely retained or renumbered. Neither version contains theorem or proof developments.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the explanation and validation of the central generative mechanism through explicit training details and component tests. Recorded-view fidelity checks, more relevant generative comparators, PandaSet evaluation, and documented failure boundaries address important gaps in v1's evidence and qualification of applicability. These benefits outweigh the loss of the real nuScenes comparison, some ablations, and reproducibility details. Some claims remain too broad: Table 2 does not show uniform superiority over FreeVS. The improvement rests on stronger explanation and assessment, rather than treating changed-protocol scores as direct performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DriveX by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision and relocation of material.

after.justification: V2 reports original Waymo and PandaSet experiments, generated-video reconstruction, component ablations, and qualitative robustness and failure analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original Waymo experiments, reconstruction of Vista-generated videos, a real nuScenes comparison, and component ablations.

results.title: Driving View Synthesis on Free-form Trajectories with Generative Prior

C1.justification: V2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion elevate learning from internal IQA activations and content-agnostic reference-image quality transfer to central contributions. V1 centers on score-conditioned generation and its degradation and adversarial applications. The claims of up to 10% quality improvement and preservation of generative capabilities are retained.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations concerning semantic leakage from reference images, the suitability of IQA embeddings for distortion transfer, attention separation, and compatibility with other improvement methods. Its limitations discussion adds artifact-classifier and latent-space assessment directions, while Section 18 extends the adversarial-risk discussion to critic-based optimization. Most earlier IQA-bias and VAE limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 Section 9 newly discloses per-GPU batch sizes of 16 and 4, training on five nodes with 40 GPUs, and reference-adapter and negative-guidance settings. The timing experiment specifies hardware, precision, resolution, and sampling steps. These improve documentation; the newly disclosed batch sizes do not establish changed training. The promised code and weights release remains unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds direct KADID-10k evaluation of reference-conditioned distortion transfer in both SDEdit image editing and text-to-image generation (Section 4.5). These introduce reference images and distortion-reproduction requirements beyond v1's score-controlled generation. KADID previously appeared as training data for pretrained IQA models. Lexica.art, PartiPrompts, GenEval, and COCO coverage is retained.

E2.justification: V2 evaluates DiffusionDPO, Q-Refine, BeautifulPrompt, and Prompt Weighting against IQA-Adapter in quality, GenEval, and COCO comparisons, including several combinations with the adapter. The new distortion-transfer comparison adds IP-Adapter and, for text-to-image generation, StyleCrafter (Table 2). V1's comparisons primarily involved the base model, gradient guidance, and IQA-Adapter variants.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a distortion-transfer protocol using one reference source, 80 target images, and 125 distortion variants, evaluated through quality correlations, CLIP comparisons, and ARNIQA embedding similarity. It also adds HPSv2 scoring, architectural control configurations, and a controlled runtime evaluation. The original training schedule and basic SDXL sampling settings are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds a direct ablation of separate qualitative attention against concatenating quality and text tokens, with quantitative and visual evidence (Table 5, Figure 16). It also adds computational-overhead analysis and reference-transfer failure comparisons. V1's positional-encoding, adapter-scale, seed-consistency, and GradCAM analyses are largely retained and reorganized, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V2 Section 17.1 and Table 8 newly report timing averages over 1,000 generations with ± values, although the meaning of those spreads is unspecified. The original 25-prompt, 100-seed analysis, subjective-study counts, and Inception Score uncertainty-reporting practice remain unchanged.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial distortion-transfer, baseline, combination, ablation, and runtime results. Retained COCO values are also revised: base-model FID changes from 21.84 to 19.92, and TOPIQ+LAION-AES FID from 23.51 to 21.36 (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 7). These are reported-value revisions without an explanation establishing an algorithmic gain. The original main GenEval table and subjective-study results are retained.

M1.justification: V2 Sections 3.3–3.4 introduce Reference-based IQA-Adapter, which conditions generation on intermediate ARNIQA embeddings extracted from reference images and uses degradation augmentation during training. This substantially extends the score-based conditioning procedure in v1. The original attention mechanism and denoising objective remain; renaming the attention mechanism does not itself change the method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related work are substantially rewritten. Discussion moves from the main paper into the supplement, while negative guidance moves into the main method description. The supplement gains a contents section and reorganizes limitations, ablations, and additional experiments. These are extensive narrative and structural changes beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 2 to include embedding-based conditioning and reorganizes comparison heatmaps with colored method categories. It adds distortion-transfer, ablation, and runtime tables, expands existing comparison tables, and introduces several qualitative comparison grids. Existing figures are relocated, while the earlier negative-guidance displays are reduced or replaced.

R1.justification: V2 adds a substantive Generation Quality Improvement discussion positioning IQA-Adapter against DiffusionDPO, Q-Refine, prompt enhancement, and other quality-improvement approaches. It also situates reference conditioning relative to IP-Adapter and StyleCrafter, with additional citations supporting the new experiments. The distinction between broad quality control and quality maximization becomes more explicit.

T1.justification: The negative-condition definition is generalized from qneg = -q in v1 Section 8 to qneg = -δq in v2 Section 3.2.1, introducing a tunable quality gap. The attention equations, denoising objective, relative-gain definition, and positional-encoding formula otherwise retain their mathematical content. No new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important evidential gaps in v1 through external quality-improvement baselines and a direct architectural ablation, substantially strengthening assessment of the method's usefulness and design choices. The reference-based extension receives quantitative and visual evaluation, and training disclosure improves. Unexplained revisions to retained scores and the Table 5 versus Section 11.1 SROCC mismatch remain reporting weaknesses; the improvement rests on stronger comparisons and controls, rather than higher reported numbers.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the IQA-Adapter research and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and supplementary material. Retained content can be matched across the substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds reference-based distortion-transfer experiments, architectural ablations, external baseline comparisons, and timing measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original SDXL experiments, benchmark evaluations, sensitivity analyses, and a subjective study involving 1,017 participants.

results.title:
IQA-Adapter: Exploring Knowledge Transfer from Image Quality Assessment
  to Diffusion-based Generative Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about training-free adaptive inference, image/video applicability, computational savings, and improved long-video performance. The stated approximately sevenfold video FLOP reduction and +4.6 MLVU result remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix B explicitly identifies incompatibility with FlashAttention because pruning requires attention values, discusses other efficiency techniques, and proposes future integration. Appendix A attributes larger Qwen2-VL performance losses to joint frame encoding and discusses LLaVA-Prumerge's incompatibility with that model. V2 also interprets the newly quantified overhead as negligible; the earlier TextVQA limitation remains.

D1.justification: The abstract changes code availability from a future promise to a statement that code is available at the same repository. Appendix A discloses a memory-driven MAX_PIXELS reduction, although its value is unspecified. Existing main-experiment hyperparameters and FLOP/prefill estimation details are retained; v2 removes the explicit statement that baseline official implementations were used.

E1.justification: The same six video benchmarks and seven image benchmarks remain in use. Appendix experiments reuse this coverage; the additional base model, frame counts, and merging configurations change experimental settings rather than datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 3 add VTW and PDrop to the evaluated pruning baselines, with PDrop omitted from the lowest-budget image comparison. They remove VILA, PLLaVA, LLaVA-N-Video, IXC-2.5, BLIP-2, and InstructBLIP comparison rows. Appendix B additionally compares pruning against FlashAttention.

E3.justification: V2 adds Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct evaluation with reduced MAX_PIXELS, controlled 128-frame comparisons, temporal-versus-spatial merging experiments, and a merging-only/FlashAttention/pruning comparison. Appendix C adds another computation-budget configuration. The original main-experiment splits, metrics, and stated defaults remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations, v2 tests whether dense frames alone explain improvements, directly compares temporal and spatial merging, and examines dependence on the base model (Tables A–C). Table 7 quantifies merging/pruning overhead, while Table D compares pruning with FlashAttention. These substantially expand the evidence examining design choices and efficiency.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests for its experiments. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial baseline, overhead, and appendix results, including Qwen2-VL+AIM scoring 52.8 on VideoMME in Table C, while removing several reference-model result rows. Main AIM scores are retained. FastV's higher-budget MMB score changes from 72.7 to 72.1 in Table 3; Table 1's relative FLOP/prefill percentages change from 62.4%/63.3% to 69.5%/69.2%, consistent with comparison against FastV.

M1.justification: Both versions use within-frame similarity-based merging before the LLM, PageRank-based visual-token pruning, preserved text tokens, and the same piecewise scheduler. V2 clarifies encoder placement and corrects a token-count expression, without establishing a different implemented procedure.

P1.justification: V2 condenses portions of related work, clarifies the merging explanation, revises baseline descriptions, and corrects the erroneous reference to Experiment 16 to Experiment 6. It adds acknowledgements and appendix sections while retaining the main section order and most existing prose.

P2.justification: V2 adds an overhead table and Appendix Tables A–E, substantially extending the displayed evidence. Tables 1 and 3 have revised comparison rows, while existing figures and tables are resized and repositioned with revised captions and highlighting. Figures 1–2 retain their substantive content, and the original adaptive-inference Table 7 becomes Table 8.

R1.justification: V2 updates related work with VTW, DyCoke, multimodal chain-of-thought work, and adaptive inference for MLLMs, and adds references supporting the FlashAttention, sparse-attention, and quantization discussion. PDrop receives explicit positioning beyond the earlier concurrent-work citation. Some background references disappear, but AIM's central positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 corrects the next-layer token-count expression from N_0 r^l to N^1 r^l, using the post-merging count instead of the original count. This is a limited mathematical correction. The PageRank equation, piecewise scheduler, and absence of formal proofs are otherwise unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for AIM's efficiency and design choices through overhead accounting, controlled dense-frame and temporal-merging tests, another base model, and additional relevant pruning baselines. Its explicit FlashAttention limitation also improves the assessment of practical applicability. These address important evidential gaps in v1 and outweigh the loss of several broad reference-model comparisons, although the new Qwen2-VL pixel setting remains underspecified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AIM with the same authors, central method, and main experiments. Text, equations, figures, and tables support reliable comparison. V1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains Appendices A–C.

after.justification: V2 retains these original evaluations and adds baseline results, computational-overhead measurements, and experiments in Appendix Tables A–E.

before.justification: V1 reports original image and video benchmark evaluations, token-merging and pruning ablations, and accuracy-efficiency results in Tables 1–7.

results.title: AIM: Adaptive Inference of Multi-Modal LLMs via Token Merging and Pruning

C1.justification: The central claims about importance-sampled Hessians/HVPs, aggregate sampling, applicability to rasterization and path tracing, and improved convergence remain. Both versions retain the headline 2.71-fold speedup; the added experiments do not introduce a new central contribution.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly discusses diminishing advantages with dimensionality and hypothesizes sparse sampling and increased Monte Carlo noise as causes. New analyses explain accuracy costs relative to analytic derivatives, sample-count versus runtime tradeoffs, and qualified robustness to rendering and compression noise, substantially expanding applicability boundaries and interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix L/Table 3 supplies previously absent per-task sampling counts, bandwidth schedules, learning rates, trust regions, and line-search settings. v3 also documents antithetic sampling, the pycma implementation, and states that all methods use Adam, although its relationship to the stated GD/CG procedures remains unclear.

E1.justification: v3 adds SUZANNE and BANANA mesh reconstruction, seven-parameter Phong BRDF fitting, a non-PSD-Hessian test scenario, caustic heightfield optimization, and bunny optimization through two mirrors. These substantially broaden the represented geometry, reflectance, and light-transport tasks.

E2.justification: CMA-ES is added throughout Table 2 and evaluated in the mesh and caustic experiments. Appendix G also introduces comparisons against analytic first- and second-order derivatives. The original Mitsuba, FR22, proposed variants, and Appendix F BFGS comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce analytic-derivative controls and controlled MUG sweeps over Hessian sample counts, rendering sample counts, and JPEG compression levels. The original Table 2 metrics remain unchanged; newly supplied hyperparameters alone do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices G-I add tests of sampled-versus-analytic derivative accuracy, optimization with non-PSD Hessians, Hessian sample efficiency, rendering noise, and compression noise. The original variance analysis is retained as Appendix J/Figure 11, moved from Section 4.3/Figure 5.

E5.justification: Both versions report 20-run ensembles and the same temporal averaging and median summaries. Appendix I newly specifies that runs use random starting points, clarifying the source of run-to-run variation. No increased run count, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: Existing Table 2 numerical entries are retained, but CMA-ES results change rankings: on QUAD, its normalized time for 99% image-error reduction is 0.13, versus 0.62 for OurHVP, previously fastest. v3 also adds mesh, analytic-reference, robustness, caustic, and mirror results, including successful caustic optimization where CMA-ES does not converge.

M1.justification: The Gaussian-convolution estimators, Hessian/HVP sampling, aggregate importance sampling, and grey-box differentiation remain unchanged. The added optimizer safeguards and implementation disclosures do not establish a revision to the proposed estimator.

P1.justification: The title changes to 'Stochastic Gradient Estimation for Higher-order Differentiable Rendering,' with author/affiliation edits and localized prose condensation. The variance section moves to Appendix J and the conclusion gains limitations, but the main narrative and derivation structure remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: Table 2 gains CMA-ES rows, bars, curves, and a revised legend; Table 3 adds a substantial hyperparameter display. New figures show mesh reconstruction, analytic comparisons, robustness, task outcomes, caustics, and mirrors. Figures 3 and 6 are redrawn, while the original variance figure is relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds the Hansen-Ostermeier CMA-ES and Jensen et al. multiview-stereopsis references, discusses CMA-ES as an alternative, and explicitly relates aggregate sampling to multiple importance sampling with the balance heuristic. The broader positioning and existing cited works are retained.

T1.justification: Section 2 adds trust-region truncation and Hessian-definiteness discussion, and Appendix H adds Gaussian-convolution reasoning for a non-PSD example. The core derivations remain unchanged. The new example contains a sign inconsistency: convolution of two negated Gaussians is incorrectly described as another negated Gaussian.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited validation and implementation disclosure through analytic-reference checks, robustness experiments, harder rendering tasks, and detailed hyperparameters. Adding CMA-ES also exposes cases where another method wins, making the comparison more informative. Explicit limitations improve qualification of the findings. The new Appendix H sign inconsistency and unclear Adam/GD/CG relationship limit particular explanations, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support and reproducibility.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same research despite the changed title. All 11 pages of v1 and 14 pages of v3, including Appendices A-F and A-L respectively, support textual and visual comparison.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, with additional mesh optimization, analytic-derivative comparisons, robustness tests, and light-transport experiments in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: Section 4 and Table 2 report original optimization experiments, and Figure 5 reports estimator-variance measurements.

results.title: Stochastic Gradient Estimation for Higher-order Differentiable Rendering

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements and conclusion retain the central claims: long-term vision-value guidance improves captions, supports inference-time scaling and enables self-training. Additional backbone results strengthen supporting evidence, while correcting the benchmark count does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations connecting object coverage to avoiding artificially favorable hallucination scores from short captions, MCTS computation to per-input search, and stronger rewards to VisVM's generality. The original long-term-value, attention and self-training explanations remain, without new substantive failure-condition analysis.

D1.justification: v3 documents MCTS expansion and iteration settings, model-specific reward choices, and ten-evaluator blind judging with a shared evaluation rubric. Core appendix training details remain, relocated from Appendix C to B. The explicit code/model availability statement and repository link in v1's abstract are removed; actual external availability cannot be inferred.

E1.justification: The COCO data, LLaVA description prompts and seven visual-comprehension plus two hallucination benchmarks are retained. Changing 'eight' to 'nine' corrects the benchmark count already represented in v1. AMBER is introduced as an object-coverage metric; the additional model backbones do not establish new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds MCTS to the caption-quality and hallucination comparisons. Appendix C, Table 7 adds HADPO, POVID, CSR and VCD comparisons. Conversely, the CLIP-BoN(6) self-training comparator in v1 Table 3 is removed from the corresponding v3 Table 4.

E3.justification: v3 adds evaluation configurations using LLaVA-OV-7B, Qwen2-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.5-7B, object-coverage and GPU-hour measurements, and a controlled candidate-selection experiment with greedy continuation. The stated self-training budget changes from five epochs to three; this documents a setting revision without establishing whether retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds the CLIP-versus-SigLIP reward ablation in Table 3 and a quantitative test of subsequent hallucinations after selecting from identical candidate sentences in Table 5. It also adds computational-cost and object-coverage analyses. The original search-size analysis and qualitative examples remain.

E5.justification: v3 Section 4.1 newly specifies that human-evaluation results are averaged across ten evaluators; v1 reports win rates without explaining cross-evaluator aggregation. This adds limited statistical reporting, without establishing increased experimental runs. Neither version reports seeds, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces human win rates against CLIP-PRM, BoN and greedy decoding from 66.0%, 63.5% and 74.0% to 62.4%, 60.2% and 75.8%. Substantial new results cover MCTS, additional backbones, reward ablation, controlled continuation and computational cost. Existing LLaVA self-training scores are retained despite the changed epoch description, so they do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The TD objective, sentence-value head and inference procedure in Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. v3 adds SigLIP as an alternative training reward component, including its use with LLaVA-OV, whereas v1 specifies CLIP.

P1.justification: v3 edits grammar, rewrites parts of the introduction and evaluation narrative, and reorganizes the appendices. The original qualitative analysis moves from Section 5 to Appendix D, while quantitative analysis becomes Section 4.3. Much of the method exposition and conclusion remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 adds the GPU-cost chart and tables for reward ablation, controlled sentence selection and additional methods. Existing comparison tables expand with model blocks and a coverage column, and Figure 3 gains an MCTS comparison. The original Figure 4 becomes appendix Figure 5, while the nine case-study tables are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for VCD, AMBER and HADPO, while removing MMed-RAG, RULE and LLaVA-Critic. It also removes the related-work distinction concerning LLaVA-Critic's response-level scoring. The broader positioning around inference-time search and self-training remains stable.

T1.justification: The MDP formulation and TD objective in Equation 1 are unchanged, and no new theorem, proof or derivation appears. v3 omits the displayed standard CHAIR formulas without changing their underlying metric definitions.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's single-backbone evaluation and qualitative mechanism evidence. Additional backbones, stronger comparators, controlled continuation, reward ablation and measured computational costs support generality, mechanism and practical efficiency more convincingly. Removing CLIP-BoN and the code-access statement, together with the unexplained epoch revision, weakens comparison completeness and reproducibility, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VisVM research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching the relocated qualitative analysis and retained case studies.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds model evaluations, comparator results, computational-cost measurements, a reward-model ablation and a controlled sentence-selection experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original caption-generation experiments, human and GPT evaluations, hallucination measurements, inference-budget scaling and self-training results.

results.title: Scaling Inference-Time Search with Vision Value Model for Improved Visual Comprehension

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: an efficient plug-and-play DiT adapter with three components that improve foreground preservation and text-aligned background generation. The Flux extension supplies evidence for the previously claimed general applicability.

C2.justification: New Appendix H identifies difficulty preserving slender objects and handling unusual viewpoints. Appendix G discusses completion or occlusion of missing parts, reconciliation of lighting conflicts, and transfer between structurally compatible models. Section 5.2 also frames text-alignment advantages against same-backbone ControlNet comparisons.

D1.justification: v2 documents Flux integration into 19 double-stream and 38 single-stream blocks, foreground compositing, and foreground-region LPIPS evaluation. It omits v1's disclosure of 24 A100 GPUs, batch size 5 per GPU, and an internal refiner. These omissions reduce implementation information but do not establish that the underlying processing stopped.

E1.justification: The 88K-image training collection, 300-item evaluation collection, and MSCOCO evaluation remain. Appendix G adds limited qualitative coverage of multiple subjects, incomplete foreground objects, conflicting lighting, and an anime-style domain.

E2.justification: Table 1 replaces the SD3 ControlNet comparator with Hunyuan ControlNet, enabling a same-backbone comparison with HY-Pinco. Appendix Figures 17–19 add Hunyuan ControlNet while retaining SD3 ControlNet and Adobe Firefly. The other comparator families and user-study competitors remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces the Flux-Pinco model configuration and tests transfer of a FLUX.1-dev-trained adapter to an anime-style fine-tune without further training. The main 300 images × 3 prompts × 2 seeds design, 1024×1024 resolution, learning rate, crop ratios, and metric suite remain. Newly explained compositing and LPIPS details do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds robustness investigations of subject-count mismatches, multiple identities, missing object parts, lighting conflicts, and transfer across styles. Table 2 broadens quantitative assessment of the existing component ablations, including a full no-RoPE result row. The earlier attention-map and convergence analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify two random generation seeds per image/prompt and retain the same user-study sample size. Neither adds repeated-training-run information, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds Hunyuan ControlNet and Flux-Pinco results; Flux-Pinco reports OER values of 7.87% and 6.84% and VQAScore 0.918. The renamed HY-Pinco retains v1's numerical results. Table 2 adds metrics for existing ablations, including no-RoPE OER values of 290.44% and 68.64%, and Appendix G adds qualitative findings. These are additional results, not same-setting improvements over v1's Pinco.

M1.justification: v1 implements Pinco through subject cross-attention in Hunyuan-DiT. v2 adds an MM-DiT adaptation that concatenates latent and subject keys/values for subject-aware MM-attention (Section 4.1, Equation 3), applied to Flux's double-stream and single-stream blocks. This changes the attention procedure, rather than merely testing the unchanged implementation on another backbone.

P1.justification: v2 revises introductory and methodological wording, generalizes terminology from subject cross-attention to subject-aware attention, and renames the augmentation subsection. Author information, acknowledgments, and appendix organization also change. The main narrative structure remains, although unresolved citations appear in Appendix B.

P2.justification: v2 adds Flux architecture and special-case figures, revises the framework graphic, and expands or rearranges the main and appendix comparison grids. Table 1 gains backbone grouping, and the two earlier ablation tables become one expanded table. Several existing figures are merely relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: Citations expand to Flux/Flux-fill, ATA, salient-object-aware background generation, and additional generation, restoration, and safety research. The related-work taxonomy and central positioning against image-prompt adapters and ControlNet-style injection remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 3 newly defines the MM-DiT subject-aware attention operation using concatenated latent and subject keys/values. The diffusion loss and Hunyuan attention remain mathematically equivalent, while Equation 4 formalizes the already described feature fusion. No theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for Pinco's claimed portability through an explicit MM-DiT adaptation and comparisons against ControlNet on both Hunyuan and Flux backbones, addressing v1's reliance on a single Pinco backbone. Expanded ablation reporting and the new robustness and limitations sections make effectiveness and applicability more assessable. These gains outweigh the lost hardware, batch-size, and refiner disclosures and unresolved appendix citations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Pinco work. Their main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support matching retained, relocated, and newly added material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Flux-Pinco evaluation, expanded ablation results, and special-case experiments in Appendix G.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark comparisons, component ablations, a 31-participant user study, and appendix convergence and qualitative results.

results.title: Pinco: Position-induced Consistent Adapter for Diffusion Transformer in Foreground-conditioned Inpainting

C1.justification: The central contributions remain TanhNorm, STRing and progressive ratio decay, with the claim that p-MoD preserves baseline performance while reducing training and inference costs. The additional evaluations support these retained claims without redefining the principal contribution or proposed mechanism.

C2.justification: V2 adds discussion of OCR sensitivity, repeated scaling as an overflow mechanism, grounding performance losses, and the requirement for training or continued fine-tuning rather than training-free deployment. It removes v1's extensive argument that attention-score pruning is incompatible with FlashAttention. The earlier single-image applicability limitation is retained in Appendix C.3.

D1.justification: Training hyperparameters, hardware, encoder-freezing policies and code/data links are largely retained after relocation. However, v2 drops the detailed FastV pruning and attention-implementation settings, the explanation of retraining on released 779K rather than original 760K data, and the explicit MME normalization instruction. These are documentation losses, not established changes to the underlying settings.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original 14 benchmarks, adds VQAv2 to the main evaluation, and introduces visual grounding on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg in Appendix A.2. Grounding substantially extends task requirements beyond the earlier question-answering and multimodal-understanding evaluations. The training datasets remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's dense baselines and FastV comparison, v2 evaluates MQT and LLaVolta in Table 5; SparseVLM, VisionZip, PyramidDrop, FasterVLM, FreeVideoLLM, iLLaVA and LLaVA-PruMerge in Table 10; and concurrent γ-MoD in Table 11. These are substantial additions to the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: V2 adds a 13B-model evaluation and visual-grounding validation protocols using ACC@0.5. Figure 3 replaces the fixed 15% retention perturbation with retention-ratio sweeps across shallow, middle and deep layers. Ablation and efficiency tables also report different benchmark subsets, making their averages noncomparable across versions. The original 7B training recipe is retained.

E4.justification: V2's Table 3 adds a cumulative, equal-computation ablation of TanhNorm, STRing and PRD. Figure 3 expands the depth-redundancy investigation from one lowered retention setting to sensitivity curves. Conversely, v1's isolated STRing-removal row is no longer reported. The token-selection visualizations in Figures 5 and 6 retain the same evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. V2 adds results without introducing uncertainty estimation; its use of 'significantly' does not establish statistical testing.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive comparator, VQAv2, 13B, grounding and ablation results while preserving the shared main benchmark scores. Reported default KV-cache usage changes from 53.8% to 53.7%. TextVQA latency changes from 5191 to 519.1 ms for the baseline and 3680 to 368.0 ms for default p-MoD, without an explained timing-protocol change; these are revised values, not established speedups. V1's FastV latency and GPU-memory results are removed.

M1.justification: The architecture and three components remain, but Eqs. (2)-(4) replace the selected-token additive term X_i with T(X_i). V1's Figure 2 already depicts reweighting the transformer output, consistent with v2's equations. The PDFs do not resolve whether this represents an actual procedural change or correction of an inconsistent mathematical specification.

P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract, introduction and conclusion, reorders the experimental subsections, and promotes method comparisons into the main text. The appendix is substantially reorganized into experiments, visualization, discussion and implementation sections. Hardware information, limitations and PRD clipping are relocated; author and affiliation text also changes.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn from a four-bar experiment into retention-ratio curves, and Figure 1's radar display is updated. Main benchmark tables are regrouped from seven-plus-seven to ten-plus-five benchmarks, ablation tables are reorganized, and several comparison tables are added. The appendix layout changes substantially, while Figures 5 and 6 preserve their original image content.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens positioning around query-based compression, token merging and newer pruning methods. Appendix A.4 newly acknowledges concurrent γ-MoD and distinguishes its layer-selection approach from p-MoD. The earlier FlashAttention-based criticism and associated citations are removed, changing an important part of the comparison with prior work.

T1.justification: The selected-token definitions in Eqs. (2)-(4) change algebraically from adding X_i to adding T(X_i), rather than merely changing notation. The routing and cosine-decay definitions remain, and the unchanged clipping equation moves to Appendix D.3. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow comparison against alternative compression methods through broader comparisons, including γ-MoD, and strengthens component validation with cumulative ablations and retention sweeps.
