The 13B and grounding experiments better test applicability, while grounding losses and the training requirement receive explicit qualification. These gains outweigh the lost FastV timing/memory documentation, although unexplained latency revisions and stale equation/table references in the overflow discussion remain reporting weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe p-MoD and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Their shared methods and experiments can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds component ablations, additional compression-method comparisons, 13B-model evaluations and visual-grounding results.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, efficiency measurements, component ablations, token-retention experiments and a FastV comparison.

results.title: p-MoD: Building Mixture-of-Depths MLLMs via Progressive Ratio Decay

C1.justification: The central claims about single-image decomposition and compatible subject/style LoRAs remain. V2's introduction additionally claims cross-image composition and generalization to KOALA, extending applicability without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: V2 explains when generic versus detailed trigger phrases suffice, proposes why separately trained LoRAs can cross-combine, and attributes lower KOALA image quality to limited model capacity. The earlier limitation concerning highly abstract styles is retained and moved into the conclusion.

D1.justification: V2 supplies more explicit trigger-phrase annotations and guidance, discloses unlabeled user comparisons with arbitrary ordering, and adds the ablation-study interface. SDXL hyperparameters, block assignments, hardware timings, and project/data access information are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds cross-image composition, combining subject and style LoRAs learned from different images (Figures 6 and 19), extending v1's evaluation of decomposition and recombination from one image. Appendix B.4 also adds human-subject evaluations. Both versions still describe a 40-image collection.

E2.justification: The decomposition comparators remain DreamBooth-LoRA, Inspiration Tree, and B-LoRA. V2 expands recontextualization comparisons beyond v1's B-LoRA comparison by reporting preferences against all three methods. Figure 8 also adds B-LoRA outputs to the existing failure cases.

E3.justification: V2 adds component-wise user comparisons, controlled trigger-phrase tests, 20/30/40% column-selection experiments, and KOALA evaluations. The original SDXL budgets and eight-input, sixteen-sample alignment protocol remain. DreamBooth's stated style-training prompt changes from 'A subject in <s> style' to 'A <c> in <s> style'; this reporting revision does not establish rerunning existing comparisons.

E4.justification: V1 primarily supports component contributions through qualitative ablations. V2 adds component preference and alignment tables (Tables 3–4), subject/style trigger-phrase sensitivity tests (Figures 10–11), and column-fraction sensitivity tests (Figure 18). Existing failure analysis also gains a B-LoRA comparison.

E5.justification: Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run uncertainty estimates. The existing generation-sample protocol and seed-selection discussion are retained; the added user-study sample counts describe new evaluations rather than a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 2's alignment scores and Table 1's decomposition preferences remain identical. V2 adds recontextualization preferences of 98.10%, 79.17%, and 77.14% over DreamBooth-LoRA, Inspiration Tree, and B-LoRA, respectively, plus component results in Tables 3–4. Cross-image, KOALA, and sensitivity experiments substantially expand the reported findings.

M1.justification: The three separation mechanisms, losses, SDXL block assignments, and direct-addition inference are retained. V2 expresses the existing column fraction as N, retaining 30% for the main experiments. The additional applications do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: prompt construction moves into the problem setup, preliminaries and comparisons are condensed, experimental subsections are restructured, and limitations enter the conclusion. The supplement gains a contents list and reorders implementation details, experiments, and compute requirements.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is reformatted, qualitative panels are redistributed, and v1 Figures 6 and 12 are consolidated into v2 Figure 13. V2 expands Table 1, adds Tables 3–4, introduces application and sensitivity figures, and expands the user-study interface display.

R1.justification: V2 adds KOALA and DiT references and removes the LEGO discussion and citation. It also revises the characterization of B-LoRA's training and its contrast with UnZipLoRA. The broader literature positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: The low-rank formulation and Equations 1–5 are mathematically unchanged. V2 adds no theorem, proof, or substantive derivation; introducing N names an experimental hyperparameter.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the retained method: quantitative component ablations replace reliance on selected qualitative examples, while prompt and column-fraction tests address previously untested sensitivities. Separate recontextualization evaluation further supports the compatibility claim. Some interpretations remain overstated: M2 receives only 39.51% style preference over M1 despite claimed style improvement, and uncertainty estimates remain absent. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UnZipLoRA. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison, including matching material that was reorganized.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds quantitative ablations, sensitivity tests, recontextualization preferences, and additional application results.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-generation experiments, human preferences, alignment scores, qualitative ablations, and computational measurements.

results.title: UnZipLoRA: Separating Content and Style from a Single Image

C1.justification: The abstract, principal contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about descriptor fusion, generalization, efficiency, synthetic references and dataset identification. The introduction clarifies that the quoted dimensionality reductions concern feature dimensions without materially redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: Section 9 interprets unstructured-reference compression as a storage and computation tradeoff with some recall loss. Section 12 attributes remaining failures mainly to visual similarity between geographically distant places. These add applicability qualifications while retaining the original explanations concerning feature reinforcement, nearby-match disambiguation and low-dimensional descriptors.

D1.justification: A HOPS repository address replaces v1's promise of code upon acceptance. The supplement specifies AnyLoc's author-released weights, 49,152-dimensional representation and omission of PCA, and identifies SALAD and cosine matching for dataset identification. Section 3.3 clarifies that core results use no random projection. These are additional disclosures, not evidence of changed implementations.

E1.justification: Section 9 adds evaluation on Google Landmarks v2 micro, extending coverage from repeated route traversals to an unstructured collection with varying numbers of reference images per place. This substantially broadens the input environment tested. Dataset identification and the three original datasets were already covered in v1.

E2.justification: Figure 4 adds pooling and distance-matrix averaging to the dimensionality comparison. Tables 9–10 add one-image and ten-image dataset-identification baselines and maximum/median distance aggregation; minimum aggregation is also displayed and matches pooling. Table 8 adds a dimensionality-reduction compression comparator. Tables 5–7 supply the AnyLoc comparisons previously mentioned without results in v1.

E3.justification: The new Landmarks evaluation fuses 7–9 images per place, reducing 23,294 references to 3,103, and compares this with retaining all references at 1024 dimensions under a similar storage budget. Dataset-identification comparisons introduce one-reference and ten-reference sampling controls. These substantially extend the evaluation design; the original datasets' sampling counts and matching tolerances remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figures 5–10 expand dimensionality sensitivity analysis beyond v1's four-descriptor RobotCar Dusk example to all six main descriptors on six additional query sets. Figures 12–14 add successful and failed retrieval cases across the three original datasets, including failures where another method succeeds. These substantially expand sensitivity and error-analysis evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates. v2's randomly selected dataset-identification baselines are reported without variability or repetition information.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their values, but v2 adds extensive numerical and qualitative results. For example, AnyLoc on RobotCar Dusk achieves 84.0 R@1 with HOPS versus 69.7 for the best single reference. The new Landmarks comparison reports 69.7 for original references, 65.8 after HOPS compression and 59.7 with 1024-dimensional references. Section 4.3 also corrects the exception count from two to three, acknowledging CosPlace Night's already-tabulated 19.4 versus 21.2.

M1.justification: The descriptor summation, cosine-distance matching and optional Gaussian random projection remain unchanged. Section 3.3 clarifies that projection is used for the dimensionality experiment, while the supplement explains existing bundling applications. No new HOPS component or altered procedure is established.

P1.justification: The main section order and most wording remain intact. Changes include localized clarification of random projection, additional cross-references, the corrected outlier paragraph, publication headers and an organized supplementary narrative. The added scientific material is not accompanied by an extensive rewrite of the original paper.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–10 and Figures 5–14, including multi-panel sensitivity plots, a dataset-identification diagram and three qualitative image galleries. Figure 4 gains comparator curves and a revised legend, while Figure 3's caption specifies error units. These substantially expand and refine the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The related-work sections and 86-work bibliography are retained. Section 11 adds a focused comparison with the already-cited approaches in references 22 and 51, emphasizing differences in reference storage and query-descriptor computation. This modestly expands research positioning.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6, the quasi-orthogonality reasoning, complexity statements and Johnson–Lindenstrauss motivation are retained. The supplement adds no formal theorem, proof, assumption or mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's empirical support through multi-reference controls in the dimensionality plots, an unstructured compression benchmark, detailed dataset-identification comparisons and explicit failure examples. Previously referenced supplementary evidence becomes inspectable, making the benefits and limitations substantially easier to assess. Code access information and implementation clarifications further help reproducibility. Minor inconsistencies, such as Table 8's 8488/8448 descriptor dimensions, do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HOPS research, and their text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends after the references; v2 includes Supplementary Material, Sections 6–12. Supplementary additions below mean newly available content in the supplied PDFs, not necessarily newly conducted experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and supplies additional original results, including AnyLoc comparisons, Google Landmarks compression, dataset-identification baselines and qualitative retrieval examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original VPR experiments on RobotCar, Nordland and SFU-Mountain, dimensionality-reduction and synthetic-reference experiments, and dataset-identification outcomes.

results.title: A Hyperdimensional One Place Signature to Represent Them All: Stackable Descriptors For Visual Place Recognition

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the three selection principles, their adaptive collaboration, and competitive performance using limited data. The abstract and introduction update the headline from 100.8% to 101.3% of full-data performance with 15% data. Informativeness is also framed more explicitly around difficult tasks.

C2.justification: V2 replaces the cognitive-load and convergence motivations with explanations involving sample difficulty, feature rank, directional diversity, and training robustness. It adds interpretations of feature-backbone stability and alternative scoring functions. Appendix D.4 newly identifies failure on extended mathematical or programming instructions when reasoning steps are omitted. Future work shifts from surrogate-model architectural features to interleaved video and audio data.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code-and-data repository link and expands GPU distance-computation, pipelining, and clustering implementation details. It revises the normalization description while retaining the principal hardware, batch-size, and epoch disclosures. Conversely, v1 Appendix D.1's explicit description of GPT-4 answer comparison and rating is no longer provided.

E1.justification: V2 adds Virgo training data and evaluations on MMMU, MathVerse, and MathVision, substantially extending coverage of difficult visual and mathematical reasoning. The original instruction datasets and OwlEval remain. MM-Vet and LLaVA-Wild are incorporated into the main table but already appeared in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: V2 adds COINCIDE and ICONS to the central LLaVA comparison in Table 1, reporting their results with 133k selected examples. Table 10 additionally compares against QVQ-72B-preview and InternVL2.5-78B. These expand the substantive comparator set; the change from E2LN to EL2N is only a name correction.

E3.justification: V2 introduces 13B and 72B model settings and controlled 1%-data addition experiments. Table 2 replaces POPE with MMMU, while aggregate reporting expands to 13 benchmarks. Table 6 changes the runtime comparison from 15% to 7.5% selected data. Appendix C.2 also reports 13 task categories instead of 10, without establishing that the underlying 665k examples changed. The original LoRA training budgets remain documented.

E4.justification: Table 3 replaces leave-one-principle-out ablations with principle-only tests and separate removals of adaptive weighting and allocation. V2 adds feature-backbone and model-scale robustness tests, weight-ratio sensitivity, quantitative principle evaluations, alternative scoring comparisons, and qualitative examples (Tables 8, 9, 11 and Figure 8). Figure 5 removes the MiniGPT4 selection-ratio sweep and adds a TIVE comparison. Existing noise perturbations and human evaluation are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report OwlEval response-score variance through Figure 7's circle sizes. Neither supplies repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional experiments do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive benchmark, comparator, scalability, and ablation results. For example, Table 10 reports Qwen2-VL-7B averages of 36.2 with DataTailor's 15% subset versus 35.8 with full data. LLaVA-Wild scores also change: full-data/7.5%-DataTailor values are 84.3/85.0 in v1 Table 7 and 67.9/69.3 in v2 Table 1, without an explanation of the scoring difference. Most original Table 1 scores merely undergo rounding; the headline 100.8% to 101.3% change uses an expanded benchmark aggregate.

M1.justification: The reported uniqueness score replaces averaging by cluster size with normalization by total cluster informativeness, and the representative score gains the same informativeness denominator (v1 Equations 3 and 5; v2 Equations 4 and 6). These refine scoring within the retained SVE, clustering, adaptive weighting, and task-allocation framework. Ward clustering and nearest-neighbor-chain optimization were already documented in v1.

P1.justification: The method motivation, related-work discussion, and experimental interpretation undergo substantial rewriting. The appendix is reorganized around principle definitions, expanded clustering subsections, and additional analyses; human evaluation moves from D.2 to D.5. Terminology, the incorrect inter-cluster uniqueness heading, and author/affiliation information are also revised.

P2.justification: Figure 1 switches from absolute MME scores to relative performance, Figures 2 and 3 gain annotations, and Figure 5 changes its panels and plotted metrics. Table 1 absorbs the earlier appendix's open-ended evaluation and adds columns and comparators. Several new tables and the substantial qualitative Figure 8 are added; the threshold table is relocated and restructured.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion adds substantive comparisons with ICONS and COINCIDE and expands its contrast with the already cited INSTRUCTMINING. Additional references support the new geometric reasoning and benchmarks, while the cognitive-load citation is removed. The overall positioning as collaborative, three-principle data selection remains.

T1.justification: V2 introduces formal local-margin and Wasserstein-based definitions of uniqueness and representativeness, plus a stated Ward-clustering monotonicity theorem and partition rule. It removes v1 Appendix B.2's gradient-descent/Taylor-expansion convergence derivation and replaces it with a spectral-concentration argument. These substantially revise the mathematical rationale, beyond restating the existing SVE formula.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the selection criteria and their applicability. Separate adaptive-component tests, alternative scoring comparisons, and larger-model reasoning experiments address v1's limited evidence for design choices and scalability. Contemporary comparators, explicit failure limitations, and a code/data link also improve assessment and usability. Unexplained LLaVA-Wild score revisions and unchanged uncertainty reporting remain weaknesses, but the additional targeted validation provides a substantial net benefit. The higher headline aggregate alone does not establish improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DataTailor and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices. The expanded and reorganized supplementary material can be matched reliably across versions.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds larger-model experiments, mathematical reasoning results, and further analyses of the selection criteria.

before.justification: V1 reports original data-selection and fine-tuning experiments, ablations, robustness tests, runtime measurements, and an OwlEval human evaluation.

results.title: Mastering Collaborative Multi-modal Data Selection: A Focus on Informativeness, Uniqueness, and Representativeness

C1.justification: Both versions claim an instance-level open-set bias-identification framework and a foundation-model-assisted strategy for learning bias-invariant representations, with effectiveness across four datasets. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain this scientific scope; the new experiments principally add support for existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly identifies sparse ImageNet9 tag-defined groups as an evaluation limitation, interprets additional dataset-specific bias patterns, and adds guidance about hyperparameter sensitivity in Supplementary Section 5. The gradient-starvation explanation and limitations concerning tagging vocabulary and sensitive-data applications largely remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds class-specific irrelevant-tag inventories for all four datasets (Tables 17–20), an implementation-availability statement naming VB-Mitigатор, baseline hyperparameters, and encoder variants such as OpenCLIP ViT-L-14. Most existing training details move into the main text. The reported ImageNet hardware also changes from RTX-4090 to A100; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: The four image datasets, seven ImageNet9 variants, and two-moon scenario remain. V2 presents its main CelebA task as hair-color prediction with gender bias, supported by blonde/non-blonde tag tables; v1 evaluates gender prediction with hair-color bias. That earlier task remains in v2 supplementary Table 13. The task descriptions are not clearly reconciled.

E2.justification: V2 adds SD and FLAC-B to the retained ImageNet9 comparison (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 3). Its new open-set comparisons also evaluate a common LfF, JTT, SD, Debian, and FLAC-B panel across three datasets, substantially broadening comparator participation. Earlier closed-set comparators, including SoftCon, DISC, and bias-aware methods, remain in the supplement.

E3.justification: V2 adds class-specific, tag-defined open-set evaluation: vanilla-model accuracy identifies biased tags, samples form two groups per class, and epochs are selected using overall accuracy without bias information (Section 4.4). ImageNet9 is exempted because some groups contain fewer than four samples. A separate new protocol measures tag-filter precision and recall against manual ground truth.

E4.justification: V2 adds a focused GPT-4o filtering diagnostic (Table 9) and broader class-specific tag analyses, while removing v1's ImageNet9 aligned/conflicting case-study results (Table 6). Existing component ablations, projection-accuracy and vocabulary analyses, two-moon demonstration, and hyperparameter study are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions state that experiments use five different random seeds and retain the same plus/minus reporting practice (v1 Appendix A.2.2; v2 Section 4.3). Additional result rows do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation procedure, repeated-run policy, or significance test.

E6.justification: V2 Table 2 adds open-set worst-group/average accuracies of 66.7/81.4 for CelebA, 75.4/87.5 for Waterbirds, and 84.4/89.3 for UrbanCars; Table 9 adds filtering precision/recall. These are new-protocol results, not gains over v1's closed-set scores. MAVias's ImageNet9 scores remain unchanged, but added baselines alter margins: MIXED-NEXT is 88.26 versus SD's 87.56. V1's Table 6 subgroup results are removed.

M1.justification: The tagging, LLM filtering, vision-language encoding, additive-logit training, and inference procedures remain unchanged. V1's regularization term is renamed the logit alignment term in v2, with the same formula. More specific encoder names do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized into separate dataset, architecture, implementation, protocol, comparison, and ablation sections. Existing appendix material moves into the main text, closed-set comparisons are condensed, and the appendix becomes separately structured supplementary material. Introduction and related-work passages are edited, with BLA/BLU and regularization terminology revised.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn as a pipeline and Figure 2 is restyled. The dog-tag visualization is replaced by broader tag tables; new comparison and diagnostic tables are added, and closed-set results are consolidated and relocated. Typography and layout change throughout. V2 Table 20 overflows the final page, visibly clipping part of the Instrument and Primate lists.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a focused distinction between a priori instance-level filtering and validation-based discovery or subgroup mitigation, and revises the comparison with OpenBias. References add OpenCLIP, VB-Mitigатор, and several bias-related works, while replacing the original CLIP citation. The overall open-set research positioning remains.

T1.justification: V1 Appendix A.1 and v2 Supplementary Section 1 retain the same gradient argument and unbiased-distribution/logit-addition derivation. Assumptions and mathematical reasoning are unchanged apart from numbering, notation, and terminology. The new grouping procedure is an evaluation protocol rather than a new theoretical result.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central open-set claim, previously assessed largely through predefined-bias benchmarks, by adding tag-defined group comparisons across three datasets, stronger ImageNet9 comparators, and a manual-ground-truth check of tag filtering. Tag inventories and implementation information also improve scrutiny and reproducibility. Inconsistent CelebA task descriptions, stale introductory performance margins, and the clipped final table are drawbacks, but the gain in empirical support is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MAVias and provide the main text, experiments, mathematical derivations, and appendices needed for comparison. V2's final tag table extends beyond the visible page, but its embedded text is recoverable, so this layout defect does not leave an evidence gap.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds open-set comparisons across three datasets and an evaluation of GPT-4o tag filtering against manually established ground truth.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification experiments on four image datasets, component ablations, and an appendix experiment using a biased two-moon distribution.

results.title: MAVias: Mitigate any Visual Bias

C1.justification: The central contribution and abstract's performance and speed claims remain. The introduction newly claims comparable multimodal behavior, while RQ2 drops fast convergence and focuses specifically on inference efficiency.

C2.justification: Appendix D distinguishes inference advantages from training convergence and tokenizer pretraining costs. Appendix G explains recovery failures through missing failure demonstrations and hesitation through short observation histories. Appendix A shifts from underdeveloped multimodal potential to claimed comparable expressiveness, while questioning how strongly existing benchmarks require multimodality.

D1.justification: Most training recipes in Appendix H are relocated from v1. New disclosures include the three-dimensional task embedding, argmax versus top-3 sampling, exclusion of visual encoders from parameter counts, and training hardware and resource accounting. Appendix K also documents AprilTag-based state estimation for the added real-world experiments.

E1.justification: v3 adds Push-T for contact-rich, multimodal pushing and FurnitureBench assembly tasks One Leg, Round Table, and Lamp, including physical One Leg execution on a Franka Panda. These substantially broaden task requirements and real-world embodiment coverage while retaining the original benchmarks.

E2.justification: Appendix F newly evaluates VQ-BeT and Consistency Policy against CARP on Kitchen and Push-T; their citations in v1 were not evaluated comparisons. Figure 12 also introduces LSTM-GMM into the data-efficiency comparison. These additions materially strengthen comparison with efficient alternatives.

E3.justification: New protocols include 30–200-demonstration subsampling, K=1–6 scale experiments with feature-map expansion, 1,024 FurnitureBench rollouts per task, and single-task Nut-Assembly/Threading evaluation using first-contact position errors. Push-T visualization uses top-3 sampling. These extend evaluation design; the original benchmarks retain their principal horizons and training budgets.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's trajectory/refinement visualization, v3 adds scale sensitivity, joint versus per-dimension tokenizer reconstruction analysis, data-efficiency tests, training and inference cost breakdowns, recovery and hesitation failure cases, and insertion-precision analysis. These directly investigate design choices, efficiency, and failure conditions.

E5.justification: Tables 8–9 newly report means and variances of first-contact position errors, adding descriptive dispersion statistics. The original top-three-checkpoint averaging and five timing runs remain; neither version provides systematic multi-seed confidence intervals or significance testing.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial result sets for the new benchmarks, baselines, ablations, and precision studies. For example, Figure 5 reports Push-T success rates of 0.88 for CARP, 0.87 for DP-C, and 0.84 for DP-T. Most original benchmark values remain, but Table 3 changes DP-T's Kitchen p2 score from 0.99 to 0.98.

M1.justification: The per-dimension multi-scale VQ-VAE, residual quantization, GPT-style next-scale predictor, and training losses remain unchanged. Collective decoding of all scales clarifies the residual aggregation already present in v1's Algorithm 1; the PDFs do not establish a redesigned method.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most method exposition remain intact. v3 tightens prose, clarifies decoding and efficiency terminology, condenses related work, and consolidates existing experimental implementation paragraphs in Appendix H. Much of the appendix expansion consists of new scientific content rather than rewriting retained material.

P2.justification: v3 adds numerous analytical plots, comparison tables, failure illustrations, and assembly visualizations. It also merges the original single-task and multi-task setup figures into Figure 4, combines real-world setup and results in Figure 7, and relocates the original UR5 execution visualization to Appendix K.

R1.justification: v3 adds FurnitureBench and From Imitation to Refinement references for the assembly experiments and explicitly discusses comparison with VQ-BeT and Consistency Policy, both already cited in v1. The broader positioning around VAR-inspired autoregression and diffusion policies remains stable.

T1.justification: The mathematical substance of Equations 1–9 and the residual quantization algorithm is retained. Prediction notation and explanatory corrections do not introduce new assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 largely supported CARP through benchmark scores and trajectory examples. v3 substantially strengthens validation through efficient competing baselines, design ablations, cost accounting, multimodal pushing, another physical robot, and explicit failure analysis. These additions make the central performance–efficiency claims more assessable and better qualified. Limited uncertainty reporting and unexplained differences between Nut-Assembly scores in Tables 4 and 8 remain, but do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CARP and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds Push-T, FurnitureBench, Franka robot experiments, ablations, and additional analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation benchmarks, trajectory analyses, inference measurements, and real-world UR5e manipulation results.

results.title: CARP: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Coarse-to-Fine Autoregressive Prediction

C1.justification: V2 strengthens the abstract and introduction from a competitive generalist policy to the first generalist policy surpassing expert models, and explicitly claims state-of-the-art results on simulated and real-world datasets. The headline CALVIN sequence-length claim changes from 1.7–3.3 to 1.7–3.5, expanding the claimed achievement and applicability.

C2.justification: V2 extends the alignment explanation by arguing that camera changes alter 2D features while preserving 3D scene features, and interprets RoboFlamingo's results as showing an inability to align input space. It also attributes physical-task advantages to stronger 3D reasoning. The existing moderate-training-scale qualification and interpretation of imperfect auxiliary predictions remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds substantial physical-system documentation: UR3/Dalu hardware, gripper and camera models, hand-eye calibration, point-cloud supervision, ROS1, and RTX 3090 operation. It newly specifies a four-billion-parameter bf16 model and RT-1 preprocessing. Reported joint-training time changes from 130 to about 50 hours under the revised experiment, and the repository pointer changes. Existing appendix hyperparameters remain.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates five simulation datasets. V2 retains CALVIN, Meta-World, LIBERO, and RoboCasa, adds RT-1 training data with SIMPLER evaluation on three task families, and adds ten physical UR3 manipulation tasks. RoboMimic results disappear, although its dataset documentation remains.

E2.justification: V2 adds jointly trained RoboFlamingo comparisons across four simulation datasets, π0 and π-Fast on LIBERO, DTP on CALVIN, and GR00T-N1-2B+IDM on RoboCasa. New RT-1 comparisons include RT-X, Octo, OpenVLA, and HPT; physical experiments compare RoboUniView and RoboFlamingo. The IBC comparison disappears with RoboMimic, while the original CALVIN/OpenVLA comparison survives in appendix Table 6.

E3.justification: The main joint-training configuration now uses the DiT head, and the alignment study is described as four-dataset training. New RT-1 experiments introduce camera-parameter supplementation and missing-wrist-image masking. Physical evaluation uses 100 demonstrations per task and ten trials per task with manual resets. The original single-frame OpenVLA protocol is retained in the appendix.

E4.justification: The existing ablation program gains an Image-plus-UVFormer configuration without occupancy supervision and an explicit MLP-versus-DiT comparison in Table 2. Table 3 extends the retained alignment analysis with aligned and unaligned RoboFlamingo controls. The RoboMimic alignment results are omitted; the other original proposed-model alignment scores remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report point success rates and average sequence lengths without independent training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new physical trial counts specify evaluation sample sizes rather than a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 reports substantially different benchmark and task-level results under its revised configuration: RoboCasa is 47.4% in Table 1 versus 30.6% in v1, with the older score retained in alignment Table 3. Table 2 retains the 3.31 MLP result and adds 3.51 for DiT. New results include 60.0% on RT-1 and 82.5%, 70.0%, and 46.6% across physical-task difficulty groups. These are not same-setting version-to-version gains.

M1.justification: V1 uses an MLP action decoder. V2 Section 2.2 and Figure 4 introduce a CogACT-style DiT alternative, which is used for the main joint-training results and explicitly compared with the MLP in Table 2. This changes a central action-generation component; UVFormer, MIM, and the auxiliary decoders remain.

P1.justification: The main narrative is substantially reorganized: Related Work and the OpenVLA comparison move to the appendix, alignment receives a separate experimental subsection, and the conclusion is rewritten as Conclusion and Outlook. The abstract and results discussion are revised, alongside the model renaming and author-header changes. Much of the technical exposition is retained.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview chart, revises architecture diagrams to display the DiT alternative, adds the physical-task montage, and updates the rollout montage. Benchmark Table 1 is reorganized, Table 2 gains configurations, and alignment results receive a separate display. New physical and RT-1 tables substantially expand the presentation; the unchanged OpenVLA table moves to the appendix.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to CogACT, π0, FAST, GR00T N1, and DTP, while removing MindBench and IBC. It adds an RT-1-X versus RT-1 argument about heterogeneous-data fusion. The dedicated related-work discussion otherwise remains largely unchanged after relocation.

T1.justification: The mathematical content of Equations 1–14, the losses, coordinate transformations, and EADM/CRMM/PCM definitions is retained. The DiT addition introduces no new formal derivation, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1's simulation-only validation and limited generalist comparisons through the ten-task physical study, jointly trained RoboFlamingo controls, and additional action-head and alignment ablations. These substantially strengthen practical validation and support for the design choices. Lost RoboMimic results, absent uncertainty estimates, and stale documentation such as Figure 9's RoboMimic caption remain weaknesses. The improvement rests on stronger empirical support, rather than treating scores from changed configurations as controlled performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RoboData and multimodal manipulation framework, renamed from RoboMM to RoboTron-Mani. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 reports original RoboTron-Mani evaluations, additional ablations, RT-1/SIMPLER results, and a ten-task physical-robot experiment, alongside retained earlier results.

before.justification: V1 reports original RoboMM benchmark evaluations, component and alignment ablations, and an OpenVLA comparison in Tables 1–3, with task-level results in the appendix.

results.title: RoboTron-Mani: All-in-One Multimodal Large Model for Robotic Manipulation

C1.justification: The abstract and six central multiscale properties retain their meaning. The conclusion changes from acknowledging highest-resolution AR generation underperformance to claiming similar text-to-image performance and improved class-conditional generation. This extends the performance claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix A adds explanations for reconstruction–generation tradeoffs and hypothesizes that larger wavelet supports cause padding and interpatch information leakage. Section 5.5 qualifies broader baseline comparisons through architectural and training differences, including VAR's larger tokenizer training dataset. These extend the retained spectral and multiscale interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 adds extensive implementation information for the class-conditional variants, including dimensions, dropout, vocabulary size, learning rates, loss weights, batch sizes, training duration, and adversarial-training onset. Appendix B.1 revises reconstruction specifications. Appendix B.2 newly discloses guidance scale 3.0 and no reranking for text-to-image generation; this disclosure alone does not establish a procedural change.

E1.justification: V2 adds class-conditional ImageNet generation at 256×256 and 512×512 in Section 5.5. ImageNet previously supported reconstruction experiments only. ImageNet, WebLI, and MS-COCO remain the datasets; 512×512 reconstruction and 16×16-input upsampling already appeared in v1.

E2.justification: V2 Table 3 introduces class-conditional comparisons against AR-ViT-VQGAN, RQ-VAE, DQ-VAE, LlamaGen-L, and VAR. Several were discussed in v1 but had no reported comparison against SIT. V2 Table 1 also adds a reproduced ViT-VQGAN row alongside the reported and no-logit-laplace baselines.

E3.justification: The reported reconstruction configuration changes from Base transformers with 12 layers and 768-dimensional features to Small transformers with 8 layers and 512-dimensional features. Table 2's generation hardware changes from TPU v5e to v6e. New class-conditional protocols introduce 650M and 350M configurations, different guidance settings, and training budgets detailed in Appendix B.3.

E4.justification: Appendix A and Table 5 substantially replace the ablation design. V1 tests entropy regularization, codebook sharing, transformer parameter sharing, and model size. V2 adds vocabulary-size, sequence-length, and Haar/LeGall5/3/CDF9/7 comparisons while removing those component ablations and retaining only part of the scale-causal attention study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeat counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Results remain scalar estimates without reported uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 replace many results under revised model or hardware settings; for example, 256×256 AR-SIT-SCD-4 FID changes from 13.7 to 12.6, which is not a controlled cross-version gain. New results include AR-SIT-4 FID 6.95 at 256×256 and AR-SIT-5* FID 5.97 at 512×512. V2 omits the former 512×512 SIT-4 result and the lowest-resolution baseline FIDs. Table 4's upsampling scores are unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 4 replaces separate transformer parameters and codebooks for every scale with approximation-versus-details groups; AR token embeddings and prediction heads change accordingly. V1's entropy regularizer is removed from the stated objective. The new AR-SIT-4* variant additionally introduces GeGLU, axial 2D RoPE, and scale-dependent loss weighting.

P1.justification: The overall narrative and much of the prose are retained. V2 labels the introductory properties P.1–P.6 and cross-references them, introduces ADTransformer terminology, merges high-resolution reconstruction into Section 5.1, and reorganizes the implementation appendix. These are localized editorial and structural revisions.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn for approximation/details parameter sharing. Table 1 incorporates the former high-resolution Table 3, while a new class-conditional Table 3 and Figures 9–10 are introduced. Table 5 is substantially redesigned, several sample grids are replaced, and retained appendix figures are reordered and relocated.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds targeted discussion of FAR, DQ-VAE, QG-VAE, and SEMANTICIST. Appendix A connects the new analyses to additional compression–generation and wavelet literature. The central positioning—operating on input DWT coefficients rather than learned latent features—remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 revises the formal quantizer definition from scale-specific Q_s to separate approximation and details mappings, and removes the defined entropy regularizers. The DWT background, patchification equations, and autoregressive likelihood reasoning remain substantively unchanged; neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical case beyond v1's narrow generative comparisons. It adds a matched class-conditional comparison—FID 6.95 versus the reproduced baseline's 8.37—broader comparisons with explicit limitations, and actual 512×512 generation where v1 demonstrated only reconstruction. New sensitivity analyses and detailed implementation specifications improve interpretability and reproducibility. Some direct component ablations are lost, and changed settings prevent simple cross-version performance claims, but the added controlled validation provides a substantial overall benefit.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Spectral Image Tokenizer by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports original reconstruction and text-conditioned generation results, revised ablations, and new class-conditional ImageNet generation experiments at 256×256 and 512×512.

before.justification: V1 reports original ImageNet reconstruction experiments, MS-COCO generation and upsampling results, editing examples, and tokenizer ablations.

results.title: Spectral Image Tokenizer

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds reconstruction and classification gains, including the 16%/23% headline claims, and sensitivity to small pixels. V2 removes classification and those quantified headline claims, retains the importance of diffraction-aware optimization, and makes interferometric/freeform applicability a main contribution. This substantially changes the claimed scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of defocus-related sampling failures and why diffraction differences matter less for aberration-limited natural images than for high-frequency inputs. New Section 4.7 identifies limitations from strong aberrations and poorly defined focal/pupil geometry, including reference-sphere sampling problems. V1's pixel-size and classification feature-extraction interpretations are omitted.

D1.justification: V2 replaces a planned code release with a reported public repository and newly documents vectorization, PyTorch checkpointing, paraxial exit-pupil estimation, and sensor resizing to maintain FoV. Hardware wavelength and incidence angles become explicit. Conversely, v1's triplet glass identities and freeform B-spline implementation details are not retained.

E1.justification: DIV2K reconstruction remains, but v1's ten-class ImageNet classification task is removed. V2 adds Fizeau surface recovery and extends optical test conditions to 35°/40° off-axis PSFs. The existing freeform study is reworked from reference-height-map recovery into target-pattern design.

E2.justification: V2 Figure 6 introduces evaluated comparisons with Zemax-FFT, the Airy disk, Yang et al.'s ray-wave model, Wei et al., and Chen et al., using Zemax-Huygens as reference. These renderer comparisons were absent from v1. V2 Figure 11 also adds a ray-trained comparator to the freeform experiment.

E3.justification: The main reconstruction evaluation replaces the triplet pixel-size sweep with a singlet/triplet/six-aspheric lens grid and replaces curvature cosine similarity with RRMSE. V1's training-versus-dense-testing interpolation study is removed; its supplementary measurement-RMSE evaluation becomes a FoV-stratified SSIM study retaining the 969-PSF reference. V2 also introduces a renderer accuracy, ray-count, and runtime benchmark.

E4.justification: V2 adds comparative defocus/high-angle stress tests and a natural-versus-sparse-image spectral analysis, and revises interpolation sensitivity analysis across FoVs and lens complexities. V1's Grad-CAM++ analysis, pixel-size PSF study, F-number training trajectories, wave/ray forward-backward timing curves, and mesh-versus-B-spline ablation are absent.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, reproducibility seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The retained Monte Carlo ray sampling does not constitute new uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V1 Table 1 reports triplet wave/ray RMSE of 0.02040/0.02406 at 0.1 mm aperture and 1 micrometer pixels; v2 Table 1 reports 0.106/0.148 for its 0.1 mm triplet comparison. Reported objectives and settings differ, preventing matched-setting gain/loss claims. V2 adds renderer and application results and hardware SSIM of 0.781/0.853 on/off axis, while classification and several appendix result series disappear.

M1.justification: The core ray-wave renderer and PSF interpolation remain unchanged. The reported reconstruction objective changes its MSE term to RMSE while retaining perceptual loss. V2 Section 4.6 also specifies an adaptation that coherently accumulates wavelets across scene points for interferometry; freeform optimization itself already existed in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten and condensed. The classification section and separate supplementary structure disappear; freeform work is reworked into an Applications subsection, and Limitations is added. Retained method explanations and captions also receive substantial editing.

P2.justification: V2 adds a first-page results illustration, a multi-renderer PSF matrix, spectral analysis, and Fizeau/freeform panels. It redraws the lens comparison as an overlay and restructures the experimental tables. Classification heatmaps and many supplementary displays disappear; core method diagrams and hardware PSF panels are largely retained with revised placement and captions.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 substantially repositions the work around competing simulators' defocus accuracy, sampling costs, and differentiability. V2 adds field-tracing, generalized-Debye, and interferometry references while removing classification-related citations and DiffuserCam. Yang's preprint-to-conference bibliographic update represents the same prior work.

T1.justification: The optical-path-length, Rayleigh-Sommerfeld PSF, and isoplanatic interpolation equations (1–7), assumptions, and derivation are retained. The added implementation and application explanations introduce no new formal theorem, proof, or analytical derivation.

The spectral analysis and explicit limitations also clarify applicability. Although classification and several training-level diagnostics are lost, the later version substantially strengthens support for its central physical-modeling claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same simulator and research work, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures. V1 includes supplementary Sections 6–9; v2 has no appended supplement but reworks some corresponding experiments into its main text. The supplied material supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original reconstruction, simulator benchmarking, hardware comparisons, Fizeau interferometry, and freeform optimization results.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction, ImageNet classification, optical simulation, hardware validation, and supplementary freeform surface-recovery results.

C1.justification: v2 specifies a 10% MVBench gain in the abstract/introduction, whereas v1's introduction describes up to 10% improvement to backbone VLLMs more generally. The conclusion replaces its explicit SOTA assertion with effectiveness and limitations, although SOTA language remains elsewhere. The four central contributions are retained.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the earlier eight-frame/eight-token optimum discussion with interpretations of frame-count saturation and a 512-token performance plateau. It adds explanations of temperature and merging effects, Q-Former versus Resampler behavior, and the accuracy–efficiency tradeoff of CLS features. New qualifications address fixed frame-count limits and stronger models' larger training datasets; the earlier multi-round and temporal-order caveats largely move to the supplement.

D1.justification: Supplementary Tables 5–6 and Section 7 add training-data composition, source attribution, benchmark statistics and setup details, including EVA-CLIP, 768 preliminary tokens and 32 selected frames with 32 spatial tokens each. Model sizes and computational costs are also newly reported. The existing training recipe is relocated, not newly introduced; some details are lost, including v1's open-ended grading description and explicit activation-free projection specification.

E1.justification: The main training datasets and scored video/image benchmark suites are retained. Supplementary Figures 7–10 add qualitative evaluation of an AI-generated video and multi-turn video conversations, extending the demonstrated input and interaction scenarios. Next-QA appears only in Table 6's dataset summary; no corresponding results establish its evaluation.

E2.justification: Table 1 removes VideoChatGPT, adds Sharegpt4Video, and adds VideoChat2 participation on VNBench and VideoMME. Supplementary Table 9 introduces comparisons with InternVideo2, InternVL2, LLaVA-OV and Qwen2VL; Table 10 compares latency with Qwen2VL. Tables 4 and 7 also introduce alternative selection architectures and frame features.

E3.justification: Section 3.2 changes the stated temperature from 0.5 to 0.1. Figure 3 replaces the earlier 4–16-frame sweep with 2–32-frame/token sweeps and explicitly evaluates VideoMME-Medium, adding controlled temperature, similarity-threshold and token-budget experiments. New protocols include eight-frame VideoLLaMA2 feature probes and latency measurements for 4-, 8- and 12-minute videos. The original two-stage training recipe is retained in supplementary Section 7.1.

E4.justification: The component ablation in Table 3 is retained, but Figure 3 substantially revises the sensitivity analysis and removes the earlier image-token-count sweep. Added analyses test temperature, merging threshold, token budget, Q-Former versus Resampler, alternative frame features including OCR/counting performance, and frame-count sensitivity across video durations. Supplementary Figures 6–10 add qualitative case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Reported B-VLLM scores change substantially: Table 1 gives MVBench 49.2 to 50.8, VNBench 13.8 to 22.6 and VideoMME-Long 44.4 to 47.9. Changes are mixed: Table 2 gives MME 1504 to 1455 and VizWiz 46.5 to 45.1. Numerous additional comparison, sensitivity and efficiency results appear. These are revised reported outcomes, not established same-setting gains, given the method and setting revisions.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 adds an explicit step restoring selected frames' temporal order using the selection matrix. The frame-selection, temporal-merging, spatial-sampling and optional spatial-merging components otherwise remain unchanged. The supplementary temporal-order limitation is not reconciled with this added step.

P1.justification: The abstract and selected introductory and discussion passages are edited. Implementation is condensed, training details move to the supplement, and limitations are redistributed between Section 5.4 and supplementary Section 8.6. Despite these organizational refinements, the main section sequence, method exposition and much of the benchmark narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is substantially redesigned with additional heatmaps and a token-budget curve. Figure 4 gains explicit frame-selection timelines, while supplementary Figure 5 and Figures 6–10 add sensitivity and conversation displays. Tables 4–10 are new; existing tables also change caption placement, styling and placement within the document.

R1.justification: v2 adds CLS-token literature, training-source references and citations concerning other vision applications, while removing the RegNet reference. The supplement adds brief positioning against newer, larger-data VLLMs. The principal related-work taxonomy and iterative-token-merging novelty assertion remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5, the Gumbel-Softmax reasoning, cosine-threshold duplicate definition and averaging rules are retained. Neither version supplies additional theorems, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v1 offered limited evidence for its specific selection mechanisms and accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. v2 substantially strengthens their assessment through controlled alternatives in Tables 4 and 7, expanded sensitivity experiments, computational comparisons and previously unavailable dataset/setup details. Newer-baseline comparisons and explicit CLS/frame-count limitations also improve perspective. Latency protocols remain underspecified and some text–table and temporal-order inconsistencies persist, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in methodological scrutiny and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same B-VLLM framework and contain readable text, equations, figures and tables. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 additionally includes supplementary Sections 7–9. All supplied pages support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds architecture comparisons, sensitivity analyses, computational measurements and qualitative evaluations, including supplementary results.

before.justification: v1 reports original video and image benchmark results, component ablations and token/frame sensitivity experiments in Tables 1–3 and Figure 3.

results.title: B-VLLM: A Vision Large Language Model with Balanced Spatio-Temporal Tokens

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion emphasize preservation of spectral properties rather than only symmetry and positive definiteness. The conclusion extends demonstrated applicability to LLM pretraining. The central Cholesky-quantization, error-feedback, memory-efficiency, novelty, and convergence claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds spectral-fidelity and computational-cost explanations. Section 5.1 changes partial support for the eigenvalue assumption into an implementation-guarantee claim, although the added positivity criterion is conditional. The untested ImageNet-ViT limitation is replaced with boundaries involving other tasks, and Appendix C.3 acknowledges shortened LLM training.

D1.justification: V2 Appendix C.3 and Table 11 document LLaMA architecture dimensions, precision, training budgets, and gradient accumulation, alongside ViT-Base training details. Appendix C.2 specifies synthetic-matrix generation and eigenvalue ranges, and the hardware description adds the A100's 80GB capacity. Existing augmentation and memory explanations are largely relocated rather than newly disclosed.

E1.justification: V2 extends evaluation from image classification to LLaMA pretraining on C4 and adds synthetic ill-conditioned matrix tests. CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet classification remain. ViT-Base on ImageNet expands model configurations within retained task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 8 adds evaluated RMSprop, RMSprop plus 32-bit Shampoo, and RMSprop plus vanilla 4-bit Shampoo comparisons. SGDM/AdamW comparison families otherwise remain. Newly cited ReLoRA, GaLore, and Wang et al.'s 4-bit Shampoo are not separately evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: New protocols include LLaMA-130M/350M/1B evaluation using perplexity, bfloat16, 10K/10K/2K training steps, and effective batch size 512; ViT-Base/ImageNet training; and NRE/AE tests on synthetic and recorded preconditioners. V1 Appendix C.1 specifies error-feedback momentum 0.9 for CNNs and 0.95 for ViTs, whereas v2 C.3 specifies 0.95 throughout. This is a reported setting change, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct quantization-fidelity analyses on synthetic and real preconditioners (Tables 1 and 10), a toy matrix illustrating loss of positive definiteness (Table 9), a joint momentum-coefficient sensitivity sweep (Table 7), and RMSprop applicability testing (Table 8). Existing CQ/error-feedback and off-diagonal quantization comparisons remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The 100 synthetic matrices in v2 constitute a new evaluation sample, not repeated-training uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds C4, ViT-Base/ImageNet, fidelity, sensitivity, and RMSprop results. Matched ViT-Small/CIFAR-100 accuracies change from 78.21/76.50/76.76 to 77.95/77.34/77.74 for 32-bit/CQ/CQ+EF (v1 Table 1; v2 Table 3). Tiny-ImageNet CQ+EF scores change from 61.91 to 62.81 for Swin-Tiny and 57.45 to 57.51 for ViT-Small. ResNet-50 CQ+EF memory changes from 11455.2 to 11445.2 MB. CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet timing results are removed.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same Cholesky quantization, error-feedback updates, triangular storage, inverse-root computation, and preconditioned optimization procedure. Additional model and base-optimizer experiments do not introduce a new method component; the changed momentum setting is an experimental-setting revision.

P1.justification: V2 tightens the abstract and contribution prose, converts contribution paragraphs into bullets, introduces numbered experimental subsections, and reorganizes Appendix C. The main section sequence, algorithm exposition, and much of the theoretical narrative remain recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the displays: wide classification tables become compact single-column tables without timing columns, ImageNet gains ViT-Base rows, and new tables present LLM, diagnostic, ablation, and architecture information. V1 Figure 2 is removed, while its CQ comparison remains tabulated. The other figures are retained, with renumbering and relocation.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Wang et al.'s 4-bit Shampoo, ReLoRA, GaLore, and the C4 source, and replaces the original LLaMA citation with LLaMA 2. These additions extend context and experimental provenance without substantially restructuring the related-work discussion or the claimed Cholesky-quantization novelty.

T1.justification: Propositions 5.1/B.2 replace the explicit lower perturbation bound with a diagonal-dominance condition for positive definiteness and add a Gershgorin-based proof, materially revising support for the eigenvalue assumption. The new proof contains a sign inconsistency in its displayed lower bound. The Frobenius-norm definition is also corrected; the principal convergence assumptions, theorems, and their proofs otherwise remain.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central memory-efficiency claim through C4 pretraining up to LLaMA-1B, including a 32-bit Shampoo out-of-memory case, and resolves v1's untested ImageNet-ViT limitation. Fidelity and sensitivity analyses add direct support for the mechanism. These gains outweigh the removed smaller-benchmark timings, although shortened LLM training and new inconsistencies limit confidence: Section 6.1 states a 0.73-point ViT-Base gain where Table 5 implies 2.73, and Proposition B.2's added positivity proof contains an erroneous inequality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-C. Corresponding content can be matched despite additions, restructuring, and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds language-model pretraining, matrix-quantization diagnostics, sensitivity experiments, and additional optimizer comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-classification accuracy, runtime, GPU-memory measurements, component comparisons, and preconditioner eigenvalue analyses.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about contextual and spatial priors, single-image reconstruction, and state-of-the-art performance. Supplementary evidence supports these existing claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v1's conclusion already acknowledges occluded or truncated regions and RealEstate10K-only training. Section 10 elaborates newly revealed-region failures and proposes generative knowledge as future work. Sections 9.3-9.4 also refine explanations concerning fabricated caption details and differences between VLMs.

D1.justification: Sections 6-8 supply previously unavailable survey procedures, dataset splits and sample counts, PointNet sampling/alignment details, and implementation settings. Examples include ResNet-50, LLaVA 13B, 256-by-384 inputs, eight attention heads, gamma 0.5, loss weights, and one A100 GPU. v2 also adds a project-site link and a prospective code-release statement.

E1.justification: Both versions use RealEstate10K, NYUv2, ACID, and KITTI for the same reconstruction and novel-view synthesis tasks. Added ablations and failure examples examine retained coverage rather than introducing another dataset, domain, or distinct evaluation scenario.

E2.justification: The main reconstruction comparator sets remain unchanged. New Table 10 introduces component-level comparisons using OpenFlamingo, BLIP2 T5, and LLaVA 7B text features against the selected LLaVA 13B configuration.

E3.justification: The supplement adds controlled prior-removal evaluations across datasets and a VLM-family/size comparison using common single-sentence prompting. No existing benchmark setting is explicitly revised; newly specified splits, sample counts, and survey controls document existing experiments.

E4.justification: Tables 8-9 newly test each prior's contribution to NYUv2 and ACID generalization, while Table 10 tests VLM choice. Figure 11 extends the cross-attention analysis with additional cases, and Figure 13 supplies concrete reconstruction failures. These substantially broaden diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Table 7 already reports identical 95% confidence intervals in v1. Supplementary Section 6 newly specifies binomial proportion intervals for preferences and normal-distribution intervals for mean ratings. Neither version reports repeated-training-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1-7 retain their numerical results. Tables 8-10 add substantial ablation results, including random-frame PSNR values of 25.06, 25.27, and 25.23 for OpenFlamingo, BLIP2 T5, and LLaVA 7B. Additional qualitative comparisons and failure cases expand the findings; these are not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1-3.4 retain the same depth-conditioned encoder, contextual and spatial cross-attention, Gaussian prediction, and losses. Supplementary PointNet details and Algorithm 1 explain the existing procedure; they do not establish an algorithmic revision.

P1.justification: The main paper remains essentially unchanged, but v2 substantially expands explanatory exposition through a supplementary overview and organized Sections 6-10. Detailed user-study and architecture walkthroughs, pseudocode, and extended discussions provide a substantial new explanatory structure. The affiliation edit is minor.

P2.justification: Main Figures 1-7 and Tables 1-7 retain their displays apart from small layout adjustments. The supplement adds Tables 8-10, Figures 8-17, and Algorithm 1, including survey examples, architectural diagrams, error maps, caption comparisons, failure panels, and enlarged qualitative comparisons.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for OpenFlamingo, farthest-point sampling, and Tulsiani et al.'s layer-structured scene inference protocol. The existing related-work discussion and positioning relative to reconstruction methods remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1-8 are retained. Algorithm 1 restates the existing computation, and the supplementary architectural explanation adds no new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v1 refers readers to supplementary implementation and evaluation details that its PDF does not contain. v2 supplies substantial architecture, data, training, survey, and statistical documentation, reducing important reproducibility gaps. Cross-dataset prior ablations and VLM comparisons strengthen evidence for central design choices, while illustrated failures substantiate existing limitations. These gains substantially improve the paper's auditability and evidential support despite unchanged headline results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CATSplat and contain readable, matching main methods, equations, and experiments. v1 ends after the references; v2 additionally includes supplementary Sections 6-10. The supplied material supports comparison of both retained content and newly documented details.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds supplementary ablations and qualitative findings in Tables 8-10 and Figures 11-17.

before.justification: v1 reports original novel-view synthesis results, component ablations, cross-dataset evaluations, and a 100-participant user study in Tables 1-7.

C1.justification: The FaceQ and F-Bench contributions remain, but v2's abstract, introduction and conclusion add a central claim: F-Eval is a unified generative-face evaluator achieving state-of-the-art performance across the tasks and evaluation dimensions. This substantially expands v1's database-and-benchmark contribution.

C2.justification: V2 revises the interpretation of existing face-IQA methods, distinguishing identity-feature extraction from alignment with perceptual quality. It attributes F-Eval's gains to dual-stream encoding, LLM fusion and dimension-specific experts. Section 12.2 adds small-face and extreme-side-view failure conditions and lack of distortion localization. The earlier privacy and resolution limitations are retained in the supplement.

D1.justification: V2 supplies F-Eval backbone, LoRA-rank/dropout, optimizer, training-budget and GPU details, and replaces the future-release statement with a project-page address. However, some original collection instructions disappear, including ELITE subject-mask generation and practice-rating trials. The detailed degradation pipelines and generative-model configurations remain in the supplement.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 12,255-image FaceQ database covering generation, customization and synthetic/real-world restoration. The nine prompt categories, demographic analyses and reduced-sampling-step scenarios already appear in v1. F-Eval is evaluated within this retained coverage; its stated failure conditions are not accompanied by new test datasets.

E2.justification: V2 adds IFQA and PromptIQA to the corresponding comparisons in Tables 2–4. Table 2 also adds a non-fine-tuned MINTIQA configuration while retaining the earlier MINTIQA results under a fine-tuning marker. The other evaluated QA methods and 29 generative models are retained.

E3.justification: The correlation metrics and stated 80:20 baseline training/testing split remain unchanged. V2 introduces F-Eval's training configuration, including 10 epochs, batch size 4 and AdamW at learning rate 0.0001, plus projector/face-encoder controls and single-, task- and dimension-based LoRA comparisons. These are substantial new experimental configurations.

E4.justification: V2 adds component ablations testing projector and face-encoder contributions and alternative LoRA specialization strategies, summarized in Table 5 and expanded in supplementary Table 8. V1's sampling-step, demographic and degradation analyses remain. The new evidence is substantial, although Section 6.4's removal descriptions conflict with Table 8's 'Freeze' labels.

E5.justification: The human-rating aggregation and outlier-rejection policy are retained. Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals or significance tests for the QA benchmarks. V2's additional benchmark and ablation scores continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Existing baseline values in Tables 2–4 are retained, including v1's MINTIQA row, now marked fine-tuned. V2 adds F-Eval, IFQA, PromptIQA, non-fine-tuned MINTIQA and ablation results. For example, v2 Table 2 reports customization-correspondence SRCC of 0.9460 for F-Eval versus the retained 0.8391 for fine-tuned MINTIQA.

M1.justification: V1 proposes a database and benchmark without its own learned evaluator. V2 introduces F-Eval: Qwen2.5-VL and ArcFace feature streams, learned projectors, instruction-based scoring, and four dimension-specific LoRA experts selected by a trained router. Supplementary Section 12 adds its language, score-regression and router-classification objectives.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, an explicit contribution list is added, and the related-work, dataset-construction and subjective-study descriptions are condensed. The narrative incorporates separate method and experiment sections. References move before a separately headed supplement, and the earlier limitations paragraph moves into that supplement.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview, regroups the rating examples, reduces the main MOS-distribution panels and resizes the radar plots. Table 1 loses rows and columns; Tables 2–4 gain rows and fine-tuning markers. A new architecture figure and two ablation tables are added. Most appendix figures are reused and renumbered.

R1.justification: V1 positions FaceQ as a foundation for developing better evaluators. V2 additionally positions F-Eval as the first unified generative-face evaluator and contrasts it with dimension-specific IQA approaches. It adds supporting Qwen2.5-VL, LoRA and visual-instruction-tuning literature, while narrowing the related-database comparison in Table 1.

T1.justification: V2 formalizes dimension-specific LoRA updates and the combined F-Eval training objective. Section 3.3 also corrects inconsistent annotator/image indexing in normalization and specifies an image-dependent valid-rater count for MOS. These are limited mathematical additions and corrections; the existing degradation and correlation formulas remain, and no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially advances the metric-alignment problem identified in v1 by providing a specified evaluator, comparisons across the retained tasks, component tests and explicit failure boundaries. The benchmark foundation remains intact, and the separate MINTIQA configurations clarify the value of fine-tuning. Conflicting ablation labels and omitted collection details weaken reproducibility, but the added, empirically supported methodological contribution provides a substantial net gain in scientific usefulness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FaceQ database and F-Bench research. The main text, tables, figures, equations and appendices support reliable comparison. V1's Appendices A–D largely correspond to v2's supplementary Sections 8–11; v2 additionally introduces F-Eval.

after.justification: V2 retains the original human-rating study and benchmarks, and adds F-Eval performance comparisons and component ablations in Tables 2–5 and 8.

before.justification: V1 reports an original human-rating study involving 180 annotators, generative-model benchmarks, quality-assessment experiments and supplementary demographic and sampling-step analyses.
