C1.justification: Both versions retain the central claims about positional bias in early pruning, benchmarks' limited assessment of fine-grained vision, and FEATHER's greater-than-fivefold localization improvement at comparable computational savings. The new contribution list explicitly summarizes findings already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 explains differing TextVQA findings through OCR inputs, suggests lost positional information explains FasterVLM/VisionZip localization failures, and acknowledges that removing RoPE may unintentionally alter attention weights. These extend the retained positional-bias and benchmark-limitation interpretations.

D1.justification: New details specify OCR-free TextVQA inputs, the existing transfer-control experiment's two-pass implementation, once-per-pruning attention calculation and FlashAttention compatibility, NVIDIA L40S hardware, and FasterVLM's SigLIP adaptation. These improve documentation without establishing changes to the original experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 12 datasets covering localization, open-ended VQA and challenge tasks. The additional encoder and positional-shuffling experiments change model configurations and controls, without adding datasets or task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix A3 adds evaluated FasterVLM and VisionZip comparators, extending the comparison beyond the retained FastV and PyramidDrop approaches to pruning before the LLM. FasterVLM is adapted to SigLIP by averaging received attention instead of using CLS attention.

E3.justification: Appendices A1-A4 add evaluation with DINOv2+SigLIP, positional-embedding shuffling controls, and measured total runtime alongside theoretical FLOPs. The original main settings remain; explicitly excluding OCR tokens clarifies the existing TextVQA protocol rather than establishing a protocol change.

E4.justification: The new shuffling ablation tests dependence on spatial position for both the unpruned model and FEATHER (Table A3). Table A1 also repeats the pruning-criteria analysis with DINOv2+SigLIP, testing whether the findings persist across encoders. Existing layer, criteria and information-transfer analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 3.3 newly reports a chi-square test of selected tokens' vertical-position nonuniformity, with p-value below 0.05. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds or uncertainty intervals for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: Existing localization values and headline comparisons are retained, with table fractions converted to percentages. v2 adds per-task criteria scores and new encoder, runtime, comparator and shuffling results. For example, Table A3 reports localization averages of 39.3 for FEATHER, 5.7 for FasterVLM and 8.5 for VisionZip at approximately comparable FLOPs reductions; shuffling reduces the unpruned model's average from 53.2 to 8.0.

M1.justification: FEATHER retains RoPE-free attention for token ranking, uniform sampling during pruning at layer 8, and further attention-based pruning at layer 16 with the same retention rule. The additional encoder experiment evaluates the existing method rather than revising its procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, analysis sections and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. v2 adds an explicit contribution list, replaces boxed findings with integrated discussion and descriptive subheadings, relocates the RoPE explanation and ensemble definition, and reorganizes the supplement into Sections A1-A5.

P2.justification: Table 1 is substantially redesigned with individual task columns, grouped headings and delta rows. v2 adds Tables A1-A3 and runtime Figure A1, removes the boxed finding/insight displays, and enlarges one qualitative figure. Original Figures 6-8 are retained as Figures A2-A4.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature on FasterVLM, VisionZip, ViT token reduction, FlashAttention and NaturalBench. Section 3.3 also contrasts its token-selection explanation with PyramidDrop's low-redundancy account, while retaining the paper's overall research positioning.

T1.justification: The VLM and pruning formulations, FLOPs equation and density-distance definition are unchanged. The RoPE mechanism discussion is reorganized and expanded, but no mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v1 supported efficiency primarily through theoretical FLOPs and evaluated one encoder setup with two principal acceleration baselines. v2 adds measured runtime, another encoder configuration, two additional baselines and a targeted positional-shuffling ablation. These address important empirical gaps and substantially strengthen the practical validation and support for the central diagnosis, while clearer presentation and explicit limitations improve assessability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FEATHER study. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, allowing reliable comparison of the methods, equations, experiments, tables and figures.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds another encoder configuration, runtime measurements, additional baseline comparisons and a positional-embedding shuffling ablation.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations across 12 benchmarks, pruning-criteria and layer analyses, information-transfer controls, and comparisons against FastV and PyramidDrop.

results.title: Feather the Throttle: Revisiting Visual Token Pruning for Vision-Language Model Acceleration

C1.justification: The three central contributions and headline gains of +98%, +67%, and +131% are retained. V2 refines TENOR's advertised role from preserving spatial semantics to preserving token order and linguistic structure, consistent with its clarified division of responsibilities between TENOR and SCOP.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly separates TENOR's structural signal from the semantic grounding supplied by SCOP (Section 3.2). Its new limitations discussion identifies viewer-centric scope, unsupported object-centric frames, contextual spatial language, and extreme size-disparity failures. V1 contains no comparable treatment of these applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Code changes from promised to stated available. V2 identifies grid search, clarifies internal descriptors and crop perturbation, and supplies the targeted adaptation budget. The main training table is retained, but v1's explicit VISOR detector and four-images-per-prompt description is omitted. Some new study procedures remain sparsely specified.

E1.justification: V2 adds DPG-Bench's long, dense prompts and a constructed benchmark of 512 three-object spatial prompts (Appendix C.4), extending evaluation beyond the retained coverage. Figure 7 also tests explicit extreme size disparities. The original COCO-derived training dataset remains.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparisons with R&B, Attention Refocusing, and Layout Guidance in the computational-efficiency study (Table 3), substantially broadening comparison to inference-only approaches. These comparisons concern overhead, not image-generation accuracy. The existing main and appendix VISOR comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a 500-image training control preserving category and relationship distributions, three-object evaluation with any/all correctness measures, and training/inference time and VRAM comparisons excluding bounding-box generation. It also adds human validation and a 100-step, batch-size-4 adaptation experiment. The original training hyperparameter table is unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds SCOP threshold sensitivity tests, reduced-data experiments, human validation of curated pairs, three-object generalization analysis, and a size-disparity failure case with targeted mitigation. These test robustness, data efficiency, curation quality, and applicability boundaries beyond v1's retained component ablations.

E5.justification: Appendix B retains the same latency measurements and accompanying ± values. V2 introduces no new run-count, seed, confidence-interval, or significance-testing information. Its human-agreement percentage is an additional evaluation outcome without uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Matched original benchmark, fidelity, ablation, and latency values remain unchanged. Substantial new results include DPG-Bench overall scores of 80.63/84.42 and three-object all-correct rates of 13.1%/31.2% for base/CoMPaSS-enhanced FLUX.1, respectively. V2 also adds human agreement of 85.2%, efficiency and sensitivity results, and new qualitative examples.

M1.justification: The standard SCOP/TENOR procedure, attention supervision, and LoRA setup are retained. V2 adds a targeted adaptation: further fine-tuning FLUX.1+CoMPaSS on size-contrast data filtered through an adapted SCOP engine (Figure 7). This additional training stage is absent from v1.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, related work, method explanations, and experimental narrative. It consolidates training documentation in the appendix, reorganizes evaluation subsections, and replaces the conclusion section with Discussion and Conclusion. Appendix organization and captions are also revised.

P2.justification: V2 merges spatial and fidelity results into an expanded Table 2, moves and extends the detailed benchmark table as Table A11, and adds several experimental displays. Figure 1 is replaced, Figure 7 is new, and Table 1 and Figure 6 are substantially compressed. The original appendix image galleries are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around reinforcement learning, preference optimization, training-based versus inference-only control, and qualitative spatial relations. It adds substantive references such as R&B and spatial-representation research. These additions go beyond the numerous bibliographic publication updates.

T1.justification: The five formal SCOP constraints and their mathematical definitions in Equations 1–5 are unchanged. V2 adds explanatory discussion of TENOR's role, but no new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for compositional generalization through long-prompt and three-object evaluations. Data-budget controls, sensitivity tests, and computational comparisons better substantiate the framework's practical claims, while the clarified mechanism and explicit failure boundaries improve scientific precision. These gains outweigh the loss of some VISOR protocol detail and incomplete specification of parts of the new studies; the original benchmark and ablation evidence is preserved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CoMPaSS, its SCOP and TENOR components, and the same four diffusion backbones. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains the original empirical studies and adds human validation, DPG-Bench evaluations, efficiency and sensitivity experiments, and three-object composition results.

before.justification: V1 reports original text-encoder retrieval tests, image-generation evaluations, component ablations, and runtime measurements in the main text and appendices.

results.title: CoMPaSS: Enhancing Spatial Understanding in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The central contributions remain semantic identity/expression separation, semi-supervised monocular capture, identity-preserving retargeting and MultiREX. V3 foregrounds the identity-aware decoder and inexpensive synthetic data, but these capabilities and their claimed advantages were already present in v1.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands the explanation of component roles and applicability boundaries. It interprets decoder-conditioning and delta-loss ablations, explicitly identifies a tradeoff between domain loss's worse MultiREX error and qualitatively better in-the-wild generalization, and acknowledges the lack of quantitative unconstrained evaluation. Appendix D.3 additionally identifies motion-blur-induced jitter and dependence on landmark-detector quality.

D1.justification: V3 replaces MultiREX's 'Coming soon' placeholder with a repository link, adds a project-page pointer, and reports hardware, batch size and component-level inference timings. Architecture Tables 4–5 are retained, although some v1 prose specifying graph pooling, upsampling and encoder–decoder skip connections is omitted.

E1.justification: V3 adds explicit qualitative testing under challenging lighting, external occlusion and motion blur in Appendix D.3 and Figure 16. Training datasets, the representation test set, MultiREX subjects and viewpoints, and the principal capture/retargeting tasks remain unchanged.

E2.justification: TEASER is added to the main in-the-wild retargeting comparison in v3 Section 5.4 and Figure 7, alongside DECA, EMICA, SMIRK and 3DDFA-V3. The FLAME representation comparison and DECA/EMICA/SMIRK MultiREX comparator set are retained. MonoNPHM is newly discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: V3 introduces controlled loss-removal and decoder-conditioning experiments and a timing protocol using batch size one on a 2080Ti, excluding bounding-box detection. It also revises the reported reconstruction-loss weight from 0.001 to 1.0 without establishing reruns. The retained benchmark sample counts, alignment procedures and metrics are unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing synthetic-only comparison and viewpoint analysis, v3 adds ablations of delta regularization, decoder identity conditioning, domain loss, eye-closure loss and edge preservation (Sections 4.4 and 5.5; Appendix C). Appendix D.3 adds challenging-condition and failure analysis. These substantially expand testing of the method's central components and robustness.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same mean-plus/minus reporting and Wilcoxon signed-rank significance criterion of 0.001. V3 extends these practices to additional result rows without introducing seed counts, repeated-training-run information, confidence intervals or a different uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Retained entries in Tables 1–3 are numerically unchanged, but v3 adds substantive findings. Without delta regularization, reconstruction error is 1.75 mm; without decoder identity conditioning, CSIM is 0.773 versus 0.791 for the full model. Without domain loss, MultiREX error is 2.10 versus 2.19 mm. New qualitative comparisons, failure examples and 26.1 ms inference timing further extend the results.

M1.justification: The reported reconstruction-loss weight changes from 0.001 in v1 Appendix A.1 to 1.0 in v3 Appendix A, revising the specified objective weighting. Architecture and component losses otherwise remain unchanged. The three-stage overview reorganizes the existing pipeline; the PDFs do not establish whether the weight revision reflects retraining or a documentation correction.

P1.justification: The introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten, the method narrative explicitly separates three stages, and experimental-procedure explanations are consolidated. The appendices are reorganized from A.1–A.4 into sections A–F, with additional subsections and acknowledgements. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: V3 replaces Figure 2 with a three-stage pipeline overview, redraws Figure 4, expands Tables 1–2 and adds a TEASER column to the main qualitative comparison. New Figures 5, 8, 10 and 16 display ablations and challenging cases. Existing benchmark, mask and synthetic-sample figures are retained but redistributed.

R1.justification: V3 adds discussion or citations for MonoNPHM, local anatomically constrained facial performance retargeting and TEASER, while removing several general representation-learning, disentanglement and capture-background references. The principal positioning against linear 3DMMs, paired expression models and expensive realistic synthetic training remains.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulations and loss definitions are retained, apart from notation and term ordering. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs that are added or revised in v3; the loss-weight revision is a training specification.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses v1's limited component-level validation with direct tests of identity conditioning and the principal losses, substantially strengthening assessment of the central design choices. Reporting the unfavorable MultiREX domain-loss result, failure conditions and runtime also improves transparency. Headline scores remain unchanged, and the unexplained reconstruction-weight revision and qualitative-only in-the-wild generalization evidence remain limitations, but the added controls materially improve the paper's empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SEREP and MultiREX. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and sufficiently complete to match retained material and identify revisions.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds component ablations, challenging-condition examples and inference-time measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original expression-reconstruction, identity-preservation and MultiREX experiments in Tables 1–3, alongside qualitative capture and retargeting results.

results.title: SEREP: Semantic Facial Expression Representation for Robust In-the-Wild Capture and Retargeting

C1.justification: The central claims remain that wildlife observations improve and complement satellite representations, benefit pretrained models, outperform competing cross-modal approaches and enable text-based retrieval. The conclusion is retained. Segmentation and multispectral experiments broaden support for the existing general-applicability claim rather than redefine the contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies poor zero-shot performance on anthropogenic classes and suggests combining wildlife and anthropogenic supervision. It also discusses African segmentation transfer and relates larger US bird-prediction gains to training geography. Conversely, it removes v1's polar-coverage and endangered-species caveats. The PEFT and location-encoder interpretations promoted into the main text already appeared in v1's appendix.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/data repository pointer and discloses negative sampling, species/location text matching, use of supplied dataset splits, and average training time of eight hours on two NVIDIA L40S GPUs. It documents missing-band handling for the new multispectral experiments. The endangered-species exclusion/location-noise disclosure is removed, without establishing that the underlying processing changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds Cashew1k plantation segmentation in Benin and SAcrop3k crop segmentation in South Africa, substantially extending evaluation beyond image classification and bird encounter rates. It also evaluates zero-shot classification on selected EuroSAT and So2Sat20k classes, previously evaluated through trained linear probes.

E2.justification: RemoteCLIP joins the existing CLIP, TaxaBind and GRAFT classification comparison in v2 Tables 2 and A3, and participates in the new zero-shot comparison in Table A5. The previously evaluated comparators are retained.

E3.justification: New segmentation experiments train U-Net-style decoders with frozen encoders and report IoU and pixel accuracy. v2 also adds zero-shot classwise F1 evaluation and multispectral runs using available bands, zero-filling only unavailable bands instead of all non-RGB bands. These are additional protocols; the original RGB classification experiments and WildSAT training budget remain.

E4.justification: The component, location-encoder and PEFT ablations and So2Sat20k confusion matrices are retained unchanged. v2 adds focused multispectral checks, a diagnostic comparison of zero-shot performance on natural versus anthropogenic classes, and segmentation case studies highlighting corrected crop predictions (Tables A4–A5 and Figure A3).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests. The connecting lines in v2 Figure 3 represent base-to-WildSAT performance changes, not uncertainty intervals.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial numerical and qualitative results. Examples include SatlasNet Cashew1k IoU of 55.2%/71.0% for base/+WildSAT, multispectral Prithvi-100M So2Sat20k accuracy of 28.7%/50.1%, and zero-shot WildSAT F1 of 87.4 on SeaLake versus 0.4 on Highway. These are newly reported evaluations, not gains over v1 under identical conditions. The original classification, bird-encounter and ablation tables retain their values.

M1.justification: The WildSAT contrastive objectives, SINR/GritLM encoders, projection heads and fine-tuning rules remain unchanged. v2 adds a task-specific segmentation adaptation: a trainable U-Net-style convolutional decoder attached to a frozen ResNet50 encoder, extending the linear-head downstream procedure in v1 (Section 5 and Appendix C.1).

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract and portions of the introduction and related work, moves Dataset from Section 3.2 into a standalone Section 4, and summarizes existing appendix interpretations in the main text. The method exposition, conclusion and much supplementary prose remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v1's main classification Table 1 moves to v2 Table A1, while a new multipanel Figure 3 visualizes those results. v2 adds segmentation, multispectral and zero-shot tables plus segmentation visualizations, and reduces the main retrieval image grid. These changes substantially reorganize the presentation of evidence beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of WikiSatNet as a close predecessor, EcoWikiRS and RemoteCLIP, explicitly credits TaxaBind's earlier combination of species locations and satellite imagery, and adds references supporting segmentation. This sharpens the distinction between wildlife and anthropogenic supervision while retaining the original research positioning.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and three contrastive-loss equations are equivalent across versions. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 introduces no substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the paper's broad representation-learning claims. Frozen-encoder segmentation tests establish transfer to dense prediction, multispectral experiments address the RGB-only restriction on compatible pretrained models, and quantitative zero-shot results reveal concrete applicability limits absent from v1's qualitative retrieval examples. Added implementation and access information also helps reproducibility. Removing the polar-coverage and endangered-species caveats reduces transparency, but this limited loss is outweighed by the stronger and better-qualified empirical evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WildSAT. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison. Renumbered and relocated material can be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds segmentation, multispectral evaluation and quantitative zero-shot classification results.

before.justification: v1 reports original satellite classification, bird encounter-rate prediction, retrieval and ablation results, including Tables 1–4 and supplementary experiments.

results.title: WildSAT: Learning Satellite Image Representations from Wildlife Observations

C1.justification: The abstract and three central contributions remain substantively stable. The introduction strengthens the compression claim by asserting fixed memory consumption and scalability to more intricate designs, and explicitly emphasizes fitting bodies without detailed body measurements.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations involving token-budget and GPU constraints, clarifies conditioning as a normalized residual, and connects baseline fitting failures to body-training and attachment limitations. The stated limitations concerning pockets, zippers and intricate sketches remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Supplementary Sections 6 and 9 newly document the canonical panel ordering, parameter-to-description thresholds, GPT-4 annotation refinement and its prompt, and PiDiNet checkpoint usage. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Hardware, training times and loss weights remain unchanged; the explicit future code-release promise is removed while the project link remains.

E1.justification: The 120,000-pattern GarmentCodeData corpus and garment-generation task remain. V2 expands input-scenario coverage with explicitly sourced Multimodal Garment Designer images and hand-drawn sketches (Figures 6, 17 and 18), providing a focused extension of the existing sketch-conditioned evaluation.

E2.justification: V2 adds direct qualitative comparisons with ChatGarment and AIpparel in supplementary Section 8 and Figure 11, substantially updating the evaluated competition. Existing comparators, including GarmentCode, remain. Design2GarmentCode is discussed but is not an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: V2 adds test-set reconstruction and simulation-failure evaluation, fine-tunes SewFormer until validation loss plateaus, and evaluates DressCode failure rate using its existing checkpoint. Section 4.2 also changes the main sewing-pattern comparison inputs from ControlNet-generated images to selected in-the-wild images. These reported protocol changes do not establish that retained Table 1 experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds an illustrative extended-versus-original representation comparison testing neckline and skirt-detail preservation (Section 10, Figure 12), plus additional sketch-generalization examples. The compression, attention, injection-depth and one-stage-versus-two-stage ablations, use case and failure examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed evaluations, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The user-study reporting practice remains unchanged; newly reported failure percentages are outcome metrics, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: New Table 2 reports Panel L2 values of 0.64 for the autoencoder, 3.13 for SewingLDM and 12.3 for fine-tuned SewFormer, alongside other reconstruction metrics. Section 4.3 adds DressCode's 11.4% failure rate. Section 8 reports comparable results to ChatGarment and better results than AIpparel. Table 1 and the renumbered compression table retain their numerical values.

M1.justification: The 29-dimensional edge representation, quantized autoencoder, DiT diffusion model, two-stage training and attention-output fine-tuning remain unchanged. Equations (1)-(4) are retained. The added panel-order listing documents implementation without establishing a procedural revision.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized language corrections and rewrites parts of the introduction and experimental discussion. It expands the supplementary organization and moves the use case from main Section 4.5 to supplementary Section 13. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure remain.

P2.justification: V2 adds reconstruction and annotation-prompt tables and figures for concurrent comparisons, representation analysis and additional sketch conditions. Main Figure 6 is replaced, while much of its earlier comparison reappears in supplementary Figure 16 with revised input illustrations. The use-case figure moves to the supplement; existing ablation and body-shape galleries are retained.

R1.justification: V2 acknowledges that concurrent methods already support complex garment features and adds substantive positioning against ChatGarment, AIpparel and Design2GarmentCode. Section 8 distinguishes category-specific parameterization and body adaptation, updating the earlier positioning centered on DressCode, SewFormer and GarmentCode.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(5), the representation definitions, quantization rule and codebook-usage calculation remain unchanged. V2 adds implementation explanations and standard evaluation-metric descriptions, without new proofs, formal derivations or theoretical results.

improvement.justification: V1's compression validation relied heavily on qualitative examples and binary reconstruction checks. V2's direct reconstruction and simulation-failure measurements substantially strengthen evidence for a central contribution. Concurrent-method comparisons and explicit panel-order and annotation instructions also improve assessment and reproducibility. Generalization evidence remains illustrative and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but the additions address important evidential gaps while retaining the established results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SewingLDM study. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and supplementary material support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds reconstruction measurements, concurrent-method comparisons, a representation ablation, and additional sketch-conditioned generation examples.

before.justification: V1 reports original garment-generation and simulation results, quantitative comparisons, a 30-participant user study, and ablations in the main text and supplement.

results.title: Multimodal Latent Diffusion Model for Complex Sewing Pattern Generation

C1.justification: The central contribution remains interactive in-context segmentation without task-specific retraining. The quantitative headline is narrowed: abstract scribble savings change from 53% to 25%, and the conclusion replaces reductions of 'as much as 50%' in interactions with 36% average click savings.

C2.justification: v2 develops practical interpretations concerning fine-tuning overhead, interactive latency and resolution sensitivity. BUID heterogeneity was already discussed in v1's appendix; v2 refines that limitation with a small-context failure boundary and explains why informative scribbles reduce context's benefit. These are bounded extensions rather than a new account of the method's mechanism.

D1.justification: v2 adds square-padding and bilinear-resizing details, SAM's ViT-b/single-mask configuration, fine-tuning hyperparameters and checkpoint selection, and A100 timing/memory measurement details. The core architecture and training recipe were already documented. The new Code appendix repeats the existing code-and-weights link rather than establishing newly available resources.

E1.justification: Table 2 adds TotalSegmentator: 1,204 CT scans covering 104 structures, substantially broadening organ, bone, muscle and vessel evaluation. The listed evaluation suite grows from 11 to 12 datasets. v1's appendix and dataset plots establish 59 sequential-evaluation tasks across seven datasets, versus 161 across eight in v2; v1 already contains an inconsistent 161-task statement in Section 6.1.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained ScribblePrompt, SP+UVS and UniverSeg comparisons, v2 actually evaluates SAM, MedSAM, SAM-Med2D, IMIS-Net and SegNext, and adds task-specific fine-tuned ScribblePrompt. Figures 3–4 and 18 report the expanded comparisons; MedSAM results appear in Section 6.2 and fine-tuning in Appendix E.4/Figure 21.

E3.justification: The principal sequential evaluation changes from 128x128 to 256x256, with model-specific input resizing and predictions rescaled before scoring; v2 also evaluates at 128x128. It adds a five-example fine-tuning protocol with a 4/1 training/validation split and 13 subsequent test images. In-context evaluations extend to 256 context examples, and interactive context-size evaluations extend from 32 to 64.

E4.justification: v2 adds resolution sensitivity analysis, inference-time and memory scaling, and a longer-sequence WBC analysis. These test sensitivity to evaluation resolution and practical scalability beyond v1's analyses. Existing context-label-quality and SP+UVS minimum-context analyses are retained as Figures 16–17, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The new fine-tuning experiment reports five random seeds and 95% confidence intervals; the runtime table reports mean and standard deviation over 1,000 predictions. Existing main experiments retain 200 simulations and the Experiment 2 description retains 100 bootstrap runs. These additions do not establish increased repetition of the existing experiments.

E6.justification: Reported click/scribble reductions change from 35.61%/52.70% to 36.41%/25.26%, with substantially revised result entries in v1 Table 7 versus v2 Figure 18. These reflect different resolution and dataset coverage, not same-setting performance changes. New comparator, fine-tuning, runtime and larger-context results expand the evidence substantially. The fine-tuning scribble mean is internally inconsistent, and Figure 21's scenario count disagrees with Appendix E.4.

M1.justification: The ScribblePrompt initialization, CrossBlock encoder-decoder, accumulating context set, segmentation loss and synthetic-task training procedure are retained. The added fine-tuning procedure is a comparator; the resolution changes concern evaluation rather than a revised MultiverSeg algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most explanatory prose remain recognizable. v2 polishes wording, relocates the fine-tuning paragraph within Related Work, adds an appendix contents list and Code/Inference sections, and reorganizes supplementary experiment subsections. The added scientific material does not amount to wholesale narrative rewriting.

P2.justification: Figure 4 changes from differences in total interactions to grouped per-image comparisons, and v1's combined dataset plots become separate click and scribble figures. v2 expands qualitative and quantitative panels and adds fine-tuning, resolution and runtime displays. v1 Table 7 becomes the expanded tabular Figure 18; the architecture and segmentation-workflow illustrations are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to SAM-Med2D, the IMIS-Net benchmark paper, LesionLocator and interactive-latency research. These support expanded comparisons and practical discussion while preserving the central positioning relative to interactive segmentation, in-context learning and task-specific retraining.

T1.justification: The task objectives, CrossConv/CrossBlock mathematics, expected segmentation loss and equivalent implementation derivation are retained. v1's first two displayed equations become inline expressions and subsequent equations are renumbered; no substantive mathematical assumption, proof or derivation is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central efficiency claim through broader evaluated baselines, whole-body CT coverage, higher-resolution evaluation, and explicit adaptation and resource-cost studies. These address important limitations in v1's comparison breadth and practical feasibility evidence. Reporting errors weaken some additions: Appendix E.4 repeats the click value for scribbles, and Figure 21 states 13/14 scenarios versus 13/16 in the text. Those defects require correction, but do not outweigh the substantial gains supported by the expanded experiments and figures.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MultiverSeg, and their main texts, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices support comparison. Internal inconsistencies in some dataset counts and result summaries can be identified and qualified using the corresponding tables and figures.

after.justification: v2 reports original segmentation experiments and adds baseline comparisons, few-shot fine-tuning, resolution sensitivity, and measured inference time and memory usage.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated interactive-segmentation experiments, held-out segmentation results and context-quality analyses in Sections 6–7 and Appendices D–E.

results.title: MultiverSeg: Scalable Interactive Segmentation of Biomedical Imaging Datasets with In-Context Guidance

C1.justification: v1 presents Minimum-Ball and adaptive-resolution Reinforce-Ball as paired central contributions. v2 centers its abstract and contribution list on efficient reconstruction, explicitly adds memory reduction and 3D point-cloud reconstruction claims, and relegates Reinforce-Ball to an experimental appendix component. Its conclusion acknowledges residual non-manifold errors instead of presenting their elimination as an available capability.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits real-image applicability because of its simple rendering model and assumed lighting knowledge, supported by the DTU failure case. It adds sparse-point-cloud and computational-cost limitations and conjectures an expressiveness/non-manifoldness trade-off. It also attributes GShell's high average error to outlier failures. v1's detailed explanation of Reinforce-Ball's difficulty in 3D is shortened to a limitation statement.

D1.justification: v2 adds density-based point-cloud initialization instructions, dedicated 3D point-cloud hyperparameters and baseline settings, an explicit triangle-quality loss formula, and Phong/directional-light rendering details. It removes v1's detailed 2D DMesh setup, four-epoch colored-reconstruction schedule, and DNA source/10K-point initialization disclosure. Hardware and the stated project access remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds dedicated 3D reconstruction from oriented and unoriented point clouds, real-image reconstruction on DTU, and a downstream bouncing-ball simulation. These extend task and input-domain coverage beyond v1's 2D point-cloud and synthetic multi-view reconstruction studies. Thingi10K, Objaverse, fonts, and complex drawings were already represented in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated point-cloud comparators PSR, VoroMesh, and PoNQ alongside DMesh. All appear in Table 2; the larger Table 3 includes PSR, PoNQ, and DMesh. The multi-view comparator set remains Remeshing, DMTet, FlexiCubes, GShell, and DMesh.

E3.justification: The 20-model hand-selected multi-view evaluation becomes evaluations on 50 selected models and 500 randomly selected models, the latter split equally between closed and open surfaces. New point-cloud protocols use 200K Poisson-disk samples and distinguish oriented from unoriented inputs. GPU memory is added to scaling evaluation. Font downsampling is now stated as 0.005 cells, whereas v1 describes approximately half the initial 0.005 grid spacing; this documentation change does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a controlled renderer translation experiment testing visibility gradients (Figure 14), a topology-evolution visualization (Figure 3), memory-scaling analysis, and a DTU failure case (Figure 21). The Reinforce-Ball ablations are retained as Table 6 and Figure 24, rather than newly introduced. v1's separate self-occluded-vase failure illustration is omitted.

E5.justification: Both versions report five trials and averaged measurements for tessellation scaling. Neither introduces reported seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for reconstruction results. Expanded result tables retain aggregate point estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds point-cloud results, 500-model reconstruction results, and memory savings reaching 96% in 2D and 75% in 3D. Its 50-model multi-view table replaces v1's 20-model aggregate: DMesh++ CD changes from 0.127 to 0.342, both scaled by 10^-3, under different evaluation conditions. These are not same-setting performance changes. Font and Reinforce-Ball numbers remain unchanged; several colored-example counts and timings disappear.

M1.justification: The reconstruction procedure changes substantively. v1 optimizes independent face probabilities, regularizes their mean, and derives point real values; v2 directly optimizes and regularizes point real values (Appendix 8). The revised pipeline also omits v1's explicit non-manifold-removal operation. Minimum-Ball, nearest-neighbor caching, subdivision, anti-aliasing, and Reinforce-Ball remain; Reinforce-Ball's relocation is not a method removal.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: Section 4 becomes a short reconstruction overview, detailed operations and losses move into Appendix 8, and Reinforce-Ball moves into Appendix 10. Experiments are regrouped by reconstruction task, the introduction is rewritten, and the discussion becomes a conclusion with revised limitations and future directions.

P2.justification: v2 adds conceptual, topology-evolution, point-cloud, simulation, renderer-test, and DTU figures, expands the timing plot with memory panels, and redraws the pipeline. It adds and reorganizes comparison tables, relocates Reinforce-Ball displays, combines earlier full-page drawings into Figure 18, and removes much of the colored reconstruction gallery.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting point-cloud reconstruction, DTU, 2D Gaussian Splatting, and t-SNE, while removing works including Meshtron and NeRF. It refines the description of earlier mesh methods to acknowledge local connectivity changes. The three-part related-work organization and central positioning as an efficient successor to DMesh remain.

T1.justification: v2 Equation (3) reverses the signed-distance definition from radius minus nearest-point distance to nearest-point distance minus radius, correcting its sign relative to the positive empty-ball test. However, Algorithms 1 and 2 retain the old sign. The real-loss definition also changes from averaging face probabilities to averaging point real values. Lemma 3.2, its proof, and the Reinforce-Ball gradient derivation remain.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence beyond v1's small, selectively chosen multi-view benchmark through broader random-model evaluation, dedicated point-cloud comparisons, memory measurements, and a controlled renderer test. The DTU failure example and clearer applicability limits also improve claim calibration. These gains outweigh lost implementation details and remaining inconsistencies: the corrected signed-distance sign is not propagated to appendix pseudocode, and the claim of outperforming DMesh on every point-cloud metric conflicts with Table 2's non-manifold-vertex values.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DMesh++ and retain its central Minimum-Ball formulation. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including the image-dominated final pages of v1.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction results, including new 3D point-cloud comparisons, expanded multi-view benchmarks, memory measurements, a DTU failure example, and a physics simulation demonstration.

before.justification: v1 reports original tessellation timings, 2D reconstruction and Reinforce-Ball ablations, and quantitative and qualitative 3D multi-view reconstruction results.

results.title: DMesh++: An Efficient Differentiable Mesh for Complex Shapes

C1.justification: v1 explicitly limits its delivered contribution to the dataset and postpones benchmarking. v2 claims completed standardized benchmarking and model releases, and adds substantive conclusions about exceeding strong from-scratch baselines, task-dependent SSL effectiveness, and the competitiveness of pre-trained transformers.

C2.justification: Sections 4–5 and Appendix A add interpretations involving global versus local representations, encoder adaptation, decoder capacity, and degradation from longer fine-tuning. v2 also explicitly qualifies classification reliability, weak evidence for data-filtering benefits, and the limited pre-training budget. These empirical interpretations and limitations were absent from v1.

D1.justification: v2 replaces deferred release statements with reported availability of data, training frameworks, and model checkpoints. Appendices B–D add image-quality sampling and aggregation rules, preprocessing exceptions, optimizers, learning rates, batch sizes, augmentations, and architectural details; Section 3 specifies GPU hardware. Resource availability is reported by the PDF, not independently verified.

E1.justification: v1 presents the pre-training corpus without downstream experiments. v2 evaluates 12 segmentation datasets and three classification datasets, covering brain and head-and-neck disease, abdominal and cardiac structures, knees, and spinal fractures across MRI and CT (Section 3.1).

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 introduce evaluated comparisons among VoCo, SwinUNETR pre-training, SimCLR, Volume Fusion, ModelsGenesis, MAE, and architecture-specific S3D or SimMIM, alongside from-scratch baselines. Table 2 also includes default nnU-Net. v1 cites several methods but reports no such comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled benchmark protocols: development versus held-out datasets, 50/50 train/test splits with additional development validation splits, common architectures, 1000-epoch pre-training, and specified fine-tuning budgets and metrics. Appendix C.2 additionally specifies five-fold classification cross-validation, although its relationship to the blanket 50/50 split statement is unclear. These protocols were absent from v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds comparisons of five fine-tuning schedules, 150 versus 1000 fine-tuning epochs, image-quality and modality filtering, and anonymization-aware reconstruction losses (Tables 4–8). Tables 10–11 add VoCo and Volume Fusion hyperparameter studies. v1 discusses possible benefits of quality scores and masks without testing them.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 newly reports five-fold cross-validation for classification, adding resampling-based performance estimation information absent from v1. Neither version supplies seed-based variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the two-rater image-quality assessment is retained.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive benchmark and ablation results absent from v1, including mean segmentation DSC of 70.91 for ResEnc-L MAE and 70.42 for Primus-M MAE after 150 fine-tuning epochs (Table 2). Table 1 also changes OpenMind's reported volume count from 114,570 to 113,921 and modality count from 23 to 24, although some v2 prose retains 23 modalities.

M1.justification: Beyond v1's dataset construction pipeline and announced benchmark, v2 introduces operational adaptations of SSL methods to ResEnc-L and Primus-M. These include 3D SimCLR, architecture-specific dense and global output heads, and a two-layer decoder for Primus-M MAE pre-training (Figure 7 and Appendix D). These are substantial additions to the presented procedures, without establishing replacement of an earlier implemented benchmark.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and dataset narrative are extensively revised and integrated into a dataset–benchmark–results–discussion structure. The original standalone DWI appendix becomes Appendix B.2 within a reorganized four-appendix document. Authorship, affiliations, and citation presentation also change.

P2.justification: v2 introduces extensive performance and ablation tables, including color-coded result matrices, and new dataset-distribution, learning-rate, and architecture figures. Figure 1 is recomposed into a single-column montage, while the retained DWI diagram is relocated and its ADC label becomes MD. These substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands its positioning around rigorous benchmarking, CNN–transformer comparisons, and data selection, adding discussion and citations for Primus, nnU-Net revisited, Touchstone, DataComp, and SemDeDup. It also adds explicit attribution to 800 source datasets through references 55–854.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical guarantees, proofs, or formal assumptions. The equations and objective descriptions added in Appendix D explain established comparison methods rather than introduce substantive new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v1 postpones the benchmark, leaving its intended comparative contribution unsupported. v2 supplies a controlled 15-dataset evaluation with strong baselines, targeted ablations, detailed implementation information, and explicit limitations, substantially resolving that evidentiary gap. Reporting weaknesses remain: dataset totals are inconsistent, and broad classification conclusions overlook Volume Fusion leading both Primus-M mean metrics in Table 3. These weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OpenMind dataset and SSL benchmarking project, and their text, tables, figures, and appendices are readable. The original DWI appendix is retained as Appendix B.2 in v2; the substantial expansion supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original segmentation and classification experiments, fine-tuning and preprocessing ablations, hyperparameter studies, and additional dataset analyses in the main text and Appendices A–D.

before.justification: Section 2.1 and Table 1 report original descriptive results from dataset curation, including 114,570 volumes, 34,191 participants, and 23 modalities. These are dataset characterization results; v1 explicitly defers the SSL benchmark experiments.

results.title: An OpenMind for 3D medical vision self-supervised learning

C1.justification: V2 makes input-view reconstruction and two-stage reconstructor training central to its generalization contribution, explicitly claims benchmark construction, and strengthens generalization to 'no domain gap' in the introduction. V1's abstract-level video and reenactment claims disappear. These changes substantially redefine the contribution framing despite retaining the principal reconstruction claim.

C2.justification: V2 adds mechanism explanations connecting input reconstruction to reduced synthetic overfitting and object pretraining to geometric diversity. It interprets the eight-view tradeoff and failed LGM fine-tuning, and adds limitations involving blurred unseen regions and excessively dark rear hair. Earlier accessory and out-of-distribution limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents the 50-degree field of view and MTCNN resizing/cropping procedure, an approximately eight-second inference breakdown, attention/transformer implementation details, and the deformation network. These improve technical disclosure; most existing training hyperparameters, hardware information and the project-page address remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The underlying training datasets, Cafca, Ava-256, real and cartoon portraits, and video reconstruction remain. V2 removes the explicit image-plus-driving-video reenactment demonstration using LivePortrait from v1 Section 4.5/Figure 9. The larger portrait galleries mostly redistribute existing examples rather than establish new coverage.

E2.justification: Cafca comparisons add GGHead, Dual Encoder and Our MV + LGM; Ava-256 adds Our MV + LGM. Supplementary Table 3 adds TRELLIS, Unique3D and InstantMesh, while Figure 22 evaluates fine-tuned LGM. These substantially broaden evaluated comparators. RodinHD and DimensionX comparisons already existed.

E3.justification: Shared aligned benchmark identities, camera lists, metrics and training budgets remain unchanged. V2 removes the unaligned 30-view Cafca evaluation and adds settings for new controls, including a 20-degree target elevation and eight-view reconstruction. Reconstructor sampling changes from 32 HDR renderings to either 32 ambient or 25 HDR renderings in supplementary Section 5.2; this reported revision does not establish rerunning.

E4.justification: V2 adds quantitative input-view reconstruction and multi-view attention ablations, a reconstructor without object pretraining, an eight-view alternative, and LGM integration/fine-tuning analyses. These investigate previously untested component contributions and transfer behavior. The lighting ablation is retained in the supplement, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's additional result tables retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Shared aligned benchmark scores are unchanged, including FaceLift PSNR of 16.61 on Cafca and 16.52 on Ava-256. V2 adds substantial comparator and ablation results: supplementary Table 4 reports ArcFace distances of 0.2367 without input reconstruction and 0.2126 without attention, versus 0.1573 for the full model. Unaligned Cafca results disappear, and autoregressive video results are added.

M1.justification: V1 reconstructs video frames independently. V2 adds an autoregressive deformation pipeline with an eight-layer MLP predicting Gaussian position, opacity and scale changes, supervised by subsequent-frame renderings (supplementary Section 3.5). This is a substantial procedural extension. Input-view reconstruction and object pretraining followed by head fine-tuning were already present in v1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten around generalization. Ablations become a separate main section, real-image inference receives its own subsection, and lighting/video material moves into a substantially reorganized supplement. This exceeds localized language editing.

P2.justification: V2 revises the pipeline diagram, restructures comparison figures and tables, expands ablation displays, and adds mesh-comparison and autoregressive-deformation illustrations. Existing portrait examples are regrouped into larger galleries, and benchmark camera tables are relocated together. These are substantial visual changes beyond numerical updates or renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion of Morphable Diffusion and HeadGAP, citations to SynthLight and LPFF, and literature supporting the expanded comparators. LivePortrait and Instant-NSR-PL references disappear. The broader positioning around synthetic heads, diffusion and large reconstruction models remains recognizable.

T1.justification: V2 supplementary Section 4.1 adds a formal joint multi-view diffusion formulation, forward/reverse Markov factorizations, Gaussian transition definitions and a noise-prediction objective (Equations 6–10). This is a limited mathematical addition to v1's descriptive treatment, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence behind FaceLift through dedicated face and mesh comparators, quantitative component ablations, and a pretraining control, addressing important gaps in v1's comparative and diagnostic support. Inference documentation and failure analysis also improve. Removing unaligned full-view Cafca results and asserting 'no domain gap' weaken balance, but the added evidence provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FaceLift. Their complete main texts and appendices, including readable tables, figures and equations, support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark results and adds comparator results, quantitative component ablations and demonstrations of an autoregressive video extension.

before.justification: V1 reports original Cafca and Ava-256 evaluations in Tables 1–2, qualitative reconstructions, ablations and video demonstrations.

results.title: FaceLift: Learning Generalizable Single Image 3D Face Reconstruction from Synthetic Heads

C1.justification: The introduction drops v1's specific average-error claims of less than 0.4 degrees rotation and 0.2 cm translation, replacing them with qualitative accuracy claims over the expanded evaluation. The central human-motion calibration contribution, progressive refinement, and claim of joint dynamic-NeRF reconstruction from unknown offsets and poses remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly explains the initialization-only EgoBody evaluation through sparse-view reconstruction difficulty and identifies moving-camera refinement as future work. It removes v1's explanation for omitting refinement on degraded videos. Appendix C introduces an inconsistency by describing EgoBody refinement, although Table 1 and Figure 9 report initialization only.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B add EgoBody clip and missing-frame processing details and specify Mobile-Stage grid resolutions and regularization scheduling. Panoptic undistortion details are relocated. Conversely, v1's explicit first-frame/one-pose-per-static-video implementation description disappears. The project-page link is unchanged.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from single-person, static-camera Panoptic scenes to three-person smartphone recordings in Mobile-Stage and two-person EgoBody scenes containing a moving head-mounted camera alongside static cameras. v2 also evaluates mixed-frame-rate inputs. EgoBody covers initialization only, not full dynamic reconstruction.

E2.justification: The reconstruction comparisons retain Sync-NeRF with ground-truth poses, the calibrated K-Planes oracle, and the no-progressive-training variant. Mobile-Stage uses this same comparison set. The DUSt3R/COLMAP illustration remains; newly cited human-calibration methods are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: v2 introduces initialization-only evaluation on sparse EgoBody views, using 200-frame clips with at least 90 overlapping frames, and unit-bounding-box translation errors for EgoBody and Mobile-Stage. It adds a 20/1 Mobile-Stage train/test split and a mixed-rate protocol with five 24-FPS videos and the others at 30 FPS. The documented Panoptic sampling, training budget, and test-time optimization remain.

E4.justification: Table 2 adds a test of initialization robustness to mixed frame rates. The progressive-training ablation is also evaluated on Mobile-Stage. Existing human-state-distance, SMPL-noise, and image-degradation analyses are retained with their previous results.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed-based variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Added experiments continue the existing practice of reporting point estimates and averages.

E6.justification: v2 adds calibration results for Mobile-Stage and three EgoBody scenes, mixed-FPS results, and Mobile-Stage rendering results: Table 3 reports 23.27 PSNR for the proposed method, 17.26 for Sync-NeRF, and 22.98 for the oracle. Panoptic Table 3 scores remain unchanged. Table 1's mean Panoptic input offset changes from 62.39 to 30.64 frames without explaining whether this corrects reporting or reflects different data.

M1.justification: v1 explicitly assumes equal frame rates. v2 adds linear interpolation of lower-rate joint trajectories before alignment and interpolation of missing EgoBody frames. These are limited procedural adaptations; SLAHMR extraction, DTW/global alignment, Procrustes calibration, and progressive K-Planes refinement remain.

P1.justification: v2 drops 'Pattern' from the title, edits and condenses several passages, adds a related-work subsection, and reorganizes supplementary material into dataset, implementation, and result sections. Dataset specifications and Algorithm 1 move to the appendix. The overall narrative and most method exposition remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 5 becomes a multi-dataset calibration display, and new Figures 7, 9, and 10 show Mobile-Stage and EgoBody results. Tables 1 and 3 gain dataset groupings and additional results, while Table 2 gains the mixed-FPS row. Existing Panoptic visual comparisons are retained as Figures 8, 11, and 12 rather than replaced.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantive 'Camera calibration with human' subsection covering CameraHMR, Virtual Correspondence, moving-person calibration, person-reidentification calibration, and HSfM. It acknowledges shared human-based calibration ideas and distinguishes synchronization, camera-motion, and reconstruction assumptions. This materially expands positioning beyond v1's human-pose and NeRF discussions.

T1.justification: The stated problem assumptions now explicitly include known cross-view person correspondences and permit unequal frame rates, replacing v1's equal-rate restriction. The mathematical formulation and Procrustes/alignment algorithms otherwise remain substantively unchanged after renumbering and relocation; no new proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 validates the approach only on static, single-person Panoptic scenes. v2 substantially strengthens evidence beyond that setting through multi-person smartphone reconstruction, initialization with sparse and moving cameras, and mixed-rate testing. The expanded discussion of earlier human-based calibration also addresses an important positioning gap. Unexplained Panoptic offset changes and Appendix C's overstatement of EgoBody refinement weaken reporting, but the validation and positioning gains outweigh these limited problems. Full moving-camera reconstruction remains unvalidated.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same human-motion calibration and dynamic NeRF work. The main texts and included appendices are readable, and corresponding equations, algorithms, figures, and tables can be matched despite retitling and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds Mobile-Stage reconstruction, EgoBody calibration, and mixed-frame-rate experiments, including supplementary visual results.

before.justification: v1 reports original calibration, novel-view synthesis, ablation, and robustness results on five Panoptic Studio scenes in Section 4, Tables 1–3, and supplementary figures.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain WAD and timely, concise walking guidance through hierarchical reasoning and adaptive triggering. v4 removes the repeated claim that WAD is unbiased and explicitly claims the first large-scale dataset dedicated to walking assistance. These are limited changes to the dataset's claimed properties and novelty.

C2.justification: The original geographic, camera and linguistic biases and generalization/efficiency limitations are retained in the appendix. v4 adds specific limitations involving event prioritization, obstacle/direction errors and fine-grained recognition. It also discusses interaction with existing walking aids, respondents' concerns about redundant or inaccurate guidance, and interprets the new walking trial as evidence of practical assistance.

D1.justification: The appendix supplies annotation interfaces, category thresholds, normalization/inference/judging prompts, temporal labeling instructions and task-specific test counts. These are substantial new disclosures, not proof of changed implementations or splits. The abstract changes code/data availability from promised to stated available; external availability was not verified.

E1.justification: The 12k-example WAD dataset and reminder/QA tasks remain. v4 additionally evaluates annotation suitability through 34 visually impaired respondents and actual walking assistance with three visually impaired participants (Sections 3.4 and 5.4), substantially extending target-population and interactive deployment coverage.

E2.justification: Relative to v1 Table 2, v4 Table 3 adds LLaVa-7B and WAD-fine-tuned DeepSeek-VL-7B, MiniCPM-V2.6 and Qwen2-VL alongside the original baselines. The subjective comparison also replaces three baseline configurations with fine-tuned versions. DeepSeek becoming DeepSeek-VL is a naming change, while the TRF comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v4 adds explicitly WAD-fine-tuned comparison controls and new survey and walking-study protocols. The walking trial counts manual reminders with and without WalkVLM, always testing WalkVLM first. Section 5.4 also changes the reported subjective-evaluation panel from nine annotators to eight; this establishes a reporting revision, not that every retained result was rerun.

E4.justification: The three original component ablations and their scores are unchanged. However, v4 adds a field case study testing whether WalkVLM reduces manual assistance, supplementary hierarchical-reasoning and streaming-inference cases, and category/text-length analyses (Table 6; Figures 15–21). These substantially broaden analysis beyond the original offline component tests and examples.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests. Added participant counts and outcome percentages concern study design and results. The walking trial's description of a significant reduction is not accompanied by statistical testing.

E6.justification: v4 adds baseline results, 88.24% positive survey responses, and manual-reminder counts of 24/22/28 with WalkVLM versus 35/33/37 without it. Subjective results also change. Existing TF-IDF, ROUGE, TRF and ablation values remain. WalkVLM's GPT scores change from 0.447/0.521 to 1.103/4.168; the pattern suggests rescaling against GPT-4o, not demonstrated performance gains, and the normalization is insufficiently explained.

M1.justification: Both versions retain MiniCPM-V2.6 with LoRA, perception–comprehension–decision reasoning, POLM object-location priors and the ConvNext3D/history-state TAP module. Appendix prompts and trigger details expand documentation without establishing an algorithm change. Event-priority modeling and retrieval augmentation are proposed as future work.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations and experimental discussion undergo extensive rewriting. Section 3.4 is repurposed for dataset applicability and participant feedback, while bias and limitations material moves to the appendix. A contents page and organized supplementary sections substantially expand the document structure.

P2.justification: Existing diagrams and qualitative comparisons are largely retained but resized or relocated, including the annotation pipeline and architecture figure. The main comparison table gains baseline groups, new survey and walking-study tables appear, and the appendix adds maps, annotation screenshots, distributions, prompt tables and qualitative panels. These are substantive display additions beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: The detection-versus-semantic assistance positioning remains largely unchanged. v4 adds LVIS and two retrieval-augmentation references for implementation context and future directions. Its additional published LLaVA reference represents an already cited work, rather than a new research connection.

T1.justification: The problem formulation and mathematical description of temporal prediction remain equivalent. No theorem, proof, substantive derivation or new formal assumption is introduced. The appendix explains the existing TRF evaluation rather than adding mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: Explicitly WAD-fine-tuned baselines substantially strengthen assessment of WalkVLM beyond the original comparisons, while the supplied prompts and annotation specifications address important reproducibility gaps. Direct feedback and walking results from visually impaired participants add relevant, though preliminary, validation. The three-person fixed-order trial remains limited, and GPT-score normalization and the relationship between detailed test counts and the retained 1.5k-sample statement need clarification. These weaknesses do not outweigh the stronger comparison controls, documentation and concrete applicability analysis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WAD dataset and WalkVLM system, and their text, tables, figures and mathematical notation are readable. v1 ends after references despite citing appendices; v4 includes supplementary material. Newly supplied details can be compared as documentation without assuming that the underlying procedures changed.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical evaluations and adds fine-tuned baseline results, a 34-person survey, a three-person walking trial and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, temporal-trigger evaluation, annotator judgments and component ablations in Tables 2–5.

C1.justification: The central contribution, 70% token-reduction claim, and less-than-3% average performance-impact claim remain. The headline end-to-end speedup range increases from 1.6–1.9× in v1's abstract to 1.6–3.6× in v2. This is a limited strengthening of the empirical claim; v1 already reported up to 3.2× in its appendix.

C2.justification: v2 adds the interpretation that token content dominates positional embeddings in determining similarity and explains efficiency scaling through attention costs and the relative contribution of other processing overheads. It also discusses performance outside the intended video setting. The existing limitations concerning complex videos and predefined metrics are retained, moving from Section 11 to Section 12.

D1.justification: Appendix 7 adds explicit per-model frame counts and NVILA similarity thresholds, while Section 3.1 specifies that the first 128 VideoMME samples are used. These are additional disclosures, not evidence that retained experiments changed. The code link remains unchanged. One new inconsistency remains: NVILA-8B's threshold is 0.75 in Appendix 7.1.2, but Table 12 marks 0.7 as the default.

E1.justification: v2 retains VideoMME, NExT-QA, and VideoNIAH and adds EgoSchema and MVBench. It also evaluates VideoMME with subtitles and introduces image evaluation on MMMU-Pro-standard in Appendix 8.1.6. These additions materially broaden task and input coverage.

E2.justification: v1 principally compares against StreamingLLM, FastV, and dense or reduced-frame models. v2 adds PruMerge to corresponding existing benchmark comparisons, including Table 1 and Figure 7, while explicitly excluding it for MiniCPM-V. It also adds measured non-cascaded merging results where v1 used an empty-cache computational bound.

E3.justification: v2 adds NVILA-2B/8B/15B, Qwen2-VL-7B, and InternVL-2.5-8B configurations and expands the main retrieval frame-count sweep from 64–128 to 8–256. The cascading experiment changes substantially: a non-cascaded baseline with a stated 30% merging rate is compared with cascaded merging at an 84% token budget under matched FLOPs, replacing v1's empty-cache limiting case.

E4.justification: v2 adds downstream accuracy tests for similarity-pair selection, distance-metric comparisons, threshold sensitivity, and a positional-embedding intervention. It broadens merging-layer and merging-order ablations across three benchmarks and implements a direct cascading comparison. The earlier top-k hit-count diagnostic is replaced by average similarity versus merging ratio.

E5.justification: Appendix 8.3.4 newly reports numerical uncertainty for the positional-embedding analysis: 0.0087 ± 0.0010 absolute change and 2.73% ± 0.66% relative change. Existing plots of variance across data items remain. The meaning of the new ± terms and any repeated-run counts are unspecified.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial benchmark, ablation, and efficiency results. For example, Table 10 reports NVILA-15B MMMU-Pro-standard scores of 32.8 for FrameFusion, 36.1 for the dense model, and 30.6 for FastV. Many matched earlier results remain unchanged, including Llava-Video-7B's 30%-budget VideoNIAH scores of 90.0, 48.7, and 87.3; expanded aggregate scores should not be treated as same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: Both versions use adjacent-frame cosine similarity, transitive token grouping, averaging into the earliest token, cascaded shallow-layer merging, and subsequent importance-based pruning. The expanded workflow explanation and additional model and image evaluations do not document a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, similarity analysis, and design rationales are extensively rewritten. Cascading discussion moves from the observation analysis into the design rationale, scalability is integrated into performance reporting, and Appendices 7–8 are reorganized into detailed setup, performance, efficiency, and ablation subsections.

P2.justification: Table 1 becomes a much broader model-by-benchmark display, Figure 6 gains a layer-placement panel, and Figure 10 adds a detailed workflow. Runtime and memory displays are redesigned, with additional comparison and ablation plots and tables. Existing radar plots, retrieval heatmaps, and video visualizations are largely retained or relocated.

R1.justification: New Appendix 11 substantially expands positioning against closely related token-merging methods: EVL-Gen, AIM, and LLaVA-PruMerge. It distinguishes FrameFusion's linear-complexity temporal merging from their quadratic similarity computations and different merging/pruning arrangements. This addresses a related-method family largely missing from v1's importance-pruning-centered discussion.

T1.justification: The cosine-similarity and retention definitions in Equations 1–3 and the token-budget and FLOP derivations in Equations 4–6 are retained. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive mathematical correction is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the retained method. PruMerge supplies a relevant merging-based competitor, broader evaluations test generality, and Table 5 replaces v1's empty-cache limiting-case argument with an implemented, FLOP-matched comparison. New metric, threshold, and positional-embedding ablations test important design assumptions. These gains resolve meaningful validation gaps, despite localized reporting problems such as the inconsistent NVILA-8B threshold default.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FrameFusion by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark evaluations, model configurations, and experiments on merging strategies, distance metrics, thresholds, and positional embeddings.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, GPU runtime and memory measurements, token-similarity analyses, and ablations in the main text and appendices.
