C1.justification: The novelty claim is qualified from being the first dataset locating question content toward being the first dataset specifically organized around focus ambiguity, alongside acknowledgment of earlier question grounding. The central contributions remain the dataset, two benchmark tasks, and evidence that current models struggle.

C2.justification: v2 substantially revises the interpretation of recognition behavior, adding hypotheses about counting/pointing pretraining, reasoning prompts, few-shot bias, visual dependence, and abstention. It also explains new localization limitations, including SAM's incomplete object segmentation and Molmo's failure with long FS-ECoT inputs. These extend beyond the earlier discussion of missed regions and question-versus-answer confusion.

D1.justification: v2 specifies model checkpoints in Section 9.1 and substantially expands prompt documentation in Figures 18–22, including the previously omitted full ambiguity definition and explicit FS-ECoT reasoning. It adds annotation-rule development details and localization output-format instructions. The advertised dataset/evaluation-server address changes, while the earlier code address remains. Training details for the new fine-tuning experiment are still missing.

E1.justification: The four source datasets and two principal tasks remain the same; increased sample counts do not constitute new coverage. However, v2 Section 9.3 adds recognition scenarios with the image withheld or replaced by a generated caption, extending evaluation to limited new input conditions.

E2.justification: The main recognition comparison expands from GPT-4o and InternVL2 to also include Qwen2.5-VL and Molmo; the appendix adds ChatGPT-o3 results. Localization adds Molmo+SAM. The earlier End-to-End and Multi-Step approaches remain as GLaMM and GPT-4o+GLaMM, respectively.

E3.justification: The reported dataset grows from 4,357 to 5,500 examples and the test split from 4,217 to 5,360, while training and validation retain 70 examples each. Recognition replaces weighted precision and recall with positive rate. The stated InternVL2 configuration changes from Pro to Llama3-76B, and enhanced-CoT instructions add a plural-form exception. New experiments introduce model-size, fine-tuning, and input-modality conditions.

E4.justification: v2 adds prompt-definition ablations, Qwen2.5-VL size comparisons and fine-tuning, GPT-4o question-only and caption-input ablations, and recognition success/failure cases in Sections 9.2–9.3. It also adds Molmo+SAM failure examples. The earlier recognition breakdowns by ambiguity label and source-specific F1 are omitted, while the existing grounding analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated benchmark runs, random seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. v2's additional question-length standard deviations describe dataset dispersion rather than introducing uncertainty estimation for model results.

E6.justification: Recognition scores and rankings change substantially: Table 2's highest accuracy is 54.4% for InternVL2 ZS-ECoT in v1 and 69.6% for GPT-4o ZS-CoT in v2. These are revised-setting results, not controlled performance gains. New results include Molmo+SAM's 24.3 mAP and ChatGPT-o3's 70.9% FS-ECoT accuracy. The original localization rows in Table 3 and grounding-agreement counts in Table 4 remain numerically unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 adds an engineered Molmo+SAM localization procedure: Molmo predicts points for plausible focus regions, which SAM converts into segmentations. This introduces a distinct inference pipeline alongside the retained direct GLaMM and GPT-4o-description-to-GLaMM approaches.

P1.justification: Beyond the title and author-contribution edits, v2 substantially rewrites the abstract, motivation, dataset description, and benchmarking narrative. It consolidates the earlier Model Design and Model Analysis appendix sections into a structured Section 9 and repairs conspicuous malformed sentences and headings in v1.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns Figure 1, merges the question-length and initial-word displays into Figure 2, restructures the recognition plots, and expands the localization figure. Table 2 changes both model rows and metric columns. New displays include the interaction-interface illustration, prompt boxes, Tables 5–6, and qualitative cases. Existing annotation screenshots and grounding examples are largely retained with relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: The related-work framework remains, but v2 adds Visual7W and explicitly distinguishes prior question grounding from its focus-ambiguity contribution. It also adds literature supporting the zero/few-shot design and the newly evaluated models, while removing the earlier Eppler visual-ambiguity citation. These are targeted positioning refinements rather than a wholesale literature reorganization.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theory, assumptions, propositions, or proofs. The localization metric definitions are retained; expanded conceptual explanations and prompt instructions do not introduce mathematical results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the narrow empirical foundation of v1 through broader model comparisons and diagnostic controls examining prompt wording, model size, fine-tuning, and dependence on visual input. Its fuller prompt specifications address an important reproducibility gap, and acknowledging Visual7W makes the novelty positioning more precise. The new fine-tuning experiment remains underdocumented, and revised settings prevent interpreting cross-version scores as controlled gains, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvements in empirical support and clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VQ-FocusAmbiguity and its recognition and localization tasks, despite the title changing from Accounting to Acknowledging Focus Ambiguity in Visual Questions. Both main texts and complete appendices, including figures and tables, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical analyses and reports additional model comparisons, prompt experiments, model-size and fine-tuning studies, and input ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset analyses, recognition experiments with GPT-4o and InternVL2, localization experiments, and supplementary qualitative analyses.

results.title: Acknowledging Focus Ambiguity in Visual Questions

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions and conclusion replace the categorical 'first' claim with 'novel.' The front matter also drops explicit 1024-resolution and real-time-rendering claims while emphasizing generation detail. The central claims of component disentanglement, layered representation, efficient generation and component transfer remain.

C2.justification: Unlike v1, Section 8.1 explicitly discusses segmentation/SMPL-X errors, body–clothing collisions, loose-clothing animation artifacts, accessory coverage and missing physical constraints. Section 8.2 attributes noise tolerance to multi-view supervision and discusses texture imbalance and limited poses as quality constraints. These materially clarify applicability and failure conditions.

D1.justification: Section 7 newly specifies feature-plane dimensions, decoder/U-Net configurations, initialization, learning rates, loss weights, batch/view sampling, six-day training on two RTX 3090 GPUs, and data preprocessing. These are disclosures rather than evidence of changed existing settings. One ambiguity remains: Section 3.2 calls the decoders MLPs, whereas Figure G describes convolutional blocks.

E1.justification: v2 retains TightCap and THuman2.0 and adds composite training data from THuman2.0, THuman2.1 and CustomHuman, with demonstrations of more varied clothing including dresses and skirts. Supplementary experiments add single-image reconstruction on unseen 4DDress, noisy-mask scenarios and multi-layer outfit composition, substantially extending the represented data and task conditions.

E2.justification: SO-SMPL, LAGA and TELA become evaluated comparators in Table 1c and Figure 3; v1 only cites these works. Conversely, EG3D is removed from both dataset comparisons and PrimDiff from the THuman2.0 comparison. EVA3D, Rodin, HumanLiff, StructLDM and E3Gen remain in their respective comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces masked inter-layer L-PSNR, a 20-participant preference study, and reconstruction experiments comparing UV resolutions 128/256 and decoder depths two/three using PSNR. It also adds a 1,954-scan composite-data experiment. The original THuman2.0 setting of 500 scans/54 views and TightCap setting of 107 samples/158 views remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original two-stage, SLMO and SLMN ablations are retained. Section 8.2 adds TV-loss removal, sensitivity to single-view versus persistent multi-view mask noise, feature-resolution/decoder-depth ablations, controlled body-shape examples and unseen-dataset reconstruction demonstrations. These substantially broaden analysis of component behavior, robustness and generalization.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2's participant count and preference scores introduce an evaluation design and outcomes, without adding an uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Retained FIDs remain 17.37 on TightCap and 12.50 on THuman2.0, and Table 2 is unchanged. New results include L-PSNR above 40 versus HumanLiff's 28.57, preference and timing results in Table 1c, and reconstruction PSNRs of 38.08, 38.55 and 37.34 for the three configurations in Figure O. Supplementary qualitative findings are added, while EG3D/PrimDiff result entries are removed. These are additional results, not improvements to the retained benchmark scores.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2–3.4 retain the three-layer Gaussian UV representation, shared geometry/texture decoders, SMPL-X deformation, joint fitting/diffusion training and existing loss terms. The supplement supplies implementation details and additional applications without documenting a revised core algorithm.

P1.justification: The five-section main-text structure and much of the prose remain. Targeted rewrites affect the abstract, introduction, representation explanation and conclusion; Section 4 gains explicit baseline and metric paragraphs. Author information is updated, and new supplementary sections organize implementation details and discussions.

P2.justification: Table 1 becomes three separate comparison panels, and the main qualitative comparison is substantially reorganized and expanded. v2 adds an E3Gen close-up comparison, architecture diagrams, a configuration table and supplementary experimental figures. v1's standalone template and expressive-animation figures are omitted, while existing ablation and component-transfer displays are reordered or revised.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting datasets, metrics, implementation, additional avatar work and possible extensions, including CustomHuman, HumanNeRF and GarmageNet. The related-work categories and distinction from entangled or optimization-based generation remain largely intact, while replacing 'first' with 'novel' narrows the priority positioning.

T1.justification: The representation, rendering, deformation and training mathematics in Equations 1–12 remain substantively unchanged. Initial-value notation and scale/rotation wording are corrected, and the v-prediction explanation is shortened, without changing the mathematical reasoning. No new theorem, proof or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 provides limited implementation information and largely visual evidence specifically addressing disentanglement. v2 substantially strengthens these areas through L-PSNR and component-focused comparisons, targeted robustness analyses, detailed implementation disclosures and explicit limitations in Sections 7–8. The user-study protocol remains sparsely documented and decoder descriptions are inconsistent, but the gains in evidential support, reproducibility information and qualification of claims clearly outweigh these shortcomings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LayerAvatar and retain matching methods and experiments. All supplied pages, figures, tables and equations support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains supplementary Sections 6–8.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds user-study results, disentanglement measurements, robustness tests and supplementary reconstruction experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original avatar-generation results on TightCap and THuman2.0, quantitative ablations in Table 2, and qualitative animation and component-transfer results.

results.title: Disentangled Clothed Avatar Generation with Layered Representation

C1.justification: The central claims about fine-grained collaborative control and four motion-related applications remain. V2 adds an explicit contribution claim that the representation is independent of base-model architecture and consistently improves controllability across benchmarks. Its conclusion also narrows the contrast with prior work to coarse or inflexible collaborative control.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations linking spatial alignment, depth, the world envelope, and staged training to the ablation outcomes (Section 4.3). Appendix E newly identifies limitations in representing rotation, producing realistic human locomotion, and dependence on preprocessing estimators, supported by failure examples. V1 contains no comparable limitations analysis.

D1.justification: V2 newly names PySceneDetect and discloses learning rates of 1e-5 for stages 1–2 and 1e-6 for stage 3. It revises reported hardware from eight A100 GPUs to one and adds integration, training, and application diagrams in Appendices B–D. These improve documentation; the newly disclosed learning rates do not establish a training-setting change.

E1.justification: RealEstate10K, WebVid10M, and the existing animation applications remain. V2 extends qualitative test scenarios with explicit large-orbit camera stress cases and object-rotation/human-walking failure cases (Figures 5 and 16). The larger reported training sample counts change settings rather than dataset coverage.

E2.justification: V1 discusses competitors but presents no evaluated head-to-head comparisons. V2 evaluates CameraCtrl, reproduced CameraCtrl*, MotionCtrl, and their ++ adaptations for camera control (Table 1), and Motion-I2V, MOFA-Video, and the ++ adaptations for object control (Table 2). Figures 5–6 add qualitative baseline comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 introduces quantitative evaluation on 1K test clips from each dataset, six quality/controllability metrics, frame-count comparison variants, and controlled ablation protocols. Section 4.1 also revises reported training sizes from approximately 6K/35K to 61K/352K RealEstate/WebVid clips. The PDFs do not establish whether these size revisions reflect expanded training or corrected reporting.

E4.justification: V2 adds representation ablations comparing point offsets, point positions, 3D spheres, and spheres plus the world envelope, and compares one-, two-, and three-stage training (Tables 3–4, Figure 7, Appendix C). It also adds a controlled focal-length comparison and concrete rotation/human-motion failure analyses (Figures 10 and 16), beyond v1's demonstrations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. V2's new quantitative tables provide point estimates without introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds the first quantitative results: Table 2 reports Ours FVD 161.076 and ObjMC 23.32, while Table 4 reports FVD 318.941, 254.907, and 161.076 for one-, two-, and three-stage training. Comparative examples and failure findings are also added. These are newly reported results, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The central representation, U-Net/ReferenceNet framework, loss, and three-stage training procedure are retained. V2 adds MotionCtrl++ and CameraCtrl++ adaptations, integrating rendered camera/object signals through separate encoders and fusion into SVD-based implementations (Section 4.2, Appendix B, Figure 13). These extend the method without replacing its core.

P1.justification: V2 extensively tightens the introduction and method explanations and reorganizes the experimental narrative around comparisons and ablations. Much of v1's case-study and application discussion is relocated and expanded in Appendices A and D, producing a substantially different document structure.

P2.justification: V2 substantially rebuilds the visual presentation with Tables 1–4, comparative and ablation figures, architecture/training/application diagrams, and failure panels. Earlier qualitative examples are selectively combined in the main text and expanded or rearranged in Figures 9–12; these are not all newly introduced results.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for FID, FVD, VBench, and PySceneDetect while retaining the main related-work coverage. Research positioning is refined by acknowledging prior collaborative controllers and distinguishing the proposed approach through control granularity, flexibility, and compatibility with other frameworks.

T1.justification: The diffusion equations, noise-prediction objective, and mathematical substance of the sphere/camera construction remain unchanged. V2 clarifies frame versus diffusion-timestep symbols and other notation; it adds no substantive derivation, formal assumption, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: V1's claims relied on selected demonstrations without evaluated competitors or ablations. V2 substantially resolves that evidentiary weakness through defined test-set evaluations, baseline comparisons, component/training ablations, and concrete limitations. Reporting remains imperfect: CameraCtrl*++ has worse translation error than CameraCtrl* (0.291 versus 0.257), qualifying the broad improvement language, and Ours SubCon differs between Table 2 (0.968) and Tables 3–4 (0.969). These limited issues do not outweigh the substantial improvement in validation and applicability assessment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Perception-as-Control and provide readable text, equations, figures, and references. V1 ends with references; v2 includes supplementary Appendices A–E. The complete supplied material supports comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original quantitative comparisons and ablations in Tables 1–4, alongside generated examples and failure cases in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original generated-video demonstrations for camera, object, and collaborative motion control and application examples in Sections 4.2–4.3 and Figures 4–7.

results.title:
Perception-as-Control: Fine-grained Controllable Image Animation with
  3D-aware Motion Representation

C1.justification: V1 presents a two-component pipeline and emphasizes empirical exploration of interleaved generation. V2 redefines the contribution around integrating multimodal autoregression with a rolling-context DiT renderer and explicitly claims state-of-the-art narrative-generation performance in the introduction. The CookGen contribution and abstract are largely retained.

C2.justification: V1 accepts an aesthetics-versus-consistency tradeoff and argues that consistency deserves priority. V2 instead explains how reference-image VAE features preserve detail while CLIP conditioning preserves semantics, and discusses a context-length efficiency/consistency tradeoff and baseline-specific visual failures. The existing ASR-noise, repeated-step, and hallucination limitations remain in Appendix H.

D1.justification: V2 identifies FLUX.1 Fill initialization and supplies the new renderer's full configuration in Appendix D, including AdamW settings, learning rate, batch size, training steps, and masking probability. It also newly specifies the existing regularization's masking/shuffling rates and noise scale estimated from 2,000 embeddings. V1's explicit director LoRA and Sora-like video-model descriptions are dropped; the project-page access information is retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same CookGen cooking data sourced from YouCook2 and HowTo100M, covering caption assessment, inverse reconstruction, narrative keyframes, and video generation. The additional renderer and baseline experiments remain within this established coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 4 adds evaluated comparisons with IC Lora, StoryDiffusion, Vlogger, and SEED-Story, alongside retained SD-XL and FLUX.1-s. V1 Table 8's SEED-X results reappear as the method without rolling-context conditioning. EMU-2 disappears from that human comparison, although its latent-space comparison remains in Appendix F.

E3.justification: The existing splits, preprocessing, and director/video-model training budgets remain unchanged. The expanded keyframe comparison adds CLIP-T/FID reporting, specifies two-epoch adaptation for IC Lora and SEED-Story, and marks SD-XL/FLUX narrative ratings as inapplicable. The new renderer introduces a four-image, 5,000-step training configuration; these are additions within the retained evaluation framework.

E4.justification: V2 adds a with/without rolling-context comparison in Table 4 and explicit regularization controls in Tables 3 and 7, including cumulative masking, Gaussian noise, and shuffling. Conversely, the EMU-2 portion of v1's loss ablation is removed. The latent-space comparison and perturbation visualizations are retained in Appendix F, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, evaluation seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The six caption-evaluation annotators are documented in both. V2's Gaussian-noise standard deviation specifies perturbation strength, not uncertainty in reported performance.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial baseline and renderer results. Table 4 reports CLIP-T/FID of 28.0/29.4 with rolling context, versus retained values of 26.1/25.3 without it; corresponding aesthetics, realism, consistency, and narrative ratings are 4.8/4.5/4.8/4.6 versus 2.1/4.3/4.5/4.4. Regularization intermediate results are added, while EMU-2 loss/human results and SD-XL/FLUX narrative scores are dropped. Matched final video-generation and caption-quality scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: V2 adds a rolling-context keyframe renderer between the interleaved director and video generator. This FLUX.1 Fill-based component combines tiled captions, predicted visual embeddings, and reference-image VAE features, using a flow-matching objective (Section 4.2). It substantially changes keyframe synthesis; the existing director and noise-regularization operators are retained.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially condensed and rewritten, the method hierarchy is reorganized around three components, and the experiments gain separate comparison and ablation sections. Dataset-quality evaluation moves from Section 3.3 into Appendix C, while much of the latent-space analysis moves into Appendix F. This is extensive narrative restructuring despite substantial retained text.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 3 to include the renderer, expands Figure 4 with regularization illustrations, adds rolling-context examples and an annotation-evaluation diagram, and replaces the main qualitative comparison. The principal comparison table gains methods, metrics, and prompting columns; the loss table loses its EMU-2 block. Several retained displays move to the appendices, whose implementation and algorithm layouts also change substantially.

R1.justification: V2 adds IC Lora, CLIPScore, and FID references and removes the LLM-grounded video diffusion reference. The narrative-generation discussion shifts from emphasizing proximity to SEED-Story toward positioning the method as an integrated multimodal-LLM/in-context-DiT approach. Most related work remains, including the FLUX work under revised bibliographic wording.

T1.justification: V2 Section 4.2 adds mathematical definitions for tiled captions, joint keyframe conditioning, and the renderer's flow-matching objective in Equations 5–7. The earlier autoregressive factorization, regression loss, and regularization mathematics remain. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical case beyond v1's mostly internal comparisons: relevant narrative baselines and explicit renderer and regularization controls address important gaps in comparative and component-level evidence (Tables 3, 4, and 7). Appendix D also documents the new renderer's training. There are material qualifications: rolling context worsens FID from 25.3 to 29.4, the prose combines best CLIP-T and FID scores from different variants, and some EMU-2 evidence is removed. These issues weaken blanket superiority claims, but the added comparative and controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VideoAuteur and CookGen. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the substantial revision.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds rolling-context renderer evaluations, external-method comparisons, and regularization ablations in Section 5.

before.justification: V1 reports original caption-quality evaluations, latent-space and regression experiments, human ratings, and video-generation results in Sections 3.3 and 5, with supplementary examples and analyses.

results.title: VideoAuteur: Towards Long Narrative Video Generation

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on jointly estimating scale, shift and pose with state-of-the-art accuracy. v2 broadens the central contribution to determining when depth information and different estimation strategies help, explicitly emphasizing scale-only alternatives, RANSAC choices and efficiency against competing affine-depth solvers. The three camera configurations remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantial conditional interpretation: when shift modelling is unnecessary, when reprojection refinement can help with reliable indoor depths, and why hybrid RANSAC trades computation for accuracy. It also tentatively attributes declining accuracy at larger iteration budgets to physically implausible scale/focal solutions that current checks admit. Existing coplanarity and pure-translation limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents Mast3r's 500 coarse/200 fine refinement iterations, its distinct CPU/GPU hardware, and exclusions from runtime measurements. Conversely, v1's statement that source code is available, accompanied by a URL, becomes only a promise of future public release in v2. This changes the documented access information without establishing the repository's actual status.

E1.justification: v2 adds ScanNet RGB-D evaluation for calibrated, shared-focal and different-focal cases (Tables 10, 12 and 15), while retaining Phototourism and ETH3D. Conversely, v1's synthetic evaluations covering controlled image/depth noise and pure-rotation scenarios disappear, including Appendix B.1.

E2.justification: v2 adds MadPose's affine-depth solvers as direct comparators for all three camera configurations and Mast3r's nonlinear optimization for focal-length comparisons. The existing P3P, Rel3PT, 3p3d, 4p4d and standard point-based solvers remain. These additions substantially strengthen comparison against competing estimation approaches.

E3.justification: The primary evaluation moves from GC-RANSAC without local optimization to PoseLib with local optimization; PoseLib already appeared in v1's appendix, but its stated threshold changes from 1 to 2 pixels. Phototourism changes from nine scenes/43,678 pairs to five scenes/24,750 pairs. v2 also adds hybrid protocols and iteration-budget sweeps, introduces RoMA/Mast3r matching, revises depth sources from eleven to five, and replaces separate real-data rotation/translation summaries with combined maximum pose error.

E4.justification: v1's numerical-stability and controlled noise-sensitivity studies are removed. v2 adds systematic comparisons of Sampson versus reprojection refinement, shift/scale modelling assumptions, iteration-dependent speed–accuracy tradeoffs, and Mast3r matches combined with MoGe depth. The inverse-depth comparison and selected fast-versus-GB results are retained, rather than newly introduced analyses.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 2 reports error distributions using medians and 25th/75th-percentile boxes; these statistical spread displays disappear with the synthetic experiments. Neither version reports seed-based uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests for the main benchmark results.

E6.justification: v2 substantially replaces and expands the benchmark results. For example, its new Phototourism SP+LG/MoGe comparison reports 40.42 mAA at 23.41 ms for 3PTs00f1,2 versus 38.89 at 44.03 ms for 4PTsuvf1,2 (Table 5). These are new within-version comparisons, not demonstrated gains over v1 under identical settings. Supplementary Tables 6–7 retain selected v1 DA V2 results unchanged.

M1.justification: The core geometric solver formulations remain. v2 extends their estimation pipeline with reprojection-error scoring and refinement, with or without shift, and integration into hybrid RANSAC. The zero-shift configurations already appear in v1's solver tables; their expanded explanation and testing do not establish an entirely new solver family.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled RePoseD and extensively rewrites its abstract, introduction, contributions and experimental narrative. A dedicated Related Work section is introduced, method sections are consolidated, and inverse-depth material is moved into a separately organized supplement. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: v1's stability and noise figures are replaced by a pipeline illustration and speed–accuracy plots. The solver-configuration tables are merged, and benchmark tables are extensively redesigned around matchers and optimization variants, with much denser supplementary displays. Selected unchanged DA V2 results are extracted into compact supplementary tables.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section substantially revises positioning, especially by acknowledging Yu et al.'s concurrent MadPose work as solving the same affine-depth formulation. v2 distinguishes its contribution through solver efficiency, additional parameter configurations and conditional disagreement about shift modelling. It also expands discussion of DUSt3R/Mast3r and depth-assisted reconstruction research.

T1.justification: Most affine- and inverse-depth reasoning is retained or relocated. Limited mathematical revisions include replacing the calibrated 3PTs00 worked example with explicit shared-focal 3PTs00f constraints and removing an extra scale factor from the four-correspondence focal-length distance constraint. The configuration table also revises reported focal-solver solution counts.

improvement.justification: Direct MadPose comparisons, systematic optimization and parameter-modelling controls, and ScanNet evaluation substantially strengthen the evidence for when depth-based estimation helps. Together with clearer positioning and more conditional conclusions, these address important limitations of v1's comparative argument. Removing synthetic stability/noise evidence and replacing the code URL with a future-release promise weaken verification, but the expanded controlled comparisons provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Despite the new RePoseD title, both PDFs describe the same underlying research, with matching solver formulations, camera configurations and retained results. Both main texts and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and supplementary Section 7 report original evaluations on Phototourism, ETH3D and ScanNet, including solver, matching and optimization comparisons.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original synthetic experiments and pose/focal-length evaluations on Phototourism and ETH3D.

results.title: RePoseD: Efficient Relative Pose Estimation With Known Depth Information

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion expand the central contribution from independent layer manipulation with motion scores or sketches to flexible composition of heterogeneous controls, including trajectories, across layers. The contribution statement and principal demonstrations now foreground simultaneous composite control, substantially broadening the claimed capability beyond the terminology change.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of control informativeness, complementary heatmap/offset representations, and the benefits of increasing layer capacity and motion information. It removes v1's explanation of weaker sketch guidance and its explicit limitation concerning control of elements absent from the initial I2V frame. Resolution/duration constraints and possible real-world transfer remain in Appendix E. Improved training-data segmentation does not itself establish that the omitted inference limitation is resolved.

D1.justification: v3 documents four-frame key-frame spacing, CoTracker3 tracking on a 60-by-60 grid, an 80% masklet-consistency threshold, control encoders, and padded-layer masking. It specifies 10% mask dropout and 20/40/40 modality-selection probabilities, and changes reported hardware from 16 to 32 A100 GPUs. Conversely, v1's explicit first/last-half allocation recipe for interpolation is no longer described. Both retain the same project-code link.

E1.justification: The four animation tasks in v1 expand to six through trajectory-conditioned I2V and trajectory-conditioned interpolation. v3 also demonstrates simultaneous heterogeneous controls across layers in Figure 6. The animation domain remains unchanged; the increased clip count is a setting change rather than additional domain coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds CogVideoX to I2V and interpolation, and AniDoc to sketch-conditioned I2V. New trajectory comparisons evaluate DragAnything, Tora, and Framer. SEINE, DynamiCrafter, LVCD, and ToonCrafter remain quantitative comparators, although SEINE disappears from the main qualitative comparison figure.

E3.justification: The reported corpus grows from 563K to 665K clips, training changes from 50,000 to 30,000 steps, and batch size increases from 32 to 96. The static threshold changes from 0.05 to 0.1 and the motion-score upper bound from 20 to 30. Sketch extraction changes from Anime2Sketch to Chan et al.'s extractor. v3 explicitly excludes motion scores from headline I2V/interpolation comparisons and specifies matched control inputs. Appendix B adds trajectory MSE evaluation. Both retain a 1K evaluation sample, without establishing identical membership.

E4.justification: v3 Table 2 adds layer-capacity tests and heatmap-versus-offset-versus-hybrid trajectory ablations. Motion assignment is examined through progressive motion-information conditions for both I2V and interpolation, replacing v1's simpler removal test. Appendix Figure 8 adds a motion-score sensitivity example. Conversely, v1's attention-fusion ablation, visual component-failure analysis, shot-filtering analysis, and sketch-style comparison are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both provide point estimates and user-vote proportions; the changed values do not constitute a change in uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces LayerAnimate's reported results: I2V FVD changes from 98.86 to 87.96, interpolation from 55.69 to 59.64, and sketch-conditioned I2V from 40.64 to 26.64. Changed training and conditioning prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains or losses. v3 adds trajectory results, including appendix MSE values of 46.58 for I2V and 24.40 for interpolation. Ablation results, qualitative examples, and user-vote distributions also change.

M1.justification: v3 replaces first-frame-only segmentation propagation with iterative key-frame segmentation that incorporates newly appearing elements. It adds trajectory conditioning through a hybrid heatmap/offset representation and trains with different control modalities selected independently across layers. These substantially extend v1's motion-score and sketch controls. The motion-coherence filtering stage is also omitted from the specified pipeline; the underlying layer fusion and motion-based assignment mechanisms remain recognizable.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, curation motivation, and method exposition undergo substantial rewriting. Section 4 is reorganized around frame decomposition, layer controlling, and feature fusion; the application narrative becomes composite control. Terminology changes throughout from layer-specific to layer-level, and the surviving limitations move into a substantially reorganized supplement.

P2.justification: The teaser, curation pipeline, architecture schematic, and qualitative comparison are substantially redesigned. Table 1 gains a six-task structure, Table 2 is rebuilt, Table 3 is added, and the user-study display expands to six charts. The merging tree moves from v1 Figure 2 to v3 appendix Figure 7; a trimmed version of v1 Figure 7 becomes appendix Figure 9. Several earlier appendix displays are removed and a motion-score sensitivity display is added.

R1.justification: The existing diffusion and controllable-generation survey remains largely intact. v3 adds CoTracker3, MIMO, DragAnything, and Tora citations, discussing trajectory control and contrasting animation decomposition with depth-based approaches. PySceneDetect and Anime2Sketch citations disappear. Framer's publication update is bibliographic; its new experimental participation is assessed under E2.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.1 introduces explicit mask-set subtraction and union-update definitions in Equations 1–2 for iterative segmentation. This is a limited addition of formal algorithmic definitions. The diffusion denoising objective is retained with revised conditioning notation, and neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence for controllability through layer-capacity and representation ablations, direct trajectory-error measurements, and broader comparisons with explicitly matched control inputs. These address weaknesses in v1's validation, while detailed control-generation and training procedures improve reproducibility. Removing the attention ablation and the initial-frame limitation reduces completeness, but the stronger experimental design and targeted validation provide a substantial net improvement. The judgment does not depend on treating changed-protocol scores as direct performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LayerAnimate and contain readable main texts, figures, tables, equations, and supplementary material. Retained components and relocated material can be matched reliably despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v3 reports original six-task benchmark results, expanded ablations, a 20-participant user study, and appendix trajectory-error measurements and motion-score experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original four-task benchmark results, component ablations, a 20-participant user study, and qualitative experiments, including appendix analyses.

results.title: LayerAnimate: Layer-level Control for Animation

C1.justification: The main novelty, unseen-prompt artifact reduction, quality preservation, and DreamBooth applicability claims remain. The third introductory contribution now explicitly includes exploring pixel-feedback choices and optional regularization against early collapse, modestly broadening the stated contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking detector false positives to downstream collapse and interpreting threshold selection and comparator weaknesses. The supplied text drops v1's detailed SD1.5 capacity/hand-avoidance explanation, warning about possible ImageReward hacking, and explicit prompt-scale resource limitation. The semantic-reasoning limitation and early-stopping/regularization tradeoff remain.

D1.justification: v2 identifies RichHF* as the authors' implementation, provides numerical mask and evaluation thresholds, and describes HPSv2 reward optimization and user-masked inpainting comparisons. It also updates inference/truncation settings. Conversely, v1's explicit statement that evaluation averages 400 generated images is absent; this does not establish a changed sample count.

E1.justification: The supplied material retains the same artifact-detection data and COCO benchmark, Qwen-generated text-to-image prompts, LAION regularization data, and DreamBooth personalization task. Replacing SD1.5 experiments with SDXL and Kolors changes model configurations, without establishing new dataset, domain or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds PAL4VST to detector comparisons, HPSv2-based optimization and Hands XL to quantitative treating comparisons, and inpainting methods to qualitative comparisons. These are evaluated alternatives absent from v1's corresponding experiments. RichHF* matches v1's 'only previous' detector baseline rather than constituting another new comparator.

E3.justification: The main evaluation replaces mean/max artifact confidence with artifact frequency based on a 0.5 maximum-confidence threshold and adds CLIP-T. FLUX.1 inference changes from five to four steps; SDXL and Kolors replace SD1.5 and use 20 steps. Gradient tracking is specified as the last 25% of steps instead of a fixed final step. The prompt split remains 3,000/100.

E4.justification: v2 adds threshold-mask and downstream detector-quality ablations, including naive-detector collapse in Figure 4 and Table 2. Table 3 adds quantitative regularization comparisons at epochs 3 and 10, complementing the retained Figure 5. v1's 4K-pseudo-label ablation, all-versus-max convergence plot, and SD1.5 shortcut case study are absent from the supplied v2.

E5.justification: v2 introduces plus/minus uncertainty values in Tables 2–4, whereas v1 reports point estimates. This adds uncertainty reporting, but the supplied text does not define the uncertainty measure or disclose repetition counts, so additional runs or a particular statistical procedure cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: v2 reports substantial new comparison and ablation results. For example, Table 4 reports FLUX.1 artifact frequency of 82.66% before and 22.00% after DiffDoctor under v2's protocol. SDXL/Kolors results replace SD1.5 results. Retained detector rows and FLUX.1 user-study percentages are unchanged. Changed metrics and inference settings prevent interpreting the revised main results as same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The two-stage detector-and-treating method remains. v2 adds confidence-thresholded pixel selection above 0.1 to v1's all-pixel and maximum-pixel alternatives and favors it experimentally. Section 3.2 also describes selecting hard cases with extremely high or low confidence, whereas v1 specifies high confidence.

P1.justification: The overall five-section structure and much of the introductory, related-work and methodological prose remain. v2 edits the abstract and detector explanation, reorganizes the final experimental subsections into comparisons and qualitative demonstrations, shortens the limitations discussion, and updates affiliations.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn, Figure 3 adds a PAL4VST column, and Figure 4 is replaced by a detector-collapse visualization. v2 adds quantitative ablation tables and restructures the main comparison table. The SD1.5 figure becomes a multi-method comparison, and the user-study bar chart becomes Table 5. The FLUX.1, regularization and DreamBooth examples are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Hands XL, SDXL and Kolors. HPSv2 and PAL4VST were already cited in v1. The related-work discussion and positioning as the first pixel-level-feedback approach to diffusion-model tuning remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 Equation (1) replaces v1 Equation (2)'s full-image normalization by an explicitly masked sum normalized by the selected-pixel count. This is a limited objective-definition revision; masking was already discussed in v1. The detector MSE, artifact definitions, and KL/rectified-flow regularization reasoning remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of evaluated competing treatments and limited evidence connecting detector quality to successful treating. The new comparisons and detector/mask ablations strengthen the central empirical argument. These gains outweigh the lost failure-case discussion, although quality remains limited by undefined uncertainty values and a contradictory sentence claiming unregularized training wins at epoch 10 when Table 3 favors regularization. Referenced appendix material remains unavailable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DiffDoctor, and all ten pages of each are readable, including equations and visual results. However, both reference appendices that are absent from the supplied PDFs, which end with references and contain no embedded supplements. Appendix-only material cannot be compared.

after.justification: v2 reports original detector and treating experiments, including comparative results on FLUX.1, SDXL and Kolors, quantitative ablations, and user-study outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports original detector ablations, FLUX.1 and SD1.5 experiments, DreamBooth demonstrations, and a 24-person user study.

results.title: DiffDoctor: Diagnosing Image Diffusion Models Before Treating

C1.justification: The central contribution remains unified appearance-geometry generation with the same downstream capabilities. v2 extends the main claims to qualitatively better inpainting than multi-step alternatives and lower memory consumption; v1 emphasized plausible joint inpainting, speed, and consistency.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations and qualifications: unbounded inverse depth is linked to long-range accuracy, range-limited ground truth is identified as a benchmark limitation, and Appendix F identifies oversmoothing on grass, fur, and hair. It also qualifies RGB quality by the pretrained model, explains excluded runtime I/O, and discloses that the inpainting baseline predicts normals without conditioning on observed normals.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly discloses distillation and KL weights of 10^-6 and 10^-3, the discriminator architecture, stage-specific dataset sampling, and filtering of examples with teacher disagreement. These improve documentation of existing training; the PDFs do not establish that these procedures were newly introduced in v2.

E1.justification: Training datasets and evaluation coverage remain the same, including COCO-caption generation, zero-shot depth and normal prediction, and joint inpainting. The new preference study, timing measurements, and PCA examine existing tasks or representations rather than introducing new model tasks or data domains.

E2.justification: v2 adds an SDXL-inpainting, Marigold-DC, and Lotus-normal pipeline to Figures 9 and 21-22, where v1 showed Orchid alone. It adds DepthAnything-v2 plus DSINE to Table 4, revises comparator participation in Figures 6, 7, and 13, and adds quantitative and preference comparisons against the pretrained RGB LDM in Table 8.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols include single-H100 timing, aesthetics and text-adherence ratings from 40 users viewing 25 images each, and PCA on 1,000 concatenated depth-normal latent samples. Ablation reporting drops FID, AbsRel, and mean angular error. The previously stated main benchmark settings and training schedules remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The existing joint-latent, distillation, and pseudo-label ablations are extended with additional geometry outcomes in Table 5. v2 adds a PCA check of depth-normal redundancy and comparative inpainting failure cases. The VAE-only pseudo-label reconstruction improvements reported in v1 Section 4.5 are no longer reported.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new preference percentages and PCA explained variance are descriptive findings rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 2-3 and the existing Table 4 scores are unchanged. v2 adds DepthAnything-v2 plus DSINE inconsistency scores of 0.059 on NYUv2 and 0.144 on KITTI, runtime results, additional ablation outcomes, PCA findings, and inpainting comparisons. Table 8 reports Orchid preference rates of 47.4% for aesthetics and 46.9% for text adherence. Some earlier ablation entries disappear, including FID values of 18.74 for joint and 17.11 for disentangled latents.

M1.justification: The joint VAE, latent diffusion model, color-conditioned finetuning, and RePaint-style joint inpainting procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 specifies the already-used distillation loss more explicitly; this does not establish a new method component.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, with substantial revisions to related work and explanatory prose. Ablations are reorganized into the main text, and the appendix is restructured into sections covering runtime, ablation details, color quality, qualitative results, and limitations.

P2.justification: Figure 9 becomes a full-width baseline comparison, and the original Figure 21 is rearranged across Figures 21-22 with comparator panels. Figures 5-7 and 13 are revised, Table 4 gains a comparator column, the ablation table is relocated and restructured, and runtime and user-study tables are added.

R1.justification: Related work substantially refocuses its inverse-problem discussion toward 3D completion, editing, and geometric diffusion priors, adding works such as Reffusion, NeRFiller, RealmDreamer, and Marigold-DC while removing several earlier references. v2 also explicitly distinguishes Orchid from GeoWizard's separate representations and from systems combining multiple appearance and geometry priors.

T1.justification: Algorithm 1 adds an explicit mathematical definition of the existing distillation loss as a weighted L1 distance between teacher and student latent means. v1 referenced this loss without defining it. The other mathematical formulations remain substantially unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked measured runtime and direct inpainting baselines, leaving important practical advantages of the joint model insufficiently tested. v2 addresses these gaps through Table 7 and Figures 9 and 21-22, while Table 8 evaluates preservation of RGB generation quality. Additional training details and explicit limitations further strengthen the paper. Removing some ablation metrics reduces completeness, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the new evidence substantially improves support for the central contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Orchid and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The shared methods and experiments can be matched despite rewriting and appendix reorganization.

after.justification: The original empirical results remain, supplemented by runtime measurements, a human preference study, latent-space PCA, and additional comparisons.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendices B-C report original depth and normal benchmarks, ablations, generated images, and joint inpainting results.

results.title: Orchid: Image Latent Diffusion for Joint Appearance and Geometry Generation

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands the mechanisms offered for the method's effectiveness: segmentation gradients improve grounding, text attention mitigates sampling noise, shared feature maps avoid dynamic-head memory costs, and time-varying text features improve temporal reasoning over static embeddings. D1.justification: V2 newly documents 16 sampling points and, in Appendix B, FPN construction, loss weights, augmentations, training epochs, batch sizes, frame sampling, optimizer settings and eight A800 GPUs. E1.justification: Both versions use RefCOCO/+/g pretraining and evaluate Ref-YouTube-VOS, Ref-DAVIS17, A2D-Sentences, JHMDB-Sentences and MeViS. Additional efficiency comparisons and visual examples do not establish new task or dataset coverage.

E2.justification: V2 introduces G-DINO+SH and G-DINO+DH, both augmented with temporal self-attention, across Tables 1–2. Grounded-SAM2 disappears from the four-dataset Table 1 and Figure 5, while its MeViS comparison survives in supplementary Table 6 alongside newly included AL-Ref-SAM2. Table 7 adds an efficiency comparison involving SgMg, MUTR and G-DINO+DH.

E3.justification: The principal training/evaluation scheme is retained, but the reported MeViS selection threshold changes from 0.2 to 0.3. Table 5 replaces the 20% and 65% pruning settings with 15% and 30%, and adds FPS evaluation at 360P. These establish limited protocol revisions without proving which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The temporal and attention-removal ablations remain, and the existing momentum-coefficient case study moves to Appendix E. V2 removes v1's isolated dot-product/CondInst mask-decoder comparisons, revises the pruning sweep, and adds comparative memory/latency analysis in Appendix D and qualitative cases in Figure 8.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, variability estimates, confidence intervals or significance tests. The results remain point estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes ReferDINO's Swin-T J&F from 66.4 to 67.5 on Ref-YouTube-VOS and from 66.8 to 66.7 on Ref-DAVIS17. Table 5 substantially replaces accuracy, FLOP and memory values and adds FPS; new baseline and efficiency results appear throughout Tables 1–2 and 6–7. These are reported result changes, not established same-setting gains. V2 Section 5.2 still quotes 66.4, conflicting with its Table 1.

M1.justification: The GroundingDINO adaptation, temporal tracker and decoder, grounding-guided mask decoder, pruning score, losses and sequence-selection procedure remain substantively unchanged. Expanded explanations of bilinear sampling and gradient propagation do not establish a new method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and substantial portions of the method explanation are rewritten. The mask-decoder and temporal-enhancer subsections and their ablations reverse order, qualitative discussion is condensed, and supplementary Sections A–F organize additional and relocated material. Affiliations and acknowledgements also change.

P2.justification: The visual presentation is substantially reorganized: Figure 1 drops the zebra example, Figure 2 is redrawn, Figure 5 removes Grounded-SAM2 rows, and Figure 7 moves to the supplement. V2 adds Figure 8 and Tables 6–7, swaps the component-ablation tables, and adds an FPS column to Table 5.

R1.justification: V2 expands positioning against parallel box/mask heads, static-text temporal modules and foundation models used primarily for preprocessing. New references include YOLO-World, DetCLIP, OnlineRefer, temporal collection and distribution, and several downstream foundation-model applications. Some earlier references, including Segment Anything and the single-scale vision-transformer work, are removed.

T1.justification: V2 Section 4.3 and Appendix A add a computational-complexity derivation absent from v1. Equations 7–11 derive a geometric-series cost bound for retaining 1/k queries per layer and argue independence from decoder depth under that model. The original method equations remain equivalent.

improvement.justification: The trained GroundingDINO baselines substantially strengthen evidence that the proposed adaptations contribute beyond the foundation model itself. Appendix B resolves important reproducibility gaps, while the complexity and timing analyses better substantiate efficiency claims. These gains outweigh the removal of some isolated controls and Grounded-SAM2 comparisons, although the unresolved Table 1 versus Section 5.2 numerical inconsistency weakens reporting reliability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReferDINO and provide readable methods, equations, experiments, figures and references. The complete supplied documents support comparison, including v2's supplementary Sections A–F; v1 ends with references.

after.justification: V2 retains original ReferDINO experiments and reports additional baseline, efficiency and qualitative results, including supplementary Tables 6–7 and Figure 8.

before.justification: V1 reports original ReferDINO benchmark results, component ablations, pruning experiments and qualitative predictions in Tables 1–5 and Figures 5–7.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of nonmonotonic lip-sync results, declining image-quality scores as greater adherence to reference images, and the effects of modality order on gesture naturalness. It specifies audio 50% and pose 25%, whereas v1 states a final pose ratio of 50%. The audio-ratio summary changes 10/50/100% to 10/50/90%, with text fixed at 90%; its full supplementary protocol is unavailable. These are reported setting changes, without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: v3 Table 1 adds systematic text-data and modality-order ablations across three benchmarks; Figures 3 and 5 add pretrained-model comparisons and hand-trajectory analysis. v1's reference-ratio study of drift in 30-second videos is not reproduced in the supplied v3. The audio-ratio study is summarized, but its referenced supplementary evidence cannot be inspected.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added quantitative tables retain the practice of reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: All numerical scores in v1 Tables 1–2 are retained in v3 Tables 2–3. v3 nevertheless adds substantial results in the training-ablation table and pose benchmark, including OmniHuman FVD 7.3184 and AKD 2.136 in Table 4. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over the earlier audio benchmark scores.

M1.justification: The core MMDiT architecture, condition encoders, reference conditioning, and staged training remain. v3 introduces region-selective CFG for choosing the speaker in Section 4.4. Section 3.4 specifies CFG scale 6.5 without retaining v1's annealing description, although it does not explicitly establish whether annealing was abandoned.

P1.justification: Existing introduction and method prose is extensively rewritten, the numbered contributions become a narrative paragraph, and the training principles receive clearer separate explanations. The experimental narrative is reorganized to put ablations before baseline comparisons, and a limitations section is added.

P2.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the displays: it adds quantitative-ablation and pose-comparison tables, adds pretrained-model and trajectory figures, and refines Figure 2. v1's Figure 7 is retained as a smaller Figure 4, while its large ablation displays and post-reference galleries are not included in the supplied v3.

R1.justification: The related-work survey is largely retained. v3 adds Panda-70M as a filtering reference, removes the standalone classifier-free-guidance and flow-matching references, and adds discussion contrasting its modality order with earlier methods. CyberHost's changed title and publication details refer to the same work.

T1.justification: The two training principles remain heuristic guidance. Neither version supplies formal theorems, proofs, derivations, or mathematical assumptions that are substantively added, removed, or revised.

improvement.justification: v1 supports its central training principles mainly through visual ablations and a preference study. v3 adds objective ablations across three benchmarks, explicit modality-order controls, and quantitative pose-driving evidence, substantially strengthening support for the central claims. Training details and specific limitations also improve assessability. The unavailable audio-ratio supplement, omitted reference-drift analysis, and underspecified pose-evaluation protocol reduce completeness, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmniHuman-1 and are readable throughout, including v1's post-reference figures. However, v3 refers to an audio-ratio study in Supplementary Section 5 that is absent from the supplied PDF, limiting comparison of that study.

after.justification: v3 retains the audio-animation benchmarks and reports additional quantitative training ablations, pose-driven comparisons, and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original portrait/body animation benchmarks, visual ablations, and a preference study involving 20 subjects and 50 samples.

C1.justification: V2 makes SBS a core contribution and explicitly focuses the introduction on cross-silo adaptation. The abstract shifts from preventing extraction through permutation to mitigating extraction through permutation and SBS, while qualifying feasibility with substantial communication and server costs. The conclusion changes from describing the challenges as addressed to stating that practical adoption still requires important improvements.

C2.justification: V2 acknowledges that neighboring representations can undermine permutation-only protection and motivates SBS through that mechanism. It interprets SBS's mixed accuracy effects as limited disruption and possible regularization, extends the existing communication caveat with a large-model/small-data applicability argument, and identifies rigorous model-privacy guarantees and malicious-client robustness as unresolved.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository link, descriptions of the evaluated baseline implementations, and substantial FHE implementation information: Tile Tensors/CKKS, 128-bit security, representation dimensions, and the benchmark machine and RAM. These are new disclosures; the PDFs do not establish a change to the implementation or hardware of the retained classification experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Fed-ISIC2019 for downstream classification, with Tiny-ImageNet and Fed-ISIC2019 auxiliary data. The additional component, similarity and cost analyses do not expand the represented datasets, domains or downstream tasks.

E2.justification: Tables 1–4 add evaluated LoRA and adapter-tuning comparators throughout the accuracy, scalability and efficiency comparisons. Appendix D.1 identifies federated LoRA as FedIT. Full fine-tuning and linear probing remain; the additions go beyond their existing citations in v1.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluation procedures for adjacent versus nonadjacent block similarity using eight-sample batches, and a separate per-block FHE benchmark at 128-bit security with single-sample and batch-of-eight measurements. These substantially broaden evaluation beyond classification and approximation testing. The retained classification experiments keep their splits, optimizers, learning rates, training budgets and balanced-accuracy metric.

E4.justification: V2 adds BlindFed-versus-BlindFed+SBS comparisons, feature-similarity heatmaps examining permutation vulnerability, and comparisons of block-sampling strategies in Appendix B. Appendix D.5 adds encryption-overhead analysis. V1's auxiliary-data, client-scalability, distillation and approximation-degree studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or empirical error bars. The added SBS sampling probabilities concern the algorithm's behavior, not uncertainty estimates for reported performance.

E6.justification: Existing accuracy entries in Tables 1–3 are unchanged under the Ours-to-BlindFed rename, but substantial LoRA, adapter-tuning and SBS results are added. For example, the new SBS row reports 0.6831 on federated Fed-ISIC2019 with in-distribution auxiliary data, versus retained BlindFed accuracy of 0.6679. Table 7 newly reports 136 seconds for encrypted block inference and 17.33 MB ciphertexts. Table 4 changes Fed-ISIC2019 memory from 17.32 to 8.71 GB for linear probing and from 8.71 to 17.32 GB for full fine-tuning.

M1.justification: V2 adds stochastic block sampling (SBS): nonadjacent block representations are selected, and unselected features are zeroed for adapter learning. Appendix B.1 additionally introduces noise masking of unselected outputs during client decryption and re-encryption. These substantially extend the privacy procedure; polynomial approximation, distillation, parallel adapters and secure aggregation are retained.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction and conclusion, names the framework BlindFed, and reorganizes the method around architecture redesign, two-stage split learning and privacy boosting. The proof moves to the supplement, existing appendix material is reorganized, and a contents page is added. This restructuring extends beyond the newly added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 adds an overall workflow diagram, an SBS state diagram, similarity heatmaps, sampling plots and an FHE-cost table, and redraws existing architecture illustrations. Tables 1–4 gain comparator rows and double-blind-status columns. V1's accuracy-versus-parameters plot is removed, new efficiency bar charts are added, and retained training curves are regrouped with clarified loss-axis labels.

R1.justification: V2 adds LoRA-GA, LoFT, linear-probing and FHE implementation/acceleration references while retaining the existing research positioning. The additional published FedIT reference corresponds to federated instruction-tuning work already cited in v1, rather than a distinct new work.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds a sampling-probability recurrence, its stationary probability of one-third, and approximate expected sampled-block counts. Proposition 1 and its non-uniqueness proof are retained and relocated to Appendix A; the distillation and approximation mathematics remains substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central feasibility and privacy claims through relevant PEFT comparisons, analysis of permutation vulnerability, measured FHE costs and a more qualified conclusion. These address important evidentiary gaps in v1. End-to-end model privacy remains unestablished, and the claimed SBS communication savings conflict with Appendix B.1's continued transmission of masked blocks. Nevertheless, the expanded evidence and clearer deployment limitations provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across renaming and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original SBS results, baseline comparisons, feature-similarity analyses and FHE measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original centralized and federated classification experiments, efficiency measurements, and appendix studies of distillation and polynomial approximation.

C1.justification: v2 adds the priority claim of being first to clearly define S2V and makes dynamic injection and resolving multi-subject confusion explicit central contributions. Its abstract and conclusion also broaden v1's competitiveness and advantage over some commercial solutions into claims of outperforming state-of-the-art commercial solutions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of identity loss in S2I+I2V, encoder-specific artifacts and multi-subject ambiguity. These substantially improve implementation transparency without establishing that previously unspecified settings changed.

The principal evaluation coverage remains single subjects, multiple subjects and facial identity across the same broad categories. Its supplement also investigates staged-generation identity loss, copy-paste failures, dataset composition and additional comparator failures, substantially expanding diagnostic evidence.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the original quality/user-study plots retain their values. New distribution results and qualitative failures expand the evidence. These are added analyses, not demonstrated v1-to-v2 performance gains.

M1.justification: v1 Section 2.2 explicitly describes modifying inputs without changing the DiT structure. v2 instead specifies window attention with dynamic reference-feature injection, shifting and output averaging (Section 3.2, Figure 5). P1.justification: The introduction and method exposition are substantially rewritten and reorganized. v2 introduces a structured contribution statement, separates related work, adds a training/inference subsection and organizes supplementary material into eight sections. Much of the original benchmark description remains recognizable within this larger narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the data pipeline, revises the architecture diagram and adds attention, ablation, distribution and supplementary pipeline displays. Earlier qualitative panels are selected and combined into Figure 7 or retained in supplementary comparisons. The unchanged v1 Figure 5 plots become v2 Figure 6; their relocation is not new evidence.

R1.justification: The brief positioning in v1 becomes a dedicated three-part related-work section covering video foundations, subject-consistent images and subject-consistent videos. Added works include DreamBooth, PuLID, OmniGen and MovieWeaver. v2 substantially develops its relationship to image-personalization methods and staged S2I+I2V alternatives, alongside the new S2V priority claim.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of implementation detail and controlled evidence for design choices through Sections 3.2–3.3, Tables 3–4 and the supplementary analyses. Specific limitations also make applicability easier to assess. The new success-rate evaluation remains underspecified, and broader superiority claims plus the weakened Dynamic Degree discussion reduce precision. Nevertheless, the gains in transparency and diagnostic support constitute a substantial overall improvement, independent of the unchanged main benchmark scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Phantom and retain matching core evaluations. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. All 11 pages of v1 and 16 pages of v2, including v2's supplementary materials, are available; v1 has no separately labeled appendix.

after.justification: Section 4 retains the original empirical evaluations and adds encoder ablations. The supplementary materials report alignment success rates, training-data distributions and additional qualitative comparisons.

Appendices add a surface-detail semantic-enhancement ablation, intermediate mask-guided optimization results and a beard failure comparison. The initialization ablation and part of the snail-shell analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests. The descriptive averaging and user-preference reporting remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 are numerically unchanged, including Text2VDM's CLIP score of 0.2556, self-intersection of 0.77%, and preference rates of 75.3% and 67.6%. Qualitative results expand substantially through the new controls, 2D diagnostics and supplementary comparisons. Some earlier outputs, including λ = 45 and CSD weight 1, are removed; these changes do not demonstrate a same-setting performance gain.

However, Equation (3) revises the stated optimization step from updating v* with (I - λL)^-1 to updating v with (I + λL)^-1. This changes the documented procedure; the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed.

P1.justification: Sections 3.2–3.3 and 4.3 undergo substantial rewriting and reorganization around Sobolev preconditioning and semantic enhancement. Terminology changes throughout, related-work headings are reformatted, and application discussion is redistributed into structured Appendices A–C. These changes extend beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: v2 revises the method diagram and several comparison/ablation panels, adds the 2D diagnostic, interface and initialization illustrations, introduces a prompt table, and expands the visual result galleries. Some displays are relocated rather than new: notably, v1's pillar example in Figure 10 becomes v2 Figure 19.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning against concurrent, image-conditioned GenVDM, introduces Attend-and-Excite into the discussion, and cites two procedural-material studies. The broader relationship to existing 3D editing and brush-generation research remains intact.

T1.justification: Equation (3) changes both the preconditioner sign and the optimization variable/gradient, constituting a mathematical revision beyond notation. Equation (2) and the token-blending formula remain. The token weight is also unchanged: v2's 1.1 squared equals v1's 1.21. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses substantial reproducibility gaps by documenting the model, camera sampling, optimization budget, prompts and baseline setup, while new controls better support its central design choices. These gains improve auditability and scientific support despite unchanged quantitative scores. A remaining flaw is that Section 4.1 claims shared initialization and masks for all methods, whereas Appendix B.2 exempts Paint-it; this inconsistency does not outweigh the substantial documentation and analytical improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Text2VDM and retain matching core experiments. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable. The comparison includes v2's Appendices A–C; the supplied v1 ends with references.

after.justification: Section 4 retains these original empirical results and adds diagnostic comparisons and supplementary qualitative results.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original generation experiments, ablations, a 40-prompt quantitative evaluation and a 32-participant user study.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the central claims: an animatable large reconstruction model, few-image avatar creation through expression cross-attention, robustness to inconsistent inputs, and single-image applications using 3D GANs. The expanded experiments support these contributions without materially redefining them.

It attributes FlashAvatar's novel-view failures to overfitting and explains adaptability to different expression signals. The earlier temporal-smoothness interpretation accompanying JOD is removed. The stated limitations concerning GAN inversion, camera poses and lighting remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix E newly explains the expression-code sources and FLAME-code fine-tuning using GAGAvatar's Metrical Tracker for NeRSemble and in-the-wild driving. Appendix C documents activation caching and RTX3090 timing hardware. v2 also identifies published baseline implementations and the internal neutral-identity data source. Existing preprocessing, architecture hyperparameters, training budget and project website are retained.

E1.justification: Ava256 and NeRSemble remain the principal datasets; NeRSemble was already evaluated qualitatively in v1. v2 adds an internal dataset of 984 neutral identities for supplementary fine-tuning, extends single-image evaluation to NeRSemble, and includes additional phone captures with glasses, rotated inputs and a headscarf. These extend coverage within the existing head-avatar domain.

E2.justification: The four-image comparison expands from GPAvatar alone to GPAvatar, HeadNeRF and InvertAvatar. Supplementary single-image comparisons retain both GAGAvatar versions and add HeadNeRF and Portrait4D-v2 on NeRSemble. FlashAvatar is newly evaluated with a full monocular video. These are evaluated comparators, not merely new citations.

It also tests the four-view-trained model with different inference view counts. The main JOD evaluation and its 100-frame video procedure disappear, although JOD remains in the retained skip-connection ablation. The original Ava256 split, evaluation resolution and base training schedule remain.

E4.justification: The original component, skip-connection and training-data/view-count ablations are retained. v2 adds extreme-expression interpolation, inference with three to six views using a four-view-trained model, challenging phone/accessory cases, a FlashAvatar viewpoint-failure comparison, and an experiment testing whether additional neutral identities improve identity preservation. Appendix C also adds an efficiency analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and scaling curves without uncertainty bands. Neither reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or statistical significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises Ava256 PSNR from 22.0 to 20.7 for Avat3r and from 20.3 to 19.4 for GPAvatar. Their LPIPS ordering reverses: 0.309 versus 0.304 becomes 0.33 versus 0.34. The reason for these revisions is unstated, so they do not establish a model improvement. v2 also adds NeRSemble, single-image, FlashAvatar, runtime and identity-augmentation results, while removing the main JOD scores. Existing ablation values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The Gaussian prediction architecture, DUSt3R/Sapiens components, expression cross-attention, skip connections and losses remain unchanged in Section 3. The single-view variant already appears in v1's supplement. Newly documented FLAME-code fine-tuning and activation caching do not establish a revision of the original algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized introduction and related-work rewrites, adds a related-work subsection, moves the single-shot discussion into Appendix A.2, and reorganizes the supplement. The abstract, method exposition, training description, limitations and conclusion remain largely intact, so this is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The few-shot comparison becomes a full-width, multi-baseline display covering both datasets, and Table 1 gains dataset groups and comparator rows while losing JOD. New figures show interpolation, input flexibility, FlashAvatar failures, phone captures and identity augmentation; new tables report supplementary comparisons and runtimes. Existing figures are also relocated, including v1 Figure 3 becoming v2 Figure 18.
