R1.justification: Related work substantially expands through a new monocular-avatar reconstruction subsection, broader coverage of 3D GANs and inversion methods, and discussion of FaceLift and concurrent CAP4D and LAM. This develops the paper's positioning against video-based reconstruction and alternative single-image avatar approaches beyond v1's narrower treatment.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation in Equations 1–18 is unchanged. Neither version contains additional theoretical propositions, proofs or derivations that change the comparison.

improvement.justification: v1's quantitative comparison relied on one baseline, while single-image and NeRSemble performance were illustrated primarily through examples. v2 substantially addresses this validation gap with multiple comparison methods, quantitative single-image and NeRSemble results, targeted generalization analyses, and measured creation/driving times. Expression-driving details also improve reproducibility. Removing the main JOD comparison weakens temporal-quality evidence, and unexplained changes to Ava256 scores limit traceability, but the broader and more informative validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Avat3r research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and supplementary material are readable and support comparison, including matching results moved between sections.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds quantitative comparisons, generalization demonstrations, identity-augmentation experiments and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original avatar reconstruction and animation experiments, quantitative comparisons, component ablations, and supplementary studies of training subjects, input views and skip connections.

results.title: Avat3r: Large Animatable Gaussian Reconstruction Model for High-fidelity 3D Head Avatars

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion replace the central claim of HR estimation solely from eye-tracking video with a method that fuses video and built-in IMU motion cues. v2 also announces released code, data, and EgoExo4D HR augmentations. The egoPPG task, dataset contribution, and claimed 14.1% egocentric proficiency improvement remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets dancing improvements through MITA and explains residual static-task errors through HR variability, blinking, and eye motion. It adds hypotheses for soccer failures involving scarce examples and unseen stop-and-go activity, discusses transfer generalization, and introduces explicit consent requirements. These substantially expand the mechanisms and applicability boundaries discussed in v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project link and announces code, dataset, and HR-augmentation releases. It supplies MITA implementation details, cross-dataset preprocessing, peak-based HR extraction, feature normalization, and inference throughput. Reported model resources change from approximately 770k parameters, 164 GFLOPS per batch, and 15 training hours to 12M parameters, 399 GFLOPS, and 20 hours.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual training and evaluation on MMPD, UBFC-rPPG, and PURE through bidirectional transfer with egoPPG-DB (Supplementary Section 16). These introduce conventional facial-video domains beyond the retained egoPPG-DB and EgoExo4D experiments. OBF and SCAMPS are added only to the related-dataset comparison, not evaluated.

E2.justification: Table 2 expands four learned baselines to ten, adding Yue et al., ContrastPhys+, RhythmMamba, RhythmFormer, PhysFormer, and FactorizePhys. Supplementary Table 9 additionally compares proficiency estimation using HR predictions from PhysFormer and FactorizePhys. The eye/skin signal-processing baselines and main Table 5 comparator configurations already exist in v1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces bidirectional cross-dataset protocols, extracting eye regions with MediaPipe, resizing to 48 by 128, and converting to grayscale. Transfer experiments use the model without MITA because the conventional datasets lack head IMU recordings. The stated signal-processing baseline bandpass changes from 0.6-3.0 to 0.5-2.8 Hz. Existing participant splits and core training hyperparameters remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds explicit spatial-attention and MITA ablations, activity-specific MITA comparisons, cross-dataset generalization tests, HR-distribution analysis, and downstream HR-source comparisons. Conversely, v1 Supplementary Table 9 is removed, eliminating sensitivity results for preprocessing, image/window sizes, losses, target signals, and augmentation.

E5.justification: Supplementary Section 15 and Figure 6 newly report prediction-MAE distributions by cross-validation split and an overall interquartile range of 1.7-10.5 bpm. This adds descriptive variability reporting; neither version reports repeated-seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The IMU-enabled model reports MAE 7.67 bpm and r=0.85, versus v1's video-only 8.82 and 0.81; the earlier aggregate scores remain as the no-MITA ablation. Activity and frame-rate results change, and substantial baseline, ablation, and transfer results are added. Table 5 changes overall Ego+Exo+HR accuracy from 42.37% to 43.94%, while Ego+HR remains 45.29%. These updates involve the revised model, rather than an unchanged-method performance comparison.

M1.justification: EgoPulseFormer becomes PulseFormer and gains motion-informed temporal attention using the headset IMU. A new ResNet18 image-embedding branch and convolutional IMU embeddings feed cross-attention that weights video frames before the retained spatial-attention CNN backbone (Section 5.2). This changes the inputs and computation substantially.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and substantial discussion passages are rewritten. Section 5 gains named component descriptions and reorganized experimental subsections; Section 8.3 becomes Broader impacts, with demographic and outdoor future work moved into the conclusion. The model is renamed throughout and the supplementary narrative is substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn to depict IMU-image fusion. Table 2 expands substantially, and Table 3 replaces its RMSE/MAPE columns with a MITA comparison. The supplement adds three experimental tables and two boxplots while removing the hyperparameter table. Existing signal traces, photographs, and dataset/protocol tables are relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 refreshes the literature with additional rPPG competitors, prior spatiotemporal-attention methods, and OBF/SCAMPS, while removing several gaze and wearable-device citations. The introduction adds Project Aria 2's contact HR sensor as context. The fundamental positioning around recovering HR from headset cameras for egocentric tasks remains.

T1.justification: Section 5.2 adds a formal definition of IMU-image cross-attention, including its embedding dimensions and query/key/value assignments (Equation 3). The optical reflection model and spatial-attention mathematics remain equivalent; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support through stronger comparators, explicit component ablations, cross-dataset HR evaluation, and downstream HR-source comparisons (Tables 2-3 and 7-9). These address important gaps in v1's evidence for component benefits and generalization. Resource access information also improves reproducibility. Removing the hyperparameter study loses useful sensitivity evidence, and reporting inconsistencies remain, such as upsampled MAE 10.20 in the text versus 10.18 in Table 4. These drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same egoPPG research, dataset, and downstream application. Both complete 16-page documents, including supplementary text, equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original heart-rate and proficiency experiments, component ablations, cross-dataset evaluations, and supplementary comparisons of downstream HR sources.

before.justification: v1 reports original heart-rate estimation experiments, EgoExo4D proficiency results, and supplementary hyperparameter analyses.

results.title: egoPPG: Heart Rate Estimation from Eye-Tracking Cameras in Egocentric Systems to Benefit Downstream Vision Tasks

C1.justification: The Introduction removes the claim of employing correlated frame coupling 'for the first time.' The principal claims of efficient, stable streaming generation through temporal flow and denoising, with quality comparable to conditional diffusion, remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 2.1 explicitly identifies noise as a surrogate for an unknown artifact distribution and qualifies the connection between coupling and straighter trajectories. The supplement interprets sparse conditioning as complementary and scaling as unsaturated within available resources. Existing context-size and manual-noise-selection limitations remain.

D1.justification: Supplemental A supplies previously unavailable backbone widths, separate prediction/denoising networks, parameter/FLOP counts, AdamW settings, learning rate, batch size, 200K iterations, BF16 training, software and approximately 80-hour training time. v2 also provides a planned code-release location; the PDF does not establish that code is already available.

E1.justification: Supplemental Table 4 adds UCF101 evaluation, extending coverage to multiclass human-action videos. The original six datasets and unconditional video-generation task are retained.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained CONDIFF and FLOW comparisons, supplemental Tables 3–4 evaluate RIVER and SVP, including comparisons on SKY/CARLA. These directly relevant prior approaches substantially broaden the comparator set. The paper specifies pixel-space evaluation and adoption of SVP's modified inference procedure.

E3.justification: The supplement adds FID over generated frames, consecutive-frame Inception-feature similarity, and controlled scaling evaluations using approximately 0.5–4 times the model size and 25–100% of training data. These substantially extend evaluation design; the original FVD sampling, sliding windows, solver tolerances and 20-step comparison remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test model/data scaling and additional past-frame conditioning, while FID/I-SIM results examine the noise-dependent realism–consistency tradeoff. Section 2.2 also newly reports that linear joint sampling outperforms solve-then-denoise and denoise-then-solve alternatives, although it provides no numerical scores for that comparison.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. The retained 128-video sample count and averaging over time are evaluation details, not new uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–2 are numerically unchanged, but the supplement adds substantial results. UCF101 FVD is 4512 for BI-FLOW, 4794 for RIVER and 5218 for SVP. The added conditioning comparison reports 436 without versus 387 with an extra past frame; frame metrics, computational costs and scaling results are also newly reported.

M1.justification: The central bilinear objective and joint sampler remain unchanged. Supplemental B adds a variant conditioned on one additional randomly selected past frame. Supplemental A's separate-UNet implementation is newly disclosed detail, rather than evidence that the original architecture was changed.

P1.justification: v2 edits the abstract, introduction and contribution bullets, expands the characteristic-curve explanation, and adds acknowledgments and supplemental sections. The main section sequence and most prose remain intact, so this is a limited narrative revision.

P2.justification: The supplement substantially expands visual presentation with computational-cost and evaluation tables, scaling plots and a characteristic-ODE illustration. Main Figure 1 is redrawn as a compact icon-based diagram and moved to the first page; main Table 2 is enlarged and reformatted.

R1.justification: Section 4.1 adds focused discussion of RIVER and SVP, acknowledging their use of previous frames and distinguishing BI-FLOW's temporal ODE from their denoising modifications. The supplement adds dataset/software citations. Most related-work positioning is retained; publication-metadata updates do not introduce additional works.

T1.justification: The transport definitions, bilinear objective and sampling mathematics retain their substance. Equations 6–8 use clearer derivative notation and an explicit chain-rule expansion, while the supplemental characteristic-curve diagram explains existing mathematics. No new theorem, proof or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important reproducibility and validation gaps in the supplied v1: it provides detailed implementation settings and comparisons with directly relevant RIVER/SVP methods, alongside scaling and broader evaluation. It also moderates the first-use claim while preserving the original results. Some supplemental protocols remain abbreviated and uncertainty across runs is still unreported, but the added transparency and evidence constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Generative Video Bi-flow and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and references. v2 additionally includes Supplemental Sections A–B, which are absent from the supplied v1 despite its references to supplemental material.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds original supplemental results on frame quality, additional baselines, UCF101, scaling and sparse conditioning.

before.justification: Section 3 reports original video-generation experiments across six datasets, including FVD, solver-step comparisons, noise-level analyses and generated examples.

results.title: Generative Video Bi-flow

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: streaming-memory online dense tracking, strong CVO and sparse-tracking performance, computational efficiency, and causal processing. The supplementary evidence supports these existing claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v1 mainly warns that prolonged occlusion can make memory unhelpful and tracking fail. v2 explains effective pairwise behavior when memory becomes unavailable, illustrates recovery after a ten-frame occlusion, and documents additional failure conditions. It also develops the interpretation that two-stage propagation and retrieval matter more than choosing forward splatting versus backward warping.

D1.justification: Section 6 supplies previously missing feature dimensions, encoder stride, mask-decoder details, bilinear-kernel formula, loss weighting, FlashAttention-2 usage, Adam with a one-cycle schedule, learning rate, batch sizes, and eight-H100 training hardware. These substantially improve implementation specificity. The abstract replaces the direct repository link with a project-page link, and the text points to animations; actual external availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions train on Kubric-CVO and Kubric-MOVi-F and evaluate on CVO, TAP-Vid's DAVIS/Kinetics/RGB-Stacking datasets, and RoboTAP. The supplement analyzes existing coverage through alternative protocols, temporal intervals, resolutions, and selected cases; it introduces no new dataset, domain, or tracking task.

E2.justification: Section 7 adds Track-On and DELTA to measured speed and memory comparisons. Table 5 also extends online comparator coverage through causal executions of TAPIR, CoTracker2, SpatialTracker, and DOT with their original window sizes. The original benchmark comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds causal evaluation that repeatedly supplies available video prefixes while preserving baseline window sizes, alongside the retained two-frame-window protocol. It also adds resolution sweeps and interval-specific DAVIS evaluation. Section 6 specifies 32 decoding iterations for Kinetics, RGB-Stacking, and RoboTAP, exceptions absent from v1's stated 16-iteration default; this changes the documented settings without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations, Table 6 tests backward propagation without attention-based retrieval. Figures 7–10 add resolution scaling, accuracy versus temporal interval, a qualitative memory-bank ablation, and analysis of recovery after occlusion exceeding memory length. Figure 13 adds explicit failure cases involving prolonged occlusion, similar textureless objects, and fast motion.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed or repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The added tables and curves continue reporting point estimates without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain identical numerical entries. New results include Table 5's causal DAVIS comparisons and Table 6's attention ablation, where CVO Extended EPE is 395.35 versus 6.42 for SPOT within that experiment. v2 also adds resolution and temporal curves, Track-On/DELTA resource measurements, and qualitative recovery and failure findings.

M1.justification: The memory-reading module, sensory memory, visibility-guided splatting, flow decoder, and warm-start procedure remain unchanged. Feature symbols are renamed, and Section 6 supplies architecture and loss details without establishing a redesign of the proposed method.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely preserved. Local edits rename feature notation, separate Discussion and Limitation paragraphs, add supplementary cross-references and acknowledgements, and append Sections 6–8. These additions do not constitute an extensive rewrite or reorganization of the existing paper.

P2.justification: v2 retains the original figures and tables, with small notation and caption changes to Figure 3. It adds Tables 5–6 and Figures 7–13, including resolution and temporal plots, memory-ablation images, an occlusion timeline, expanded qualitative comparisons, and failure-case grids. This substantially expands the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Track-On, DELTA, FlashAttention-2, and the one-cycle training schedule. Section 7 distinguishes SPOT's online dense setting from Track-On's online sparse and DELTA's offline dense tracking. The main related-work discussion and broader novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical procedure in Equations 1–7 is retained apart from notation. The supplement spells out the existing bilinear kernel and loss implementation, but adds no substantive theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important reproducibility and validation gaps in v1. Section 6 supplies essential architecture, loss, and training specifications; Table 5 tests online comparisons without shrinking baseline windows; and the added memory analyses and failure cases strengthen the evidence for the mechanism while clarifying its limits. Together these substantially improve the paper's assessability and experimental support, even though the main benchmark scores remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPOT research, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures. The main sections closely correspond. v1 ends after its references; v2 adds supplementary Sections 6–8, which are fully available for comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds causal baseline evaluations, attention ablations, efficiency measurements, temporal analyses, and qualitative failure cases in its supplement.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.4 report original tracking evaluations on CVO, TAP-Vid, and RoboTAP, together with efficiency measurements and component ablations.

results.title: Online Dense Point Tracking with Streaming Memory

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: replacing most self-attention with ConvAttn, integrating Flash Attention into lightweight SR, and preserving transformer-like representational capacity and data scalability. The headline performance and novelty claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 4.2.4 shifts the mechanism interpretation from reduced inter-layer similarity to LK providing broader spatial influence and DK providing greater input-dependent diversity. The supplement additionally attributes Flash Attention training instability to missing relative positional bias and discusses applicability to constrained devices and larger models. These refine the existing scientific interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 identifies SwinIR-light as Figure 2's source, expands Flash Attention documentation, and supplies larger-model configurations and device/input specifications. Existing core training details and the code-access link remain. The new hidden-dimension disclosure is internally inconsistent: Section 7.1 assigns ESC-FP both 8 and 4, leaving that setting unresolved.

E1.justification: Real-world image coverage expands substantially: v1 evaluates RealSRSet, whereas v2 additionally evaluates RealLQ250, RealSR, and DRealSR (Section 9, Table 8). These introduce additional real-degraded image collections; the existing classic and arbitrary-scale benchmark coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 10 introduces comparisons against EDT-B, CAT-A, ART, ACT, and full-size SwinIR and SRFormer for the larger ESC model. This substantially extends the evaluated comparator set. The established lightweight and arbitrary-scale comparisons retain their methods; RealESRGAN's relabeling as RealESRGAN+ alone does not establish a new comparator.

E3.justification: ESC-Real's reported initial L1 training increases from 400K to 1M iterations; its subsequent 400K phase remains. New protocols include nine real-world quality metrics, MacBook/iPhone tests with different input sizes, and a 12.5M-parameter ESC using 48×48 attention windows and 64×64 pre-training followed by 96×96 fine-tuning. These are substantive setting additions and revisions.

E4.justification: v2 adds an isolated dynamic-kernel removal ablation (Table 3) and compares Flash Attention without positional encoding, with RoPE, and with relative positional bias (Table 6). Figure 6 replaces the ConvAttn inter-layer CKA analysis with kernel-specific gradient/receptive-field and input-wise similarity analyses. Figure 9 also replaces the building case with a dog example.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 100 repetitions for the existing GPU measurements. Neither introduces training-seed variability, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; the added results continue using point estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 2, 4, 5, and the renumbered arbitrary-scale appendix table retain their numerical results. v2 adds substantial real-world, device, larger-model, and ablation results. For example, removing DK yields 33.36 versus ESC's 33.46 dB on Urban100×2, while Table 8 reports the highest CLIPIQA for ESC-Real on all four datasets. These additions are not longitudinal same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The core ESC/ConvAttn procedure remains intact. The specified ESC-Real skip branch changes from a three-convolution sequence in v1 Section 6.3 to a sequence including LeakyReLU(0.2) in v2 Section 7.3. The added larger ESC variant also specifies extra normalization before ConvFFNs.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain largely intact, with grammar corrections, terminology standardization, and localized rewrites. Flash Attention implementation discussion moves into an expanded supplementary section, existing supplementary sections are renumbered, and new evaluation sections are appended.

P2.justification: Figure 6 is substantially redesigned into feature, gradient, and input-similarity panels; Figure 9 replaces a visual example. Table 3 gains an ablation row, and new Tables 6 and 8–10 introduce several substantial displays. The original supplementary Table 6 becomes Table 7 and is relocated, rather than newly added.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature supporting RoPE, real-world datasets and quality metrics, ConvFormer, and larger-model comparisons. Section 3.3 more explicitly distinguishes ConvAttn from attention-map sharing and large-kernel CNNs with pixel attention. The central research positioning and novelty claim remain stable.

T1.justification: Equation 4 corrects the fusion definition: v1 feeds F_fuse into its own defining concatenation, whereas v2 correctly uses F_res. This removes a circular mathematical definition and matches the existing prose description. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 supports its real-world claims mainly with selected visual examples and its deployment argument with GPU measurements. v2 substantially strengthens this evidence through four-dataset quantitative evaluation, MacBook/iPhone tests, and targeted controls for dynamic kernels and positional encoding. These address important gaps in empirical support while preserving the established benchmark results. The inconsistent hidden-dimension disclosure and metric-dependent real-world advantages limit the conclusions but do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ESC super-resolution work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, references, and supplementary material are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds positional-encoding experiments, quantitative real-world evaluations, device benchmarks, and larger-model results.

before.justification: v1 reports original classic, arbitrary-scale, and real-world super-resolution evaluations, together with ablations, feature analyses, and efficiency measurements.

results.title: Emulating Self-attention with Convolution for Efficient Image Super-Resolution

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction stop presenting mIoUobj as a newly introduced metric and instead frame evaluation around object recall and point-level IoU. The central claims about TOP pre-training, transferability, potential task generalization and improvement up to 28.77% remain.

C2.justification: v2 corrects the explanation of recall and false positives, removes v1's confused UnO false-negative/false-alert interpretation, and expands the explanation of ego-induced IoU inflation. The supplement adds limitations involving class imbalance, geographic bias and temporal error propagation. Conversely, Section 5.4 makes the attribution of baseline failures to flow overfitting more assertive without adding a causal test.

D1.justification: Supplementary Sections 2 and 4 supply labeling speed thresholds, optimizers, learning-rate schedules, batch sizes and epoch budgets missing from the supplied v1. v2 also documents constant input features and the checkpoint-selection validation split. The abstract replaces a future code/model-release promise with a stated public code repository. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changed experimental settings.

E1.justification: Both versions use nuScenes for pre-training, few-shot MOS and semantic segmentation, and SemanticKITTI for cross-dataset MOS transfer. Additional qualitative examples and ego-inclusive scoring remain within this existing coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain training from scratch, ALSO, 4DOcc and UnO; spelling and capitalization changes do not identify different methods. The added ego-point analysis uses the existing training-from-scratch comparator.

E3.justification: Section 4 revises the stated object metric from mIoUobj with TP/(TP+FP) to Recallobj with TP/(TP+FN). Supplementary Table 5 adds conventional ego-inclusive IoU scoring. The main numerical entries remain unchanged, so these reporting changes do not establish that the experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Supplementary Section 5 adds a direct analysis of how including ego-vehicle points affects IoU, and Figures 7–8 expand the qualitative cases. The two-objective ablation is unchanged. Figure 6 displays a distribution analysis whose principal findings were already reported in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions state that experiments use a fixed random seed. Neither supplies repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests; the supplement does not change this reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their numerical entries, while Table 4 changes only rounding. New Table 5 reports conventional IoU of 68.89 versus 70.28 at 10% training data and 63.68 versus 68.13 at 20%, for scratch versus TOP. Additional labeling statistics and qualitative cases extend the reported evidence rather than demonstrate improved main benchmark scores.

M1.justification: The sparse 4D UNet, beam-divergence preprocessing, overlapping-point sampling and two occupancy-prediction objectives remain the same. Clarified point terminology, mathematical corrections and newly supplied implementation details do not establish a changed training or inference procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations and experimental prose receive extensive rewriting, with particularly substantial restructuring of Section 4. Terminology is standardized, the introduction is condensed, and an organized supplement and acknowledgement are added, while the main section sequence remains recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with temporal correspondence lines; the beam illustration and pipeline are revised and reordered. Figures 4–5 move and reverse their false-positive/false-negative legend assignments. v2 also adds the cumulative-distribution plot, a training-settings table, the conventional-IoU table and expanded qualitative grids, combining new displays with retained examples.

R1.justification: v2 adds T-MAE and explicitly recognizes temporal pre-training in that work and the already-cited Nunes et al. work. Section 2 replaces the blanket statement that existing 3D pre-training lacks temporal information with a narrower claim that TOP specifically targets dynamic tasks such as MOS.

T1.justification: Equation 7 adds wconf < 1 to disambiguate occupied versus free states, and Equation 12 corrects the object metric's denominator from TP+FP to TP+FN. Supplementary Equations 13–15 explicitly derive the overlap-segment starting point using approximations already described in v1.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evaluation and reproducibility deficiencies: it repairs the central object-metric definition and error interpretation, supplies previously missing labeling and training specifications, and directly demonstrates ego-point inflation through Table 5. These substantially improve readers' ability to assess and reproduce the work despite unchanged main benchmark scores. The more assertive, still untested overfitting explanation is a limited drawback that does not outweigh those gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TOP method and matched experiments, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. The supplied v1 ends after references despite appendix cross-references; v2 includes supplementary material. Newly available documentation can therefore be identified without assuming that the underlying implementation changed.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and additionally reports ego-inclusive IoU results in supplementary Table 5 and expanded qualitative examples.

before.justification: Tables 1–4 report original few-shot MOS, cross-dataset transfer, semantic segmentation and training-objective ablation results, supplemented by qualitative examples.

results.title: Temporal Overlapping Prediction: A Self-supervised Pre-training Method for LiDAR Moving Object Segmentation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: open-set language-guided dexterous grasping, generalizable-instructive affordance, the two flow-matching models and superior open-set generalization. Supplementary evidence and application examples do not redefine these headline claims.

C2.justification: D.1 newly interprets flow matching as offering better performance and faster inference than diffusion, with modest affordance-generation overhead. D.4 discusses applicability to planned manipulation. Existing affordance and optimization interpretations remain; no substantive limitations discussion is added.

D1.justification: Sections A-C and E substantially improve documentation through attention wiring, loss definitions, the previously referenced MLLM prompt, texture-generation prompts, category lists, camera placement, evaluation sampling and thresholds, baseline adaptations and robot execution details. These disclosures mostly clarify existing experiments rather than establish implementation changes.

E1.justification: The open-set, closed-set, zero-shot and one-shot grasping evaluations are retained. D.4 and Figure 14 add a real-world manipulation task involving pouring. The newly supplied category lists and one-shot dataset counts primarily document coverage already described in v1.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds DDIM and DDPM comparisons against flow matching. The original comparator sets remain. Contact2Gen becoming ContactGen and GraspCAVE becoming GraspCVAE are naming corrections, verified against their references, rather than new baselines.

E3.justification: The additional experiments introduce train/test Point IoU and component inference-time evaluation. Appendix B.1 reports 11 unseen categories for Open Set A, versus 10 in v1, constituting a reported setting correction without establishing a rerun. The 80/20 split and detailed retained evaluation procedures are newly disclosed information.

E4.justification: Supplemental D substantially expands the analyses: flow matching versus diffusion and computational cost, direct train/test affordance generalization, optimization before-and-after examples, and a downstream manipulation case study. These address questions beyond the retained representation, pre-understanding and optimization ablations in Table 2.

E5.justification: Table 7 newly reports timing values with ± quantities. Their statistical meaning and repetition counts are unspecified, so additional training runs or a particular uncertainty estimator cannot be inferred. Existing grasp-diversity standard deviations remain unchanged and measure output diversity.

E6.justification: Tables 1-5 retain their numerical results, and Table 6 reuses the unoptimized flow-matching results from Table 2. Substantial additions concern diffusion comparisons, inference cost and intermediate-map generalization: Table 8 reports test IoU of 0.508/0.502 versus contact-map 0.359/0.315 on A/B. Figure 14 adds a qualitative manipulation outcome.

M1.justification: The core affordance representation, AFM, GFM and grasp optimization remain unchanged. Supplemental D.4 adds a manipulation procedure combining grasp generation with ReKep-style keypoint constraints, MLLM planning and an optimization solver. Other architectural elaborations document existing components.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are retained, with localized wording corrections, corrected method names, a rewritten split description, expanded author information and acknowledgements. Detailed explanations are appended in separately organized Supplemental Sections A-E rather than extensively rewriting the main paper.

P2.justification: Figures 5-15 and Tables 6-8 substantially expand the visual presentation with training and evaluation diagrams, prompt examples, dataset construction, comparative visualizations, hardware photographs and execution sequences. The original figures and tables largely retain their organization.

R1.justification: Adds citations including DDPM, DDIM, Perceiver, InfoNCE, G-DexGrasp, AffordPose and newer interaction work. ReKep, already cited in v1, gains an explicit role in the manipulation extension. The related-work organization and principal novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix C.1 newly formalizes the evaluation encoder's multi-positive InfoNCE objective and category/action matching predicate in Equation 18. Appendix A.3 supplies explicit definitions for previously described optimization losses. Core Equations 1-7 are retained; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves important reproducibility gaps by supplying the previously referenced prompts and documenting evaluation sampling, success criteria, data construction and baseline adaptations. Added model-choice and affordance-generalization analyses strengthen validation while preserving the main results. Timing uncertainty remains undefined, and D.1's broad superiority interpretation exceeds the mixed grasp-quality evidence in Table 6, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial improvement in verifiability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable and describe the same AffordDexGrasp work, with matching core methods and main results. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally includes Supplemental Sections A-E. Text, equations, tables and rendered figures support comparison.

after.justification: Retains the original empirical results and adds diffusion comparisons, inference timings, affordance prediction measurements and a manipulation demonstration.

before.justification: Tables 1-5 report original simulation comparisons, ablations, zero-shot and one-shot evaluations, and real-world grasping outcomes.

results.title: AffordDexGrasp: Open-set Language-guided Dexterous Grasp with Generalizable-Instructive Affordance

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same RFM/DIP proposal, architecture-agnostic accuracy/efficiency claims, and 7,333-pair, eight-category LRS-VQA contribution. New experiments support these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantial explanations and qualifications: CLIP baselines' referring-expression and global-context limitations, incomplete visual information as an explanation for training-pruning degradation, and interference from mixing resolutions. The supplement also discusses long-context constraints, text-fusion inconsistency, vocabulary sensitivity and why higher resolution need not help global classification.

D1.justification: Appendices A–C supply previously unavailable construction thresholds, annotation prompts, training-data processing, batch size 128, learning rate 2e-5, sequence-length limits, positional-padding details, Flash Attention extraction, caching and compute accounting. These materially expand reproducibility information without demonstrating that the retained experiments changed settings.

E1.justification: v3 adds localization evaluation using DIOR-RSVG and RRSIS-D, plus region-box localization tests on LRS-VQA. This extends v1's VQA evaluation to directly assessing text-guided region coverage. The original training datasets and four VQA evaluation sets remain.

E2.justification: v3 adds CLIP-L14 and RemoteCLIP-L14 sliding-window pruning baselines to main Table 3 and supplementary comparisons. Teacher LLM attention also becomes a comparator in localization evaluation. These substantially broaden tests of the central guidance mechanism; the original LVLM and token-reduction comparators remain.

E3.justification: New localization tests use 25% token retention and count success when retained tokens cover over 50% of the ground-truth region. Added controlled experiments introduce anyres-p36/p49, further layer configurations, training-time pruning and text fusion. Original VQA metrics and documented main settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds quantitative attention-localization validation and ablations of distillation losses, pruning at larger resolutions, concatenating tokens across pyramid levels, and training with pruning/text fusion. v1's layer-pair ablation is retained and expanded in supplementary Table 6, rather than removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added experiments do not introduce an uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Existing headline scores are retained, including the 32.16 average for Ours (LLaVA-Next) in Table 2. v3 adds RFM localization recalls of 47.99%, 64.76% and 61.17% on LRS-VQA, DIOR-RSVG and RRSIS-D, respectively, alongside new baseline scores, ablation outcomes and per-question-category leaderboards.

M1.justification: The DIP construction, RFM architecture, distillation losses and Algorithm 1 are retained. Supplementary implementation explanations do not establish a changed method. Training-time pruning, text fusion and multi-level token concatenation are tested alternatives, not replacements for the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose are retained. Section 4.1 gains clearer coarse-to-fine transitions, experimental discussion is reorganized, and layer-pair discussion moves into the new supplement. Author affiliations, contact information and acknowledgments also change; the main manuscript is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: Figures 1–6 retain their visual content. However, Table 3 expands, a localization table occupies main Table 7, and the original layer-pair table moves into an expanded supplementary display. The supplement adds a prompt box and numerous ablation, localization and category-level tables, substantially expanding the presentation of evidence.

R1.justification: v3 adds an adaptive/superpixel tokenization thread, references for CLIP/RemoteCLIP and localization datasets, and additional remote-sensing works such as SkySense and MEET; SkyEyeGPT is removed. The main research taxonomy and positioning relative to LLaVA-Mini and FlexAttention remain.

T1.justification: Appendix C adds explicit token-count and FLOPs derivations for the pyramid/RFM/LLM computation, culminating in the previously reported 36.61 TFLOPs. The original method equations remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves important validation and documentation gaps: direct localization comparisons test the central distillation rationale, additional ablations examine design choices and failures, and Appendices A–C make construction and implementation substantially easier to audit. These gains matter despite unchanged headline performance. Appendix C introduces a limited inconsistency between the 2ndm feed-forward term in prose and 3ndm in its equation, but this does not outweigh the stronger evidence and reproducibility documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RFM/DIP method and LRS-VQA benchmark, with readable text, equations, figures and tables. v1 ends after references despite appendix cross-references; v3 supplies Supplementary Sections A–D. This supports comparison of newly documented material without assuming changes to previously unspecified implementation.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds localization evaluations, further ablations and detailed benchmark results in the supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original VQA evaluations, token-reduction comparisons, efficiency measurements and ablations in Tables 2–7.

results.title: When Large Vision-Language Model Meets Large Remote Sensing Imagery: Coarse-to-Fine Text-Guided Token Pruning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims about compact latent representations, two-stage autoencoding, uncertainty-guided pruning, up to 16-fold compression and 20.8-fold generation speedup. Figure 1’s caption changes from 8-fold to 16-fold compression, but the latter claim already appeared in v1’s abstract and introduction.

C2.justification: The supplement adds interpretations of latent-size versus generation-quality tradeoffs and explanations for the training and uncertainty-objective ablations. It also discusses thin-structure failures, diminishing benefits from additional latents, VAE resource costs and possible texture extensions. Appendix F.4 explicitly limits comparisons with text-generation methods because their training data sizes and output capabilities differ.

D1.justification: Appendices C–E supply substantial missing implementation and reproducibility information: token merging, triplane reconstruction, loss weighting and clipping, normalization, optimizer settings, learning-rate schedules, batch sizes, metric thresholds and evaluation sample counts. v2 also specifies decoder patch size and replaces v1’s promised code release with a stated repository link.

E1.justification: Appendix F.4 adds text-conditioned 3D generation using captioned objects, substantially extending the original reconstruction, class-conditioned generation and unconditional generation tasks. Existing ShapeNet and Objaverse coverage remains; the added per-category results concern categories already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: Table 11 introduces three PerceiverIO compression configurations as evaluated comparators. Figure 11 adds qualitative comparisons against 3DTopia-XL, LN3Diff and GaussianAnything for text-conditioned generation. The original VecSet, 3DILG and GEM3D comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds protocols for near-surface IoU using 50K queries, controlled PerceiverIO comparisons, and multiresolution decoding timings at batch size 64. Text-conditioned evaluation introduces a 128-latent configuration, object filtering, approximately 20K training objects and unseen validation captions. These extend the evaluation design; newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish protocol changes.

E4.justification: Beyond v1’s encoder, decoder and pruning-ratio ablations, v2 tests latent count, positional embeddings, single- versus two-stage training, and confidence- versus reconstruction-based uncertainty objectives in Table 13. It also adds near-surface pruning analysis, thin-structure failure cases, multiresolution sampling analysis and VAE runtime/resource breakdowns.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or variability across runs. The uncertainty head concerns token pruning, not statistical uncertainty in experimental results.

E6.justification: Numerical entries in Tables 1–7 remain unchanged, but Tables 8–14 add substantial results. For example, Table 11 reports 96.1% IoU for COD-VAE versus 94.0% for the strongest listed PerceiverIO variant, and Table 13 reports 94.4% versus 96.1% for single- and two-stage training. v2 also adds per-category scores and text-conditioned qualitative outputs.

M1.justification: The original COD-VAE procedure is retained. Appendix F.4 adds a text-conditioned variant using CLIP embeddings, 128 latent vectors, two additional layers before pruning, and convolutional triplane refinement. Appendix C mainly discloses previously unspecified base-model details rather than establishing that the original architecture changed.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and narrative remain intact. Changes include sentence polishing, typo corrections, a clarified latent-decoder description, author contact information and acknowledgments. The new supplement organizes additional material into Sections A–F without extensively rewriting or reorganizing the original exposition.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 8–14 and Figures 9–15, including diagnostic tables, failure cases, text-generation comparisons and expanded qualitative grids. Figures 1 and 5 are revised, with changed teaser examples, rearranged renderings and clearer Objaverse latent-count labeling. The original main-text displays largely retain their locations and structure.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references including PerceiverIO, 3DTopia-XL, GaussianAnything, DUSt3R, layer normalization and Earth Mover’s Distance. Supplementary discussion positions COD-VAE relative to generic latent compression and possible integrations with other 3D methods. The main related-work organization and central positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds explicit mathematical definitions of the weighted two-stage objectives, including near-surface reconstruction weighting and normalized-feature MSE in Equations (8)–(10), beyond v1’s component-level prose description. Equations (1)–(7) remain unchanged, and no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v1 directs readers to supplementary objectives and analyses absent from its PDF. v2 supplies essential implementation and evaluation details, tests previously unsupported design choices, adds a generic compression comparator, and documents failure and resource tradeoffs. These changes substantially improve reproducibility and support for the unchanged core results. The text-generation comparisons remain qualitative and use different training data, limiting their comparative force, but the broader documentation and diagnostic gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same COD-VAE work, and their text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends with references and contains no supplement despite referring to one; v2 includes supplementary Sections A–F. The supplied documents support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds compression comparisons, further ablations, runtime analyses, failure cases and text-conditioned generation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original ShapeNet and Objaverse reconstruction and generation results, efficiency measurements, and encoder, decoder and pruning ablations.

results.title: Representing 3D Shapes With 64 Latent Vectors for 3D Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: reconstructing usable, temporally consistent 4D mesh assets from fixed-view monocular video using native 3D mesh generators. Additional supporting experiments do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix B.1 newly interprets generator substitutions as evidence of extensibility and better base meshes as improving robustness. It also interprets component and VGGT results as beneficial, although Table 6 shows mixed metric effects. Existing limitations concerning initialization, topology changes, and fixed temporal sampling remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly discloses use of a single A100 GPU, provides component runtimes in Table 4, clarifies mesh decoding during embedding optimization, and specifies collected sequence lengths exceeding 200 frames. Existing hyperparameters and metric implementations remain documented as before. The project link is relocated without an access change.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 40-video benchmark: 20 Consistent4D videos and 20 Mixamo/Sketchfab videos. The added experiments vary components and generated-mesh perturbations within retained coverage. The statement that collected sequences exceed 200 frames adds detail rather than establishing changed coverage.

E2.justification: Table 5 adds naive CraftsMan3D, TripoSG, and Hunyuan3D-2.0 comparisons against their corresponding V2M4 variants, substantially broadening the native-generator comparator set. The original naive TRELLIS and DreamMesh4D comparison in Table 2 and qualitative L4GM comparison in Figure 6 remain.

E3.justification: Appendix B.1 introduces controlled quantitative designs involving generator/stereo substitutions, component removals, DreamSim and ARAP weights of 0.1, 1, and 10, and Gaussian-noise levels labeled 0.1×, 1×, and 10×. The original benchmark, metrics, preprocessing, interpolation, and FVD segmentation protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V1's qualitative component analyses are retained as Appendix B.2. New Tables 5–8 test generator dependence, component contributions, loss-weight sensitivity, and robustness to mesh-generation noise. The failure figure also adds one example for each existing failure category: topology changes and poor initialization.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. The added tables continue reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 retain exactly the same scores and runtimes. Tables 4–8 add substantial results, including component timings, alternative-generator scores, and ablation/sensitivity/noise outcomes. For example, Table 5 reports All-set FVD 377.14 for V2M4 with Hunyuan3D-2.0 versus the retained TRELLIS value 576.73; these are different configurations, not a same-setting version improvement.

M1.justification: The default five-stage TRELLIS/DUSt3R pipeline and losses remain unchanged. Appendix B.1 adds evaluated variants replacing TRELLIS with CraftsMan3D, TripoSG, or Hunyuan3D-2.0, and replacing DUSt3R with VGGT. These extend the component choices without redesigning the workflow.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely retained, with limited copy edits, expanded appendix pointers, a shortened affiliation, and added acknowledgements. Appendix B gains quantitative and qualitative subsections, while Failure Cases and More Qualitative Results exchange their C/D positions.

P2.justification: Five new tables substantially expand the quantitative presentation. Main Tables 2–3 move, and the failure figure is expanded and rearranged from v1 Figure 12 into v2 Figure 10. The unchanged qualitative comparison figures become Figures 11–12, with broader appendix layout changes.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to CraftsMan3D, TripoSG, Hunyuan3D-2.0, and VGGT for the new experiments and extensibility discussion. The related-work narrative and Table 1's positioning of native mesh generation against multi-view/video-prior approaches remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 newly states linear time complexity O(T) and almost constant memory usage O(1) with respect to frame count. No derivation or proof accompanies this characterization; the existing mathematical definitions and algorithm remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: Tables 5–8 address v1's reliance on qualitative component checks by adding quantitative tests of component contributions, generator dependence, sensitivity, and robustness. Runtime/hardware disclosure and additional failure examples further improve transparency. Some interpretations overstate the mixed results in Table 6, and noise settings remain incompletely specified, but the new diagnostic evidence substantially strengthens the paper's empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe V2M4. All 16 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable. Corresponding methods, equations, tables, and figures can be matched despite additions and relocation.

after.justification: The original experiments are retained, with additional original generator comparisons, component ablations, sensitivity and noise tests, and component runtimes in Tables 4–8.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original reconstruction-quality and runtime experiments on 40 animation videos. Appendix B reports qualitative component analyses.

results.title: V2M4: 4D Mesh Animation Reconstruction from a Single Monocular Video

C1.justification: v2 withdraws v1's repeated claim to the first density-map-based VIC method and reframes the methodological contribution around shared-density-map learning. It also drops explicit first-dataset assertions. These materially narrow the novelty claims, while retaining the dataset contribution and performance claims.

C2.justification: v2 attributes FMDC's weaker performance to difficulty predicting inflow/outflow masks. Supplementary Section D newly acknowledges shared-map errors, ambiguity from similar pedestrian appearances, and expensive cross-frame attention. These qualify the otherwise retained interpretations and applicability claims.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly documents frame intervals, resolution limits, learning rate, weight decay, scheduling, ImageNet initialization, PyTorch and A800 hardware. The abstract changes a promised code/data release to a reported release with an access link. These substantially improve reproducibility documentation, although v1's specific positional-encoding implementation reference is removed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate individual counting on MovingDroneCrowd and UAVVIC. Dense and sparse crowds, static and moving cameras, and varied lighting are already represented in v1. The supplementary examples do not introduce another dataset, task or distinct evaluation environment.

E2.justification: v2 adds the density-based FMDC method to the MovingDroneCrowd comparison in Table 2. All previously evaluated comparators remain, and the UAVVIC comparator set in Table 3 is unchanged. This is a targeted addition of a particularly relevant baseline.

E3.justification: Supplementary Figure 11 adds an evaluation varying the test frame interval from 2 to 10. Existing benchmark splits and metrics remain unchanged. Appendix A's training interval range, test interval and resizing limits are newly disclosed settings, not evidence that the retained experiments changed.

E4.justification: v2 adds frame-interval sensitivity analysis and qualitative cases examining low-light dense/sparse scenes and a nearly static UAVVIC scene. The backbone, positional-encoding, DCFA-versus-SCFA and learning-strategy ablations in Table 4 remain unchanged; 'Subtraction' is renamed 'SDNet'.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty bars. The added interval analysis also presents point estimates without uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing numerical entries in Tables 2–4 are unchanged. v2 adds FMDC results, including MAE 120.31 and RMSE 183.57, interval-sensitivity results and qualitative predictions. Figure 3 also changes dataset-distribution bars: the training-set bin for 150–199 pedestrians moves from below 1% to above 1%, without an explanation.

M1.justification: The DCFA architecture, shared-density subtraction, decoders, four MAE losses and counting procedure are retained. SDNet names the existing method. The residual term added to Equation 3 matches the residual module already depicted in v1's Figure 5, rather than establishing a new architectural component.

P1.justification: The abstract and multi-paragraph introduction and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten and condensed around shared-density learning. SDNet terminology is introduced, explanations are edited throughout, and supplementary Sections A–D and acknowledgements are added. The main six-section outline remains intact.

P2.justification: v2 revises Figures 1–5, including clearer architecture labels and a redrawn distribution plot; reformats comparison tables with underlining and red improvement annotations; and relocates Figure 7. Four supplementary figures add dataset examples, prediction panels and an interval-sensitivity plot, substantially expanding the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 introduces Wan et al.'s FMDC as the closest density-based predecessor and distinguishes shared-map estimation from flow-mask prediction, substantially revising the first-of-kind positioning. Smaller citation changes add Zhan et al.'s survey and remove the Twins, original ViT and Sreenu survey references.

T1.justification: Equation 3 adds the omitted residual term after cross-attention, correcting the formal recurrence to match the existing architecture diagram. No new theorems or proofs appear. Equation 1's shift from zero-based to one-based frame indexing is otherwise an equivalent reformulation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps by recognizing and evaluating the closest density-based predecessor, narrowing the novelty claim, and supplying substantial training/testing documentation and reported code/data access. The sensitivity analysis and explicit limitations further strengthen assessment of the method. Although Figure 3's statistical revisions are unexplained and positional-encoding source detail is lost, the attribution and reproducibility gains provide a substantial overall improvement without relying on higher retained benchmark scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MovingDroneCrowd dataset and video individual counting method. All pages, equations, tables and figures are readable, including v2's added supplementary Sections A–D; v1 ends after its references.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds an FMDC comparison, frame-interval sensitivity results and supplementary qualitative predictions.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset statistics, evaluations on MovingDroneCrowd and UAVVIC, backbone and attention ablations, and qualitative predictions.

results.title: Video Individual Counting for Moving Drones

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the state-of-the-art claim to GroundingYouTube and YouCook-Interactions. The central contributions—automatic grounded-data generation, GROVE, and iGround—and the claimed value of pre-training followed by fine-tuning remain intact.

C2.justification: New Appendix C explains limitations from eight-frame training on long videos and difficulty disambiguating similar referring expressions. Figure 10 identifies objectness, localization, object-label, and action-label failures. Section 6.4 and Appendix B also replace v1's inconsistent AP50 explanation with a precision-recall interpretation supported by caption and noun-phrase counts.

D1.justification: v3 adds video-ID disjointness assurances, VidSTG supervision-adaptation details, and a sliding-window inference disclosure. It explicitly states code/data availability and locates supplementary videos. However, it removes v1's explicit 50,000-clip ablation pre-training budget without specifying a replacement. Most implementation settings and annotation prompts are retained.

E1.justification: v3 adds actual evaluations on YouCook-Interactions and GroundingYouTube (Table 8), alongside the retained iGround, VidSTG, and ActivityNet-Entities coverage. It also adds interrogative-sentence grounding on VidSTG (Table 4), substantially broadening the evaluated data and query scenarios.

E2.justification: New evaluated comparators include PG-V-L (13B), GLaMM+SAM2, and VideoGLaMM in Table 4; What When and Where with S3D and CLIP in Table 8; and a VideoLlama-3-based annotation alternative in Table 7. The original benchmark comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: v3 adds a no-VidSTG-training evaluation condition using transformed pre-training supervision and selects a difficult iGround validation subset. It revises the reported iGround split from 2000/500/1000 to 2013/500/1000. The established metrics and general optimization settings remain unchanged; these disclosures do not establish which existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained scaling and component analyses, v3 tests a video-captioner alternative for annotation (Table 7), evaluates ambiguity from similar referring expressions on a Hard subset (Table 9), and illustrates four failure modes (Figure 10). Appendix B also adds caption-length and noun-phrase statistics to examine the full-caption versus SVO tradeoff.

E5.justification: Figure 5 retains the same error bars. Neither version explains their estimator or repeated-run count, and v3 adds no seed information, uncertainty-estimation procedure, or significance test.

E6.justification: Existing results change: Table 2 all-frame PT+FT CIDEr changes from 85.4 to 83.5, and Table 3 GROVE PT+FT msIoU from 62.9 to 63.7. ActivityNet-Entities, model-ablation scores, and Figure 6 also change. New results include interrogative VidSTG msIoU of 43.0 without fine-tuning and 55.5 with fine-tuning, two additional benchmarks, and Hard-subset outcomes. Revised sample reporting and an unspecified ablation budget prevent treating every update as a matched-setting performance change.

M1.justification: v3 Appendix E adds a task-specific pre-training adaptation for evaluation without VidSTG training data: Llama-3 rewrites captions into declarative/interrogative forms, paired with the first mentioned subject or object's bounding boxes. The core architecture, losses, and three-stage annotation pipeline remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. v3 condenses the annotation-ablation discussion and moves its detailed treatment into Appendix B, adds an appendix roadmap and limitations section, and updates cross-references, terminology, and acknowledgments.

P2.justification: v3 adds comparison and diagnostic Tables 4, 8, and 9 and the four-example failure Figure 10. It redraws and relocates the architecture diagram, arranges the VidSTG tables side by side, expands the annotation-ablation table, and changes Figure 6's plotted axes. The original qualitative examples and prompt displays are largely retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to PG-Video-LLaVA, VideoGLaMM, SAM 2, and VideoLlama 3. Section 2 distinguishes GROVE's fully automatic bounding-box annotations from concurrent VideoGLaMM's mask grounding and semi-automatic annotations. The broader positioning remains stable; the added published What When and Where entry represents an already cited work.

T1.justification: The adapter equation, model tensor definitions, and loss equations (1–6) are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v3 introduces no substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation through direct comparisons with additional video-grounding models and evaluation without VidSTG training data (Table 4). The measured Hard-subset analysis, failure examples, and explicit long-video limitations address v1's limited characterization of reliability and applicability. The corrected annotation-ablation interpretation also improves scientific clarity. Table 8's unspecified metric/protocol and the lost ablation-budget disclosure weaken reproducibility, but the stronger comparative evidence and substantive failure analysis provide a clear overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GROVE, HowToGround1M, and iGround. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite additions and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark comparisons, an annotation ablation, difficult-subset evaluation, and failure examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, pre-training scaling experiments, component ablations, and qualitative predictions in Section 6 and the appendix.

results.title: Large-scale Pre-training for Grounded Video Caption Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: the diverse, finely annotated OmniDiff dataset, the plug-and-play MDP module within M3Diff, and strong performance across IDC benchmarks. The new experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: New Section 9.2 tentatively attributes LLaVA-OneVision's competitive performance to greater use of multi-image pretraining data and discusses MDP's effectiveness across backbones. The existing OCR failure discussion and proposed extension to video remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 adds a project homepage link and supplies the complete GPT-4o evaluation prompt in Figure 6. The existing implementation details and hyperparameter table are retained. Both abstracts still describe code, data, and model release as forthcoming, so the PDFs do not establish that those resources became available.

E1.justification: The training datasets, benchmark coverage, and image-difference-captioning tasks are retained. The new appendix experiments reuse OmniDiff-Real, OmniDiff-Render, IEdit, and CLEVR-DC; they add model configurations and evaluation procedures rather than new data domains or tasks.

E2.justification: The original comparison tables retain their comparator sets. Supplementary Table 11 newly includes FINER-MLLM in the CLEVR-DC comparison, while Table 12 adds InternVL3-8B comparisons and fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL controls without MDP, extending the earlier zero-shot Qwen comparison.

E3.justification: New supplementary protocols include reproducing FINER-MLLM with the same 896k training samples as M3Diff, testing MDP with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B, and scoring captions with GPT-4o on a 0–100 ground-truth-aspect-coverage rubric. These substantially expand the evaluation design; the original splits, metrics, and main-model training budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the original single-backbone ablations in Table 6, Table 12 tests whether MDP remains beneficial on two additional backbones. Table 13 evaluates training with versus without OmniDiff using semantic judgments from GPT-4o. These add substantial evidence about module portability and dataset utility; the existing qualitative cases are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The new appendix tables continue reporting point scores.

E6.justification: Tables 11–13 add controlled FINER-MLLM results, cross-backbone ablation results, and LLM scores; for example, OmniDiff-Real scores are 12.3 without OmniDiff training and 37.3 with it. Table 5 changes M3Diff's BLEU-4/METEOR/CIDEr/SPICE from 33.9/26.3/135.2/26.5 to 33.6/26.5/136.6/27.5, matching the already-existing Table 6 values. Table 11's FINER-MLLM scores use different training conditions from Table 3 and are additional results, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The MDP operations, multi-scale integration, and one-stage fine-tuning procedure remain unchanged. The additional backbone experiments test the existing module without introducing a new algorithmic component or adaptation procedure.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized wording corrections, including changing '324 scene pairs' to '324 scenes', and adds corresponding-author information and acknowledgements. A new supplementary Experiments section precedes the retained Case Study, renumbered from Section 9 to Section 10. The main narrative is largely preserved.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 11–13 and the evaluation-prompt Figure 6, redraws the Figure 4 word cloud, and relocates Figure 3 and Table 3. The two-column design, existing table structures, and qualitative case-study panels are retained, with localized layout adjustments.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to the LLM-as-a-judge survey and InternVL3 to support the new evaluations. The related-work narrative and research positioning remain largely unchanged; most other reference edits update metadata for already-cited works.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and operations in Equations 1–8 are retained. No new theorem, proof, derivation, or formal assumption is introduced; the GPT-4o scoring rubric is an evaluation-protocol addition.

improvement.justification: V1 did not establish matched training data for its FINER-MLLM comparison and tested MDP on only one backbone. V2's identical-data comparison and two additional backbone ablations address important gaps in comparison fairness and support for the plug-and-play claim. It also resolves the IEdit discrepancy between Tables 5 and 6. These substantially strengthen the central empirical argument, although uncertainty reporting and detailed settings for the new evaluations remain limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OmniDiff benchmark and M3Diff model. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material are readable and support a complete comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains the original empirical evaluations and adds controlled comparisons, backbone ablations, and LLM-based evaluation in supplementary Tables 11–13.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations and dataset/module ablations in Tables 3–8, together with dataset analyses and qualitative case studies.

results.title: OmniDiff: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Fine-grained Image Difference Captioning

C1.justification: Both versions make the same central claims: introducing HIS-QA and HIS-Bench, proposing a joint human-scene foundation model, and achieving superior HIS-QA performance. The new appendix evidence supports these retained claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets human ratings as validating benchmark quality, evaluator correlations as demonstrating accuracy and reproducibility, and the remaining fine-tuned baseline gap as supporting unified 3D modeling. Existing interpretations of AInt, LTP, frozen-LLM training and rendered inputs are retained.

D1.justification: The abstract adds a repository address for a planned code and data release. Appendix D.1 identifies reuse and format conversion of HIS-GPT training data for baselines, but supplies no detailed fine-tuning recipe. Existing implementation settings and prompts remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix A.4 newly evaluates 100 OpenEQA samples in a human assessment of benchmark quality; v1 only discussed OpenEQA. HIS-GPT's training datasets and the 800-question HIS-Bench task coverage remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The HIS-QA comparator methods remain unchanged. New Table 8 evaluates existing Chat-Scene, LLaVA-OV and LLaVA-OV+GPT-4 baselines under additional fine-tuning conditions. Qwen2.5-7B is introduced as an evaluator, not a competing HIS-QA method.

E3.justification: v2 adds substantial evaluation protocols: three-person, four-dimension ratings of all HIS-Bench samples and 100 OpenEQA samples; human assessment of GPT-4o answers; alternative judging with Qwen2.5-7B; and baseline fine-tuning using converted HIS-GPT training data. These supplement the retained original evaluation.

E4.justification: New Appendices A.4–A.5 investigate benchmark quality and evaluator validity, while D.1 tests whether the comparison survives baseline fine-tuning. These address questions absent from v1's analyses. Existing component, loss-weight, LoRA and video-format ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A.5 adds Pearson correlation estimates for human–GPT and cross-evaluator agreement, and the human studies report three raters. The original three-evaluation averaging remains unchanged; no confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Original performance and ablation results remain unchanged, including HIS-GPT's 48.7 average. New Table 8 reports fine-tuned baseline scores of 13.4, 19.7 and 20.8. Table 5 adds human quality ratings, including correctness scores of 4.35 for HIS-Bench and 4.64 for OpenEQA. Appendix A.5 adds correlations of 0.54 and 0.75, and Table 6 adds Qwen-judged scores. These are additional results under new protocols.

M1.justification: The scene and motion encoders, AInt auxiliary objectives, LTP encoding, frozen backbone and two-stage HIS-GPT training remain unchanged. The additional experiments do not introduce a new proposed method component.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is unchanged. v2 updates affiliations and contact information, lightly rewrites the conclusion, adds acknowledgements and appendix subsections, and places the appendices before the bibliography instead of using a separately headed supplement.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5, 6 and 8, adjusts figure sizing and placement, and reflows supplementary figures alongside the relocated bibliography. Existing supplementary Figures S1–S13 become Figures 6–18; their substantive contents and existing result displays are retained.

R1.justification: The same 72 referenced works and the same positioning relative to scene-only and human-only understanding are retained. The added studies reuse existing citations without revising the central novelty argument.

T1.justification: The task formulation, model equations, losses and spatial definitions are unchanged. The added empirical correlation analysis introduces no new theoretical result, assumption or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 did not quantify benchmark quality or human–judge agreement and compared trained HIS-GPT with zero-shot baselines. v2's human assessments, alternative-evaluator checks and matched-corpus baseline fine-tuning address central validation and fairness gaps, substantially strengthening the empirical foundation. The 0.54 human correlation warrants more cautious interpretation than the paper gives it, and fine-tuning details remain sparse, but the added evidence provides a substantial net benefit.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HIS-QA, HIS-Bench and HIS-GPT work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices A–E are readable and can be matched despite supplementary-material reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds human quality assessments, evaluator-validation results and fine-tuned baseline evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original HIS-Bench evaluations, component and training ablations, input-format comparisons and qualitative results.

results.title: HIS-GPT: Towards 3D Human-In-Scene Multimodal Understanding

C1.justification: The abstract and four introduction contributions retain the same claims: efficient vector-set representation, explicit outpainting, cross-scene blending and NuiScene43 curation. The shorter conclusion preserves this scope; the new appendix experiments primarily supply additional support.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds substantive qualifications concerning floating artifacts, larger-batch overfitting, height-prediction failures and decoder capacity. It also explains why marching-cubes thresholds and differing chunk distributions limit CD/F-score comparisons across settings, favoring IoU for those comparisons. These materially deepen the interpretation beyond v1's mainly dataset-size, controllability and global-context limitations.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies 50 DDPM denoising steps, 12-view retrieval embeddings, camera field-of-view and clipping settings, and TRELLIS-image-large without decimation. It adds dataset-visualization and sampling-configuration links and documents the new decoder variant. These disclosures do not by themselves establish changes to previously performed experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions study outdoor-scene reconstruction and generation using NuiScene43. The new 13-scene experiment expands the training subset within this collection, but does not identify a distinct new domain, dataset or task; its scene and chunk counts are experimental-setting changes.
