E2.justification: Triplane, RePaint and Trellis remain the comparison methods. Within the existing four-scene setting, v2 adds quantitative triplane comparisons in Tables 10–11, whereas v1 presents vector-set generations and a qualitative Trellis comparison.

E3.justification: v2 completes the 128-by-128 triplane experiment using four L40S GPUs instead of the unsuccessful two-GPU setting. New experiments vary batch sizes and inference resolutions, evaluate four-scene diffusion with 30k quad-chunks per distribution, and train on 280k chunks from 13 scenes. The original single-scene split and principal training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds substantial sensitivity and failure analyses: high-resolution triplane artifacts, larger-batch overfitting and height errors, inference resolutions of 13/25/50, and the decoder upsampling comparison for 13-scene training. These extend considerably beyond v1's resolution comparisons, RePaint analysis and qualitative examples.

E5.justification: Table 5 first specifies that generation times are averaged over five runs; v1 gives no repetition count. This establishes a reporting change, not an increase from a known earlier run count. Neither version reports timing dispersion or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 retain their numerical results, but Table 5 revises timings: explicit vector-set generation/decoding changes from 217.79/76.59 seconds to five-run averages of 215.92/87.76 seconds. New entries in Tables 7–11 report high-resolution, larger-batch and four-scene outcomes. The 128-by-128 triplane achieves predicted-height F-score 0.879 versus vecset's 0.864, while the new 13-scene decoder variant raises IoU from 0.968 to 0.983 within that experiment.

M1.justification: Appendix C.3 introduces a decoder variant for 13-scene training: a channel projection and pixel-shuffle-like reshape expand features to 512 vectors, followed by three additional self-attention layers. This is a localized architectural extension; the original encoder, losses and conditional outpainting framework remain.

P1.justification: v2 tightens prose, shortens the conclusion, separates Limitations into its own section and brings a scene-texturing summary into the main text. The supplement is reorganized from S1–S3 into A–C, while the overall narrative and much of the wording remain.

P2.justification: The supplementary presentation expands substantially with Tables 7–11, height-error and resolution comparisons, decoder-comparison panels, and aerial/street-level views of 13-scene generations. Existing meshes are widely re-rendered in blue, Figure 6's detail annotations are revised, and earlier galleries are reduced or replaced. Main-text tables are also relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Objaverse-XL, DreamFusion and pixel-shuffle super-resolution. Its limitations discussion expands positioning relative to 2D-prior methods and directly supervised 3D generation, while the main related-work coverage and novelty framing remain.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, normalization, losses and diffusion equations remain substantively unchanged. Algorithm 1 clarifies the denoising call, but no new formal assumptions, derivations, propositions or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 supports multi-scene generation mainly through qualitative examples and leaves its highest-resolution triplane baseline unevaluated because of memory limits. v2 adds four-scene quantitative comparisons, 13-scene validation and completed high-resolution and larger-batch experiments, alongside specific failure analyses and metric caveats. These substantially strengthen empirical scrutiny and reproducibility; the benefit is better-supported, more qualified evidence rather than uniformly higher performance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NuiScene work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and can be matched despite reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds reconstruction, scaling, sensitivity and multi-scene results in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction and generation experiments, resource measurements, timing comparisons and generated-scene examples.

results.title: NuiScene: Exploring Efficient Generation of Unbounded Outdoor Scenes

C1.justification: v2 removes a central claimed benefit: mitigating catastrophic forgetting disappears from the abstract, introduction's stated challenges and contributions, and conclusion. The conclusion also drops the specific rare-disease applicability claim. The unified multimodal, multitask, pan-cancer contribution and overall performance claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 removes the speculative forgetting/overfitting explanation for performance gains and qualifies untested modality extensions as possible in principle. New discussion links text-training benefits to architecture and attributes the RCC clinical-input degradation to potentially less relevant clinical features. The original computational-cost and convergence limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a public-code repository link, newly specifies HSV thresholding for foreground patch selection, and documents the clinical covariates and their two-layer encoder. HSV thresholding is newly disclosed rather than established as a changed procedure. The shared hyperparameter table is unchanged.

E1.justification: The same six TCGA cohorts and the same subtyping and survival tasks remain. Supplementary Section 13 adds an input scenario using clinical covariates alongside WSIs and transcriptomics; the TITAN experiments introduce no additional cohort or prediction task.

E2.justification: v2 substantially broadens the controls: Gigapath linear probing joins both in-domain and OOD comparisons in Tables 2–3; Table 8 adds LoRA and ABMIL with text embeddings; Tables 9 and 11 introduce TITAN linear-probing, tuning, and fusion comparators. The original comparator rows are retained.

E3.justification: New evaluation configurations include pretrained-feature linear probing, TITAN-specific re-extraction of patch features, and controlled adapter, text-training, and clinical-input variants. The existing patient splits, balanced-accuracy/C-index metrics, and original training settings remain unchanged. These are additions to the evaluation design, not documented revisions of the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of adapter choice using LoRA, whether text-based multitask training benefits ABMIL, transferability to TITAN, and the value of additional clinical inputs. These substantially extend validation of the framework's design and extensibility. The original ablations and qualitative analyses remain, although v1's untabulated observation about single-task text targets is removed.

E5.justification: The stated three-seed mean/standard-deviation reporting and median-risk Kaplan–Meier analysis with a log-rank threshold of 0.05 are unchanged. New trained-model rows follow the existing uncertainty format; no increased run count or new statistical procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results in Tables 2, 3, 7, and 8 are unchanged, but numerous results are added. Table 9 reports ModalTune TITAN overall balanced accuracy/C-index of 0.942/0.735. Table 10 reports 0.950/0.755 for the clinical-input variant versus 0.954/0.750 for the retained default. These and the new baseline and ablation rows expand the evidence rather than improve the original scores.

M1.justification: The original Modal Adapter, task prompts, feature fusion, text targets, and KL objective remain unchanged. v2 adds a clinical-input extension using a two-layer MLP to produce a token concatenated with transcriptomics features (Supplementary Section 13), and instantiates the framework with TITAN.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites affect the abstract, introduction, selected method and results passages, and conclusion. Two supplementary sections are inserted, moving Qualitative Analysis from Section 12 to Section 14. Affiliation and terminology edits accompany these changes, while the overall narrative structure remains stable.

P2.justification: Tables 2, 3, and 8 gain rows, and Tables 9–11 are added using the existing presentation style. Captions, sizing, and float placement receive limited adjustments. All six figures retain identical underlying artwork, including the relocated appendix visualizations.

R1.justification: v2 adds the LoRA reference and removes the Alfasly et al. retrieval and de Jong et al. medical-center robustness references while narrowing the introduction's motivation. The related-work survey largely remains intact. The additional CLIP bibliography entry duplicates a work already cited in v1.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations (1)–(5) are retained. Supplementary Section 11.5 preserves the same random-projection and Johnson–Lindenstrauss reasoning; no new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through pretrained linear-probing controls, alternative-adapter comparisons, and direct tests of another slide encoder and additional clinical inputs. Removing the unsupported catastrophic-forgetting claim also improves the match between claims and evidence. Section 12 nevertheless overstates the TITAN OOD advantage over the next-best baseline by overlooking the stronger linear-probing comparator in Table 11. Despite that qualification, the added controls and extensibility tests substantially strengthen the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ModalTune study. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and the methods, equations, tables, and figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds linear-probing controls, further ablations, TITAN experiments, and clinical-input experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original TCGA cancer-subtyping and survival experiments, OOD evaluations, ablations, and qualitative analyses.

results.title: ModalTune: Fine-Tuning Slide-Level Foundation Models with Multi-Modal Information for Multi-task Learning in Digital Pathology

C1.justification: The central ClaraVid and DSP-correlation claims remain. v2 emphasizes complexity estimation from 2D measurements before reconstruction, recasts the third introductory contribution as demonstrating both dataset and DSP utility, and removes the introduction/conclusion's explicit method-selection and pipeline-optimization promise.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's general uncertainty discussion, v2 explicitly qualifies DSP's reliability under blur, resolution changes, unbounded scenes, spatial contraction, and mismatched acquisition policies. The UAVid analysis explains weaker correlations through capture artifacts and incomplete coverage, while Supplementary Section 8.2 specifies conditions for meaningful cross-scene comparison.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies Gaussian preprocessing with a 3×3 kernel and sigma 1.0, 3×3 Sobel filters, and 256 histogram bins per axis. It also clarifies depth rendering, reduced segmentation palettes, Zip-NeRF reimplementation, and UAVid setup, and states that code/data are available rather than promising release after acceptance. Conversely, v1's method-of-moments/Newton–Raphson fitting details disappear.

E1.justification: v2 adds Dronescapes to semantic-segmentation evaluation and extends UAVid coverage to reconstruction on six continuous-video sequences with non-grid trajectories. UAVid previously appeared in segmentation and distribution-model motivation. ClaraVid and the existing Mill19/UrbanScene3D analyses remain.

E2.justification: Shannon pixel entropy and GLCM texture entropy become directly evaluated competitors to delentropy in Figure 4, with corresponding comparisons on UAVid in Figure 6. v1 discussed these alternatives without this quantitative comparison. The original reconstruction baselines and ClaraVid-versus-Syndrone segmentation comparison are retained.

E3.justification: Supplementary Section 10.4 introduces a UAVid reconstruction protocol using six 901-frame sequences, specified training/testing frame offsets, stationary-frame exclusion, endpoint inclusion, twofold downsampling, and COLMAP. Section 4 also revises reported point-cloud sampling units from meters to centimeters. These changes do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds comparative validation of the complexity proxy, robustness evaluation under UAVid's unstructured capture conditions, and two illustrated failure cases involving blur/registration and incomplete coverage. Supplementary Section 8.2 additionally reports resolution- and scene-area-sensitivity observations. The original viewpoint ablation is retained.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 and Figure 4 newly describe and compare predictive-interval widths for the entropy measures. This is a limited reporting addition: interval construction and coverage are unspecified, and neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds entropy-comparator correlations, six-sequence UAVid reconstruction results in Table 5, and Dronescapes segmentation results in Table 4, including mIoU 37.30 for ClaraVid training versus 34.11 for Syndrone training. Matched numerical entries in Tables 2–3 and the existing Table 4 rows are unchanged.

M1.justification: DSP still computes gradient-based delentropy and models its scene-level distribution with a four-parameter Beta distribution fitted by maximum likelihood. Reconstruction models and semantic heads are retained. Newly specified filtering and histogram settings document implementation details without establishing a procedural revision.

P1.justification: v2 substantially revises the introductory/DSP framing and experimental discussion, reorganizes the dataset description into labeled paragraphs, moves the Beta-distribution motivation from the main text to Supplementary Section 8.1, and consolidates segmentation settings within the experimental-setup appendix. These changes reshape the explanation and organization beyond simply inserting results.

P2.justification: Figure 4 is redesigned with normalized entropy axes and overlaid comparators; new UAVid correlation and failure-case figures and Table 5 are added. Table 2 gains complexity-based ordering and color shading. The final RGB montage is replaced by an eight-mission multimodal overview, while several retained figures and tables are relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Dronescapes, InfoNeRF, aerial tracking/LiDAR work, evaluation metrics, and COLMAP, while removing the OMMO reference. It explicitly distinguishes image-only DSP estimation from complexity computed during or after reconstruction. The broader related-work organization and positioning remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 retain the gradient, deldensity, delentropy, Beta-profile, and maximum-likelihood definitions. The expanded complexity-profile framing and acquisition-condition discussion provide conceptual explanation and applicability qualifications, without substantively changing the mathematics or adding proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central DSP contribution by addressing v1's lack of direct entropy-baseline comparisons and adding original real-video reconstruction validation, explicit failure conditions, and reproducible computation details. These gains improve evidential support and appropriate use of the metric. Localized reporting problems remain: the new Dronescapes entropy results contradict the retained all-dataset superiority claim, and the domain-gap averages still reflect the earlier three-dataset evaluation. These inconsistencies temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial validation and documentation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ClaraVid dataset and Delentropic Scene Profile (DSP) study. Their complete main texts and supplementary materials are readable, and corresponding equations, experiments, tables, and figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds Dronescapes segmentation, UAVid reconstruction experiments, entropy-comparator evaluations, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original ClaraVid reconstruction benchmarks, viewpoint-generalization experiments, synthetic-to-real segmentation results, and scene-complexity analyses.

results.title: ClaraVid: A Holistic Scene Reconstruction Benchmark From Aerial Perspective With Delentropy-Based Complexity Profiling

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about retrieval-augmented generalization, part-aware generation, and prior-guided refinement. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining their stated scope.

C2.justification: Supplementary Section 3.3 newly explains the tradeoff between diversity and task-aligned, natural grasps, acknowledges room to improve joint-angle diversity, and justifies restricting diversity comparisons to seen categories. Other additions interpret descriptor and reduced-data results as evidence of flexibility and scalability. The original part-segmentation limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the full GPT-4o prompt and action definitions, plus user-study details including the 0–5 scale, two viewpoints, and 20 examples across 19 unseen categories. It also documents preprocessing and supervision settings for added experiments. Conversely, Section 4.1 removes v1's batch size of 90, and the Fast Version configuration remains unexplained.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on filtered Objaverse-tiny objects pre-segmented by PartField, extending the original curated object coverage to another open-set population. Supplementary Section 3.1 also evaluates parsing and grounding with point and press added to the original five affordances; it does not establish full grasp-generation evaluation for those additional actions.

E2.justification: Main Table 1 retains AffordPose, GrabNet†, GraspTTA†, and Ours*. Supplementary Table 1 adds Ours-BPS as an internal comparison method against the original Ours-OBB. Newly cited AffordDexGrasp and Dexterous Grasp Transformer are not evaluated as baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds held-out seen-category evaluation with a stated 8:1:1 AffordPose split, parsing/grounding metrics, and diversity metrics evaluated on the AffordPose test set. New protocols also filter and rescale the first 500 Objaverse-tiny candidates and test 30 intrinsic configurations per affordance or one-tenth extrinsic supervision. These are additional evaluation designs, not evidence that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The supplement adds OBB-versus-BPS sensitivity testing, reduced-supervision scalability tests, five-versus-seven-affordance parsing analysis, and grasp-diversity analysis. A microwave case traces intermediate processing, while additional ablation visualizations examine penetration, contact, and initialization failures beyond v1's bucket example.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new standard deviations of translation, rotation, and joint angles measure generated-grasp diversity, rather than uncertainty in reported performance. The stated 30-participant study size is unchanged.

E6.justification: Main Table 1 adds seen-category scores while preserving the original unseen-category values; for example, Ours now reports seen/unseen part accuracy of 82.6/71.6%. Main Table 2 is unchanged. Supplementary results add BPS comparisons, diversity, parsing accuracy, Objaverse-PartField, reduced-supervision settings, and a Fast Version row. These are newly reported results, not improvements under the original settings.

M1.justification: The main retrieval, CVAE generation, and two-stage optimization pipeline remains unchanged. Supplementary Section 3.2 adds an implemented retrieval variant using Basis Point Set features and cosine similarity instead of OBB-size distances, a limited procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: v2 locally condenses related-work, method-overview, and dataset prose while retaining the main section organization. It adds acknowledgments and organized supplementary sections, updates affiliation ordering and equal-contribution markings, and makes bibliographic corrections. The existing narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: Main Table 1 changes to paired seen/unseen entries with ranking colors based on their averages. The supplement adds three tables and five figures, including the prompt, survey screenshot, intermediate-stage visualization, and extensive comparison and ablation grids. Main figures are largely retained, with limited label corrections such as Figure 3's feature dimension.

R1.justification: v2 acknowledges concurrent AffordDexGrasp in Section 2.2 and adds Dexterous Grasp Transformer to the data-driven literature. The supplement introduces citations for Objaverse, PartField, and BPS. These are limited additions; the main research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The formal problem setup, retrieval-distance definitions, and losses in Equations 1–7 remain unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the supplement adds empirical analyses without new formal derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for central assumptions that v1 left largely untested: parsing reliability, retrieval-descriptor sensitivity, scalability with fewer labels, and generalization with automated segmentation on open-set objects. The disclosed prompt and user-study procedure also materially improve reproducibility. The removed batch-size disclosure and underspecified Fast Version and filtered Objaverse sample count are weaknesses, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe G-DexGrasp and retain matching methods, equations, experiments, and figures. All pages are readable, including v2's added supplementary material; v1 ends with references and contains no appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds seen-category comparisons and supplementary experiments on retrieval descriptors, diversity, parsing, open-set objects, and reduced supervision.

before.justification: v1 reports original grasp-generation comparisons, simulation metrics, ablations, and a perceptual user study in Section 4 and Tables 1–2.

results.title: G-DexGrasp: Generalizable Dexterous Grasping Synthesis Via Part-Aware Prior Retrieval and Prior-Assisted Generation

C1.justification: The central contributions remain GPCT for consistent single-pass patch refinement, BFM for avoiding synthetic-label bias, strong zero-shot depth performance, and approximately 12× faster inference than PatchRefiner with 177 patches. The added experiments support the existing generality claim rather than redefine it.

C2.justification: Supplement A newly explains that poor transparent-object predictions from DA1 can undermine refinement: DA1-based PRO has Booster AbsRel 0.0500 versus unrefined DA1's 0.0482. It also interprets the BFM transfer experiments as evidence of broader applicability and patch-count variation as a speed/detail adjustment available without retraining.

D1.justification: New Supplement C fills important implementation gaps by specifying rejection of samples with more than 50% unreliable pixels, native-resolution crop and patch geometry, overlap scaling, and assembly into a 2072×2072 depth map followed by bilinear upsampling. Supplement A also states that replacing the base model requires retraining. These are newly disclosed details, not demonstrated changes to previously run experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions use UnrealStereo4K for training and evaluate on Booster, ETH3D, Middlebury 2014, NuScenes, DIS-5K, UHRSD, and internet images. UHRSD and internet examples already appear in v1's appendix. Alternative base models and patch counts change configurations within retained coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparison methods remain unchanged. New supplementary comparisons evaluate standalone MiDaS v3.1 and DepthAnythingV1 alongside their refinement variants, BFM-trained PatchFusion and PatchRefiner, and a two-patch diagonal-consistency control (Tables 5, 6, and 8). These extend the comparisons without replacing the original baseline families.

E3.justification: Supplement A adds substantial experimental controls: retraining with two alternative base models, enabling BFM in other architectures, testing 3×3/4×4/5×5 inference grids, and comparing diagonal regularization with GPCT. Existing primary evaluation settings remain. Section 4.4 also changes the stated overlap interpretation from its shorter side to a square-region size; this does not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of base-model generality and transparent-object failure, BFM transfer to other methods, patch-count sensitivity, and GPCT versus diagonal consistency (Supplement A, Tables 5–8 and Figures 6–7). The original component, overlap-size, and frequency-fusion ablations are retained; v1's FFM Table 5 becomes v2's Table 9.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. The added experiments continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 and the relocated FFM results are numerically unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results in Tables 5–8. For example, diagonal consistency has CE 0.075 versus GPCT's 0.049, while achieving better D3R, 0.0787 versus 0.0803. Table 7 reports DIS boundary recall of 0.125, 0.156, and 0.162 for 3×3, 4×4, and 5×5 grids. These are additional comparisons, not revised headline scores.

M1.justification: The residual refinement architecture, four-patch GPCT, BFM, frequency fusion, and losses are retained. Explicit patch arguments in ROI operations and additional indices clarify existing notation. Newly documented preprocessing does not establish a change to the underlying procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and portions of the method receive extensive language editing and paragraph rewriting. The appendix is reorganized into supplementary Sections A–D, with dedicated experiment and implementation sections, while notation, terminology, and captions are clarified throughout.

P2.justification: v2 adds four supplementary tables and two qualitative figures, substantially expanding the displayed experimental evidence. It places the retained FFM table beside its architecture discussion and updates diagram labels. The original qualitative panels are retained and renumbered, including v1 Figures 7–10 becoming v2 Figures 9–12.

R1.justification: The same 49 cited works and substantive positioning relative to previous depth-estimation methods are retained. The new experiments use already cited methods; added citation markers and changed reference back-links do not expand the literature coverage.

T1.justification: Equations 1–10 retain the same refinement, consistency, masking, and frequency-fusion operations. Explicit ROI patch arguments and patch indices are equivalent notation changes. No new assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's broad integration claim was tested principally with DA2, and its GPCT ablation lacked a direct diagonal-consistency control. v2 addresses both gaps through alternative-base experiments and a targeted comparison, while reporting a DA1 failure case and metric-dependent tradeoffs. The newly specified sample filtering and reconstruction steps also materially improve reproducibility. Together these changes substantially strengthen the paper's validation and clarify applicability, despite unchanged headline results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PRO research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, references, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite supplementary-section reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds experiments with alternative base models, BFM transfer, inference patch counts, and diagonal consistency training.

before.justification: v1 reports original depth-estimation comparisons, component and overlap ablations, and an appendix experiment comparing frequency fusion with convolutional fusion.

results.title: One Look is Enough: Seamless Patchwise Refinement for Zero-Shot Monocular Depth Estimation on High-Resolution Images

C1.justification: The introduction adds an explicit Python-toolkit contribution whose scope includes localization, detection, tracking, alignment and visualization, and the abstract now emphasizes the toolkit. The central claims about unified data, voxel-level flows, cooperative support and ground-truth-free evaluation otherwise remain.

C2.justification: v1 Section 4.3 broadly emphasizes benefits across domains and improved background forecasting. v2 qualifies this interpretation: its generalization discussion focuses on mixing real datasets, while simulation mixing can degrade temporal consistency. It explicitly discusses the already-reported nuScenes IoUbg decrease from 59.56 to 55.07 and investigates speed mismatch as a potential explanation in Section 8.

D1.justification: v2 supplies previously undocumented flow-computation formulas, GMM fitting with EM/BIC selection over 1–20 components and four covariance types, voxel-scale perturbations, PCA pseudocode and tracking-distance thresholds. It also specifies localization's RANSAC threshold and iteration limit. These substantially improve technical disclosure without establishing changes to existing experiments. Data/code access instructions switch from direct dataset/repository links to a project website.

E1.justification: The four data sources and principal occupancy tasks remain. v2 adds training and evaluation involving highway-focused CARLA scenes generated with Town06, supporting speeds up to 55 mph (Section 8, Table 6). This extends the represented driving conditions within the existing simulation domain.

E2.justification: v2 adds an object-level-flow OccWorld comparator alongside no flow and voxel-level flow on both nuScenes and Waymo (Tables 2 and 8). v1 Table 3 compared only with and without voxel flow. Cam4DOcc, CVTOcc and CoHFF remain in their corresponding evaluations.

E3.justification: v2 adds nuScenes-plus-Waymo-only training configurations, a standard-versus-highway CARLA comparison, and evaluation through a weighted UniOcc Score (Section 9). These supplement the existing protocol; the stated 200×200×16 grid, 0.4 m resolution and three-second observation/forecast horizons remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The new object-flow comparisons test whether fine-grained voxel motion offers benefits beyond coarse object motion. Section 8 adds a substantive investigation of simulation–real compatibility through speed-distribution histograms and highway-scene training experiments. These directly examine two central explanations behind the benchmark's reported benefits.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added GMM-fitting and RANSAC details describe algorithm computation rather than uncertainty reporting for experimental performance.

E6.justification: v2 adds object-flow, real-only mixed-training, highway-training and composite-score results in Tables 2, 3, 6, 8 and 9. It also changes same-source Pcar values from 75.52 to 82.57 for nuScenes and 71.23 to 86.68 for Waymo between v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 3, resolving discrepancies with v1's flow table. Other retained benchmark values match.

M1.justification: Supplementary Section 7.3 introduces an ego-localization procedure that estimates rigid transformations from static-voxel flows using Kabsch and RANSAC, inverts them into ego motion and accumulates poses. This substantially extends the processing toolkit. The existing OccWorld flow encoder, cross-attention fusion, decoder and L2 supervision remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Main Sections 1–5 retain their order and much of their wording. Editing concentrates on the abstract and contribution list, the rewritten and reordered Section 4.3 discussion, expanded Broader Impacts moved into the supplement, and explanatory cross-references. This is localized restructuring rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 gains a distinct toolkit stage, Figure 2 is redrawn, and Figure 6's existing examples are rearranged. New supplementary diagrams, speed histograms, pseudocode and result tables substantially expand the presentation. The label table moves to the supplement, and the original flow comparison is split between main-text and supplementary tables.

R1.justification: Section 2.5 and the expanded supplementary Broader Impacts substantially broaden connections to trajectory prediction, aerial–ground collaboration, point-cloud completion, vision-language models and generative world models. Added references include AirV2X, LangCoop and TrajEvo; STAMP is removed. The principal positioning against existing occupancy benchmarks remains.

T1.justification: v2 substantially extends the mathematical development with explicit dynamic/static flow transformations, rigid-registration and inverse-ego-motion derivations under a static-scene assumption, and a formal definition of the composite UniOcc Score (Sections 7 and 9). The original tracking and individual evaluation equations remain; no new theorem or proof is presented.

improvement.justification: The flow-granularity controls and simulation-speed investigation strengthen previously incomplete support for central arguments. Section 7 substantially improves methodological transparency, while Sections 4.3 and 8 replace overly broad simulation-benefit interpretations with evidence-based qualifications. Together these materially improve the benchmark's credibility and usefulness. The new composite score has a limited reporting defect—its weights sum to 1.10 despite being described as a weighted average—but this does not outweigh those gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniOcc and contain matching datasets, framework components and core experiments. Their text, equations, figures and tables are readable. Inspection of both complete PDFs, including v2's supplementary material, supports reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical evaluations and adds object-level-flow comparisons, real-only mixed-source training results and highway-focused CARLA experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of flow-augmented OccWorld, cross-source training, camera-based occupancy prediction and cooperative prediction in Tables 3–6.

results.title: UniOcc: A Unified Benchmark for Occupancy Forecasting and Prediction in Autonomous Driving

C1.justification: The introduction broadens the third contribution from outperforming event-based SLAM approaches on TUM-VIE to doing so on TUM-VIE and VECtor. The central claims about temporal supervision, MCTS, robust descriptors, and integration into frame-based SLAM retain their meaning.

C2.justification: Appendix C newly explains higher-rate performance through increased temporal overlap and reduced motion-dependence effects. v2 also qualifies RPE results when ground truth is discontinuous and explains their omission for loop-floor sequences. The existing limitation concerning descriptor matching under strong motion changes remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents compilation, float16 precision, runtime input cropping, online calibration for VECtor, and settings for the added experiments. It changes the advertised project/code address from the Smart Robotics Lab host to the ETH MRL host. Existing optimizer, training duration, hardware, and model hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds large-scale VECtor SLAM evaluation and an actual HVGA ATIS homography experiment, whereas v1 only discusses the latter dataset. It also extends TUM-VIE evaluation to mocap-shake, mocap-shake2, and floor2-dark, testing fast-motion and low-light operation. Training coverage and the ECD/EDS pose-estimation tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Table 10 adds plain frame-based OKVIS2 using BRISK as a quantitative comparator. Appendix C also explicitly contrasts SuperPoint plus SuperGlue with SuperEvent under adverse imaging conditions. The original pose-estimation and TUM-VIE comparator sets remain unchanged; VECtor comparisons reuse DEIO and ESVO.

E3.justification: Runtime evaluation changes from plain PyTorch measurements on ECD/EDS to compiled float16 inference across four cropped input resolutions. v2 adds consecutive-sample RPE, SLAM comparisons at 20 and 40 Hz, and a homography protocol using 400 keypoints, 50 ms separation, and five RANSAC thresholds. The original training recipe and pose-estimation protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix C tests matching under HDR and fast motion, SLAM under fast motion and low light, and sensitivity to processing rate. Figure 9 adds a RANSAC-threshold analysis relating reprojection error to inlier ratio. The original training-data, representation, architecture, and loop-closure ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report five runs and selection of the median-error trajectory for small-scale TUM-VIE experiments. v2 introduces no new seed information, uncertainty intervals, error bars, significance tests, or repeated-run procedure.

E6.justification: Original pose-estimation, TUM-VIE ATE, and ablation table values are retained, while v2 adds VECtor, RPE, robustness, and homography results. For example, Table 10 reports mocap-shake ATE of 43.71 cm for SuperEvent versus 50.83 cm for frame-based OKVIS2 at 20 Hz. The previous 2.9 ms inference and 0.2 ms NMS figures are replaced by resolution-dependent 1.3–23.2 ms inference and 0.4 ms NMS under changed execution settings, not a same-setting speed comparison.

M1.justification: Temporal pseudo-label generation, MCTS construction, the MaxViT/FPN architecture, detector and descriptor heads, losses, NMS, and OKVIS2 integration remain unchanged. Compiled float16 runtime testing changes execution settings without introducing a new method component.

P1.justification: v2 makes grammatical and terminology corrections, updates affiliations, and consolidates runtime reporting into the implementation discussion. It inserts an event-versus-frame appendix and shifts the former Appendices C/D to D/E. Most existing paragraphs and the main narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds displays for runtime scaling, VECtor results, adverse-condition comparisons, RPE, and RANSAC sensitivity, including a new matching-example figure and six VECtor trajectory panels. Existing method diagrams and result tables remain; the former trajectory Figures 8–9 become Figures 10–11, with layout adjustments.

R1.justification: v2 adds the VECtor benchmark citation and removes the U-Net citation previously included among methods using homographic adaptation. The broader related-work organization and positioning against existing event detectors, trackers, and odometry systems remain stable.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(7), the pose-sampling construction, and the argument about homography reprojection error remain substantively unchanged. The added RANSAC experiment provides empirical support rather than a new definition, derivation, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the paper’s practical motivation. Appendix C adds direct, same-rate comparisons against frame-based OKVIS2 under fast motion and low light, addressing a gap in v1, while VECtor evaluation extends downstream validation beyond TUM-VIE. More specific runtime reporting and explicit ground-truth caveats improve interpretability. Cross-rate RPE values use different temporal intervals, limiting that particular comparison, but the broader validation provides a clear substantial quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SuperEvent and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary appendices. Corresponding content can be matched despite added experiments, renumbering, and layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds VECtor SLAM evaluation, adverse-condition comparisons, relative pose errors, and a homography-estimation analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original pose-estimation experiments, TUM-VIE SLAM results, runtime measurements, and ablations of training data, event representations, and network architectures.

results.title: SuperEvent: Cross-Modal Learning of Event-based Keypoint Detection for SLAM

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: compact superquadric scene representations, superior object decomposition with class-agnostic training, generalization beyond training categories, and usefulness for robotics and controllable generation. Rewording and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the hierarchical example as evidence of potential for unsupervised hierarchical decomposition and concludes that random sampling is sufficient for practical applications. Earlier interpretations, including limited LM improvements and possible trapping in local minima, are retained.

D1.justification: A new Training Details appendix supplies the two-stage epoch schedule, rotation/translation augmentation, optimizer, one-cycle learning-rate schedule, batch size 128, and four-A100 hardware configuration. The main text additionally specifies feature dimension, decoder depth, and existence threshold. This substantially expands implementation disclosure, without establishing changes to previously undocumented settings.

E1.justification: The established datasets and downstream tasks remain. V2 adds a distinct scenario involving hierarchical decomposition of an unsegmented scene containing grass, a table, and chairs (Figure 9). Replica was already evaluated qualitatively in v1; its new numerical results alone do not introduce another dataset.

E2.justification: The ScanNet++ comparison in Table 2 expands from EMS alone to EMS, SQ, and CSA, substantially broadening the test against learning-based alternatives. These methods also participate in the newly quantitative Replica comparison. ShapeNet and path-planning comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 3.2 changes the stated normalization from a unit sphere to a sphere of radius 0.5. V2 adds ground-truth-mask Replica evaluation and controlled existence-head and sampling variants. Existing ShapeNet splits and planning procedures are retained; newly disclosed training details do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New appendix Tables 4–5 test predicted versus segmentation-derived existence decisions during training/inference and FPS versus random sampling. Figure 9 tests hierarchical decomposition without instance segmentation. These substantially extend component and applicability analyses. The earlier LM and compactness–accuracy analyses are retained, with the latter moved to the appendix.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The added experiments continue the existing practice of reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes SUPERDEC's displayed in-category L2 from 0.051 to 0.047 and changes the caption's scaling factor from 10^3 to 10^2. Table 2 replaces its ScanNet++ L1/L2/primitive-count values of 1.37/0.07/5.41 with 1.70/0.11/5.18 and adds baseline and Replica results. New ablation and hierarchical findings further expand the evidence. These are reported revisions, not established same-setting performance gains; planning results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 4.3 adds a hierarchical inference adaptation: SUPERDEC first decomposes an entire scene, then processes the resulting segments again, without an external instance-segmentation model. The principal PVCNN/Transformer architecture, training losses, and LM refinement remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Editorial rewriting is concentrated in the abstract and introduction. Scene-results subsections are consolidated, the appendix is reorganized, and the compactness–accuracy discussion moves there. Most method and downstream-application prose, along with the overall main-text narrative, remains recognizable.

P2.justification: Table 2 expands to four methods and two datasets; two ablation tables and the hierarchical figure are added. New appendix Figures 13–14 display scene reconstructions. Overview and architecture graphics are revised, while the existing trade-off plot moves to the appendix and the t-SNE figure is relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to Video Perception Models for 3D Scene Synthesis, Search3D, and Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization. It removes a duplicate EMS bibliography entry while retaining that work. The principal positioning against learning-based, optimization-based, and scene-level decomposition methods remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix Section 1 adds an explicit angular surface parameterization and its parameter domains, supplementing the existing implicit superquadric definition. Equations 6–7 also correct primitive summation indices. These are limited formal additions and corrections; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V1's scene-level evidence relied on an EMS comparison and qualitative Replica examples. V2 substantially strengthens this central generalization claim through learned-baseline comparisons and quantitative Replica results, while component ablations and extensive training disclosure improve assessability. Reproducibility remains imperfect: conflicting parsimony weights persist, and the newly stated existence threshold of 24 conflicts with normalized assignment mass. These documentation problems temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SUPERDEC with the same core architecture and research objectives. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding equations, experiments, tables, and figures can be matched despite reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds quantitative Replica evaluation, existence-head and sampling ablations, and a hierarchical decomposition demonstration.

before.justification: V1 reports original decomposition results on ShapeNet and ScanNet++, planning experiments on 15 scenes, a robot demonstration, image-generation examples, and additional analyses.

results.title: SuperDec: 3D Scene Decomposition with Superquadric Primitives

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about adaptive grounding, noise prompts, modality adaptation, and open-world prediction. The claimed 4.09 mIoU advantage on the closed-world nuScenes benchmark is unchanged; the additional experiments support existing claims.

C2.justification: New Appendix A.4 attributes POP-3D's lower reported score to the stricter Occ3D evaluation protocol. Appendix A.5 further explains the supervision underlying SelfOcc's zero unknown-class performance. Existing modality-conflict interpretations and future directions concerning temporal information and richer prompts remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-availability URL and baseline reproduction details in Appendices A.4-A.5: borrowed versus retrained scores, POP-3D's 200×200×16 retraining resolution, and the baselines' losses and supervision across stages. These clarify retained experiments without establishing configuration changes. AGO's existing hyperparameters, hardware, and pseudo-label processing instructions are retained.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates occupancy prediction only on Occ3D-nuScenes. V2 adds closed-world and staged open-world evaluations on Occ3D-Waymo, substantially broadening the driving data and category coverage (Appendix B.4, Tables G-H). Figure C also adds an open-vocabulary streetlight retrieval example.

E2.justification: VEON, previously compared only in the closed-world benchmark, becomes a direct open-world comparator in new Table F. The existing POP-3D, SelfOcc, and GaussTR comparisons remain. The change from PoP3D to POP-3D is a naming correction, not a new baseline.

E3.justification: New Table F introduces VEON's 0/17, 9/8, and 13/4 seen/unseen settings, with ground-truth supervision for seen categories, extending the original pseudo-label-based evaluation design. The new Waymo open-world evaluation excludes GO. Section 4.1 also revises the reported nuScenes scene split from 600/150/150 to 700/150/150; this does not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Figure C supplies a streetlight retrieval case study with average prediction entropy before and after the modality adapter, 0.582 and 0.497. Existing training-paradigm, inference-rule, component, backbone, resolution, loss-function, and adapter-depth ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions state that each few-shot experiment is repeated five times and averaged. V2 adds no new seed disclosures, variability estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retrieval example's prediction entropy does not change statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing nuScenes benchmark and ablation values are retained. New Table F reports AGO versus VEON mIoU of 22.42 versus 15.16 at 9/8 and 25.90 versus 19.94 at 13/4. New Waymo results include 16.02 versus GaussTR's 13.97 closed-world mIoU and 12.81 versus 9.16 after few-shot tuning (Tables G-H). These are additional settings, not improvements over v1 under identical conditions. VEON's reported parameter count also changes from 406.4M to 678.1M.

M1.justification: The encoder architecture, noise-augmented grounding, modality adapter, training losses, and entropy-based inference rule remain unchanged. The added evaluations and baseline implementation explanations do not establish a change to AGO's procedure.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized grammar, terminology, and notation edits, standardizes POP-3D's name, and adds appendix subsections explaining comparisons and new evaluations. The main narrative and section organization are largely preserved rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: V2 adds appendix Tables F-H and the retrieval Figure C within the existing visual format. V1's Table F and Figure C are retained as Table I and Figure D. Existing main figures, tables, and appendix plots remain visually stable apart from caption edits and modest reflow.

R1.justification: V2 adds six references: TQD-Track, PETR, DETR3D, UniOcc, RenderWorld, and AutoOcc. It also moves the VEON discussion after the statement that preceding methods lack open-world prediction, excluding VEON from that criticism. The broader research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation in Equations 1-9, including the losses and entropy-based selection rule, is unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 adds no substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: V1's empirical support was confined to nuScenes and its own open-world protocol. V2 substantially strengthens that support through a second dataset and VEON's alternative evaluation setting (Tables F-H), addressing important limits in experimental scope. Baseline retraining explanations and the code-access statement also improve reproducibility. Although documentation of the new benchmarks remains brief, the broader validation and clearer comparison procedures provide a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AGO framework. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds AGO evaluations under VEON's open-world setting, Occ3D-Waymo experiments, and a retrieval example.

before.justification: V1 reports original AGO occupancy-prediction experiments, zero-shot and few-shot evaluations, and component ablations in the main text and appendix.

results.title: AGO: Adaptive Grounding for Open World 3D Occupancy Prediction

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the design-alignment framing, solver-feedback approach, and headline 93% versus 34% and 8.9% fully-constrained results. Changing 'without alignment' to 'without SFT' clarifies the same baseline rather than changing the scientific claim.

C2.justification: V2 newly identifies dimension-based reward hacking in the successful RL models, extending beyond v1's failed-PPO discussion. It distinguishes high solver scores from designer preferences and explains the tradeoff between reduced dimensional locking and lower fully-constrained/stability scores. Appendix B.2 also adds a substantive rationale for functional evaluation instead of exact constraint matching.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the AWS instance, GPU memory, CPU count, and system memory, discloses random test-set selection for Figure 5, and adds a project-page link for additional results. The three-day runtime discussion is relocated to Appendix B.1, while existing training hyperparameter tables remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The SketchGraphs corpus, CAD domain, and constraint-generation task remain unchanged. V2 adds a professional-designer evaluation population and a preference study using 30 sketches, a limited extension beyond automated evaluation.

E2.justification: The seven models compared in Tables 1 and 2 are unchanged. V2 adds reward-penalized RLOO to the evaluated alternatives; the new human study compares it with SFT, DPO, ExIt, and original RLOO.

E3.justification: V2 adds Pass@4 evaluation across temperatures 1.0/1.5 and top-p thresholds 0.5/1.0, plus a forced-choice study excluding unstable outputs. C.6 reports five designers, 30 sketches, and 1,500 judgments, although Figure C.4's 180-comparison instruction conflicts with the implied 300 judgments per participant. Existing benchmark settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendices C.4–C.6 examine sampling sensitivity, excessive dimension generation and reward penalties, and whether designers prefer the generated constraints. These substantially extend validation of robustness and design alignment. Earlier diversity analyses, iteration studies, training curves, and failed attempts remain.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains its eight-sample evaluation and standard-deviation reporting. V2 introduces no new seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-training uncertainty procedures; the human study reports preference percentages without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 2, and C.1 retain their earlier scores. V2 adds constraint-type frequencies, sampling Pass@4 results, and reward-penalized RLOO results of 72.79% fully constrained and 82.83% stable. Table C.3 adds human preferences: ExIt beats original RLOO in 94% of comparisons, and penalized RLOO beats it in 92%.

M1.justification: Appendix C.5 introduces an RLOO variant with two additional penalties: total constraints and dimensions normalized by entity count, and dimensions as a fraction of all generated constraints and dimensions. This is a targeted objective extension; the architecture, solver-feedback pipeline, and original algorithms remain.

P1.justification: V2 edits the solver and qualitative-results explanations, clarifies ExIt/DPO notation, subdivides the appendix, relocates runtime discussion, and updates the author list. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain, so the additions do not constitute extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Figure 5 gains red input-geometry overlays that expose distortion directly. V2 also adds the stability illustration, preference chart, and study-interface screenshot; introduces sampling and preference tables; and expands Table A.2 with constraint-type distributions. These substantially extend the visual presentation of evidence.

R1.justification: V2 adds two Hoffmann and Joan-Arinyo constraint-solving references supporting the formal definitions. The principal research positioning remains unchanged. Its additional Bouma bibliography entry duplicates a work already cited in v1 rather than introducing another distinct source.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds formal constraint-state definitions using Jacobian rank and residual rigid-body degrees of freedom, beyond v1's verbal descriptions. No proofs are added. The new over-constrained criterion, rank(J_C) > n-r, is problematic because redundant equations need not increase rank.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's missing validation that solver success reflects design intent. Sections C.5–C.6 expose over-dimensioning, test a remedy, and establish strong designer preferences against original RLOO despite its leading solver scores. This materially improves empirical validity and interpretation. The small, stability-filtered study, inconsistent study reporting, and problematic new rank definition require correction, but do not outweigh that central gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CAD constraint-generation study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–C support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds sampling sensitivity results, a modified-reward experiment, dataset analyses, and a professional CAD designer preference study.

before.justification: V1 reports original SketchGraphs experiments comparing constraint-generation models, including benchmark scores, diversity measurements, training curves, and failed approaches.

results.title: Aligning Constraint Generation with Design Intent in Parametric CAD

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about verifier-free early seed selection, BIS, and MLLM-assisted prompt selection. The headline 41% average/61% maximum computational reduction and approximately 40% recovery of failed cases are unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds explanations of global editing through structural coherence, attributes uncommon under-editing to editing models' modification bias, and discusses noisy-latent CLIP failures and excessive foreground changes. It also motivates future multi-objective selection. The original over-preservation limitation and main interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly supplies a code-repository link after the abstract, adding explicit code-access information absent from v1. Existing experimental setup descriptions, algorithms, and MLLM prompt templates are largely retained. The PDFs alone do not establish the repository's contents.

E1.justification: v2 adds human preference data from 34 participants evaluating 52 selected PIE-Bench cases. Image benchmark and editing-task coverage remain PIE-Bench and MagicBrush; the new global-edit analysis examines PIE-Bench's existing style-transfer task rather than introducing another benchmark.

E2.justification: The five editing models and original Vanilla/Best-of-N/ELECT comparisons are retained. Appendix C.6 and Figure 17 newly compare background-based selection against foreground-MSE selection, CLIPScore selection, and a background/foreground hybrid.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a human-evaluation protocol: 34 participants classify ten seed outputs for each of 52 high-variance, category-balanced cases, with preference aggregated from positive and negative responses. Additional experiments extend candidate pools to N=25, 50, and 100 for IP2P and UltraEdit. The original benchmark settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C substantially expands validation through background-MSE ranking analyses and human judgments, larger-pool sensitivity tests, global-style-edit analysis, a concrete under-editing failure, and alternative-score ablations. The earlier timestep and mask-extraction analyses are retained, including the full stopping-step plot relocated to Figure 13.

E5.justification: The new human study reports inter-rater agreement using Krippendorff's alpha=0.7535 and a preference/background-consistency Pearson correlation of r=0.534. These statistical summaries are absent from v1. Repeated-run uncertainty reporting for the retained benchmark results is unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 3, and 4 retain their numerical values. v2 adds human-preference findings, N=25–100 performance curves, global-edit subset results, and alternative-score comparisons. For example, Appendix C.4 newly reports 26% lower MSE and 3.4-point higher SSIM for IP2P versus fixed-seed evaluation; Figure 17 ranks the hybrid highest across its three models. These are additional comparisons, not improved values for the original experiments.

M1.justification: The core BIS framework and Algorithms 1–2 remain. Appendix C.6 adds an evaluated hybrid selection variant choosing between minimum-background-MSE and maximum-foreground-MSE candidates using a preliminary score. Section 4.3 also corrects the written rectified-flow update increment from t to Δt; an implementation change or rerun is not established.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the overall section sequence are retained. Changes include localized introduction edits, reversing the Performance/Efficiency discussion order, reorganizing Appendix E, and expanding Appendix C's subsection structure. This is not an extensive narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 switches to a two-column layout, places Figure 1 before the abstract, reconfigures the pipeline and qualitative-comparison displays, and relocates the prompt demonstration and full stopping-step plots to the appendix. It also adds the validation, scaling, global-edit, failure-case, and alternative-score figures.

R1.justification: The cited research and substantive positioning against prior editing and candidate-selection methods remain the same. Appendix A's positioning text moves into Table 2's caption; reference metadata and formatting updates do not introduce new related work.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 changes the rectified-flow denoising update from z_t−v_theta·t to z_t−v_theta·Δt, correcting the mathematical step increment. The BIS definitions, other diffusion/flow equations, and Appendix D are otherwise retained; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 primarily supports its central background-consistency criterion through automatic metrics. v2 adds direct human validation and competing-score comparisons, substantially strengthening that justification while examining larger candidate pools, global edits, and a concrete failure. These additions improve the evidence for both usefulness and limitations. The selected 52-case study and incompletely specified hybrid score still limit generalization and reproducibility, but the overall evidential gain is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ELECT research, with matching authors, methods, and principal experiments. All pages, including Appendices A–F, are readable, and relocated or reformatted material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds a human preference study, larger candidate-pool experiments, and further diagnostic analyses in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative and qualitative editing experiments on PIE-Bench and MagicBrush, including seed-selection, prompt-selection, and ablation results.

results.title: Early Timestep Zero-Shot Candidate Selection for Instruction-Guided Image Editing

C1.justification: Both versions claim the first T2V backdoor framework exploiting redundant video information, combining attack effectiveness, content preservation, benign utility, and evasion of frame-based moderation. The shortened conclusion and added experiments do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: Supplement A explicitly discusses framewise CLIP's possible failure to capture temporal semantic changes and describes the generation pipeline as model-agnostic. Supplement C.2 extends the stealthiness interpretation to input-level trigger detection. Existing defense explanations and proposed watermarking applications remain.

D1.justification: Supplement A newly supplies Kling 1.6 identification, I3D-based FVD preprocessing at 224×224, CLIPSIM aggregation details, and full generation and evaluation prompts. Section 5 changes A100 to A800. Conversely, Section 3.5 removes the statement that human evaluation uses 100 randomly sampled videos. Overall, implementation and evaluation documentation expands substantially.

E1.justification: Panda-2M training/attack evaluation and MSR-VTT benign evaluation remain unchanged. Supplement C.2 adds Unicode-substitution and benign-phrase trigger scenarios, including text-input screening rather than video-output screening. CogVideoX and Wan expand model configurations, not dataset coverage.

E2.justification: The original clean-model controls and four output-moderation comparators remain. Supplement C.2 additionally evaluates input-level trigger-detection defenses using GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-VL in Table 5. These models were already evaluated on video outputs, but screening prompt text constitutes an additional defense procedure.

E3.justification: The original splits, metrics, poisoning ratio, and training budgets are retained. Supplement C adds CogVideoX-5b and Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B configurations and text-trigger screening experiments. Section 5 changes the stated cost-analysis hardware from A100 to A800 without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: Existing fine-tuning, prompt-perturbation, epoch, poisoning-ratio, multiple-backdoor, and output-defense analyses remain. Supplement C.2 adds a focused investigation of trigger choice and detectability. Supplement B supplies additional qualitative examples, and Figure 4 replaces its SCT example.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability estimates for the experimental scores. The added tables continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their values, but supplementary Tables 4–6 substantially extend the reported evidence. Added-model ASRMLLM values range from 86.1% to 90.1%. Table 5 reports GPT-4o trigger-detection rates of 25.1%, 3.1%, and 1.0% for rare-word, Cyrillic, and phrase triggers. These are additional results, not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The target-generation modules, STC/SCT/VST strategies, frozen-text-encoder fine-tuning, and inference procedure remain unchanged. The supplement identifies the generation model and tests alternatives within the already modular text-trigger mechanism; it does not establish a redesign of BadVideo.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized prose edits, repairs the VST explanation, shortens the conclusion, updates author information, and adds acknowledgments. The main section sequence remains intact, while the supplement is organized into A–D with a contents list. The existing narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds three supplementary result tables, three grids of video examples, four instruction panels, and a notation table. It also replaces Figure 4's SCT example, resizes and relocates Figure 7, and compacts Tables 2–3. These constitute substantial visual additions and layout changes.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds general-backdoor context and citations including BadCLIP and sample-specific invisible triggers; Sora and Wan references also appear. BackdoorLLM and the adversarial-diffusion survey cited in v1 are removed. The positioning relative to image-generation backdoors and claimed T2V novelty remain stable.

T1.justification: The diffusion equations remain unchanged. Supplement D.1 supplies a short complexity derivation, concluding O(p·n·r) for poisoned-data construction under fixed diffusion steps and negligible prompt-processing cost. v1 references an appendix analysis but does not contain this derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves an important documentation gap by supplying the generation and evaluation specifications referenced but absent from v1, making the central pipeline and scores substantially more inspectable. Tables 4–6 broaden checks of model generality and directly test input-trigger stealthiness. These gains outweigh the limited reporting loss from removing the human-evaluation sample count and sampling statement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of BadVideo with matching methods and main experiments. v1 ends at its references despite citing appendices; v2 includes Supplementary Material A–D. The supplied contents support comparison, with supplement-only material treated as newly available documentation rather than automatic evidence of changed procedures.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds experiments on CogVideoX and Wan, alternative triggers, and input-level trigger detection in supplementary Tables 4–6.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack, utility, content-preservation, human-evaluation, and defense experiments on LaVie and Open-Sora, including Tables 1–3 and Figures 5–7.

results.title: BadVideo: Stealthy Backdoor Attack against Text-to-Video Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and scientific claims, including differentiable beam tracing, material-aware visual guidance, and sparse-measurement performance. The comparison against models trained with ten times more data and the 16.6%–50.9% gain range are unchanged.

C2.justification: The appendix substantially expands interpretation and limitations: visual features are interpreted as primarily helping early reflections and requiring sufficient views; aggregate metrics can miss waveform distortion; nearby source–listener pairs challenge first-arrival prediction. It also attributes an anomalous training-scale trend to a failed-speaker recording.

D1.justification: v1 defers important implementation and training details to supplementary material absent from that PDF. v2 supplies tracing pseudocode, basis-point sampling, frequency sampling, optimizer settings, batch size, progressive reflection depth, training/inference beam counts, hardware, model sizes, and timings. It also adds a project-page link, without establishing the linked resources' availability.

E1.justification: Appendix A.1.6 adds a rendering-time test on the substantially larger Gibson Hennepin scene, approximately 600 square meters. The six-room RAF/HAA accuracy evaluation and training coverage remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Corresponding RAF and HAA comparisons retain NAF++, INRAS++, AV-NeRF, AVR, and, for HAA, Diff-RIR. The added timing and waveform comparisons reuse existing baselines; ResNet18 is an internal encoder ablation.

E3.justification: The original splits, training fractions, HAA listener counts, and accuracy metrics remain unchanged. Added evaluations specify image-count and encoder controls, timing comparisons on the same GPU, an 8-second Gibson rendering test, and a diagnostic reanalysis excluding one failed-speaker recording.

E4.justification: v2 adds vision-count and encoder ablations, waveform fidelity comparisons, a failed-recording analysis explaining an anomalous scaling trend, and direct-sound/early-echo failure cases. These substantially extend the diagnostic evidence. Table 8 repeats the existing Table 3 ablation rather than introducing another experiment.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The appendix continues the existing practice of reporting point results.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–3 remain unchanged, but v2 adds HAA EDT results, RAF metric curves, vision-ablation scores, waveform examples, and computational measurements. Table 5 reports inference times of 66 ms for AV-DAR, 376 ms for DiffRIR, and 100 ms for AVR. New Table 6 gives INRAS++ Dampened Room T60 as 382.9%, conflicting with 187.1% in retained Table 2.

M1.justification: The beam-tracing renderer, integrated positional encoding, multi-view feature aggregation, and position-dependent residual remain unchanged. Appendix A.1 documents their implementation and training recipe without establishing a change to the underlying method or objective.

P1.justification: The main sections retain their order and largely identical prose, with limited wording and typo corrections. Additional explanations are organized into Method Details and Additional Results appendices, rather than an extensive rewrite of the main narrative.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn to clarify rendering operations, aggregation, and gradient flow. The appendix adds geometric diagrams, waveform panels, failure visualizations, Algorithm 1, and timing, full-metric, and vision-ablation tables. Table 8 redisplays Table 3, while Figure 5 receives smaller formatting changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for spherical sampling, ResNet, Hearing Anywhere in Any Environment, Gibson, and Open3D. The main relationship to learning-based and physics-based prior work remains unchanged; publication updates to existing references do not constitute new positioning.

T1.justification: Appendices A.1.1–A.1.2 add beam-hit and time-of-arrival expressions and a derivation of the local Gaussian covariance used for beam footprints. These supply supporting mathematical details; the main formulation and assumptions remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves substantial documentation and evidential gaps in the supplied v1: previously deferred renderer/training details become inspectable, measured timings support the central efficiency claim, and vision ablations and failure cases clarify effectiveness and limitations. These gains outweigh localized weaknesses, notably the conflicting INRAS++ T60 entry in Tables 2 and 6 and the inconsistent percentage identifying the failed-recording subset.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AV-DAR and contain readable text, equations, figures, and tables. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally includes Appendices A.1–A.2. The matching main sections support reliable comparison of retained content and newly supplied material.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds runtime measurements, vision ablations, additional metric results, waveform comparisons, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original RIR prediction experiments across six RAF/HAA rooms, component ablations, and qualitative acoustic visualizations.

results.title: Differentiable Room Acoustic Rendering with Multi-View Vision Priors

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same principal claims: a domain-specific multimodal knowledge benchmark, training-free autonomous graph retrieval, and improved MLLM performance. V3 supplies supporting detail and evidence without materially redefining those claims.

C2.justification: V3 develops explanations involving query-aware perception, retrieval quality, and the importance of validation relative to summarization. It also identifies shallow reasoning requirements, computational inefficiency, dependence on contextual hints, prompt sensitivity, and failures despite retrieving relevant knowledge. V1 offers only general perception/retrieval conclusions and future directions.

D1.justification: V3 adds graph-construction and annotation procedures, capture settings, image resizing, model/API identifiers, path limits, agent and evaluator prompts, and hardware information. The supplement provides substantial implementation detail. V1's promised future release is replaced with a code/data repository address; availability beyond that statement was not verified.

E1.justification: The Monster Hunter domain and 238-question benchmark are retained; v3's enumeration of six sub-tasks does not establish dataset expansion. However, Table 17 adds evaluated scenarios withholding monster names and contextual hints, introducing requirements such as identifying the retrieval root without a supplied monster name.

E2.justification: V1 mentions experiments on leading MLLMs without reporting specific comparator results. V3 supplies Vanilla and Vanilla+ comparisons across 13 MLLMs, knowledgeable and novice human comparisons in Table 3, and InternVideo2.5 and VideoChat-Flash caption-source comparisons in Table 4. This substantially expands the reported comparative evidence.

E3.justification: Newly reported analyses introduce controlled path budgets, BFS versus DFS with three paths, frame sampling at two frames per second capped at ten frames, and cross-model agent substitutions. Section 8.3 also introduces judge validation using two human raters and 200 sampled judgments per model. These are additional evaluation designs, not evidence that v1's unspecified experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds captioning and keyframe analyses, path-count and traversal ablations, prompt-wording robustness, name/context removal, agent-model swaps, human checks of automated judging, and success/failure examples. Sections 5.3 and 8 provide substantive diagnostic evidence absent from v1's general discussion.

E5.justification: V3 Table 18 introduces mean and standard-deviation reporting for retrieval time, agent-call counts, and response time. This describes computational-cost variability, not demonstrated repeated-seed performance uncertainty. Neither version reports repeated-run accuracy intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: V1 supplies only broad qualitative findings. V3 adds extensive numerical results: Table 3 reports GPT-4o accuracy of 0.3122 for Vanilla, 0.4050 for unaided-offline, and 0.5105 for unaided-online. Further tables quantify ablations, judging accuracy, computational costs, and agent substitutions. These are newly reported results, not measured performance improvements between versions.

M1.justification: Both versions propose training-free multi-agent graph retrieval. V3 first specifies the perceiver, summarizer, topic-selection, expansion and validation agents, BFS traversal, and caption handling. V1 lacks enough procedural detail to determine whether these components change the earlier algorithm or document its existing implementation.

P1.justification: V1 moves directly from introduction to conclusion.
